name: Washington State Standard
title: Midterm losses push Republicans into superminority in the WA House
description: When this century began, Republicans held half of the 98 seats in the Washington state House of Representatives and shared power with Democrats. They will soon occupy 29.  The Grand Old Party’s descent to superminority in the chamber has been a decade-in-the-making journey, coinciding with the Trump era, and hastened by the whopping loss of […]
text:
Washington State Republican Party Chairman Jim Walsh said the midterm elections were bad but not an "epic tsunami." While Republicans face the loss of at least nine seats in the state House, Walsh said he will seek another term as party chair. Here he is pictured at a 2024 election night party in Bellevue, Wash. (Photo by Washington State Standard)When this century began, Republicans held half of the 98 seats in the Washington state House of Representatives and shared power with Democrats. They will soon occupy 29. 
The Grand Old Party’s descent to superminority in the chamber has been a decade-in-the-making journey, coinciding with the Trump era, and hastened by the whopping loss of nine seats in the Nov. 3 election.
Rep. Jim Walsh, R-Aberdeen, who easily won re-election, is also the chair of the Washington State Republican Party. He’s getting pressed these days on how the party will respond while fending off critics who think more could have been done to lessen the political damage.
“The midterm was bad. It was not this epic tsunami,” he said. Incumbents who are losing “got caught in the riptide of statewide mania of Trump, Trump, Trump.”
Walsh’s term ends in January. Some, including a former state party chair, want him to step aside so the organization can reboot. He intends to seek re-election.
“We are going to continue to rebuild the party to make it a true bottom-up operation,” he said. “We’re getting there. The process is not quite done.”
Diagnosing the damage
Blame for what happened on Nov. 3 is apportioned to many, with Walsh getting a larger piece.
“If you lose, they come for you. That’s politics,” said Mathew Patrick Thomas, one of Washington’s two members on the Republican National Committee and the former chair of the King County Republican Party. “Donors really want to know ‘what’s the new plan’ after we get our butts kicked.”
A similar diagnosis of what transpired and what to do now emerged from interviews with Republican lawmakers, donors, activists and party chairs. 
The state party needed to have raised more money and started earlier to build its get out the vote operation, they say. And Walsh, along with House Minority Leader Drew Stokesbary, R-Auburn and others engaged in the political operations for the House Republican caucus,  should have been in greater sync.
But President Donald Trump’s decade-long dominance on the national landscape posed the single largest obstacle facing Republican candidates. His presence has been souring the GOP brand for years; many candidates struggled to escape his shadow. 
Trump urged people to vote like he was on the ballot. In Washington many did. Swing voters disillusioned by the president’s use of tariffs and the war in Iran sided with Democrats. Meanwhile, moderate Republicans disaffected by Trump’s policies likely sat out partisan races. 
People rejoice at the Washington State Democratic Party election night gathering in Seattle, Washington on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard).
“We thought we had the right messaging but it was too complicated for the average person. It was too easy to blame what’s happening nationally,” said Rep. David Stuebe, R-Washougal, one of the House Republicans getting ousted.
With Democrats turning out in higher numbers, a controversial redistricting map forged by a federal judge was another factor. Those redrawn lines shifted more than 300,000 people across 13 legislative districts on both sides of the Cascades. It put more Democrats into the 12th, 14th, 17th and 18th districts located across central and southwest Washington. In all those places, Republican lawmakers are getting unseated.
Matt Brown, chair of the Yakima County Republican Party, said an electoral shellacking like this requires a commitment to finding a way to ensure voters can hear the message of Republicans campaigning in their community above the uproar of national politics.
“You won’t win every election. You are going to have losses. The key is moving forward with clear expectations,” Brown said. “The small things will catapult you to the bigger wins.
What does a party chair actually do? 
There’s no handbook or style guide for running a state political party. Generally, the chair is counted on to be a spokesperson, a strategist and a fundraiser.
 Chairs cozy up to the donor class using money raised to elect candidates, pass or defeat ballot measures, and build an operation to turn out a party’s voters. Some chairs will try to build unity among like-minded forces that don’t all agree on the right messaging, the best marketing and the targets for the most resources. 
Chairs let legislative caucuses recruit their candidates, though they may encourage individuals to run for statewide and federal offices. But, in the end, only individuals will decide if they want to run and for what office.
The state Republican Party will pick a chair in January.
Walsh earns around $105,000 annually as party chair, in addition to his legislative salary of $72,494.  Washington State Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad declined to share her annual salary.
To get elected, Walsh or other GOP party chair candidates must receive a majority of votes from the 117 people on the party’s central committee: a panel made up of the chair and two state committee members from each of the state’s 39 county Republican parties.
These are Walsh’s bosses, described as “the most conservative of the conservative” Republican activists. 
“In fairness to Jim, there certainly exists within the Republican Party not only Trump voters but ones who believe wholeheartedly in the Trump agenda,” said Steve Gordon, a Pierce County precinct committee officer who led the unsuccessful efforts to repeal the income tax on higher earners. “Jim can’t afford to alienate those folks.”
Walsh hasn’t so far. First elected in August 2023, he was re-elected in January 2025. He’s a conservative who can fire up a crowd with his orations. 
Though some view his rhetorical rants on social media as self-serving, those pokes draw reactions. Gov. Bob Ferguson recently predicted Walsh would step aside but said he hoped he did not, calling Walsh a “weak, ineffective” leader.
Walsh laughed when asked about this. 
“Part of the job of party chair is be a lightning rod for the neurotic governor to strike at,” he said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Outraised and outspent
Walsh has been criticized for less than robust fund raising. Some blame his embrace of the MAGA agenda for driving some donors to withhold money from the party and instead contribute to other organizations working to elect Republicans.
Walsh said he’s made all the fundraising goals set for him. Those goals, however, have still left the GOP well behind Democrats in the competition for cash this election cycle.
The state Democratic Party hauled in roughly $2.5 million through the end of October compared to the Republican Party total of $1 million, according to records from the state Public Disclosure Commission.
Adding party totals to the political operations of the House and Senate caucus campaign committees shows Democrats had a sizable financial edge. Those figures show Democrats outraising Republicans by a wide margin: $10.2 million to $6.6 million.
 A similar picture emerges on the federal level. Washington’s Democratic Party outraised the state Republican Party, $7.4 million to $3.1 million, between Jan. 1, 2025 and Oct. 14, 2026, according to filings with the Federal Election Commission.
A challenger emerges
In August 2023, Dave McMullan, chair of the Pierce County Republican Party, said he nominated Walsh to be the new leader of the state party. After the party’s midterm faceplant, he now wants the job and will challenge Walsh in January.
“The way things turned out, I decided change would be good,” McMullan said. “I just feel the state party is stagnant and going backwards. I don’t feel it has done enough to promote our candidates. It has not been able to raise the money to do many things.”
McMullan called Walsh an “excellent legislator. There’s no animosity, just disappointment,” he said.
Pierce County is home to two Republican-held seats that are being lost this cycle. A third is at risk.
Looking back to the future
In 2001, when Republicans and Democrats shared power in the state House, Chris Vance, then chair of the state GOP, started pushing a strategy of winning seats in the crescent of communities around Seattle. 
It would be easier said than done. The party recruited candidates with strong local ties whose messages would resonate with voters in their neighborhoods. They had to be honest brokers of ideas who would be accountable to their communities rather than every provision of the state Republican Party platform.
Rep. Peter Abbarno, R-Chehalis, served as executive director for the state party from 2001-2005 and was at Vance’s side in pushing this approach. In 2004, Dino Rossi, a business-minded Republican state senator from Sammamish, came oh-so-close to becoming Washington’s first GOP governor in two decades. It’s now been 40 years.
To be successful in the next two and four years, Republicans need to start thinking about and recruiting good candidates, Abbarno said. They will need to brand themselves “and not let the winds of change at the national level” impact them as much,” he said.
It’s a tall order. Filling it cannot be done by the party alone, regardless of who is in charge. Republicans in elected office and leaders of their ally organizations will need to work in tandem.
“After an election like this, you really have to show you can do things. You have to show you are reasonable and you have a plan. Republicans haven’t been in charge for so long, you have to prove you can lead,” Abbarno said. “It’s not an overnight thing.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri hemp businesses clear shelves, close shops as new restrictions take effect
description: Hemp retailers across Missouri slashed prices, cleared shelves and, in some cases, gave away products this week as they prepared for a new state law restricting the sale of hemp-derived THC. Clearance bins appeared on gas station countertops. Smoke shops emptied display cases. And in one small Missouri town, those who served in the military […]
text:
Brian Riegel, owner of South Point Hemp, has farmed hemp since 2018 near Union. He had hoped to specialize in full-spectrum CBD products, which are marketed as sleep aids and pain relievers. But those products contain small amounts of hemp-derived THC, which is now banned in Missouri (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).Hemp retailers across Missouri slashed prices, cleared shelves and, in some cases, gave away products this week as they prepared for a new state law restricting the sale of hemp-derived THC.
Clearance bins appeared on gas station countertops. Smoke shops emptied display cases. And in one small Missouri town, those who served in the military were offered free products on Veterans Day.
The law, which took effect Thursday, prohibits many hemp-derived THC products from being sold outside Missouri’s licensed marijuana dispensaries. Certain hemp beverages are temporarily exempt, while broader federal restrictions are scheduled to take effect Dec. 11.
Brian Riegel, owner of South Point Hemp in Union, grows hemp at his farm and manufactures his products at his warehouse. 
On Wednesday, Riegel closed his doors and liquidated his products.
“It’s just basically been a sad day,” Riegel said. “We’ve tried to get most of our customers to come in beforehand. We reached out to a lot of them to make sure they were aware of the laws that were coming into place.”
Riegel is also the treasurer of the Missouri Hemp Trade Association, which represents businesses selling and producing hemp products. This week has been hard for all the members, he said.  
“They’re calling, crying because they’re firing people that have been working with them for five years,” he said. “There’s some people with multiple stores, so they had managers, multiple families relying on the income from this.”
Among his products is an intoxicating hemp seltzer, which can still be sold in Missouri until Dec. 11 unless Congress delays the federal ban again. Another federal delay could extend the reprieve for qualifying hemp beverages under Missouri law. 
Throughout the state, “Last Chance” signs appeared in store windows, selling products for 70% off or more. 
John and Kara Grady owned Slaphappy Hemporium in Rosebud. But they’ve now renamed it to Gradys, where they sell specialty food items. (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).
In Rosebud, John and Kara Grady were giving away their products for free to veterans. Many of their products were full-spectrum CBD, which have about 2 mg of THC to enhance the pain-relief and soothing properties of CBD. These products are still in limbo on a federal level, but in Missouri, they are now banned. The Gradys are both veterans and pride themselves on being a veteran-owned hemp business. 
“The insult of all insults is today is Veterans Day,” John said, “and this is the last day we can sell any of our hemp products in the state of Missouri outside of beverages.” 
While stores were clearing out their shelves, Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said enforcement efforts would focus on businesses selling prohibited products, rather than consumers who purchased them.
“Certainly no one enforcing the law is particularly concerned about the consumers,” Hanaway said. “It’s really the store owners and the sellers that we want to make sure are complying with the law.”
Hanaway’s office has primary jurisdiction over enforcement of the act’s provisions, according to a memo the Missouri Department of Public Safety sent out to industry members.
It states the attorney general may authorize the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, the public safety department, Division of Alcohol and Tobacco Control, the Missouri State Highway Patrol, “or any other state agency it deems necessary, to aid in enforcement efforts.”
Amy Moore, director of the Division of Cannabis Regulation, which is part of the state health department, said it is ready to take direction from Hanaway’s office regarding lab testing or other resources needed.
On Wednesday, one gas station was selling a $50 box of “THCA” vape carts for only $5, and the product also contained CB9A – a synthetic compound made from cannabis. 
Things like the vape carts, Moore said, highlight the evolution of products since Missouri lawmakers began talking about regulating intoxicating hemp in 2023. 
“There’s the things that you can make by extracting what’s in the [cannabis] plant,” she said, “and then there’s a whole other world of things that you can recreate — and you can create them through conversion of things that come out of the plant.”
Most people traditionally think of these compounds as “synthetics,” she said, and they are created by adding some agent that causes a chemical reaction. Her team is most concerned about the byproducts that could come from the conversion process and how they affect the human body.
“In an unregulated environment, the kinds of solvents and agents that could be in there that we’re not requiring them to be taken out or tested for,” she said. “So yes, from the health perspective, there’s a lot going on that the department has been concerned about.”
Moore believes it’s more cost effective to create those synthetics or semi-synthetics.
“A lot of the product that is on the market now, online, in stores,” she said “is probably in that semi-synthetic or even synthetic realm now.” 
Hanaway said her team has tested some of the products and found that they’re much more potent than the labels claim.
“Sometimes there’s heavy metals in it, and it’s a dangerous product,” Hanaway said. “And like any other food or drug, you want a regulated market so it doesn’t hurt people.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: The unsung heroes who make Missouri elections possible
description: “Elections are miracles.” With a bit of enthusiasm and wonder, that’s something a former boss of mine used to always say. As I think back over last week’s elections, I was reminded just how right she was. I was lucky enough to spend almost a decade working in Missouri’s election administration. I got to see […]
text:
(Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)“Elections are miracles.”
With a bit of enthusiasm and wonder, that’s something a former boss of mine used to always say.
As I think back over last week’s elections, I was reminded just how right she was.
I was lucky enough to spend almost a decade working in Missouri’s election administration. I got to see firsthand what goes into making an election happen.
We’ve all heard the saying “All politics is local”. Elections are local, too.
They happen in our communities, carried out by people who know their neighbors and take pride in doing the job right.  It’s a lesson that carries into our public affairs work both here in Missouri and across other states.
I had the opportunity to work with county clerks from across the state, representing a wide range of political backgrounds. County Clerks and Election Boards run the elections in each of Missouri’s 116 local election jurisdictions. Regardless of their politics, I encountered countless dedicated election administrators  who took their jobs seriously and understood the importance of running free and democratic elections.
Think about it. On Election Day, we’re basically opening thousands of small businesses across each state, all at the same time, asking them to serve the public. Each one needs a location, supplies, equipment, trained staff, and a list of their customers.
One election. Millions of people. Thousands of polling places. An extraordinary amount of work.
These operations are mostly run by our neighbors.  Many of them are retirees and senior citizens who work for little pay.  These people show up early, work long hours, and take their responsibility seriously.
Long before Election Day, ballots were being designed, printed, and delivered, voting equipment tested, voter records checked, and poll workers recruited and trained. All of this happens with very little room for error.
After the polls close, the work doesn’t stop. Ballots must be secured and counted. Results must be reconciled and accounted for. Election officials review the numbers, conduct canvasses, and complete the certification process according to state law. It’s a process involving checks, balances, and multiple layers of accountability.
Election officials also have to expect the unexpected. Court decisions and legal challenges can sometimes require last-minute changes to ballots or election processes. Inclement weather and power outages can disrupt voting locations. Whatever the circumstances, local officials have to adjust quickly while keeping everything else on schedule.
Somewhere along the way, like a sporting contest, the reporting of election results has turned into election entertainment.
Television networks provide scorecards and projections. Campaigns and politicians use social media to focus on winners and losers. We watch the vote totals change and wait for someone to declare a victory.
But here is something we forget. In elections, there are no come-from-behind victories.  There are no last-second field goals or walk-off home runs. The winner was already decided when the last voter cast his ballot. The counting that follows simply tells us the decision the voters made.
I’ve stood in election offices on nights when my friends won, and on nights when they lost. I’ve certified results that made me smile, and results that made me cry. Here’s what that taught me: In a democracy, voters don’t make wrong decisions.
A ballot isn’t a test, and a vote isn’t wrong because someone else disagrees with it.
People vote according to their own beliefs, values, and hopes. I don’t get to invalidate the outcome simply because I question the judgment behind it or I don’t like the result.  That’s the point of democracy.
My boss was right. Elections are a miracle. Thanks to those local election officials, we just pulled off another one.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Health advocates pack state Medicaid Advisory Committee to protest restrictions, work requirements
description: LINCOLN — Bennett Martin Public Library staff had to bring in extra chairs for Nebraska’s Medicaid Advisory Committee meeting Thursday as guests flooded in to share their concerns about new restrictions on Medicaid. Roughly 50 attendees, many wearing red or white shirts bearing phrases like “We sow solidarity, they sow misery” and “Healthcare is for […]
text:
Protesters walking to Centennial Mall on Nov, 12. 2026 in Lincoln. (Juan Salinas II | Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Bennett Martin Public Library staff had to bring in extra chairs for Nebraska’s Medicaid Advisory Committee meeting Thursday as guests flooded in to share their concerns about new restrictions on Medicaid.
Roughly 50 attendees, many wearing red or white shirts bearing phrases like “We sow solidarity, they sow misery” and “Healthcare is for everyone now,” packed the library’s fourth-floor meeting space. Jacob Kawamoto, deputy director of policy and plan management for the state Department of Health and Human Services’ Medicaid division, called it “record attendance,” as committee members agreed their meetings rarely see many attendees.
The attendees were there as part of a planned protest against cuts to Medicaid spurred by funding cuts under the federal “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which included an evening rally in downtown Lincoln.
Protesters holding “Medicare for All” sign on Centennial Mall on Nov, 12. 2026 in Lincoln. (Juan Salinas II | Nebraska Examiner)
Seventeen people spoke during the committee’s one-hour public comment period, with a majority expressing fear for the future well-being of themselves or their loved ones, who are either on Medicaid, or have had their coverage revoked.
A common concern among the testifiers was the lack of transparency from DHHS about how the changes would impact them. Several testifiers said they have stayed on the phone for hours trying to get clear answers, and frequently get different answers from DHHS staff for the same question.
Amanda Gershon, a sponsor of the 2018 ballot initiative that authorized Medicaid expansion in Nebraska, said the changes are not what Nebraskans voted for. She said the paperwork for Medicaid participants is too complex for the average person. After 12 years in the healthcare system, Gershon said she doesn’t understand how to properly fill hers out.
“I went to college, got A’s, and this is confusing,” Gershon said. “How is anyone with a developmental disability supposed to do this?”
Several testifiers criticized the implementation of new federally mandated work requirements for Medicaid recipients that took effect in Nebraska earlier this year. Broadly, the federal requirements mandate that certain adults receiving Medicaid who are between the ages of 19 and 64 will need to work, volunteer or attend school for at least 80 hours per month, earn at least $580 a month or qualify for an exemption.
Melanie Knight, a mother of an autistic son, said although her son works part-time and is considered high-functioning under state standards, there is “no way” he could handle working 80 hours per month. She said her son relies on Medicaid for medication that allows him to function, and even with it, he needs her help regularly.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Cheila Ditzler, a psychiatric nurse who clarified that she was speaking on behalf of herself and not her organization, said she felt the work requirements ignored some of the barriers rural Nebraskans face in locating job opportunities in their area. She asked the committee to advocate for the state to allow Medicaid participants to demonstrate that they have attempted to find work in order to obtain an exemption.
As the meeting went on, some of those testifying expressed sympathy for the committee, with several people calling them “scapegoats” for the public to vent their frustrations on while state and federal leaders with the power to make decisions remain unchecked.
“It feels like you guys are going to be the scapegoats for our legislators and Jim Pillen and Republicans on Capitol Hill,” said Katrina Siefken. “And you guys don’t deserve that. And DHHS employees, they don’t deserve that.”
Committee member Philip Gray explained that their committee is mostly made up of Medicaid members — including himself — and healthcare providers who are tasked with making recommendations to the state on how to improve the Medicaid system. However, while the formation of the committee is a federal mandate, it is not a mandate that “anybody listen to us,” he said.
Several testifiers questioned the point of providing public feedback if the committee lacked “teeth” to enforce any meaningful change.
“I really appreciate that you guys are hearing us out,” said dental assistant Nehemiah Gage. “But it just feels like it’s for nothing.”
Several committee members addressed this concern, saying they shared a lot of the testifiers’ frustrations. Members noted that their committee has openings, as well as one of their subcommittees, and encouraged attendees to consider applying. Gray recommended attendees also look into applying for the Developmental Disabilities Advisory Committee.
“We may not have a lot of teeth, but you guys showing up here, that has teeth,” said committee vice chair Jennifer Hansen.

name: WyoFile
title: Court decides to let legal battle over Wyoming’s school-choice program proceed
description:
Voucher supporters hoped a district court judge would dismiss lawsuit challenging Wyoming’s new Steamboat Legacy Scholarship, which gives state money to families for private-school costs. 
The post Court decides to let legal battle over Wyoming’s school-choice program proceed appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
District Court Judge Peter Froelicher has again refused to dismiss the lawsuit against Wyoming’s universal school-choice program, leaving the fate of the controversial law uncertain as enrolled families accrue costs for private-school expenses the state program has pledged to fund. 
Froelicher’s Nov. 6 decision is the latest bump in the road for advocates of the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Program. Through the program, Wyoming residents can apply to receive up to $7,000 in state funds per student to pay for costs associated with private K-12 education. The money covers not only private-school tuition, but also things like admission fees to zoos or internet classes for homeschooling children not enrolled in public education.
The 2025 law passed amid objections that it would violate the Wyoming Constitution, which bars the state from handing out public funds to individuals, corporations or associations “except for necessary support of the poor.” Shortly after it passed, a group of parents and the Wyoming Education Association sued to halt the program. The lawsuit, which named Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder, Wyoming State Treasurer Curt Meier and the State of Wyoming as defendants, asked the court to block the program. 
The lawsuit set off a flurry of motions and hearings. The one the judge responded to last week was from defendants asking him to dismiss the case for a failure to establish standing. 
Froelicher declined. That means he will continue to weigh whether the program aligns with constitutional mandates that obligate the Legislature to fund public education and explicitly prohibit the use of public funds for private and parochial schools. 
Jett Schulte, an upper elementary student at Powder River Prep, prays with his classmates during Bible study. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
The Wyoming Education Association celebrated Froelicher’s decision, which association President Kimberly Amen said allows the case to move forward toward trial. 
“We remain confident in the strength of our case and steadfast in our belief that public dollars belong in public schools,” Amen told WyoFile in a statement. 
School-choice advocates, including Wyoming families that intervened on behalf of state defendants, still find promise in a May decision by the Wyoming Supreme Court that reversed Froelicher’s 2025 block of the program’s rollout. 
“The Wyoming Supreme Court already held that the [educational savings account] program does not affect the public school funding model and that the plaintiffs cannot claim an educational injury from a program they do not intend to use,” EdChoice Director of Litigation Thomas M. Fisher, who represents the intervening families, said in a statement to WyoFile. “The district court’s denial of our motion for judgment on the pleadings in order to wait for further evidence will not change the governing law in this case.”
A turbulent path
The 2025 Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act represents a significant expansion of school choice in Wyoming. It arrived on a wave of advocacy nationwide, particularly among conservatives, and has been dogged by debate regarding proper use of state funds. 
Even in Wyoming’s majority-Republican statehouse, the measure created ample tension in the 2025 legislative session as lawmakers grappled with whether it would adhere to the state’s constitution, which makes public education a paramount state commitment.
Lawmakers had created an income-qualified voucher program in 2024. Supporters said the income qualifications in the measure provided constitutional safeguards. 
Rep. Ocean Andrew, R-Laramie, however, called it too narrow when he proposed expansion in 2025. His bill ultimately passed. Along with $7,000 per child annually for K-12 non-public-school costs, the scholarship offers money for pre-K costs, but only to income-qualified families at or below 250% of the federal poverty level. For a family of four, that’s an income of roughly $80,000 annually.
When the state opened Steamboat Legacy Scholarship applications in 2025, nearly 4,000 applicants signed up to receive the money for the 25/26 school year. Then in June 2025, parents and the WEA filed their legal challenge.  
Laramie Republican Rep. Ocean Andrew and Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder chat Monday, Feb. 9, 2026, before the start of the budget session in Cheyenne. Both supported a school-choice bill. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
“The Program violates multiple elements of the Education Article of the Wyoming Constitution,” their lawsuit stated. “The state cannot circumvent [constitutional] requirements by funding private education that is not uniform and that meets none of the required state constitutional standards for education.”
Thus began a back-and-forth of legal maneuvers. Asserting the program would cause irreparable harm to plaintiffs, the lawsuit asked the court to block the voucher program while the case proceeds. Defendants, meanwhile, asked that the case be dismissed. 
Froelicher granted that plaintiff’s preliminary injunction request in July 2025, barring the state from releasing any money while the case is litigated.
The state, however, fought his injunction, and further challenges led to the Supreme Court taking up the matter. The higher court in May reversed the injunction, concluding the group of parents challenging the state program “failed to clearly show they might be irreparably and personally injured.” 
The Supreme Court determination that plaintiffs failed to make a clear showing of such possible injury spurred defendants to ask Froelicher once more for dismissal. (He had rejected a defendants’ motion to dismiss in 2025.)
On the heels of the higher court’s decision, meanwhile, the state restarted the program. Again, several thousand applications were submitted for costs related to everything from tutoring to online classes and private school tuition. Parents like intervening defendant Nikki Leck told WyoFile the program allows them the flexibility to tailor education to their children’s specific needs.
That flexibility will come at a cost to public education in the state, critics say, because the program will draw students away from public schools, and shrinking enrollment leads to smaller state budget apportionment.

name: WyoFile
title: A bird in hand remains a mystery in stone
description:
The Miocene Epoch specimen is a rare find in Wyoming, and a paleontologist is determined to learn its identity.
The post A bird in hand remains a mystery in stone appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
J.P. Cavigelli, a paleontologist at the Tate Geological Museum in Casper, opened a metal locker, pulled out a drawer containing dozens of specimens and retrieved a flat stone embedded with a small, rare-for-Wyoming fossilized bird.
“It’s the back end,” said Cavigelli, donning his trademark bandana and bushy, grey beard. “We got the pelvis, one really nice back leg and a not so nice back leg. We don’t know what it is yet.”
Tate Geological Museum paleontologist J.P. Cavigelli retrieves a rare bird fossil from the archives. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
The fossil, discovered on private property in Laramie County, found its way to the Tate Museum a couple of years ago. The bird — definitely from the Miocene Epoch, according to Cavigelli — remained in the locker, its identity a mystery to be solved. Itching for answers, he attended a conference in New Zealand earlier this year where the topic was fossilized birds, determined to find an expert who might identify the specimen.
“We’re talking to a student in Chicago who is probably going to work on it,” Cavigelli said. “It basically entails looking at the dimensions of all the leg bones and the details of the joints on these things — that’s kind of what they look at when they do this stuff.”

name: WyoFile
title: What’s painted in the clouds
description:
A Laramie mural tells an incomplete story of the frontier, writes columnist Jessica Brauer.
The post What’s painted in the clouds appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In the Laramie Plains Civic Center, the theatre’s north wall is covered in four framed oil-on-canvas paintings. The panels, painted by Florence Ware of Salt Lake City, depict frontier people across the Wyoming plains. 

Opinion

In the murals, women in hoop skirts wave handkerchiefs at a passing steam engine. Children play — a young boy with a bow and arrow, a young girl with a bonnet-clad doll. Men and their dogs rest on a prairie hill, while others move cattle in the background. 
Throughout the landscape, Indigenous and settler caricatures stand alongside historic figures from the state’s past — Jim Bridger, Jacques La Ramie, Father DeSmet, Chief Washakie. Yet, the paintings don’t depict the grim truths of settler colonization. That absence unsettles me.
It is my job to steward this building, and thus, these paintings and the story they tell. In one panel, cowboys and their border collie take a break in the foreground. In the distance, there’s a heavenly scene reminiscent of a Renaissance painting. Half a dozen figures in feather headdresses float in a towering pink cumulus cloud. One man stands, while the rest sit in a half circle, with their legs crossed. To me, it would seem, this scene depicts a peaceful gift of the Indigenous land to the plainsmen. The figures ascend from what was once their residence to the sky, passive witnesses to what would become Wyoming.
The artist, granddaughter of a Laramie pioneer couple, is said to have painted the western scene in honor of her aunt who taught in the original school building. She was teaching art and interior decorating in Utah, when she was commissioned in 1929 by Wilbur A. Hitchcock, the architect for the building’s addition, to paint the murals for the auditorium.
“The cut stone and brick building would bring some formal education to the western frontier cubs,” the building’s nomination for the National Register of Historic Places states. What is now the Civic Center was once East Side School, the Wyoming Territory’s first brick schoolhouse. 
In 1928, University of Wyoming President Dr. A.G. Crane dedicated the building:
“To truth that shall make men free;
To knowledge in combat against ignorance and superstition;
To America’s search for and development of genius;
And to the great posterity of Laramie.”
Dawn Stagner, Indigenous Affairs writer and enrolled Cheyenne Arapaho Tribe member who is also Eastern Shoshone, wrote “Letter to a future ancestor,” in reflection of America’s 250th this summer. “The government made our ceremonies and traditional ways illegal, and the boarding school system tried to strip us of our languages and traditional ties to our lands. Our languages are now endangered and might disappear in the span of a generation.”
“‘Equality’ did not exist for us here in Wyoming,” she continues. 
In the Laramie Plains Civic Center, the theatre’s north wall is covered in four framed oil-on-canvas paintings by Florence Ware. (Jessica Brauer)
In 1969, Ware told the Laramie Boomerang, “I painted them as a matter of historical record of the state of Wyoming.” She researched the area for many months and aimed to include “as much of the history as she could,” the article states. I don’t know why she painted this scene, or with what intent she painted Indigenous figures floating above the prairie, but it invokes a sense of peace that couldn’t be further from the truth of their violent displacement from this place.
“The weight of this reality is uncomfortable; the misery of guilt makes one hurry toward any reprieve,” scholars Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang wrote in “Decolonization is not a metaphor.” Their article aims not to soothe my unsettled conscience, but rather to remind me that decolonization returns Indigenous land. That act decenters settlers like me entirely. “Decolonization is not an ‘and.’ It is an elsewhere,” they say. 
Shoshone Chief Washakie is celebrated throughout the state as a man of peace. In the murals, he stands in a sea of American flags alongside cattlemen, fur trappers and explorers. The 1863 Treaty of Fort Bridger granted the Eastern Shoshone around 44 million acres. Five years later, the 1868 Treaty of Fort Bridger shrank this allotment to roughly 3 million acres in the Wind River Valley. In 1878, the same year East Side School opened its doors, Northern Arapaho arrived by Army escort to what is now the Wind River Reservation, despite being promised sovereign land of their own.
Ware’s murals are an artistic feat and a visual asset to a gathering space. Yet, I am haunted by my responsibility to the fabricated history they depict. Stagner’s letter invited an avenue for the settler anxiety this art evokes in me. She reminds me to look closer, not away from this history. 
My tools in community building — connective storytelling, philanthropy, mutual aid, attempts to divert the negative impact of harmful policy — aren’t innocent of that history. Ware’s depictions of Indigenous men in the Wyoming clouds don’t make their presence unreal. 
The path of least resistance would be to call these painted figures and my disturbances a product of a very old building. I could remove the paintings in an attempt to eradicate any further examination of them. I could avoid drawing any attention to their fraught imagery. But these painted figures are not distant, foggy memories; they are living communities. This peaceful painted story is not the full history. 
Stagner writes, “True equality demands a hard look at the past.” 
We will not find that past painted on oil canvas panels in historic school buildings. Our innocence is make-believe.
The figures floating in the prairie clouds, for better or for worse, force me to question the stories we tell about the West every single day.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama infant mortality rate increases slightly, remains above national average
description: Alabama’s infant mortality rate worsened slightly in 2025 and remains above the national average, according to data released Thursday by the Alabama Department of Public Health. State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris said that the state’s infant mortality rate, the number of infants who died in the first year of being born, was 7.4 deaths […]
text:
Dr. Scott Harris, Alabama State Health Officer, at the Oversight Commission on Opioid Settlement Funds meeting on Feb. 18, 2026, in the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. Harris on Thursday said that the state’s infant mortality rate was 7.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2025, an increase from 7.1 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabama’s infant mortality rate worsened slightly in 2025 and remains above the national average, according to data released Thursday by the Alabama Department of Public Health.
State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris said that the state’s infant mortality rate, the number of infants who died in the first year of being born, was 7.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2025, an increase from 7.1 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024.
“When we’re dealing with all these statistics, we talk a lot about statistical significance, and did things really change, or does the number look a little different,” Harris said during a meeting of the State Committee on Public Health. “But it’s not really statistically significant. Please understand what we mean when we say insignificant. Every death of a child is significant.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He said that while the rate increased, it was not statistically significant. The three-year average gives a “smoother curve” with 0.2 to 0.4 jumps over the last 10 years, and showed improvement from 2003 to 2015, when the state’s rate was between 8.3 deaths per 1,000 live births and 9.5 deaths per 1,000 live births.
Alabama’s infant mortality, a three-year average, from 2003 to 2025. (Alabama Department of Public Health)
Harris said the infant mortality rate is an indicator of overall health in Alabama and is a fair way to compare states. 
“There’s so many different factors that go into this number that you’re going to see that you can look at that number and sort of get an idea of how public health is looking in Alabama,” Harris said.
The nation’s infant mortality average is 5.5 deaths per 1,000 live births, up from 5.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024. Harris said the gap between Alabama and the national average has always been there, but the state roughly matches the nation’s trend.
In 1970, about 20 babies died per 1,000 births nationwide and about 24.5 died in Alabama. The rate started to descend after the implementation of Neonatal Intensive Care Units in the 1960s. In the late 1980s, Medicaid coverage was extended to pregnant women.
Infant mortality rates for the United States and Alabama from 1970 to 2025. (Alabama Department of Public Health)
Harris said in an interview that the gap could close, and the state got close at its lowest rate in 2022 of 6.7 deaths per 1,000 live births.
“We absolutely have the ability to improve that, and we have a lot of people working on it,” he said. “We have a lot of people in Alabama outside of our agency who are really invested in these projects, but it’s going to take all of us.”
There were 57,192 total births in 2024, and 422 of those babies died before reaching their first birthday in 2025. The 2026 rate is still being calculated because all babies born in 2025 have not yet reached their first birthday. 
A ‘stubborn statistic’
Racial disparities continue to be a challenge. Of the 422 infant deaths, 229 of them were white babies while 183 were Black babies. The mortality rate for Black babies in Alabama is 13.1 deaths per 1,000 live births, nearly 2.5 times as high as that of white babies at 5.5 deaths per 1,000 live births, Harris said.
“This is a really stubborn statistic. We spend a lot of time and effort thinking about how to address this. We’ve not really made a big difference in that,” he said. “The white infant mortality rate is right at the U.S. average, but because we’ve not done the job we should do with the Black infant mortality rate, we’re typically in that bottom tier of states overall, unfortunately.”
About 72.1% of babies were born to white mothers in Alabama, and about 24.5% of babies were born to Black mothers in 2025, according to the data. Harris said the birth rate, regardless of race, has been on a steady decline since 2021.
Alabama’s infant mortality, by race, from 2016 to 2025. (Alabama Department of Public Health)
Dr. Marquisha Jarmon, a Hoover-based pediatrician and member of the committee, said the department should work directly with Black groups to raise awareness to reduce the mortality rate.
“I love hearing this information about infant mortality because it just sheds a light on the problem, especially in the African American community,” she said. “The question that we’re all asking is: What really is the problem in our community when everyone else is getting better and we’re staying the same?”
Harris called closing the racial gap the “million dollar question.” He said in an interview that some of the social determinants – poverty, race, education, ZIP code – is not something that the health department can address, but it can educate mothers-to-be on a healthy pregnancy.
“It’s challenging to know how to address that. The way we address it is by trying to find specific reasons that we’re losing our babies that we can intervene with,” he said. “That might be prenatal vitamins and safe sleep education, trying to get people connected to healthcare for chronic disease management. That’s our approach.”
Risks and causes of death
Harris said that ensuring adequate prenatal care is crucial for a successful pregnancy. According to the data, 75.7% of live births in 2025 received adequate prenatal care, and only 2.8% of pregnancies with no prenatal care resulted in a live birth. 
The top three causes of infant deaths are congenital abnormalities, preterm births and low birth weights, and sudden infant death syndrome, according to the data. About 23.2% of infants died by SIDS, a 7-point increase over 2024 when the cause of death was the lowest ranked. The deaths often occur while the infant is asleep, often caused by accidental suffocation, strangulation or an unknown cause.
“We really believe that sleep-related deaths ought to always be preventable. We think education is the way to get there,” he said.
Harris said safe sleeping, babies sleeping alone, on their back and in a crib, is important to prevent SIDS.
Many things can contribute to infant mortality, like maternal age, smoking and chronic disease; preterm birth, low birth weight and congenital abnormalities. A mother’s income, race, level of education and ZIP code impact her baby’s chance of survival, according to the data. These factors also impact a mother’s access to health care. 
Alabama’s infant mortality, by county of residence for 2025 (right), and a map of counties with delivering hospitals for 2025. (Alabama Department of Public Health)
According to the data, the infant mortality rate is much higher in rural counties like Pickens, Sumter, Hale and Washington in the Black Belt, and Geneva County in the southern part of the state. Those counties directly correlate with counties without hospitals that can deliver babies, according to the data.
According to the University of North Carolina’s Sheps Center, nine rural hospitals have closed in Alabama since 2009. Only 30% of the state’s rural hospitals have labor and delivery units, leaving many expectant parents to drive long distances for care. One labor and delivery unit in Mobile closed this summer. 
“We aren’t necessarily able to prove a statistical association because the numbers are really small, but it doesn’t seem like a coincidence that when you live really far away from a delivery hospital your infant mortality rate is higher, and that’s what we see,” Harris said.
The department has nine programs related to infant mortality: Safe Sleep initiatives; Well Woman; family planning services; newborn screening; sexually transmitted infection/disease diagnosis and treatment; Women, Infant and Children program; Children’s Health Insurance Program; Fetal and Infant Mortality Review; and Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho independent Achilles fell short against Republican US Sen. Risch. Can independents win here?
description: Idaho’s Todd Achilles was one of a handful of major independent U.S. Senate candidates in red states to generate national attention ahead of the 2026 general election.  Although he and the other high-profile independents lost their races, Achilles argues there’s still a future for independents to be a competitive alternative in a two-party system, and […]
text:
Campaign signs greet attendees at the election night watch party for independent U.S. Senate Candidate Todd Achilles on Nov. 3, 2026, in Garden City, Idaho. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho’s Todd Achilles was one of a handful of major independent U.S. Senate candidates in red states to generate national attention ahead of the 2026 general election. 
Although he and the other high-profile independents lost their races, Achilles argues there’s still a future for independents to be a competitive alternative in a two-party system, and a viable way to win in such a Republican state. 
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, talks to an Idaho News 6 reporter at the Idaho GOP election night watch party at the Grove in Boise, Idaho, on Nov. 8, 2022. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
Achilles, a former Democratic state legislator, ended with 33.57% of the vote, compared to incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch’s 56.6% in the four-way race with no Democrat on the ballot. The other independent candidate, Natalie Fleming, received around 7% of the vote. 
In an election year where many Republicans struggled in nationwide federal races, Idaho voters stood by their GOP incumbents. 
“Idaho is different because, it’s just the advantage for Republicans among voter behavior is so outsized compared to even states in the South,” said Robert Jones, a partner and political strategist at Boise-based GS Strategy Group.
Nearly 62% of Idaho voters are registered with the Republican Party, and 12% are registered Democrats, according to the Idaho secretary of state’s office. More than 24% aren’t affiliated with either party. 
Voters who deeply align with a major political party tend to stick with that party, even when they aren’t necessarily satisfied with their performance, said Idaho State University political scientist Edward Greer. Greer researches American politics, political psychology, and political behavior. 
“If a political party is not meeting those needs, then there’s not typically going to be a lot of crossover to the other side,” Greer said. “Usually, people will just kind of sit out.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Was this race different from past Idaho U.S. Senate elections? 

The win, although still comfortable, was Risch’s closest general election race since he first won his U.S. Senate seat in 2008. 
In 2008, Risch won with 57.7% of the vote against Democratic challenger and former congressman Larry LaRocco, who had 34.1% of the vote, with three other candidates on the ballot. 
Achilles, speaking to the Idaho Capital Sun the day after the election, said his campaign “built a great foundation” for the independent movement in Idaho. 
Independent candidate for U.S. Senate Todd Achilles speaks with attendees at an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, at Iconic Bistro and Bar in Garden City. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“We went from zero to 33% in 18 months,” he said. “… We got a lot of people excited. We had hundreds of meetings and town halls and events across the state. Everything I’m seeing in my inbox this morning is, ‘Let’s keep going.’ ‘We like what this independent movement is about.’” 
Achilles said he hasn’t decided if he would run again, but that he plans to continue to be involved in politics. 
His campaign garnered a similar share of votes as Democrats in other statewide races. Risch’s last challenger, Democrat Paullet Jordan, finished with a similar vote share, with 33.2% in the 2020 election.
Achilles this year narrowly outperformed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens, who won 32.25% of the vote in her five-way contest against incumbent Republican Gov. Brad Little. 
In two-way statewide races, Democrats consistently won about 34% of the vote, with the highest coming from attorney general candidate Lori Hickman, who received 40.21% against incumbent Republican Attorney General Raúl Labrador.  
 Some Idaho Dems pressured their candidate to drop out of the Senate race and rally around Achilles, then Achilles lost. Now what? 

After he won his May primary, Democrat David Roth withdrew from the U.S. Senate race in August, days ahead of the deadline to have his name removed from the general election ballot. He told the Sun he dropped out because he lacked support from his own party.
Leaders of the Ada County Democrats wrote Roth a letter asking him to drop out, arguing Achilles had the better chance to oust Risch, the Spokesman-Review reported. 
Jared DeLoof, executive director of the Idaho Democratic Party, speaks to attendees during the general election watch party Nov. 5, 2024, in Boise. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Ada County Democrats Chair Jared Deloof told the Sun he’d still probably send the letter today, because Roth wasn’t raising the money to be competitive. But he also thinks the future lies with more work within the Democratic party, and not with independents. 
“This was, I really think, an experiment year, given the stakes of what’s going on in the country,” DeLoof said. “Folks seeing is this a path forward to confronting the threats that we’re seeing to freedom across the country?  So I totally understand the want to try to do something new.”
“I will say now the results are in after last Tuesday, and we saw across the country independent candidates not doing well against Republican opponents, and actually saw Democrats in some of the deepest, reddest parts of the country fare very well, even in places like South Carolina, Mississippi, and Texas,” he said. “And so, my takeaway from this is that in deep red places like Idaho, we have to continue to do the work within the Democratic Party to build a party that can win here.” 
Idaho Democratic Party Chair Lauren Necochea told the New York Times ahead of Nov. 3 that she thought “independent candidates will generally fade away after the election.” 
“The Democratic Party will still be here doing the work to hold Republicans accountable,” Necochea said. 
 Is there a meaningful way forward for major independent candidates? 

The Achilles campaign raised nearly $2 million, more than any other Senate challenger in recent years. However, Risch’s campaign surpassed $5 million, as of Oct. 14 Federal Election Commission data. 
Greer, the political scientist, said it’s not impossible for independents to win in Idaho, but it is more difficult without the party infrastructure Republicans and Democrats have. 
“I wouldn’t completely rule out the possibility of independents potentially doing better down the line,” Greer said. “There are some notable independent senators that have gotten elected before, closer to the East Coast. But it could be a question of, if the Democratic brand is unpopular in states like Idaho, it would be a matter of if independents could win over would-be Democrats while still keeping the Democratic brand at arm’s length to make it credibly seem that they’re not Democrats.” 
The nation saw a blue wave this election. Idaho saw a ripple.

“And then at that point,” Greer said, “they might be able to win people over that are truly independents that aren’t wanting to align cleanly with either party.” 
Jones, with GS Strategy Group which has worked with Republican-aligned campaigns and PACs, said Republicans are likely to keep winning in statewide elections in Idaho for the foreseeable future. 
“Those things take a long time to change,” Jones said. “It doesn’t mean there won’t be a candidate or a single race where something happens that’s anomalous and somebody can get elected. But structural change, where Democrats are competitive up and down the statewide ballot, is a fair ways off.”
DeLoof noted that even among some victories for Idaho Democrats this year, it’s a “really tough uphill battle” to win in statewide elections. 
“This is a similar trajectory to what Georgia did, what Texas did, states that you never could imagine showing up blue on the map,” he said. “I believe if we stick to it, we’ll eventually get there someday.” 
Jones noted that Risch’s victory against Achilles was the slimmest among statewide general election contests in Idaho. One could argue he had a better chance than a Democrat, he said.  
“So Achilles did the best, I guess if you want to put in that framework,” Jones said of the vote margins, “but an independent campaign is still a long way off from beating a Republican.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Even solidly red Saline County saw a shift toward Democrats in Arkansas’ midterm election
description: Located a short drive from Democrat-leaning Little Rock, Saline County has been a Republican stronghold of central Arkansas for years. The county hasn’t voted for a Democrat for president since Bill Clinton’s 1996 reelection, and has been the epicenter of fights over book restrictions. But an unexpected thing happened in the county that Donald Trump […]
text:
Campaign signs for the 2026 midterm elections line the grass outside the Saline County Courthouse in Benton, Arkansas on Oct. 19, 2026, the first day of early voting. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Located a short drive from Democrat-leaning Little Rock, Saline County has been a Republican stronghold of central Arkansas for years. The county hasn’t voted for a Democrat for president since Bill Clinton’s 1996 reelection, and has been the epicenter of fights over book restrictions.
But an unexpected thing happened in the county that Donald Trump won with 69% of the vote just two years ago. The county’s voters swung 17 percentage points in favor of Democrats. The GOP nominees for U.S. House and Senate saw their numbers drop from two years ago, and a Republican state lawmaker in the county barely survived a bid to oust him. 
And a Republican-led effort to cut the county’s library funding failed.
The results don’t amount to a blue wave in a county where Republicans still control county offices. But last week’s midterms in Saline County highlight how even the reddest of counties were touched by an election where Republicans suffered major losses around the country.
How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to The AP Voter Poll

Former state Republican party chairman Richard Bearden said it’s too early to draw conclusions about Arkansas’ political trajectory.
“I don’t know that we can look at one election cycle and say, ‘Golly, the state’s trending back to being sort of a yellow-dog Democrat state that it was 20 years ago,’” Bearden said.
National polling has indicated that Democrats’ takeover of congressional seats and governor’s races across was a repudiation of the president and his policies. Arkansas voters chose Trump in the past three presidential elections, winning about 69% of Saline County’s vote each time.
Despite Democrats’ attempts to tie U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton and U.S. Rep. French Hill to the increasingly unpopular Trump, Saline County’s double-digit voter shift isn’t necessarily a rebuke of the president, at least not in elections for state-level offices, said Shane Broadway, chairman of the Saline County Economic Development Corporation.
“One thing I noticed watching all of the ads [was], especially on the Democratic side, they were focusing on costs of gas, groceries, those kinds of things, and nobody ever mentioned Donald Trump on either side,” Broadway said.
Sen. Kim Hammer (R), candidate for Arkansas Secretary of State, answers questions at the press conference following the debate at Arkansas TV studios on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
But Republican Sen. Kim Hammer of Benton, who won his race for secretary of state last week, said Saline County voters’ leftward shift might have been simply “a protest vote” against Trump. 
Nearly 44,000 Saline County residents voted in the midterms, with nearly 34,000 setting a county record for early voter turnout, County Clerk Doug Curtis posted on Facebook. Turnout is typically lower in midterms than general elections, and nearly 58,000 Saline County residents voted in 2024.
Broadway, a former longtime Democratic state legislator and former House speaker, said his decades of experience in Arkansas politics have taught him that the state’s voters “tend to have an independent streak.”
“I’ve seen red waves, I’ve seen blue waves, and I’ve seen a lot of times where Arkansas was not a part of either,” he said.
 Changes in northeast Saline County

Republicans kept all 13 seats on the Saline County Quorum Court, with seven members and the county judge running unopposed. All six state House seats and both Senate seats in the county will continue to be held by Republicans.
Gina Thomas-Littlejohn (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
But GOP Rep. RJ Hawk of Bryant won reelection over Democrat Gina Thomas-Littlejohn by only 96 votes, two years after he defeated her by more than 2,300 votes.
Hawk’s razor-thin victory in the Saline County district closest to Little Rock came on a night when most of the state capital’s northern suburbs voted blue. Democrats flipped two House seats and one Senate seat in north Pulaski County, breaking Republicans’ House supermajority with 10 House seat flips statewide.
Democrats nationwide ran on lowering the cost of necessities such as gasoline and healthcare. Saline County residents of all political persuasions shared frustrations about the cost of living, said Thomas-Littlejohn, a former Alexander city council member, and Joshua Irby, a Democratic first-time candidate who ran for Hammer’s Senate seat.
NORC polling takeaways: Arkansans worried about economy, healthcare, data center impact

“Some Republicans [said] they have voted Democrat this year,” Thomas-Littlejohn said. “I’ve never heard that before. The two years prior, I never heard that.”
Bearden said independents who voted Republican in the past likely chose to vote Democrat this year because they believed the GOP wasn’t sufficiently “addressing kitchen table issues.”
Demographic changes in Saline County might have played a role in the election results. The northeast part of the county that includes Bryant, Alexander and Shannon Hills has seen an influx of new residents moving from Little Rock seeking a lower cost of living, said Thomas-Littlejohn and Lela Chism, who won a Shannon Hills city council seat last week.
This means the area doesn’t have the “reactionary Republican voting base” present in other parts of Saline County, so voters are less receptive to right-wing talking points about immigrants and the LGBTQ+ community, said Chism, one of the most vocal opponents of the failed ballot measure to reduce library funding.
“The culture stuff might hype you up and get reactionary people out to the polls because it scares them, but the policy itself isn’t popular,” she said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Shane Broadway, vice president for university relations has been appointed, interim chancellor of ASU Three Rivers. (Photo courtesy of Arkansas State University)
 Increased Democratic presence

Democrats held a majority of Arkansas’ state and federal offices from 2006 to 2012, but Republicans had taken over by 2014. The Democratic Party of Saline County “pretty much died out” around that time, said Broadway, who unsuccessfully ran for lieutenant governor in 2010.
However, the party has been rebuilding a presence in the county over the past few years. Broadway said he’s seen Saline County Democrats man booths at local festivals, and Thomas-Littlejohn said the party knocked down a wall in its Benton headquarters to make room for new members.
Chism said the issues that motivated Arkansas’ Democratic voters this year are not going away anytime soon.
“If the Republicans in Arkansas continue to neglect the needs of working people and average people, they’re going to lose again,” said Chism, who ran for a quorum court seat as a Democrat in 2024.
The four Saline County quorum court members who ran in both 2024 and 2026 defeated their Democratic opponents by lower margins this year, according to the secretary of state’s website.
Hammer said he believes Democrats’ progress in Saline County will be short-lived over the next two years.
Joshua Irby (Photo courtesy of Arkansas Secretary of State)
“I think we’re going to see the pendulum swing back the other direction because people will realize we were going in the right direction” under Republican leadership, Hammer said.
Saline County Sheriff Rodney Wright defeated Irby in the race for Hammer’s Senate seat, but Wright received 3,321 fewer votes than Hammer did in 2022.
Irby said he learned while campaigning that Arkansans want “solutions and not sound bites” from their elected officials.
“People are just feeling like, ‘Where’s the help?’” Irby said. “Where are the people who are representing us, and what are they doing to improve this situation? I think that was the key takeaway, the biggest concern anyone and everyone had.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee’s gerrymandered election maps hold up, but not as well as in past cycles
description: Tennessee Republicans won the popular vote in down-ballot races last week, but gerrymandering  allowed them to win even more seats than vote totals would have indicated. The GOP received around 54% of the vote in Tennessee’s nine congressional races while likely winning eight of them, or 89% of the seats, an analysis of election data […]
text:
Tennessee Republican won more seats then the party's popular vote totals in Tennessee's U.S. House and state House elections. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee Republicans won the popular vote in down-ballot races last week, but gerrymandering  allowed them to win even more seats than vote totals would have indicated.
The GOP received around 54% of the vote in Tennessee’s nine congressional races while likely winning eight of them, or 89% of the seats, an analysis of election data by Lookout shows. In the state House, state Republicans received 58% of the votes cast while winning 69 of the 99 districts, or 70%.
Republicans achieved this outcome by drawing a state House map in 2022 and a U.S. House map in 2026 that gerrymandered districts to dilute Democratic Party votes. Democrats won 44% of congressional votes cast and 41% of state House votes. But Republican margins of victory were narrowed, particularly in the state’s congressional races.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
During the 2022 and 2024 election cycles, Republicans handily won eight of the state’s nine congressional seats. This year’s mid-cycle redistricting narrowed Republican margins of victory in U.S. House districts 5 to 9 because of gerrymandering.
Democrats lost those five districts by less than 5% this year, compared to 2024, when President Donald Trump won those same districts by 20-25% over Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris. 
The narrow margins were also boosted by a political environment in which Democrats won the popular vote by 13%, versus 2024, when the party lost it by 1.5%. 
Kent Syler, a political science professor at Middle Tennessee State University, said Republicans were fortunate to lose only one congressional seat Tuesday night. 
“Tennessee was an afterthought, but this is what can happen in wave elections,” he said. 
The new map, enacted during a May legislative session, allowed Republicans to flip Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District, previously held by Memphis Democratic U.S. Rep. Steve Cohen. But the party likely lost Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District, resulting in no numerical change in House seats held by each party statewide.
Democrat Victoria Broderick currently leads U.S. Rep. Scott DeJarlais in the 4th district by about 285 votes, but the race has not been officially called. About 700 provisional ballots remain to be counted in the 4th as of Nov. 12, and about 600 are in the Democratic stronghold of Nashville, where Broderick won about 75% of the vote on election night. 
Those ballots will be counted on Monday, Nov. 16, after which the race can likely be officially called.
Broderick’s win would be the only Democratic win in Tennessee’s U.S. House map. It would effectively neutralize the redistricting enacted to help Republicans win all nine of the state’s congressional districts. 
Democrats did manage to flip six state House seats, and should control up to 30 of the lower chamber’s seats. The party officially won 29 seats, but in a Memphis state House district, Democrat G.A. Hardaway’s death meant neither party nominated a candidate, and write-in candidate John Bradley won.

name: Mississippi Today
title: What did Colom get right in his win over Hyde-Smith? Pretty much everything
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom greets people in line at a President Donald Trump rally for Colom's opponent, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026 in Corinth.
text:
Democratic challenger Scott Colom’s upset win over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, in red, red Mississippi of all places, will be studied by Deep South politicos from both major parties for years to come. 
I predict it will be a blueprint, a road map for Democrats and a bogeyman of what not to do for Republicans.
So what did Colom’s campaign get right? Well, pretty much everything, it would appear as the dust settles.
First, and foremost, he worked. He campaigned hard, while Hyde-Smith hardly campaigned, at least until the homestretch.
Colom crisscrossed the state nonstop, shook every hand and kissed every baby, so to speak (and he didn’t get the two mixed up, lol). He met the voters where they were, and he listened to them. That’s becoming more and more rare, in the age of big-money campaigns.
Colom adopted a clear message, and he stuck to it: It’s affordability, stupid. When you get a gift from Republicans, don’t overthink it. He expanded his messaging here and there, but he kept the main thing the main thing.
READ MORE: Turns out, Mississippi voters were paying attention in the Colom, Hyde-Smith Senate race
Speaking of money, Colom had little to start with, and national Democratic interests had, as usual, written Mississippi off as too Republican to bother with.
But what resources he did secure early on, he deployed wisely. If he and his crew ever want a new career, they could start an ad agency. The don’t pick another protein/pick another senator, and other ads drew national attention and campaign donations. 
His wise use of resources and sticktoitiveness helped convince national Democrats to sink resources into his campaign. It was kind of late in the game, but he was ready and seized on it.
In Mississippi, even before national resources flowed in, Colom didn’t try to reinvent the wheel. He relied on decades of others’ organizing work before him, and he united many different groups that helped organize and get-out-the-vote. If there was infighting, it didn’t spill out into the public or slow the campaign’s momentum. That is a feat.
Colom also appeared to keep his own counsel. He most certainly was advised to follow some conventional Mississippi Democratic campaign wisdom, and appeared to often ignore it. For many years, some statewide Democratic candidates have tried to keep the national party and its leaders at arm’s length. I recall one time many years ago when a Democratic candidate tried to keep it under wraps that the chair of the Democratic National Committee was coming to Mississippi, and their campaign folks got a little perturbed when news of it leaked to the media.
Colom read the tea leaves correctly: Americans wanted change from the current GOP led by President Donald Trump, including those in Mississippi. He embraced support from his party. He reportedly shrugged off advice to not have former Vice President Kamala Harris campaign for him. He embraced a who’s who of national party leaders past and present.
But Colom also appeared to get a sizeable amount of crossover votes. It’s hard to say exactly how many, but he overperformed other Democratic candidates by more than 25,000 votes. That wasn’t all just turning out Democrats.
He campaigned in Republican strongholds, didn’t write them off. For God’s sake, the man gladhanded with folks in line for a Trump rally in Corinth. Hyde-Smith, by the way, didn’t.
He flipped seven counties from R to D, including some big ‘uns. DeSoto County, which Hyde-Smith had previously won by 16 points, saw a well over 20-point swing, with Colom winning the normally GOP stronghold. He thwarted Hyde-Smith from running up big numbers on the Coast. 
Colom won in many of the suburbs, including Madison County and the aforementioned DeSoto, and he did well in college communities in Lafayette, Forrest and Oktibbeha counties. He held his own in many rural Republican areas, and he amped up turnout in the Delta and other rural Democratic areas.
Over many years in Mississippi, we’ve seen many Democrats play the woulda-shoulda-couda game and do some fingerpointing after (or even during) elections, even ones where they lost by fairly narrow margins. I think we’ll be seeing a good bit of that from Republicans now, although most of their fingers could point to President Trump.
It would appear Colom, of course building on the work of others over many years, helped solidify some infrastructure for the state Democratic Party and get the national party’s attention and resources, the lack of which Mississippi Democrats have long lamented. 
Will it last? Time will tell, but having a Democratic U.S. senator from Mississippi, and a blueprint that worked in the Deep South, will help.
