name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: Braun, leaders should reject Chicago Bears
description: It’s time to punt, Indiana. Take your ball and go home because the Chicago Bears don’t deserve us. Gov. Mike Braun and a bipartisan team of lawmakers crafted a package to lure the NFL team to Indiana with little notice and a lot of effort in February. Indiana’s deal involves about $1 billion in public […]
text:
A giant flag for the Chicago Bears is seen during pregame festivities at Soldier Field in Chicago. (Photo by Jonathan Daniel/Getty Images)It’s time to punt, Indiana. Take your ball and go home because the Chicago Bears don’t deserve us.
Gov. Mike Braun and a bipartisan team of lawmakers crafted a package to lure the NFL team to Indiana with little notice and a lot of effort in February.
Indiana’s deal involves about $1 billion in public funding.
But since the bill passed, the Bears have dragged out their supposed “due diligence” for nearly nine months.
I think everyone knew the bid was a bit of a Hail Mary, but Indiana entered into good faith negotiations and voted to raise tolls and local hospitality taxes to attract the team to the Wolf Lake/Hammond area.
Illinois lawmakers, meanwhile, squandered months of time and left town in June with no deal for the Bears.
And yet, Indiana is still waiting in the red zone.
The team on Friday released this statement: “We appreciate the recent engagement from Illinois leadership to explore legislation which has allowed us to share our feedback. We expect productive dialogue with both leadership teams in the coming weeks.”
In the coming weeks? I’ve definitely heard that before. And so has Braun, who reacted with umbrage.
“We encourage the Chicago Bears to fully commit to a stadium in Indiana because it is nearly time for the state to shift its energy and resources to the next opportunity,” he said in a statement.
‘Our focus is on Hammond’: Bears keep stadium sights on Indiana

To add insult to injury, it appears Illinois will essentially lift the framework of the deal Indiana passed and use it to secure the Bears. We all know it’s coming.
So instead of being strung along anymore, Braun and legislative leaders should spike the offer and reduce the leverage they gave the team to get a deal in Illinois.
While having a second NFL team would be a feather in our cap, it’s fair to say it’s unclear if Indiana taxpayers would be better off. They would pay additional tolls, restaurant, admission and hotel taxes in northwest Indiana with what return? Some temporary construction jobs? After that, only low-wage part-time jobs would remain.
In an analysis of the economic impacts of sports stadiums over four decades, through the early 2020s, researchers found little to no economic benefits for taxpayers or communities, including per capita income. Other research has concluded that effects on job growth have similarly been negligible.
Instead, Indiana should take that $1 billion and invest it in Hoosier students, improved roads, energy expansion or other worthwhile causes.
Some of the fees have already been raised, as state officials moved forward with an amendment to the Indiana Toll Road lease increasing rates to free up some infrastructure cash. Indiana already has $300 million in hand from the road’s private operator and an additional $400 million will be paid in 2027 and 2028.
It’s too late to reverse those hikes, but lawmakers should call an audible and apply that money to other important infrastructure projects or send a small rebate back to Hoosiers.
Indiana has an amazing track record of high-quality sports in this state, and we don’t need to wait around for the Bears to fumble the ball even further.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: More than ABCs: How students are falling behind before they enter kindergarten
description: The foundation for a child’s lifetime of learning is built from birth to age 5. By the time they reach kindergarten, there are certain expectations about the skills they should possess.  But what happens when they come in not knowing what they are supposed to know?  Early education and kindergarten teachers say the gaps among […]
text:
Children are entering kindergarten at different educational starting points, and teachers are finding it difficult to get them all on the same level. (Photo courtesy of Rhienna Miscio)The foundation for a child’s lifetime of learning is built from birth to age 5. By the time they reach kindergarten, there are certain expectations about the skills they should possess. 
But what happens when they come in not knowing what they are supposed to know? 
Early education and kindergarten teachers say the gaps among students entering kindergarten are often wide and can be wider if it is a child’s first time in a classroom setting. They say while everyone starts at a different point, it is becoming harder to get them all across the finish line at the same time. 
Day one looks different for every student
Caitlyn Greene is a kindergarten teacher in Franklin and has spent all of her teaching career in the city. She understands the array of circumstances from which students arrive in her classroom.
The rural city has a high percentage of students from low-income backgrounds, and the school also operates under a tax cap, which limits the available resources. 
Greene said she and her colleagues share the idea that kindergarten is “the gift of a year.” She knows she has the opportunity to make an impact on their lives, especially because her classroom is often the first time children have been in a formal learning environment. 
The different starting points and curriculum guidelines like Common Core do not always meet students where they are when they enter Greene’s classroom. Greene said that some of the standards teachers have to reach are not “developmentally appropriate for 5-year-olds”. 
“The biggest challenge is that some of the things we ask of (students), they’re just not ready for. We always assume that, when a child is 5, they are ready for all of these things,” Greene said. “But as an educator, we know that a child at 5 can look different across spectrums.” 
Some children, Greene said, have fine motor skills that let them write their name, can sit and listen to a story, take instruction and express their emotions. Others are not fully potty trained despite being 4 or 5 years old.  
“It’s oranges and apples, even though they are the same age,” she said. 
She continued: “We find that there’s a wide spectrum, and because of that wide spectrum, we are starting at different areas for each child. The issue is if a child is already significantly behind in kindergarten when they enter, it puts them at a disadvantage for the rest of the grade levels.” 
New Hampshire is one of five states nationwide that do not have state-funded preschool programs. The only preschool programs that receive government funding are those that cater to special education children. These classrooms can have non-special-needs children but are required to maintain certain child ratios to receive funding, which is mostly federal.
Rhienna Miscio, who works at one of these public preschools in Bethlehem, is well-versed in the realm of child development. She works two jobs, as a half-day public preschool teacher and speech pathologist assistant. 
Both her jobs follow a similar theme: preparing children for what’s next. What she hears from the kindergarten teachers reflects the traits of Greene’s advanced students. 
“They’re like, ‘I just want them to be able to come in and ready to learn. They have their social emotional under control. They’ve been with other kids before. They know maybe how to hold a pencil,’” Miscio said. 
Miscio partially attributes the gap to children not having access to early-learning services. Early-education programs are expensive, if families can even find them. According to the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute, average childcare costs for an infant and a 4-year-old in center-based care are more than $31,000, and the state is short at least 9,000 slots. 
“We’re finding that not all kids have access to preschool, especially where we’re from,” she said. “And some kindergartens are still half-day, so when we talk about what we want kindergarteners to know, we also have to say, ‘Is it equitable?’” 
For those who can attend publicly funded preschool, students may need to meet other developmental milestones before they can start preparing for kindergarten. 
“I think that sometimes when we are talking about kindergarten-ready, we also have to remember they’re 5 and maybe focus on the basic skills first,” Miscio said. 
Concerns about readiness from early-education and kindergarten professionals culminate in another problem: preparing students for first grade. (Courtesy Rhienna Miscio)
The very real concern of falling behind
Concerns about readiness from early-education and kindergarten professionals culminate in another problem: preparing students for first grade. 
New Hampshire’s kindergarten offerings vary. School districts are not required to have full-day kindergarten, so many only offer half-day. Variation in schedules may give teachers less time to hit their curriculum requirements. 
Greene will sometimes have students who are not ready for first grade by June. She said she recommends at least two students a year to repeat kindergarten. 
“Every year, we catch that some kids, they come in and they can’t sit and they’re missing their instruction because they’re just learning how to operate in a more restrictive environment. We’re doing things at certain times, and so if a child has missed a portion of their education, or we find it clicks in the spring but they haven’t mastered it yet, and there’s significant gaps,” she said. “Then we will talk to a parent.” 
The school makes sure recommendations for a child to repeat a grade are not a shock to parents. Pre- and post-assessments are sent home, sometimes with notes about having a meeting to discuss a child’s progress, as well as constant communication through parent-teacher communication apps. 
“As much as technology has been a deficit in education, when it comes to parents and our ability to communicate back and forth, (it) has really opened up a conversation for there to be better understanding of a child’s needs,” Greene said. 
Greene makes sure to provide parents with data ahead of and along with any conversations about progress. “We always kind of start flagging around January. … You can usually tease out who is struggling. So having those conversations with parents, the open communication is key to not surprise them. It’s a parent’s choice at the end of the day though.” 
Miscio said that as a childcare provider, her philosophy is that she is “in the business of taking care of people.” For her, that extends to parents. 
“So wherever the challenge may be, we’re in it with the parents.” she said. “We’re in the trenches with them.” 
Greene said that while she understands children need to hit early-learning and kindergarten standards, she is worried about the emotional and psychological impact it has on students. She said putting pressure on children to “be at a certain place that sometimes they’re not developmentally ready for” could cause them to “lose the love for learning they should always have.”
Misico said she is worried about the pressure on teachers that comes with children being behind, and the long-term effects on children who lack certain skills. 
“There’s not a lot of time when you’re going from a blank slate to first grade, so I think (teachers) are feeling the pressure, especially when you’re screening them when they first come in, ” Miscio said. “If there’s a gap in kindergarten that goes into first grade, it goes into second grade, and it ends up being kind of a domino effect when we’re not supporting and meeting kids when they’re in kindergarten.” 
She continued: “(But) they’re really little, and some of these kids have never had the opportunity to even be in the classroom, or to have teachers, new adults around. We’re expecting them to be ready. I think that also can be very dangerous because they’re still kids. … We take the kids where they are because that’s what we do.” 
Little institutional support
Early-education advocates have suggested looking up the school administration chain to address issues on the ground. Based on the structure of education and childcare governance, kindergarten readiness is not being addressed, they say. 
In a statement, the Department of Education said that decisions about whether to offer preschool programs, as well as how those programs are “designed and implemented,” are determined at the local level by individual school districts. They also said their oversight of preschool is specific only to special education.
Jake Leon, spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, specified the department “supports school readiness” through its childcare oversight activities, which include licensing and compliance for childcare programs, administering the childcare scholarship assistance program for families, and providing resources to “help programs strengthen early-learning environments.” 
Leon also pointed to the health and education departments’ participation in the Council for Thriving Children, a committee started by former Gov. Chris Sununu during the pandemic that is supposed to serve as the state’s advisory on early childhood education. (This is separate from the Child Care Advisory Council, which was enacted by the Legislature in 1995.) The group’s goal is to address infrastructure, workforce and family matters within the field. The last time the group met was in February, and its website does not point to any active initiatives on kindergarten readiness. 
“DHHS and the Department of Education participate on the Council for Thriving Children and other cross agency workgroups that focus on aligning early childhood systems, supporting families and promoting possible outcomes for children birth to age 5,” Leon said. “While local school districts and private childcare programs determine curriculum and instructional approaches, DHHS’s role ensures that the early-learning settings children experience prior to kindergarten are safe, stable and supported in delivering high quality care.” 
Some groups, such as the National Education Association of New Hampshire and regional childcare coalitions, are trying to address classroom concerns themselves, but have yet to find success due to several factors. For example, childcare programs all have different curricula to give parents a variety of options. Additionally, children all develop at different rates, and while access to early support and services and childcare can help, it may not immediately translate into success in kindergarten. 
At the end of the day, Miscio knows that she and her fellow teachers will continue to work with what they have under the circumstances they are given, because “that’s what teachers do.” But she knows that education gaps are going to continue to be a problem. 
“My old boss, her motto was 3 years old to third grade, and that’s where you need to put in all of everything you got because that gives them the best foundation, and that doesn’t mean put things on them that are impossible, but that means make sure that they have a really good foundation,” she said. “And when you’re rushing it, there’s going to be bigger gaps that are going to be seen the older they get.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: A rare request for clemency in Rhode Island could help 2 refugees fight deportation
description: For two Cambodian refugees fighting to remain in the U.S., an extraordinary request made to Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee could help them overcome criminal convictions that have put their ability to stay at risk.  They’re asking for pardons in a state where the power of clemency has largely gone unused for decades. Chansareth Hong […]
text:
Chansareth Hong, center, sits on the steps of the Rhode Island State House as advocates call for pardons for him and fellow Cambodian refugee Thorng Chann on Nov. 5, 2026. Both men face possible deportation stemming from decades-old criminal convictions. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)For two Cambodian refugees fighting to remain in the U.S., an extraordinary request made to Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee could help them overcome criminal convictions that have put their ability to stay at risk. 
They’re asking for pardons in a state where the power of clemency has largely gone unused for decades.


What the Rhode Island Constitution says
Article Seven, Section 4 of the first Rhode Island State Constitution in 1842 includes the power of clemency for the executive office: “He shall have power to grant reprieves after conviction, in all cases except those of impeachment, until the end of the next session of the General Assembly.”
Prior to that, researchers at the Rhode Island State Library say it appears the Royal Charter provided the “government of the people” (which included the Governor, Lieutenant Governor and  General Assembly who shared a “common seal”) with the responsibilities “to alter, revoke, annul or pardon, under their common seal, other otherwise, such fines, mulcts, imprisonments, sentences, judgments and condemnations, as shall be thought fit.”


Chansareth Hong and Thorng Chann filed their requests Nov. 2 and 3, seeking relief from convictions dating back roughly 30 years. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said in court filings it intends to deport Hong because of convictions in 1995 and 1997 for possession of heroin with intent to deliver. Chann is also facing deportation over convictions including 1995 possession of cannabis with intent to deliver and a 1997 assault with a dangerous weapon.
Hong came to the United States as an infant in 1976, and Chann arrived at the age of 7 in 1985 as hundreds of thousands fled the aftermath of the Khmer Rouge’s rule in Cambodia. Under the regime, an estimated 1.7 million people were killed through executions, forced labor, starvation and disease between 1975 and 1979. Hong and Chann have spent decades building lives in Providence. 
Now their refugee status has been revoked and they face the prospect of being deported to a country they have never really known.
“I made some serious mistakes as a teen and young adult. Mistakes that resulted in my convictions,” Hong, 50, wrote in his appeal to the governor. “I never could have imagined being at immediate risk for deportation now 29 years later for those same convictions.”
Andrea Palagi, a spokesperson for McKee’s office, confirmed receipt of the pardon requests and told Rhode Island Current the governor’s legal counsel was reviewing them.
“As a reminder, unlike in many other states, granting a pardon in Rhode Island requires the advice and consent of the Senate, which means the Senate must be convened to consider and act on the matter,” Palagi wrote in an email.
Court documents show Hong was scheduled to be removed from the country by ICE by Thursday. But on Tuesday, a Rhode Island federal judge temporarily barred the government from deporting Hong while the court considers his request to reopen his immigration case. 
An ICE spokesperson declined to comment on the ruling, citing pending litigation.
Federal immigration officers took Hong into custody during a July 22 check-in and transferred him to the Donald W. Wyatt Detention Facility. A federal judge ordered his release nearly two weeks later. 
Chann, 49, said he has been advised that he faces an immediate risk of deportation ahead of an ICE check-in scheduled for Nov. 17.
A sign reading “End All Family Separation” rests on the steps of the Rhode Island State House during a Nov. 5, 2026, rally supporting pardon requests from Cambodian refugees Chansareth Hong and Thorng Chann. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
A power rarely used
Rhode Island’s most recent pardon came in 2011, when then-Gov. Lincoln Chafee, an independent, granted clementy to John Gordon, who was hanged in 1845 for the murder of Amasa Sprague. Before that, the only successful pardon the State Library could identify in its review of Providence Journal archives was granted in 1956.
But Rhode Island governors once granted pardons with some regularity. 
A State Archives ledger of state prison discharges records dozens of pardons between the 1860s and 1920, for offenses ranging from murder and manslaughter to obstructing railroads, passing counterfeit U.S. Treasury notes, “mingling poison with drink” and “sending obscene literature by mail.”
Records show at least one pardon request a year was considered by the Rhode Island Senate until around the late 1950s.
Steven Brown, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Rhode Island, said the absence of a formal process for seeking a pardon may help explain why the state has granted so few in recent decades.
“It’s completely open-ended,” he said in an interview.
While the Rhode Island Constitution gives the governor exclusive authority to exercise pardoning power and requires the advice and consent of the Senate, it does not spell out how pardon requests should be evaluated or what standards should guide the decision.
Rep. Cherie Cruz, a Pawtucket Democrat, said she ran into uncertainty when she unsuccessfully tried to seek a pardon for herself around 2010 for a 1993 felony drug conviction. 
She recalled being told to submit a letter of intent and supporting materials, such as letters of recommendation, but said she never received clear instructions on whom to contact or how to move the request forward.
“There was nothing,” Cruz said in an interview.
Which is why Cruz co-sponsored a 2024 bill that would have created a nine-member Commission on Pardons to oversee applications and recommend candidates for clemency to the governor. The commission would have been responsible for establishing eligibility standards, deciding what documents applicants needed to submit, setting timelines for decisions and creating an appeals process.
“We really need to work to get this process transparent and working because it’s not working now,” she said. 
The 2024 proposal failed to advance out of committee during the legislative session. Cruz said she intends to reintroduce the bill after the 2027 legislative session begins in January.
Rhode Island once had a Senate committee devoted specifically to pardons. The standing Senate Committee on Pardons appeared in state government manuals from 1900 through 1968, according to the State Library — though staff found few records documenting its work or explaining why it became inactive.
One glimpse into the panel’s work comes from 1943, when the committee was asked to study ways to allow some people serving lengthy prison sentences to be released sooner. A Providence Journal editorial at the time criticized the proposal, arguing that people convicted of the most serious crimes should not be released after only a few years behind bars.
Sen. Sam Bell, a Providence Democrat who represents Hong’s district, said he hopes a resolution won’t be needed to get the governor to take action.
“I have every expectation the governor’s treating it seriously, giving appropriate vetting,” Bell said in an interview. “I think it’d be a great legacy move for him.”
McKee has already intervened once on Hong’s behalf, writing to ICE in July urging officials not to detain him at a scheduled check-in. Immigration officials detained him anyway.
Hong and Chann both read their requests to the governor aloud inside the State House rotunda on Nov. 5.
Dozens of advocates organized by the Pardons for the People campaign joined the two refugees, chanting to the beat of a lone drum and urging state leaders to consider the clemency requests.
The campaign is led by Providence Youth Student Movement and supported by a coalition that includes the Immigration Coalition of Rhode Island, the Rhode Island Deportation Defense Network, Cambodian Society of Rhode Island, ARISE, Clean Slate Rhode Island and AMOR.
Speaking to advocates after a chamber floor session on Nov. 5, Senate President Valarie Lawson said the Senate was prepared to review the requests, but that the process had to begin with the governor’s office.
A T-shirt calling for an end to the deportation of Chansareth Hong hangs from a railing at the Rhode Island State House on Nov. 5, 2026. Hong is seeking a gubernatorial pardon for decades-old criminal convictions that have put him at risk of deportation to Cambodia. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
A pardon isn’t a shield
For Hong, deportation would mean leaving behind a son who is nonverbal and requires around-the-clock care, as well as his 79-year-old mother who depends on him for housing, transportation and financial support. Chann has four children with his wife and is the parent responsible for much of their daily transportation and activities. 
“My family means everything to me,” Chann wrote in his pardon request to the governor. “I want to be there for my children, watch them grow, and support them. I want to give them a better life and be the father they need.”
A pardon would not automatically stop Hong and Chann’s deportations. But Amy Romero, chief legal counsel for the Lawyers’ Committee for Rhode Island, said it could give their attorneys another way to challenge the removal orders that have kept them at risk of being sent to Cambodia.
Romero said a pardon could provide grounds for asking an immigration court to reopen and vacate an order based on a criminal conviction that has since been pardoned.
“They were kind of complying with their order of supervision,” Romero said of Hong and Chann. “They were checking in, and they were allowed to remain here for decades. But now we have repatriation agreements, and we also have an administration that is very hell-bent on sending people to third countries.”
In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul pardoned a Laotian refugee in July 2025 whose decades-old manslaughter conviction had left him facing deportation. His lawyers said the unconditional pardon blocked his removal and restored his lawful permanent resident status, according to The New York Times.
A different outcome followed in Minnesota. The state’s Board of Pardons unanimously granted a full pardon in June to Tou Lue Vang, a Laotian immigrant convicted of sexually abusing a 10-year-old girl. But federal authorities deported him the following month, despite the pardon.
Hong said in his request to the governor that a pardon could help him remain with his son and mother. If allowed to stay, he hopes to establish a nonprofit teaching young people electrical skills and other life skills to help them find work.
“I will always have remorse for my convictions, and I have spent the rest of my life trying to make it right — by working hard, taking care of my family, my neighborhood, and my community,” Hong wrote.
Chann said a pardon could improve his employment prospects and give his family a better chance of staying together. He wants to be here as his four children grow up and to provide them with the parental support he lacked as a child.
“I have learned from my mistakes,” Chann wrote. “I want to continue being a good father, a responsible person, and a positive part of my community.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Commentary: Gov. Shapiro’s popularity and ‘GSD’ attitude might not cut it in crowded 2028 Democratic field
description: The 2026 midterm elections swept Democrats into office around the country in such numbers that journalists were running out of synonyms for “massive.” In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection by 22 percentage points, winning more than 60% of the vote – something that has been accomplished only twice before in the modern era in […]
text:
Gov. Josh Shapiro, pictured as his Election Day party on Nov. 3, 2026, cruised to victory — but will it be enough for 2028's competitive Democratic presidential primary? (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The 2026 midterm elections swept Democrats into office around the country in such numbers that journalists were running out of synonyms for “massive.”
In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection by 22 percentage points, winning more than 60% of the vote – something that has been accomplished only twice before in the modern era in the Keystone State.
Not only did Shapiro wipe the floor with his opponent Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer, but he also helped flip four U.S. House seats from red to blue. His coattails benefited down-ballot candidates, helping Democrats solidify their control of the state House and flip the state Senate as well.
Shapiro’s political stock in Pennsylvania is riding high.
I’m a political science professor and political media researcher in central Pennsylvania, and many of my former students work in Harrisburg. Some are Democrats working for or around the governor; others are Republicans working in different corners of state government. All are finely tuned to the political gossip that swirls around a successful politician whose star is on the rise. It is the worst-kept secret in American politics that Josh Shapiro wants to be president.
I’ve met the governor a handful of times and can attest to his George Clooney-level charisma. He’s a hard worker, has maintained a remarkably clean political profile, and is from many accounts a genuinely nice dude.
And yet, there are plenty of reasons his ambitions may require some careful timing, regardless of his personal strengths.
A reputation for getting stuff done
Shapiro’s political victories didn’t just happen. Over the past four years, he has worked to demonstrate bipartisan competence as Pennsylvania’s chief executive, adopting an expression he uses frequently: “get sh-t done.”
Now, with Democrats holding the governor’s office and both chambers of the General Assembly, Shapiro told reporters: “We got the power now, the House, the Senate. We have to deliver.”
Shapiro’s approval ratings have remained strong, consistent with his reelection margins. That’s unusual in a state that has swung back and forth between supporting Donald Trump in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024, each time by fewer than 2 percentage points.
If Shapiro is indeed seriously eyeing the White House, his current popularity will certainly serve him well. But winning the presidency is an enormous undertaking, particularly in a crowded field.
Stiff competition in 2028
With Trump unable to run in 2028, the next presidential election will feature open seats for both parties and likely attract many candidates. Democrats, in particular, have a deep bench of attractive potential contenders.
There are so many possibilities that Shapiro could find himself running against people very much like him: younger centrists, swing-state politicians and accomplished elected officials with solid records. Consider just a few names that could be part of the conversation: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel.
Shapiro would have to find a way to distinguish himself in a field filled with candidates who can make many of the same arguments about their experience, political appeal and accomplishments. That’s a tall order. A Plan B might be wise.
Governor Josh Shapiro signs a bell-to-bell cellphone ban into law at Lenape Middle School in Central Bucks School District on Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo from PACast)
Options beyond the White House
Fortunately for Shapiro, other choices abound.
He could run for the Senate in 2028 against incumbent John Fetterman, if Fetterman seeks reelection. This would be a twofer: Shapiro would continue his rise in politics, and he would likely beat a guy he apparently does not like. The two reportedly don’t speak, much less get along.
Shapiro could also position himself for a vice presidential nomination by attaching himself to another 2028 hopeful. This would buy him time to build his national profile, allow the presidential field to sort itself out and potentially put him in a strong position for another run at the White House down the road. It would also give him an opportunity to demonstrate that he can work effectively on a national stage.
Or he could angle for a Cabinet post. The federal government has undergone significant restructuring under DOGE and Trump’s executive orders. Should a Democrat win the White House in 2028, rebuilding federal agencies and restoring institutional capacity will be a monumental undertaking. Shapiro could be an attractive candidate for a major administrative role.
The bottom line for Shapiro is that he will need to distinguish himself from a crowded field of Democrats by emphasizing his statewide victories in a major swing state, impressive fundraising ability and a political voice that can evoke Barack Obama without alienating either his party or the broader electorate. That’s a tricky feat, even for the most talented politicians.
But Nov. 3, 2026, showed us that he knows how to make sh-t happen. Whatever he decides, the next two years will be important for Shapiro, consequential for Democrats, and fascinating for political scientists like me, who will be watching events unfold with a keen eye and, probably, a bucket of popcorn.
Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania, or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack.
Alison Dagnes, Professor of Political & Social Inquiry, Shippensburg University

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Scout Motors’ SC factory is 85% complete and first test vehicles are rolling off the line
description: EV-maker Scout Motors has started its transition from building a factory to building vehicles in South Carolina.
text:
Covered by a sheet, one of Scout Motors' first test SUVs undergoes testing for wheel and headlight alignments Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at the nearly complete electric vehicle assembly plant in Blythewood. It marks one of 30 test vehicles to be assembled this year at the plant, with more planned for early 2027. This vehicle is not a finished product that will be sold to customers in 2028. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)BLYTHEWOOD — South Carolina-based electric vehicle maker Scout Motors has started its transition from building a factory to building vehicles, with plans to hire a few hundred more assembly line workers over the course of the next year.
The Volkswagen subsidiary is nearly finished putting together its first round of 30 to 40 test vehicles and will begin a second round of testing in early 2027, CEO Scott Keogh said Thursday, following a tour of the nearly complete $2 billion assembly plant in Blythewood.
One of the assembly lines Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at the nearly complete Scout Motors electric vehicle assembly plant in Blythewood. The assembly shop is the final building in need of completion at the plant. At full capacity, 2,000 assembly workers will build about 40 Scouts per hour. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)The view from inside one of the glass paint booths Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at Scout Motor's nearly complete electric vehicle assembly plant in Blythewood. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
“This is the very first prototype, the prototype that’s working its way out to America to get the software installed, start going on roads, and testing and validating things like durability, things like safety, and all of the electronic hardware,” Keogh said.
Testing will continue in phases throughout 2027. The first vehicles are now expected to hit the market in 2028.

At full capacity, Scout plans to produce 200,000 vehicles annually. That will include a mix of fully electric and hybrid-like models.
Some 212,000 people have already signed up and paid the deposit to buy the first Scouts that roll off the line, Keogh said. Most of those are asking for the Scout Traveler SUV and 95% want the combination gas and electric option.
Today, Scout employs upwards of 18,000 workers across its three locations — the Blythewood assembly plant, corporate headquarters in Charlotte and an engineering and design center in Michigan.
Of those employees, 900 work in South Carolina: 600 in engineering and management and 300 factory workers.
That South Carolina number will grow to 4,000 workers when the assembly plant reaches full capacity.
Meanwhile, German-headquartered Volkswagen, the financiers of the Scout project, and Swedish automaker Volvo, which has an assembly plant in the Lowcountry, are both struggling financially.
Volvo posted larger-than-expected operating losses last month and Volkswagen’s profit margin fell to its lowest in at least a decade, as both face joint headwinds from increased competition in China — the world’s largest electric vehicle market — and global tariffs increasing the cost of vehicles in the U.S.
“We are not in a naive position. We quite know the automotive dynamics are tough and you have to compete,” Keogh said.
But unlike Volvo’s Ridgeville plant, which is operating at less than 20% of its capacity as it shifts from building electric vehicles for export to building them for the U.S. market, Keogh said Scout won’t need to be at full capacity — or even 80% capacity — before it expects to start turning a profit.

And unlike other startup electric vehicle brands, such as Rivian, Scout benefits from the cost savings that come with tapping into Volkswagen’s bulk buying power.
While Keogh declined to name the capacity percentage the factory needs to reach before its profitable, he said “we can make money at dramatically less volume.”
Scout did face a recent setback in its plans to sell its vehicles directly to consumers, similar to Tesla, rather than through the traditional dealership network.
Tennessee, this month, denied the company a license, and legislation allowing direct sales in South Carolina stalled in a House committee in February 2025. The bill officially died earlier this year with the end of the legislative session. To renew the effort, the bill would need to be reintroduced next year.
Laws governing direct sales vary by state — 18 expressly allow it and 17 expressly ban it, with the rest falling somewhere in between, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Still, Scout is confident it can still reach all buyers, even if customers have to cross state lines to test drive them and have them shipped at a later date.
One of about 900 robots, pictured Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, inside the body shop of the Scout Motors electric vehicle assembly plant in Blythewood. The robots work in teams to put together the parts making up the vehicles frame, with a new frame moving between each station every 90 seconds. Between 150 to 180 workers also will work alongside the robots in this shop, largely loading parts into the machines. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Black voting advocates in the South say the midterm surge was not just a ‘blue wave’
description: States across the Deep South, a region steeped in a legacy of racially-based voter suppression, reported high and in some cases historic Black voter turnout for the Nov. 3 election, contributing to the Democratic takeover of the next Congress. But advocates who worked to ensure all voices were heard on Election Day say this strong […]
text:
Election commissioners check the identification of a voter at the BREC Church Street Park polling location in Zachary on Tuesday, Nov. 6, 2026. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)States across the Deep South, a region steeped in a legacy of racially-based voter suppression, reported high and in some cases historic Black voter turnout for the Nov. 3 election, contributing to the Democratic takeover of the next Congress.
But advocates who worked to ensure all voices were heard on Election Day say this strong showing should not only be labeled as part of the “blue wave.” Rather, they see it as the fruit of a decades-long effort to boost Black voter access.
“If your analysis on what happened Tuesday is that this is a mandate against Trump, I think it’s a bit lazy. Dig deeper,” said Charles Taylor, executive director of the Mississippi NAACP. “… Because this is not just about Trump. This is about years in the making.”
Taylor and four other voting rights activists from the South spoke with reporters in a video conference Thursday, a day after the Associated Press declared Democrat Scott Colom the winner of Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race over Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. 
Colom will be the state’s first Black U.S. senator since the Reconstruction era.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Black voters cast 33% of Mississippi’s ballots on Nov. 3, up from 30% in the 2024 presidential election, according to New York Times estimates. Colom’s narrow victory over Hyde-Smith came in a state President Donald Trump won by 24 points two years ago.
His win also comes after Mississippi election officials, just days before the election, declared more than 230,000 voters inactive after Secretary of State Michael Watson used questionable Experian credit rating data to vet voters’ addresses.
In North Carolina, 23 of its 100 counties eliminated early voting on Sundays for this election cycle. Chris Shenton, senior counsel for the Southern Coalition of Social Justice, said this was a direct tactic from elections officials to lower Black voter participation, as many churches in the state organize “Souls to the Polls” events to bring people to early voting locations.
“You see all sorts of tools, mechanisms, old poison in new bottles being used to suppress Black turnout,” Shenton said. “ … Despite that, black voters increased their share of early voting turnout in the state.”
Democrats in North Carolina flipped four U.S. House seats and will represent nine of the state’s 14 districts, including five that had been drawn to favor Republicans.
Official data reflecting voter turnout in North Carolina through Nov. 3 have not been made available, but Black voters outpaced the white counterparts 39% to 36% in the early voting period, according to an analysis from Shenton’s organization.
Louisiana also reported record turnout among Black voters during early voting, making up 33% of participants. Their showing resulted in a tighter-than-expected U.S. Senate race, in which Black Democrat Jamie Davis finished less than 2 percentage points behind Rep. Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge.
Ashley Shelton, founder and CEO/president of the Power Coalition for Equity and Justice, said she believes voters looked past party affiliation throughout the South to propel their preferred candidates to wins. 
“Voters went out and voted for their families, for their communities and themselves,” Shelton said. “They did not go hit an R-button or a D-button. They picked the candidate that was going to give them the best opportunity at a better life.”
Jace Woodrum, executive director of the South Carolina ACLU, said the Election Day results in his state reflect years of frustration from Black voters. Earlier this year, they fought to block an attempt from Republicans to take away one of the state’s two majority-Black U.S. House districts out of its seven seats.   
“Black voters were still pissed off and still turned out,” Woodrum said. “I do think (Republicans) will be dissuaded because I think they have seen what will happen when you threaten our democracy. These are the voting rights that people have been fighting for for generations, and voters are standing up and saying, “We’re not going to let you keep chipping away at this.” 
South Carolina reported its highest Black voter turnout for a midterm election, with a 29% increase from 2022. It contributed to Democrat Annie Andrews’ U.S. Senate win over Trump-endorsed Republican candidate Darline Graham, who was an interim replacement for her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham. 
Rep. Joe Wilson, South Carolina’s longest-serving Republican in Congress, narrowly avoided an upset, winning by less than a percentage point over Democrat Zyon Khalifa, a 25-year-old Southern University law school graduate. 
Democrats also flipped 10 seats in the South Carolina House of Representatives, ending the GOP’s supermajority in the chamber.
Alabama gained a Democrat in Congress through redistricting, only after a U.S. Supreme Court decision forced legislators to add a second majority-Black seat, which Shomari Figures won. Voters also flipped four seats in the Alabama Legislature to Democrats and elected their first transgender state lawmaker, though Republicans still hold supermajorities.
Anneshia Hardy, executive director of the civic engagement group Alabama Values, said Figures’ victory should not be seen solely as a triumph for Black voters through redistricting.     
“We weren’t fighting for permission to participate in somebody else’s democracy,” she said. “We were fighting for the right to exercise collective power in a country that our ancestors helped build but whose institutions have repeatedly tried to deny us that power, and that struggle doesn’t disappear because of an election victory.”
The Black voting surge for the midterms should also not be labeled as retaliation for the Supreme Court’s Callais decision, which gutted a key part of the 1965 Voting Rights Act, or other measures that have diluted minority voting strength, Hardy said. Reducing Black political participation to simply backlash overlooks generations of political organizing and action, she added.     
“This moment is bigger than a blue wave,” Hardy said. “It’s bigger than any political party because a democracy that cannot protect Black political power cannot claim to have resolved the question of equal representation, and that is why this struggle should matter to every person in this country.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Detroit residents urge delay as city council advances RenCen redevelopment agreement
description: DETROIT – City council members advanced an agreement between developers and residents tied to a $2.2 billion plan to transform Detroit’s Renaissance Center and surrounding East Riverfront into a residential and entertainment district.  In a 3-2 vote, the City Council’s Planning and Economic Development Committee voted to send the community benefits agreement[...]
text:
Teron Haynes Jr. was amongst the protestors demanding that the city council delay its Nov. 12, 2026, vote on the $43.5 million community benefits agreement. He is the only member of the NAC who didn't approve the agreement. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)DETROIT – City council members advanced an agreement between developers and residents tied to a $2.2 billion plan to transform Detroit’s Renaissance Center and surrounding East Riverfront into a residential and entertainment district. 
In a 3-2 vote, the City Council’s Planning and Economic Development Committee voted to send the community benefits agreement to the full council without a recommendation.
Committee Chair Latisha Johnson said sending the agreement to the full council would allow members to raise additional questions and concerns during a public discussion.
“If we determine that we’re not ready to move forward, then we know how to address that in the committee of the whole,” Johnson said. 
Councilmember Gabriela Santiago-Romero opposed advancing the agreement, saying she wanted more time to review the proposal and ensure questions raised by council members and residents are answered.
“People don’t move to cities for their downtowns. They move to cities because of their transportation, their neighborhoods, their culture, their people, all of that,” Santiago-Romero said. “That’s what I’m trying to make sure that we have at the forefront here and this does feel very, very rushed.” 
Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield joined members of the project’s nine-member Neighborhood Advisory Council at a press conference on Nov. 5, where they signed the CBA, which dedicates $15 million to housing, $10 million to small businesses, $8 million to a community hub, $6 million to workforce development and education, and $4.5 million to parking, totaling $43.5 million. 
Developers also pledged an additional $90 million in voluntary payments in lieu of taxes or “PILOT” payments over 30 years, bringing the total announced commitments to $133.5 million.
Dozens of residents, community organizers and business owners urged the city council to delay its vote on the community benefits agreement and give the community more time to provide input. 
“There are things that we have asked for over the last 10 weeks and all of a sudden they have disappeared out of the CBA,” said Nicole Small, of Save the RenCen, during a rally outside of the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center Thursday morning.  “This is not a community benefits agreement, this is a developer benefits agreement. The mayor should be outraged. City Council should be outraged and the people of Detroit should definitely be outraged,” Small said. 
Protestors chanted “Whose riverfront? Our riverfront!” during a rally outside of the Coleman A. Young Municipal center on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)
The agreement is part of the city’s Community Benefits Ordinance, which requires developers of large-scale projects to engage residents who could be affected by the development. The Neighborhood Advisory Council is responsible for representing residents throughout that process. Its nine members include three City Council appointees, four appointees from the city’s Planning and Development Department and two elected neighborhood representatives.
Still, some residents felt that they were left out of the process, especially after released text messages between council members showed they agreed not to make public the recordings or transcripts from closed negotiations with developers, at least until after the council voted to approve the CBA. 
“We got two months of public input on this process for a project that’s about to exist for the next 50 years,” said Jeremiah Wheeler of Detroit Action during the rally. “The money is coming from all around the city but the benefits are not going all around the city. The benefits are limited to … downtown and that’s not acceptable,” Wheeler said.
Not every member of the NAC is in support of the agreement. Teron Haynes Jr. was the only council member who didn’t sign the CBA. 
“Those buildings don’t look obsolete to me. They’re standing and I’m not waiting for them to collapse,” Haynes said during the rally, pointing to the Renaissance Center. “We shouldn’t be waiting for Detroit to collapse either but that’s what’s going to happen if we keep giving billionaires this money and not investing into the community.” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The agreement follows weeks of negotiations between the council and developers Bedrock Detroit and General Motors. During Thursday’s committee meeting, officials described it as the largest community benefits agreement in Detroit’s history.
“We have community benefits in the agreement but the reason why I voted no was because I did not think that the benefits were substantial enough for, what we are giving to these developers but also what people in Detroit … have missed out on in the past decade as far as community development and investment,” Haynes told the Michigan Advance. 
The project calls for the demolition of two of the complex’s five towers, with plans to convert the remaining three into 934 mixed-income housing units and office space. Additional plans include a marina, an observation deck and 18 acres of proposed civic space across the broader 46-acre development site.
Bedrock and GM are expected to invest more than $1.6 billion in the project, while the Downtown Development Authority will contribute $75 million. The remaining $505 million is expected to come through debt.
Developers are also seeking more than $473 million in tax breaks over 30 years. Additional commercial tax incentives would bring the total requested subsidies to approximately $548 million.
If approved by Detroit City Council, demolition work is expected to begin next summer. The project is expected to take at least 10 years to complete. City Council members are aiming to approve the plan before Thanksgiving, when the council will go on recess until next year. 
Billionaire Dan Gilbert, who founded Bedrock, pledged an additional $1 billion to establish a new nonprofit organization dedicated to redeveloping and operating the Renaissance Center and East Riverfront.
Despite the donation, protesters said they would rather the new development be publicly owned and that there be more investment into developing housing throughout the city instead of downtown. 
“If the word philanthropy meant anything, then he (Dan Gilbert) would pay property taxes,” said Russ Bellant, of Detroiters for Tax Justice during Thursday morning’s protest. “Why isn’t he using those tax benefits that he’s looting from us … for an investment instead of coming back to us and saying, ‘Let me screw you for another half a billion dollars.’”
Bedrock is the largest private property owner in Detroit, operating roughly 100 properties, most of them in the downtown area. 
Dozens of community leaders, advocates and residents spoke during public comment at Thursday’s Planning and Economic Development Committee meeting, with many urging council members to delay the proposed Renaissance Center redevelopment and give the community more time to weigh in on the project. Despite commenters being limited to 45 seconds, the meeting lasted more than five hours. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)
The redevelopment has drawn both support and concern from residents. Some question whether the project represents another major investment in downtown Detroit while neighborhoods elsewhere in the city continue to grapple with vacant lots and deteriorating homes.
Another major concern, especially early in the community benefits process, was that the estimated area of impact was too small and did not include residents in surrounding areas. The Renaissance Center, located along Woodward Avenue in the city’s downtown area, is in District 5. Developers estimate that nearly 4,700 residents live in the impacted area.
“The NAC should have considered bus riders who use Jefferson as a route. If this project goes through without any consideration, it would jeopardize access to jobs, access to city and county services and transit connections across Detroit and our county,” said Renard Munchinski, an organizer with Detroit People’s Platform, during virtual public comment at Thursday’s committee meeting. 
Supporters view the development as an investment in Detroit’s future. 
“In TechTown we see every day that local entrepreneurs don’t lack talent. They lack affordable storefronts, capital and coaching and this CBA delivers all three,” said Ned Staebler, President and CEO of TechTown.
Ryan Sullivan, CEO of the Detroit Riverfront Conservancy also spoke in support of the project and urged the committee to pass the agreement. 
The project marks a significant turning point for one of Detroit’s most recognizable landmarks.
The Renaissance Center opened in 1977, featuring a 73-story central hotel tower surrounded by four office towers. Two additional office towers opened in 1981. General Motors purchased the entire complex in 1996 for $73 million and established its global corporate headquarters there.
But as hybrid work schedules became more common following the COVID-19 pandemic and office occupancy declined, GM announced in 2024 that it would relocate its global headquarters to Hudson’s Detroit, another Bedrock development. The 49-story skyscraper was also developed by the Detroit-based real estate firm, owned by billionaire Dan Gilbert.
GM’s planned departure raised questions about the future of the Renaissance Center. Now, those questions have evolved into a multibillion-dollar redevelopment proposal that could reshape Detroit’s riverfront for decades.

name: National
title: This time, rural voters ‘just weren’t there’ for the GOP
description: LAMPASAS, Texas — Standing at the edge of his family’s 300-acre cattle ranch in Central Texas, Clayton Tucker is characteristically attired in a white Stetson western hat, a beige shirt with pearl snaps, and lightly faded Wrangler jeans. At 35, Tucker is poised to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to serve […]
text:
Clayton Tucker, elected last week as Texas agriculture commissioner, poses at his ranch in Lampasas, Texas. Tucker is the first Democrat in more than three decades to hold the position. Across the country, rural voters — staunchly Republican in recent decades — either defected to Democrats or stayed home. (Photo by David Montgomery/Stateline)LAMPASAS, Texas — Standing at the edge of his family’s 300-acre cattle ranch in Central Texas, Clayton Tucker is characteristically attired in a white Stetson western hat, a beige shirt with pearl snaps, and lightly faded Wrangler jeans.
At 35, Tucker is poised to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to serve as Texas agriculture commissioner, a post from which he will oversee policies affecting much of rural Texas. The last Democrat to serve as agriculture commissioner left office in January of 1991— a month before Tucker was born.
Tucker, who takes office in January, benefitted from the Democratic wave that swept across Texas and other states in the midterm elections, propelled by widespread disenchantment with Republican policies, both in the cities and on the farm.
Across the country, rural voters — staunchly Republican in recent decades — either defected to Democrats or stayed home to protest the spread of data centers, rising fuel prices, the war in Iran and other grievances.
In Texas, about 90% of the counties where turnout decreased were rural, according to The Texas Tribune. While many rural voters stayed faithful to GOP candidates, their diminished numbers at the polls helped clear the way for Democratic victories: In the state’s U.S. Senate race, the Democrats improved their performance in all 254 Texas counties, compared with the 2024 U.S. Senate contest.
“People felt like they were being treated as sacrificial lambs for Wall Street, for Silicon Valley, for all these tech bros and oligarchs and everyone else,” Tucker said in an interview behind the steering wheel of his parked 1982 GMC pickup truck, “and they just weren’t being supported by our government anymore.”
Rural disenchantment also helped drive epic Democratic victories in other states.
In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton was elected to the U.S. Senate, the first Kansas Democrat to win a Senate seat since 1932. Analysts attributed Hamilton’s victory to a rural backlash over high fuel and fertilizer prices and cheap imported beef. In Montana, former smoke-jumper Sam Forstag flipped one of the state’s two congressional seats, becoming the first Montana Democrat to win a U.S. House seat since 1994.
Partisan control also shifted in Iowa, where agriculture-related jobs employ roughly 1 in 5 residents. Iowa Democrats won the governor’s race, a U.S. Senate seat and three of the state’s four congressional seats. Republicans maintained their grip on both chambers of the state legislature, but Democrats narrowed the gap.
Iowa Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson won just over half of rural and small-town voters in her unsuccessful bid for one of Iowa’s U.S. Senate seats, according to The Associated Press. But that was a smaller percentage of rural and small-town voters than the GOP got in 2022, and the diminished margin helped secure a victory for Democratic candidate Josh Turek.
“It was a setback for Republicans and now they have to figure out how they’re going to get back some of the voters they probably lost,” said Abhishek Chatterjee, an associate professor of political science at the University of Montana.
Texas the epicenter
Texas, the nation’s second-largest state, was an epicenter of the midterm upheaval. Voters there turned against three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott to choose state Rep. Gina Hinojosa as the state’s first Latina governor and the first Democrat to hold the office since Ann Richards left in 1995.
Texas voters also elected Democratic state Rep. James Talarico to the U.S. Senate and placed Democrats, including Tucker, in all of the top statewide offices. Democrats also took over the Texas House, which has been controlled by Republicans since 2003.
Republicans still hold the majority in the Texas Senate and are considering rule changes to undercut the power of incoming presiding officer Vikki Goodwin, a Democratic legislator who defeated incumbent Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick for the state’s number two post, which includes leadership of the legislature’s upper chamber.
Young, diverse voters showed up for midterms as older, Trump voters stayed home

In the aftermath of what she called a “nationwide Republican defeat,” Texas Republican Party Chair D’rinda Randall announced the formation of an invitation-only Texas Mandate Committee composed of statewide leaders charged with “examining what occurred and developing a strategy to win Texas back.”
“This is not about placing blame,” she said in a statement. “It is about planning to win.”
Kendall Scudder, chair of the Texas Democratic Party as well as the Democratic National Committee’s Rural Council, told Stateline that his party’s Texas triumph resulted in part from a concentrated campaign that included a heavy focus on rural Texas.
“What I think happened was folks in rural Texas gave Democrats an opportunity to state our case, and we hadn’t had that in while,” said Scudder, who grew up in Sulphur Springs in largely rural East Texas.
“I think we started making inroads, and part of that could be because Republicans weren’t worth showing up and voting for. But I think another piece is that Democrats were talking about things that were important to rural Texas.”
Top issues that resonated strongly in rural Texas, he said, included the spread of data centers, “mass surveillance” by mounted Flock cameras that read license plates, and inadequate funding for state schools. As result, he said, 21 largely rural counties that voted red in previous elections “went blue this time.”
“I think we moved the needle in a good way, and I think if Democrats deliver for those communities, we can start to unlock more and more gains,” he said.
Outgoing Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller, a Republican who lost his primary race for re-election, echoed Tucker and Scudder’s assertions that rural voters are up in arms over data centers, artificial intelligence, Flock cameras, and soaring fuel prices. Tucker says he will push for a moratorium on data centers after he takes office in January.
“We’ve never had any real property tax relief,” Miller said in a phone interview “Diesel’s the highest it’s ever been. Fertilizer’s the highest it’s ever been. I don’t think the Democrats took anything away from the Republicans,” Miller said, “we basically gave it to them.”
Miller put much of the blame for rural dissension on Abbott’s policies.  Abbott endorsed Miller’s Republican primary opponent, Nate Sheets, who in turn was beaten by Tucker in the general election.
A $1 billion publicly funded private school voucher program that Abbott pushed through the Texas Legislature in 2025 also stirred dissent in parts of rural Texas, amid fears that it will siphon money from public schools.
Voters across the country reject data centers

“There was a lot of hard feelings about the voucher program out there,” said Snapper Carr of Austin, a managing partner and general counsel of Focused Advocacy, a lobbying firm that represents cities and communities throughout the state. The Republican downturn, he said, was particularly evident in what he said are typically “bright red areas of West Texas,” where residents “talk about the price of diesel like we all talk about the weather.”
“The Republicans still carried them,” he said, “but their margins were much less than what they’ve been in the past…There was a large number of past Republicans that didn’t show up this time.”
‘Totally surprised’
In Briggs, an unincorporated Central Texas community with around 100 residents, Ray Bizzell, 83, offered his thoughts on the election outcome as he left Sunday’s services at the Briggs Baptist Church. Bizzell, who runs a floor covering business about 20 miles away in Georgetown, Texas, said he voted “Republican, straight ticket” and “was totally surprised” by Democrats’ strong showing in the state.
“I really thought we might hold it,” he said. “I just think my beliefs align better with the Republican Party.”
In Williamson County, which stretches from the high-growth Austin suburbs to patches of rural Texas further east, the unexpected Democratic surge propelled first-time candidate Chris Jimenez, 42, into a state legislative victory over a Republican incumbent backed the governor.
In this year’s U.S. Senate race, Williamson County swung nearly 19 points toward the Democrats compared with the Senate race in 2024, according to The Associated Press.
Jimenez, who lives on a pecan farm with his wife and 16-year-old daughter near the town of Elgin, is headed to the statehouse after defeating Republican state Rep. Caroline Harris Davila for the House seat once held by Talarico. Jimenez’s opponent was endorsed by Abbott.
Jimenez grew up on a ranch near Sanderson and served in the Marine Corps. He said his thoughts of running for office intensified after he was “pulled over and profiled by a police officer,” he told Stateline. “I was very concerned on multiple levels. I  figured, ‘Hey, if this is happening to me, a Marine Corps veteran just trying to make my life here on the farm, it’s got to be happening to multiple people.’”
“Did I expect to win? I felt our message resonated with people, regardless of their political affiliation,” he said. “It was never about being red or blue.  It was about survival in Texas and it’s gotten hard for a lot of folks.”
Democrats romped in state elections. What will they do with their newfound power?

Jimenez has joined other incoming lawmakers in pre-filing bills before the January start of the legislature. His measure call for repealing “the private school voucher scheme,” eliminating a sales tax exemption for data centers and expanding Medicaid benefits in Texas.
Republican data analyst Derek Ryan said Republicans needed to win by “a very large margin” in rural counties to counter strong turnout in predominately Democratic urban areas.  The GOP only had 32-point advantage in those counties in this year’s mid-term elections,  he said, compared to 55 points in 2022 and 46 points in 2018.
Ryan estimated that about 625,000 Republicans sat out the election, according to the Texas Rural Report.
“We knew there was going to be a slight shift towards the Democrats in rural Texas,” Ryan told Stateline. “I didn’t think it was going to be this significant, but it comes down to the economy and gas prices.
“When you live in rural Texas, it’s a long drive anywhere you go. So when it’s costing you more to fill up your tank, you know you’re going to vote with that in mind.”
Suzanne Bellsnyder, who owns and runs a newspaper in the small town of Spearman near the Oklahoma state line, said she has analyzed all 184 Texas counties with a population under 50,000 and found signs of Republican slippage in areas that have typically served as Republican bulwarks.
“Republicans have always depended on the rural counties to kind of be their firewall, their insurance policy,” she said. But this time, she added, “they just weren’t there.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Engineers give Indiana infrastructure a D+ amid warnings of aging systems, funding gaps
description: Indiana’s roads and bridges are holding up better than those in much of the country, but aging water systems, deteriorating dams and mounting pressure on the state’s electric grid have earned its overall infrastructure a D+ in a new assessment released Thursday. The 2026 Report Card for Indiana’s Infrastructure, prepared by the American Society of […]
text:
Indiana Secretary of Transportation and Infrastructure Matthew Ubelhor speaks Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at the Indiana Statehouse during the release of a new infrastructure report card. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana’s roads and bridges are holding up better than those in much of the country, but aging water systems, deteriorating dams and mounting pressure on the state’s electric grid have earned its overall infrastructure a D+ in a new assessment released Thursday.
The 2026 Report Card for Indiana’s Infrastructure, prepared by the American Society of Civil Engineers, found that years of transportation investments have helped preserve highways and bridges. But engineers warned that billions of dollars in needed repairs, increasingly severe weather and growing demand for electricity are threatening other critical systems.
The findings also raise concerns about how Indiana will pay for future improvements as federal infrastructure funding winds down and the state’s suspension of gasoline taxes creates additional uncertainty for road construction and maintenance.
The D+ grade falls below the C assigned to the nation’s infrastructure in 2025. The national assessment, however, covers 18 infrastructure categories, compared with seven evaluated in Indiana.
Engineers presented the findings Thursday at the Indiana Statehouse, joined by state transportation officials, as well as representatives from U.S. Sen. Todd Young’s office and Indiana American Water.
Story continues below.
2026-indiana-report-card-full
 
The report examined seven areas: bridges, dams, drinking water, energy, roads, stormwater and wastewater.
Bridges earned the highest grade, a B-, followed by roads and drinking water at C-. Dams, energy and stormwater received D grades, while wastewater received a D+.
The analysis says D means poor and at risk.
“A ‘D+’ grade is a reminder of the importance of Indiana’s infrastructure and the successes in some areas and challenges other sectors face in the future,” said James Tradup, a report card co-chair. “This report card shows the positive impact investment has sparked in some sectors, while a reminder of where additional funds are needed to improve these systems every Hoosier depends on.”
The assessment is the first state-specific infrastructure report card published by the engineering group for Indiana. Engineers said they evaluated infrastructure conditions, capacity, funding, future needs, maintenance, public safety, resilience and innovation.
The report notes that while Indiana has benefited from more than $9 billion in federal infrastructure investments under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, those resources are temporary — and the engineers said sustained funding will be critical for preventing infrastructure from deteriorating.
Roads and bridges outperform, but funding questions remain
Transportation was among Indiana’s strongest areas in the report card, following years of state investment and efforts meant to maintain existing infrastructure before major repairs or replacements become necessary.
About 95% of Indiana’s more than 19,500 bridges are in fair or good condition, according to the report. State-owned bridges generally fare better than those maintained by counties, cities and towns.
Just 1% of state-owned bridges are rated poor, compared with 7% of bridges owned by other agencies.
Still, the report identified a substantial funding gap for locally maintained bridges.
Engineers estimated that local bridges need approximately $580 million annually to reach a state of good repair, but receive only about $67 million, leaving a $513 million annual shortfall.

Local roads face similar challenges. While the state’s major highways are generally in relatively good condition, nearly one-third of city, town and county roads are rated poor.
The report estimates that deferred roadway maintenance costs Indiana motorists $1.6 billion annually through additional vehicle repairs, fuel consumption and depreciation.
Funding is another concern.
The engineers warned that the ongoing suspension of Indiana’s gasoline taxes threatens a major revenue source for transportation improvements at a time when aging infrastructure already requires significant investment.
Indiana Secretary of Transportation and Infrastructure Matthew Ubelhor, who spoke at Thursday’s announcement on behalf of Gov. Mike Braun, said the extended suspension is expected to create a roughly $1.1 billion funding shortfall.
He said the administration intends to use available reserves to keep planned transportation work moving, including projects and maintenance scheduled for fiscal year 2027. Lawmakers will have to make that happen, though.
Ubelhor said no projects have been removed from the state’s construction schedule because of the funding uncertainty.
“We are not taking one project off,” Ubelhor said, emphasizing that Braun has insisted the state’s planned construction and maintenance work continue despite the revenue losses.
He also acknowledged that Indiana will need to identify a sustainable source of transportation revenue in the longer term, particularly as fuel efficiency improves and more electric vehicles enter the market.
“We need to look at that yesterday,” Ubelhor said of finding alternatives to the gasoline tax, which he indicated will become a less dependable source of revenue as vehicle technology changes.
The administration is examining possible alternatives, including tolling, although Ubelhor said questions remain about the potential approach and federal approvals.
He said the state is still awaiting a federal waiver decision related to a proposed I-70 reconstruction and rehabilitation program.
The report’s recommendations include expanding programs such as Community Crossings, providing local governments with additional revenue options and establishing more predictable long-term transportation funding.
Billions needed for drinking water, sewer systems
Some of Indiana’s largest infrastructure challenges are underground.
The report estimates that Indiana needs more than $8 billion in drinking water improvements and more than $10 billion for wastewater infrastructure.
Those needs include replacing aging water mains, removing lead service lines, addressing emerging contaminants such as PFAS, upgrading treatment plants and repairing deteriorating sewer systems.
Much of the funding for drinking water systems comes from customers’ utility bills, which must also cover daily operations. That leaves utilities facing difficult decisions about how to finance major improvements without making water service unaffordable.
Indiana’s wastewater systems face similar pressure.
Americans’ water bills are growing faster than groceries, overall inflation

More than 4 million Hoosiers rely on municipal wastewater systems, many of which are approaching the end of their intended service lives.
In 2024, communities sought more than $2 billion in wastewater funding, but only about $300 million was available statewide, according to the engineers’ assessment.
Stormwater infrastructure also faces growing challenges as heavy rainfall overwhelms drainage systems built decades ago.
The report estimates $531 million in stormwater infrastructure needs, with available funding covering only a small share.
Engineers recommended expanding state revolving loan programs, pursuing additional federal grants, encouraging partnerships among utilities and investing in flood-management improvements.
Matthew Hobbs, senior director of engineering for Indiana American Water, said Thursday that the utility plans to invest more than $1 billion in water and wastewater infrastructure across Indiana over the next five years.
The company serves approximately 1.5 million Hoosiers in more than 75 communities.
“Water infrastructure is fundamental to public health, fire protection, economic development and quality of life,” Hobbs said. “Maintaining that infrastructure requires consistent, long-term investment — not simply responding when something breaks.”
Hobbs pointed to a new $60 million water treatment plant in Seymour, expected to enter service this month, as an example of the investments underway.
He emphasized that replacing aging infrastructure before it fails can help prevent emergencies and reduce long-term costs.
“Proactive investment is also more efficient than waiting for infrastructure [to] fail,” Hobbs said, adding that replacing aging equipment and pipelines before emergencies occur can reduce service disruptions and costly repairs.
But he also said affordability must remain central to decisions about future upgrades.
“Infrastructure investments and affordability cannot be viewed as competing priorities,” Hobbs said. “We have to do both.”
Data centers add pressure to Indiana’s electric grid
Indiana’s energy infrastructure earned a D. Engineers noted increased electricity demand rises, aging coal-fired power plants near retirement and higher utility bills for Hoosiers. They warned that the state’s power grid will need significant upgrades to keep pace with growing demand while maintaining reliable service.
One of the biggest concerns is the growth of data centers.
The report projects that data centers could account for approximately 41% of Indiana’s electricity consumption by 2030, dramatically increasing demand on a grid already facing major changes.
At the same time, coal-fired power plants are approaching retirement, requiring utilities to replace generation capacity while maintaining reliable service.
The engineers also pointed to growing electricity costs for households.
Tradup said the projected growth of data centers is a major driver of future electricity demand, alongside the retirement of existing power plants and rising costs for customers.
Residential energy costs increased by more than $28 per month between 2024 and 2025, according to the report, prompting an investigation by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission.
Severe storms present additional risks to transmission and distribution systems, potentially leaving homes and businesses without power.
Engineers recommended investing in transmission infrastructure, modernizing the electric grid, expanding energy storage and diversifying power generation sources.
Jessica Eichhorst, with ASCE Indiana, said growing demand from data centers, industrial development and electrification will require investments in transmission infrastructure and grid modernization.
She also emphasized the need to diversify electricity generation and improve the system’s ability to withstand disruptions.
The report further outlined workforce shortages as a concern across infrastructure sectors, with retirements, competition for skilled workers and limited training pipelines making it harder to maintain and operate increasingly complex systems.
Aging dams raise safety concerns
Indiana’s dams were another area of concern, earning a D.
The state has 1,641 regulated dams, nearly two-thirds of which are privately owned.
