Of those, 278 are classified as high-hazard dams, meaning their failure could result in loss of life or significant property damage. The designation reflects the potential consequences of a failure, not necessarily a dam’s current condition.
Only 55% of Indiana’s high-hazard dams have emergency action plans, compared with a national rate of 83%, according to the report.
State-owned dams also have a maintenance backlog exceeding $80 million.
The engineers warned that many dams are approaching or have exceeded their original design lives, while private owners often lack access to financial assistance for expensive repairs.
Indiana does not have a dedicated loan or grant program to help rehabilitate privately owned dams, according to the assessment.
The report recommends expanding rehabilitation funding, increasing inspections and prioritizing structures that present the greatest potential risks to public safety.
Engineers call for long-term planning
Beyond individual infrastructure categories, the report emphasizes that Indiana’s challenges can’t be addressed just with short-term spending.
Its six broad recommendations include:

more dedicated local transportation funding;
faster modernization of water and wastewater systems;
stronger flood protection;
electric grid improvements;
dam rehabilitation; and
more coordinated infrastructure planning.

The engineers also urged policymakers to account for changing weather patterns and future demand when designing projects, rather than relying on conditions that existed when much of the state’s infrastructure was originally built.
Even so, the funding question extends beyond Indiana.
The federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act provided billions of dollars for projects across the state, but its authorization expired Sept. 30. Congress has not yet approved a comparable long-term replacement.
ASCE representatives said Thursday that they plan to take the report’s findings to Washington in March 2027 as federal lawmakers consider future infrastructure legislation.
Jennifer Sharkey, an Indiana ASCE leader and report card co-chair, said the assessment is intended to give policymakers a clearer picture of where investments have worked and where additional attention is needed. She urged state leaders to consider the findings when making decisions about future infrastructure spending, particularly as communities confront growth and increasingly severe weather.
“The future of our state relies on our ability to maintain and improve upon the current conditions of our infrastructure, while also maintaining focus on that growth for our state and for our communities,” Sharkey said. “These systems, they drive economic growth, they create jobs, they improve our public health, and they also protect us from environmental threats.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Offshore wind offered a ‘limitless’ future for CT. Trump scuttled the plan
description: New London was poised to become a regional hub for offshore wind development. The Trump administration's war on offshore wind changed things.
text:
This article was produced in collaboration with ProPublica’s Sustainability Desk, a project of the Local Reporting Network. The Connecticut Mirror, The New Bedford Light and Ocean State Media worked together to understand how the Trump administration’s war on offshore wind has hurt workers and communities across New England.From The New Bedford Light: Fishermen’s offshore wind work drying upFrom Ocean State Media: Offshore wind saved a struggling New Bedford union. Now its future is uncertainAnd in ProPublica: Trump’s war on offshore wind has hurt thousands of workers
On a tour a few years ago through the North Sea coast of the United Kingdom, New London Mayor Michael Passero caught a glimpse of what a resurgence of manufacturing might look like back home in Connecticut.
At a factory in Hartlepool, he watched workers assemble underwater cables that deliver power from the country’s numerous offshore wind farms to shore. To the south, he visited a workforce development center run by the shipping giant Maersk, where workers received specialized training to work at sea on gigantic turbines.
There was even a lab developing submersible robots capable of completing jobs in rough seas that are too dangerous for humans, Passero recalled. 
In the port of Blythe — which, like New London, had seen its maritime trades wither due to decades of deindustrialization — the harbor had been repurposed as a staging area for the UK’s surging offshore wind industry, one of the world’s largest.
“I think the future just looked limitless,” Passero said. “You could almost look to Europe and really see the future here, see everything that can be done. And we have some of the best wind in the world right off the Northeast here, so the industry really looked good there for a while.
“Until Donald Trump got reelected,” he said.

New London Mayor Michael Passero poses for a portrait along New London Waterfront Park with New London State Pier in the background on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026.  New York’s Sunrise Wind, an Ørsted project, is currently being staged at the pier but beyond that there are no projects planned. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Before last year’s efforts by the Trump administration to grind America’s offshore wind industry to a halt, New London was poised to become a regional hub for developers looking to take advantage of the Atlantic’s abundant winds.
The state of Connecticut, through the use of public borrowing, invested more than $211 million to expand a state-owned pier in the city to handle the loading and offloading of parts onto specialized installation vessels. The Danish energy developer Ørsted, partnering with local utility company Eversource, signed on to launch its first three U.S. offshore wind projects from New London, kicking in another $100 million toward the redevelopment of the State Pier.
In addition to employing thousands of workers during construction, the wind projects were billed as a way to wean the region off its historic dependence on oil and natural gas to meet its growing energy needs.
Revolution Wind, the second of the three Ørsted projects launched from New London, is contracted to sell 704 megawatts of electricity — enough to power 350,000 homes — to customers in Connecticut and Rhode Island. The other two projects, South Fork and Sunrise Wind, are connected to New York through underwater cables.
As those connections get up and running, much of the work will dry up. If the Trump administration succeeds in its ongoing efforts to end future offshore wind development in the United States — which by recent accounts is likely — it will eliminate thousands of current and future jobs on America’s waterfronts from Massachusetts to Virginia. Many of these jobs are located in struggling seaports like New Bedford, Mass., and New London, Conn., where states invested hundreds of millions of dollars in port infrastructure and workforce training to court giant offshore wind companies.
The resulting uncertainty has led international wind developers to redirect investment towards other countries or even sell back their leases. Workers who have undergone specialized training or pinned their futures on the promise of steady offshore wind construction could find themselves unable to continue working in the industry. Meanwhile, the states that invested heavily in offshore wind infrastructure are at risk of seeing their purpose-built piers sitting empty, as is the case in New Bedford. 
Today, the State Pier in New London remains a bustling hive of activity. Turbine blades that stretch the length of a football field are stacked on the heavy-lift platform, ready to be transported out to sea on the specialized installation vessel Wind Scylla — named for one of the mythic sea monsters from Homer’s “Odyssey.”
That initial run of offshore wind projects is only scheduled to last through 2027. Officials are searching for a future tenant that can take over Ørsted’s position at the pier, but no contracts have been announced.
Just a few years ago, however, the investment in wind was touted by local leaders as a long-term vision for New London’s waterfront. 
“This is going to be a major facility for decades and decades to come,” Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont triumphantly declared during a visit to the then-active construction site in 2022.

Elements of wind turbine towers for offshore wind projects are staged at New London State Pier is seen on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

A new purpose for the port
New London is an old port city of irregular streets and 19th-Century buildings squeezed into a 10-square-mile strip of land where the Thames River meets Long Island Sound. Like New Bedford, the city was once home to a large whaling fleet but struggled to compete with larger trading ports like New York and Boston after that industry declined.
Across the river, in Groton, the waterfront is dominated by the Navy’s primary East Coast submarine base and General Dynamics Electric Boat’s sprawling shipyard.
But prior to the launch of the offshore wind industry, New London’s maritime trade had mostly dwindled to a few ferries shuttling passengers to and from Long Island alongside the underutilized State Pier, which had been used to import wood pulp, road salt and other products.
All that seemed destined to change by the time Passero joined a delegation of state and local officials on a tour of the U.K.’s offshore wind industry in 2024.
Between community host agreements, docking fees and crews coming ashore to spend money in the bars and restaurants along Bank Street, Passero said he estimated the economic benefit would amount to around $1 million a year for the city — a modest sum that would nonetheless provide a boost to Passero’s efforts to reinvigorate the city’s struggling downtown. 
“You’re not going to fit much in New London, but we got the pier,” Passero said.
Passero was thinking beyond the city’s borders, too. North of New London, the Thames River once powered textile mills that served as one of the birthplaces of the Industrial Revolution.
“We’d get our share of what was appropriate to put in New London, but then the whole area — think of this whole river, all the empty factories along the river — I had visions of these factories being repurposed, you know to be able to, provide some of the materials and equipment that’s needed for this industry,” he said.
Before entering politics, Passero worked as a union laborer on several area projects, including the redevelopment of an old railroad bridge and erecting a new laboratory building at Pfizer’s research campus across the harbor in Groton. 
“It was good money,” he said. “My BA wasn’t going to get me anything.”
Passero’s son, Thomas Passero, followed his father into the building trades and wound up working on both the redevelopment of the State Pier and the subsequent staging of offshore wind projects through Laborers Local 547. 
With the exception of a short diversion to work on an unrelated highway project, the younger Passero said the activity at the State Pier has provided him with a steady stream of income for more than five years, a rarity in the industry. Even when the Trump administration ordered its halt to the work taking place miles offshore, he said workers at the pier never experienced even a single-day layoff. 
“As a New London man, I’ve never seen it so busy,” the younger Passero said. “And it’s not just the pier, you go down to Ocean Beach and see the cargo ships — cargo ships! It’s pretty cool.” 

Staging for Sunrise Wind, an Ørsted project, is seen at New London State Pier on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

30 gigawatts by 2030
By all accounts, the revitalization Mayor Passero imagined on that trip to the U.K. had hit a few bumps before Trump took office the following January.
Ørsted, the developer behind the three New London-based projects, pulled out of two similar projects off the coast of New Jersey in 2023, citing rising interest rates and supply chain issues that plagued much of the industry during the COVID-19 pandemic. Elsewhere cost overruns, project delays and technical challenges threatened to slow the progress toward reaching President Joe Biden’s goal of deploying 30 gigawatts of offshore wind power by 2030.
Still, work was moving forward on projects off the coast of Massachusetts, Rhode Island, New York and Virginia.
The first of those projects, Ørsted’s South Fork Wind, began sending power to the electric grid in 2023. It was followed over the last year by Revolution Wind, Dominion’s Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind and Avangrid’s Vineyard Wind. The final two projects under construction, Ørsted’s Sunrise Wind and Equinor’s Empire Wind, are scheduled to reach commercial operation sometime next year.
Trump’s unsuccessful efforts to halt each of those projects have scuttled the long-term outlook for U.S. offshore wind. The completed projects are slated to supply a total of 6 gigawatts to the grid by the end of next year, far from the 30-gigawatt goal established by Trump’s predecessor.

Instead of planning new projects in American waters once its current work in New London is complete, Ørsted announced last year that it would instead shift its focus to “core markets” in Europe and Asia. During an earnings call with the investors in February, Ørsted chief executive Rasmus Errboe delivered a blunt assessment of his company’s future in the U.S.
“We have no expectations whatsoever to increase our exposure to offshore wind in the U.S.,” he said.

Worker Thomas Passero speaks to reporters at the Connecticut State Pier in New London on Aug. 25, 2025. Credit: Dana Edwards / CT Mirror

Standing on the sidelines
Thomas Passero, the mayor’s son who works at the pier, said he wasn’t too anxious about the future of offshore wind construction. “Being in the trade unions… it’s kind of beaten into us that we’re gonna just build ourselves out of a job and go to another one anyway,” Passero said. “So how permanent is anything, you know?”
Still, he said it was hard to find a job site like the one he had — with consistent hours, years of work, and all only a 10 minute drive from his home and two young children. 
“I hope it stays busy forever. I hope they keep building windmills or something that we can participate in here.” 
Speaking at Yale University in May, Eversource’s president of transmission Bill Quinlan said the industry had been severely weakened by macroeconomic forces and “nonconstructive federal policy.” (Eversource exited the offshore wind industry in 2024, selling its stake in two projects for $745 million.)
While the current slate of projects is likely to be completed, he said, it would could some time before any new projects are announced. 
“I would set that aside for the time being, I don’t see [wind] making a significant comeback in the near term in this country,” Quinlan said. 
“I think developers — the international developers who have the expertise — are probably going to stand on the sidelines for a period of time here in the U.S.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: SEIU Wisconsin calls for bill to restore UW Health union rights
description: After a seven-year campaign to reinstate union rights at UW Health hospitals in Madison, organizers are looking to the incoming Democratic governor and majority in the Legislature to help finish the job. Service Employees International Union’s Wisconsin branch mobilized support across the state for winning candidates — from Gov.-elect David Crowley on down t[...]
text:
Madison residents posted yard signs in 2022 in support of a campaign by nurses at UW Health seeking union representation. SEIU Wisconsin and the union's UW Health members are urging Democrats who will control the Legislature starting in January to enact a law restoring their union rights. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)After a seven-year campaign to reinstate union rights at UW Health hospitals in Madison, organizers are looking to the incoming Democratic governor and majority in the Legislature to help finish the job.
Service Employees International Union’s Wisconsin branch mobilized support across the state for winning candidates — from Gov.-elect David Crowley on down to incoming Assembly members who flipped seats on Nov. 3 and put the Democrats in charge of both houses in the Legislature.
In an announcement issued Thursday, SEIU Wisconsin members and leaders spelled out their next goal: passing legislation to restore collective bargaining rights at the UW Hospital and Clinics Authority — the corporate parent of UW Health hospitals and clinics.
“This moment represents the beginning of a new era,” Colin Gillis, SEIU Wisconsin vice president for nursing and a nurse at UW Health for nine years, told the Wisconsin Examiner.
“I’m really excited to have the opportunity, at long last after years of organizing and campaigning — knocking doors, doing phone banking, organizing with my co-workers — to have the opportunity to have a Democratic trifecta that can restore our collective bargaining rights,” Gillis said, “so that we can advocate for our patients and our community and ensure that Wisconsin has the healthcare system it deserves.”
The UW Health hospital system’s employees are not classified as state employees. Nevertheless, former Gov. Scott Walker’s 2011 Act 10 — which stripped collective bargaining rights from most public employees in Wisconsin — also eliminated state laws that had guaranteed union rights for UW Hospital & Clinics Authority employees since 1996.
SEIU Wisconsin is calling for the new Democratic majority in the Legislature to reintroduce and pass a bill that would “restore full collective bargaining rights for thousands of nurses and over 25,000 total UW Health employees,” the SEIU Wisconsin announcement Thursday said.
An email inquiry to UW Health about the SEIU announcement and the prospect of such a law did not get a response Thursday.
Nurse cites assurances from Dem leaders
Legislation to restore UW Health employees’ union rights was last introduced in February, toward the end of the current legislative session. The bills, AB 999 and SB 965, were never taken up. The SEIU announcement Thursday identified them as the union’s objective.
Gillis said that at campaign events before the Nov. 3 election, he and other SEIU members spoke with the Legislature’s Democratic leaders, Sen. Dianne Hesselbein and state Rep. Greta Neubauer, along with David Crowley, now the governor-elect.
“And they gave me and my coworkers, assurance, directly to our faces, verbally, that this would be a top priority,” Gillis said. He said he hasn’t yet heard about a timeline, however.
Rep. Lisa Subeck (D-Madison), who has been the lead Assembly author on the previous bills, said Thursday the timeline for action and the exact form it might take still has to be determined.
“I’m definitely still committed to restoring collective bargaining rights for our UW Health nursing staff and others,” said Subeck. “I think there is broad support among Democrats for restoring collective bargaining rights broadly.”
Subeck, who has been elected Speaker Pro Tempore in the next legislative session, added that it is “a little too soon to say exactly how these bills may be introduced and exactly what that timing would be.”
She also said that it “remains to be determined” whether simply repealing Act 10 — as Democratic leaders have said they intend to do — would be sufficient for restoring the UW Health workers’ union rights.
“It’s unfortunate that this hasn’t happened already,” Subeck said. “We all know that when the people who care for us, and in this case that’s our nurses at UW, have a voice in their workplace and can have a role in working conditions, it is good for patient care.”
Gillis said that he and other union members believe the legislation introduced in February would offer stronger protections for the rights of UW Health employees to union representation than simply repealing Act 10.
AB 999/SB 965 include provisions that would allow a majority of employees to win union recognition by signing a petition rather than through an election — the only mechanism for unionizing under current state law, according to the Legislative Reference Bureau analysis of the bill.
The measure, if enacted, also would require UW Health to allow unions that represent current employees to provide information at new employees’ orientation sessions, and to allow them to use the work email system to discuss workplace issues, administer union contracts and organize employees.
After 2019 launch, union drive escalates
After Act 10 ended the UW hospital system’s collective bargaining guarantees, the last contracts expired in 2014. Five years later, in 2019, UW Health nurses announced they were joining SEIU Wisconsin.
Initially they sought voluntary talks on working conditions with the hospital system’s management. UW Health rejected their demand.
A series of legal memos followed arguing that, despite Act 10, there was a stronger case in existing Wisconsin laws to support union rights for UW Health employees.
Encouraged by those arguments, nurses sought union recognition from the hospital system’s management and were rebuffed. On the verge of a threatened three-day strike in September 2022, Gov. Tony Evers brokered a deal between UW Health and nurses affiliated with SEIU Wisconsin.
That agreement set in motion a court case that concluded with a unanimous 2025 decision in which the Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed that because of Act 10, state law does not require the hospital system to recognize or bargain with unions representing its employees.
The 2022 agreement also included a provision for voluntary meetings between union representatives and UW Health management. Gillis, who has participated in those meetings, said they have continued since then.
“Every other month we sit down for a process, a two-hour meeting called ‘meet and discuss,’” Gillis said. “We have enjoyed a productive and collaborative relationship with our counterparts across the table in that process, but that process is no substitute for negotiation at the bargaining table.”
That’s because it doesn’t lead to a formal contract, he said.
“Nurses know that a contract is, collective bargaining is, the most powerful tool they have to advocate for their patients and their co-workers and their communities,” Gillis said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: How Maine’s two-decade old school consolidation effort continues to unravel
description: Next year, the town of Kingfield will leave MSAD 58 to form its own school district. The move will allow the western Maine community of roughly 1,000 people to keep its elementary school building and operate its own district, which will serve about 80 students. Kingfield was the only one of more than a dozen […]
text:
A classroom at Woodrow Wilson Elementary School in South Salt Lake City, Utah, on March 12, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)Next year, the town of Kingfield will leave MSAD 58 to form its own school district. The move will allow the western Maine community of roughly 1,000 people to keep its elementary school building and operate its own district, which will serve about 80 students.
Kingfield was the only one of more than a dozen Maine towns to successfully withdraw from or reorganize its school district in the Nov. 3 election. At least 12 other communities considered similar changes, driven by concerns that their schools could close, that their local tax dollars were being spent on improvements at other schools in their district, or that they lacked control over school governance.
Kingfield voters overwhelmingly supported the ballot measure to withdraw from the district, with  over 70% voting in favor.
The trend highlights a broader trade-off facing small towns: leaving larger districts can give communities more control over their schools, but smaller districts may struggle to provide the specialized services and academic support available in larger ones. 
It is the latest chapter in a decades-long debate about how to govern rural school districts, since former Gov. John Baldacci signed sweeping school consolidation legislation in 2007, penalizing those that chose to go their own way. 
In a state facing enrollment declines and aging school buildings with insufficient state funding available for improvements, that challenge is only expected to get worse.
“A lot of communities place a really big value on their schools, which is wonderful because schools, in my opinion, are the backbone of public education,” said Laura Columbia, superintendent of MSAD 58.
“But I think what’s really important for people to think about is: At what cost? At what point are we keeping buildings at the expense of not providing services to students?”
The challenges for smaller districts extend beyond student services to the cost of maintaining a certain level of funding, said Janet Fairman, a University of Maine professor and co-director of the Maine Education Policy Research Institute.
“The state’s funding formula gives (small districts) enough money based on a certain staff-to-student ratio, and when these communities choose to be smaller than that, they have to pay the difference,” she said. “That means they have to tax themselves more or they have to somehow come up with more revenue to cover the difference in cost.”
When a town decides to separate, Columbia explained that it can also strain the existing school district.
Most rural districts in Maine are already facing a yearslong staffing shortage, and starting next year, MSAD 58 will have to compete with the newly formed Kingfield district for the few special education teachers, bus drivers and occupational therapists in the area. Under the agreement, Kingfield will still send its students to the MSAD 58 high school, so Columbia expects staffing challenges to be most acute at the elementary level.

“People really like to have local schools, I think that’s kind of aligned with a lot of Mainers’ philosophy on local control,” she said. “But we have limited resources to start with in many of our rural schools, and so it can often stretch those resources even further when we have smaller districts in the same area.”
Financial repercussions
School districts are financially incentivized to leave their larger consolidated school units, according to Amy Johnson, a professor at the University of Southern Maine and co-director of MEPRI along with Fairman. 
Most Maine districts, 109, are typical school administrative units, with more than one school. But there are also 81 districts that have only one school. This typically means these districts operate their own schools for younger grades and use a tuition model, under which the Maine Department of Education mandates towns pay tuition for their residents to go to another town’s public school, or an approved private school. 
One-school districts enroll anywhere between 2 and 600 students, with the median student population being 129, according to MEPRI data.
That’s similar to the plan for Kingfield, where the new school will enroll about 80 students.
But there are also 59 school units with no schools. That means a town withdraws from a school unit and does not form its own, instead choosing to send all of its students to other districts under the tuition model.
“What they gain from that is they only have to pay for the costs for their students, and they only have a handful of students,” Johnson said.
These school districts have the lowest per pupil spending, according to MEPRI data. 
A typical school unit spends about $18,000 per student, not including transportation or career and technical education. Costs jump up for a one-school district to about $21,000, because, as Johnson explained, “you’re not sharing any costs, you’re trying to be an entire school district with one school plus some tuition students.”
But zero-school districts spend the least, about $15,000 per student, which is the higher end of the state average for tuition. But even at that level, that tuition often does not cover the cost of special education or other services that their students may need, leaving the district accepting them to cover those costs.
“There is this real financial benefit to pulling out of a school unit and becoming your own district, because then you can pay less towards the cost of education because you have fewer kids,” Johnson said. “Because all they’re doing is taking their tax dollars and sending their kids elsewhere.” 



Quotation







“There is this real financial benefit to pulling out of a school unit and becoming your own district, because then you can pay less towards the cost of education because you have fewer kids. Because all they're doing is taking their tax dollars and sending their kids elsewhere.


– Amy Johnson, professor at the University of Southern Maine and co-director of Maine Education Policy Research Institute


Similarly, Kingfield’s withdrawal from MSAD 58 will create a financial burden for the district, Columbia said. 
Not only will it reduce per-pupil state funding, but also because Kingfield’s local contribution to the district was relatively large because of the town’s high property values. 
And because the roughly 60 students being pulled from the district are spread across multiple grades, Columbia said it won’t result in any reduction in staffing or classroom space, and their associated costs.
Towns attempting joint withdrawal 
Three towns about an hour south of Kingfield also attempted to leave their consolidated district, RSU 10, to form their own smaller school unit. 
Buckfield, Hartford and Sumner proposed forming their own district because RSU 10’s central office is about a 40-minute drive away. Buckfield voters approved the change, but since the other two towns did not, all three will stay with the district. 
This is not the first withdrawal from that regional district. In 2017, four towns — Canton, Carthage, Dixfield and Peru — withdrew from the district to form their own. 
In the case of the Buckfield-area towns, they did not want to spend tax dollars on improvements within the district that their students would not benefit from, said RSU 10 Superintendent Matt Gilbert. 
“They’re the smaller communities within our district, and they also have the smallest tax base,” Gilbert added. “They were focusing on the desire for control of their tax dollars to be closer to home.”
If the three additional towns had withdrawn and formed their own school district, Gilbert said they would have had about 500 students, which may have been a challenge, “and they would have lost all the benefits that they get from being part of a larger district and the economy of scale that comes with that, like central office services and supports.”
In the aftermath of last week’s election, the withdrawal committee discussed an alternative budgeting model with Gilbert, under which they would have more autonomy over improvements to schools in their communities, but share administrative costs with the larger district. 
That means if they want to build a track or add a foreign language program to a school in their community, they would not rely on approval from the entire district school board. 
“We were all forced into this consolidation because of the threat of being penalized financially,” Gilbert said.
Will Maine’s next governor reshape local control in education to improve test scores?

According to Johnson from MEPRI, school consolidation is a reality many towns have to face due to declining enrollments, due to aging populations and people moving away from rural areas. 
Baldacci attempted to address this challenge by mandating that roughly 300 districts be consolidated to 80. Even though that effort was not completely successful, as there are now more than 200 districts, Johnson said it’s not realistic to expect all towns to be able to independently meet their students’ needs.
“In small communities, you don’t start with an economy of scale. If there’s only one school to begin with, it’s much harder to close because there would be nothing left,” Johnson said. “But it’s more expensive to operate that way, and it’s less efficient.”
Consolidation vs. local control
Mount Desert Island-area schools still operate under an alternative organizational structure or AOS. That model allows each of the 10 schools to pass their own budgets but share a superintendent. 
The AOS model was offered as an alternative to Baldacci’s consolidation mandate, but there are currently only eight AOSs left in Maine, according to the Maine School Management Association. 
Several towns and islands around Mount Desert Island considered consolidating into a regional school unit, but many communities last week rejected the plan.
Superintendent Michael Zboray said many communities were reluctant to give up control over their community schools. 
“I tried to argue that all the same people that are caring for your school now will continue to be the people caring for your school, you’ll just have a larger pool of money to help in that care if something catastrophic happened to your building,” Zboray said, “rather than having to rely on the tax base just within your town.” 
Zboray said at least some communities on the island as well as neighboring Tremont agree they will eventually need a consolidated school unit because of declining class sizes and lower enrollment in all schools except Bar Harbor.
“It’s a very challenging situation, and we can apply that to police departments, fire departments and school departments,” said Maine School Management Association Executive Director Eric Waddell.
Waddell said he heard from people all over the state struggling to maintain local services amid affordability challenges and declining populations.
“I don’t know what the answer is other than to find alternate revenue sources for funding schools other than leaning so heavily on local property taxes.”

title: Opinion: Telling local stories — on Kansas college campuses and elsewhere — demands elusive courage
description: “I should write about that,” I said to my wife as we walked through our Leawood neighborhood a few weeks ago.  “Yeah,” she agreed. “You should.” With our dog leading the way, we had just walked past a front yard decorated for Halloween — but with a bizarre political twist. Fake cemetery headstones jutted from […]
text:
(Illustration by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)“I should write about that,” I said to my wife as we walked through our Leawood neighborhood a few weeks ago. 
“Yeah,” she agreed. “You should.”
With our dog leading the way, we had just walked past a front yard decorated for Halloween — but with a bizarre political twist. Fake cemetery headstones jutted from the lawn, draped with decorative spiderwebs. Halloween-themed lighting gave the front of the house a spooky glow. 
At the far end of the yard, arranged MacBeth-style, three yard ornament witches encircled a decorative cauldron. The cauldron was labeled: “Cornell 7.” 
Halloween is a dark holiday, I told my wife, but a diorama to alleged college gang rape in your front yard? That is somehow more sinister than skeletons and headstones.
In the same front yard were other Halloween figures propped up on the lawn. One of them held a “No Kings” protest sign, denouncing facism.
In our pocket of Johnson County where we walk our goldendoodle (almost too on-the-nose), the decorations stood out as a unique blend of festive and political. What was the homeowner thinking?
I told myself that I would circle back before my next deadline. This front yard deserved a column.
 
A national audience
The next bullet point on the projection screen read: “Local. Local. Local.” 
Earnest students — from Texas, Iowa, California and at least a dozen other states — scribbled down my advice last week at the College Media Association’s national convention in Kansas City, Missouri.
More than 1,000 students, according to organizers of the event, gathered to hear presentations from college instructors like me, along with professional journalists and academic researchers. According to the event’s app, Kansas student journalists and faculty attended from Washburn University, Wichita State University, Kansas State University, Johnson County Community College, McPherson College, Cowley College and the University of Kansas, where I teach.
The topic I chose for my second session was about this. Literally this: the columns I write for Kansas Reflector. Many collegiate publications have opinion sections and opinion editors, voicing the heartfelt beliefs of the young people on their staffs.
For these college audiences, I always deliver the advice of writing locally. In decades of reading high school and college journalism and judging it for awards, I know what to expect. Students often aim the fire hydrant of their commentary at national news.
The most recent blockbuster Hollywood movie. The hot new pop album by everyone’s favorite starlet. Hot takes on national professional sports. Opinions on international issues. And so, so, so much national politics.
The donut hole that is so often missing? Commentary about what is happening on campus.
On the websites for many college publications, it’s almost impossible to find out how people feel about their university, its spending, its policies, its classes, its sports and its campus life. Instead, the opinion sections read like less-polished, less-cogent and less-informed versions of, say, the New York Times opinion page.
“Why would I read your opinion on the latest Olivia Rodrigo album when the writers for national publications are better writers?” I asked at the convention.
Some nodded along. Others looked at me quizzically.
At the end of the session, I invited students to email me samples of their work. What I received from a handful of the students was inspiring in many ways. Some students were vulnerable, telling wrenching personal anecdotes. Other students dove into controversy, tackling divisive political issues. (It turns out, unsurprisingly, that college journalists don’t love MAGA politics.)
Only one of the columns, however, directly addressed a campus debate: should a retrograde misogynist who is consumed with personal appearance be allowed to appear on UCLA’s campus? The student bravely took a stand: “The university should not have allowed” the social media bully “to protest on its grounds.”
This is the part of my column where I could write something thoughtlessly generational about how contemporary students are uniquely backing down from writing about local controversy. “College students these days …” But I don’t believe that. 
Writing about local politics has always been challenging. After all, we’ve been swimming in nonstop national news for decades: daily national newspapers like USA Today, broadcast news each evening, cable news like CNN, talk radio like Rush Limbaugh and more.
The buffet of topics — Bill Clinton’s infidelity, George W. Bush’s rush to war, Barack Obama’s quietly aggressive immigration policy — has been alluringly convenient for writers who should be focused more locally because the national stories are constantly shoveled toward us.
Local commentary, however, often means doing the research yourself. As college instructors, we beg students to leave their dorm rooms, meet people, explore areas of town away from campus. Be there in person and describe what you see locally.
 
Right next door
If not local, the coverage of Kansas Reflector is stubbornly statewide. I can’t count the number of times I have pitched a story to my exceptional opinion editor Clay Wirestone to have him reply with something like: “Remember that our focus is Kansas.”
Sometimes that means deleting a column idea completely. Other times it means doing extra research that narrows the focus to Kansas, which is our mission, after all.
Last night, I was thinking about my advice — my tone so confident and expert — to the student journalists in that hotel conference room last week. I was also replaying the emailed coaching that I had sent earlier in the day to the students who asked for critiques.
And then, dog leash in hand, I walked past that same house, the one with the political Halloween display. With all of the lights in the house off, it was far too late to ring the doorbell and ask about the Cornell 7. And, I told myself, the decorations weren’t even up anymore.
With that, a local story faded because it didn’t get the courage it deserved — not from a rookie college journalist but from me. Even the guy dispensing the supposedly expert advice sometimes needs an additional shot of courage to knock on a neighbor’s door and tell a local story.
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

title: Indiana to hold key financial aid award at current rates
description: Indiana’s primary need-based college scholarship will maintain the same award schedule for the third consecutive school year, while several other popular scholarships are under review. The Indiana Commission for Higher Education voted Thursday to freeze the Frank O’Bannon Grants award schedule at current rates for the 2027-28 school year, so as to not exhaus[...]
text:
Indiana Education Secretary Katie Jenner, left, speaks to the Commission for Higher Education on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. (Screenshot courtesy of State of Indiana)Indiana’s primary need-based college scholarship will maintain the same award schedule for the third consecutive school year, while several other popular scholarships are under review.
The Indiana Commission for Higher Education voted Thursday to freeze the Frank O’Bannon Grants award schedule at current rates for the 2027-28 school year, so as to not exhaust the $168 million in available funding.
The schedule now awaits final approval from the State Budget Committee when it meets in December.
Pressure on scholarship fund
The scholarship is Indiana’s most popular need-based financial aid award, supporting more than 35,000 students last school year.
Lawmakers have appropriated $168 million toward the scholarship each year since 2021. But changes in federal financial aid eligibility led to unexpectedly high demand for the scholarship in 2024, forcing the commission to trim the award and dip into reserves.
Then a grim financial forecast pushed lawmakers to revert the scholarship fund’s reserves to the state General Fund, further squeezing the dollars and prompting the commission to freeze what it offers students who qualify.
The scholarship can be used at public and private colleges alike, though award amounts vary by institution, credit hours and student need. The maximum grant amount is $10,600 and the minimum is $400.
Students must maintain satisfactory academic progress at their chosen college, maintain Indiana residency and file a Free Application for Federal Student Aid by April 15 each year to qualify.
Cody Robison, the commission’s chief deputy financial officer, said the agency is projected to spend $165 million on the Frank O’Bannon Grants for the 2027-28 school year — just shy of the $168 million appropriated to the fund.
Other scholarships subject to review
The commission is also expected to review completion rates and graduate outcomes for other popular financial aid programs like the Workforce Ready Grant, awarded to returning adult students pursuing short-term credentials, as it prepares for the 2027 legislative session.
Robison said the grant has produced mixed results despite its growing popularity.
Most programs participating in the Workforce Ready grant are designed to be completed within six to 12 months, yet only 52% of recipients finished a degree or credential within three years, Robison said.
The commission restricted new applications this fall as demand for the grant outpaces available funding.
A similar problem is happening with the state’s scholarship for children of disabled veterans and public safety officers. The state received $44 million in claims for 6,000 students receiving the award last year, far exceeding the $32 million in available funding.
Robison said 60% of these students complete their chosen degree within six years.
“We want to be thinking about the ROI that students are getting from the program and making sure that our recommendations are really informed by that,” he said.

title: Ohio Republican lawmaker wants to make it easier for legislature to override the governor’s veto
description: An Ohio Republican lawmaker is trying to change the state’s constitution to make it easier for the legislature to override the governor’s veto. State Rep. Ron Ferguson, R-Wintersville, recently introduced House Joint Resolution 11, which would decrease the number of votes required to override the governor’s veto. This comes less than a week after Democrat […[...]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by Megan Henry/ Ohio Capital Journal)An Ohio Republican lawmaker is trying to change the state’s constitution to make it easier for the legislature to override the governor’s veto.
State Rep. Ron Ferguson, R-Wintersville, recently introduced House Joint Resolution 11, which would decrease the number of votes required to override the governor’s veto. This comes less than a week after Democrat Amy Acton was elected governor, the Ohio Democrats broke the Republican supermajority in the Ohio House for the next General Assembly, and a Democrats were elected to the seats of secretary of state, treasurer, and attorney general.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Currently, a three-fifths majority vote from the members of the House and Senate is necessary to override the governor’s veto.
H.J.R. 11 would change it to a simple majority.
If both the Ohio House and the Ohio Senate pass the resolution, the issue would go before voters as a constitutional amendment in a special election on May 4.
Unlike a bill, this would not require Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine’s signature. DeWine said last week he does not support any attempt by lame-duck Republican supermajority lawmakers to dramatically change the powers of governor before January.
Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman, R-Lima, did not sound optimistic this would pass.
“To be able to put together a campaign by next May, I think would be almost impossible,” he said.
But Huffman did not rule out other potential reforms coming forward during lame duck.
“We’re sort of gathering those and deciding what is constitutional, what practically makes a difference to make sure that the legislature — which is the representatives of the people — still has the appropriate authority, and the executive branch has the appropriate authority too,” Huffman said.
When asked if the Ohio House is looking at trying to change the authority in other executive offices, Huffman said he told his Republican caucus to write up specific proposals if they have things they want to see change.
“There are a lot of people who’ve called up and said, ‘Oh, we should do this or we should do that,’” he said. “Great, let’s see a specific proposal.”
Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, R-Napoleon, does not think the house resolution will pass.
“I don’t know that they would have the support, quite frankly,” he said. “So I can tell you on that, probably not going to happen.”
Ohio House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn, D-Cincinnati, called attempts to limit the governor’s authority anti-democratic and said it was “the worst possible time to ignore the will of the voters.”
“Anything that would overturn the will of the voters is an insult to the people of Ohio and a detriment to the state, and I think that is certainly how Governor-elect Acton feels, and we share that sentiment,” Isaacsohn said.
Ohio Senate Minority Leader Nickie Antonio, D-Lakewood, agreed with Isaacsohn.
“I think to game the governor’s powers at this point would be a slap in the face to the voters,” she said. “Whatever you do right now, there are ramifications and consequences for next year. So I think everybody needs to keep that in mind as well.”
University of Cincinnati political science professor David Niven doesn’t think the proposed constitutional amendment would pass if it was on the ballot.
“The voters have shown they are skeptical about Republican power-grabs,” he said. “It makes (Ohio Republicans) feel good to think they can take away the power of the governor as soon as a Democrat is in office.”
Professor David Cohen, a political science professor with the University of Akron, said the constitutional amendment would be “a really dark stain on the Republican party.”
“A real tone-deafness as to what the election results mean,” he said.
In 2023, Ohio Republicans tried unsuccessfully to make it harder to amend the Ohio Constitution by requiring future amendments to be approved by 60% of voters instead of the simple majority. Ohio voters rejected the proposal by 57%.
Reporter Susan Tebben contributed to this report.

title: Ohio’s U.S. Senator-elect Sherrod Brown could get an early start in Washington
description: Ohio’s U.S. Senator-elect Sherrod Brown could assume office about two weeks earlier than the rest of Ohio’s new congressional delegation. It may have no impact on proceedings, but with a narrow margin in the Senate, Republican leaders could face some difficult math in the final few days of the current session. Gov. Mike DeWine appointed […]
text:
Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. Sherrod Brown speaking at a Cleveland rally. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)Ohio’s U.S. Senator-elect Sherrod Brown could assume office about two weeks earlier than the rest of Ohio’s new congressional delegation. It may have no impact on proceedings, but with a narrow margin in the Senate, Republican leaders could face some difficult math in the final few days of the current session.
Gov. Mike DeWine appointed the seat’s current occupant, Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, to fill the vacancy left when then-U.S. Sen. J.D. Vance became vice president. That promotion came with a daunting road ahead. Because there was so much time left in Vance’s term, Husted would have to run in 2026 to keep the seat, and then again in 2028 if he wanted to be reelected to a new term.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In the end, he wasn’t able to fend off Ohio’s once and future U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, who will now represent Ohio through the end of Vance’s original term in office. If he wants to keep the seat, he’ll have to run in 2028 as well.
“We will fight to end the tariffs, end this war, and lower costs so that working families don’t have to pay for this corruption in Washington,” Brown said in a statement. “My pledge to all Ohioans — whether they voted for me or not — is that I will always be on their side.”
Husted’s term ends Dec. 15 under state law. The Capital Journal reached out to Husted’s office about his priorities for the lame duck session, and the prospect of Brown finishing out the term in his place, but got no response.
So far as the U.S. Senate is concerned, Brown can be sworn in once he presents credentials signed by the governor and secretary of state. The official canvass in Ohio is Nov. 24, and election certification happens by Dec. 4. So, technically Brown could take over even before the statutory expiration of Husted’s term.
But that’s not going to happen. In an email, Ohio Secretary of State spokesman Dan Lusheck said Secretary of State Frank LaRose “will follow the law, which requires Senator Husted to fulfill his full term.”
Even if Brown has to wait until mid-December to take office, his presence could have a significant impact.
What’s ahead?
Republicans currently hold a 53-seat majority, and that already narrow margin shrinks once Husted leaves office.
“If we were talking about a 10-seat majority that Republicans had, Sherrod Brown’s vote wouldn’t matter,” University of Akron political science professor David Cohen said, “But it’s such a close margin in the Senate, it absolutely could have an impact.”
GOP Congress faces funding deadline, farm bill, lengthy to-do list in year-end session

The Senate calendar currently has lawmakers adjourning Dec.18, and there’s a lot they want to get to by then.
Particularly in the Senate, Republicans are running out of time to confirm judges and other executive appointments. They’ll likely want to advance as many as possible before they give up the gavel.
Congress is also grappling with a major energy permitting reform bill and a college sports overhaul. They’re hammering out a new farm bill — a five-year measure pairing funding for agricultural interests and food assistance — and the annual defense policy bill known as the National Defense Authorization Act.
And if that wasn’t enough, they’re facing a Dec. 11 federal funding cliff.
Political science professor David Niven, of the University of Cincinnati, agreed that Brown’s vote could be important.
“The Senate is close enough,” he said. “It could matter on appointment of judges and other vacancies.”
“It’s going to depend on what level of panic the administration is in,” Niven added, “how many judges they put (up for confirmation).”
No official announcement has been made about when Brown will be sworn in.
Reporter Susan Tebben contributed to this report.

title: The GOP lost its iron grip on Ohio. What’s the outlook for clean energy?
description: This story was originally published by Canary Media. Democrats have finally managed to gain footing in Ohio’s halls of power — a shift that bodes well for clean energy in a state that’s become particularly hostile toward solar and wind. Last week, voters ended Republicans’ 15-year-long trifecta in Ohio, picking Democrat Amy Acton to be their next governor (a[...]
text:
Solar panels. (Photo by Evan Houk/ Maine Morning Star)
This story was originally published by Canary Media.
Democrats have finally managed to gain footing in Ohio’s halls of power — a shift that bodes well for clean energy in a state that’s become particularly hostile toward solar and wind.


Last week, voters ended Republicans’ 15-year-long trifecta in Ohio, picking Democrat Amy Acton to be their next governor (and the first woman elected to that office). While the GOP still controls the state House and Senate, Democrats won enough seats to break Republicans’ supermajority in the House, meaning the party can no longer unilaterally override the governor’s vetoes.


From 2011 until now, Republican control of all three branches of state government has increasingly favored the oil and gas industry while limiting the growth of renewable power and scaling back energy-efficiency standards.


Acton campaigned on a different vision. Her affordability plan pledged to promote ​“the lowest-cost and cleanest sources of energy readily available” and to reinstate energy efficiency measures, renewable portfolio standards, and demand response programs, which incentivize customers to reduce or shift their energy consumption when the grid is strained.


In a Substack post last month, Acton wrote, ​“Ohio politicians have made it nearly impossible to advance zero marginal cost generation such as wind and solar,” so most of the state’s electricity comes from higher-cost fossil-fuels. ​“I will reexamine these obstacles that, in the long run, hit Ohio families in their pocketbooks.”


The question is what Acton can actually do to move the needle.


The main obstacle to utility-scale solar over the past five years has been a 2021 law, Senate Bill 52, that lets counties ban almost all such new projects within their territories. Even without an outright ban, counties can block most projects before a developer can proceed with a permit application at the state level. SB 52 also applies to wind farms of 5 megawatts or more, though almost all proposals for large-scale wind projects stopped after a 2014 budget law more than doubled the distance that turbines must be from neighboring property lines.


Over a third of Ohio counties have now designated large swaths of land as off-limits to renewables under SB 52. Acton can’t change that law and others on her own, since doing so requires legislative action.


Still, clean energy advocates are optimistic that the new governor will be able to knock down some roadblocks.
“It’s a brand-new day here,” said Neil Waggoner, Midwest manager for the Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal campaign, who’s based in central Ohio.


SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.Very soon, Acton will choose leaders for various regulatory agencies, subject to confirmation by the Ohio Senate. Those include the directors of the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency and the departments that deal with health, natural resources, agriculture, and development. The Ohio EPA handles permits for fossil-fuel plants and other polluting facilities, while the Ohio Department of Natural Resources decides matters dealing with hydraulic fracturing, injection wells, and coal mining.


Most notably for energy, those five agency directors will make up a majority of the voting members of the Ohio Power Siting Board, which issues permits for electric generation projections and other energy infrastructure. The board has seven standing voting members; the other two are the chair of the Public Utility Commission of Ohio and a member that represents the public.


Acton will eventually get to pick those last two members, too. The utility commission’s current chair, Jenifer French, can stay on as a regulator there until 2029, but the governor can at any time designate a different chair, who will then also head up the Power Siting Board. The term for the current public member ends in 2030.


Those personnel swaps could make Ohio friendlier to clean energy developers. In recent years, the siting board and its staff have mainly deferred to local governments on whether a solar or wind project is in the public interest. That has allowed the mere existence of local government opposition to derail projects, even when objections lack factual support or have been addressed by the developer.

Miranda Leppla, who heads the environmental law clinic at Case Western Reserve University School of Law, said she hopes the new board will take a genuinely broad view of the public interest, including a more critical examination of energy projects’ health and environmental impacts and the costs of climate change.


Acton will also appoint at least four of the Public Utilities Commission’s five members during her term, as their tenures come to an end. That agency is tasked with making sure Ohioans have reliable, affordable utility service. Leppla said new members could push utilities to embrace energy efficiency and demand response and pursue more equitable service across their territories.


 At the legislature

While Acton cannot enact laws on her own, her election could force Republicans in the legislature to compromise more on energy policy.
“The majorities in the House and Senate are going to have to work with the governor,” Waggoner said. ​“That’s a good thing. That’s the way government is supposed to work.”


Democratic Rep. Tristan Rader, ranking minority member on the current House Energy Committee, said he expects there will be some cooperation and actual movement toward the ​“all-of-the-above strategy that at least Republicans have given lip service to these last couple of years.” Otherwise, nothing would get done.


Even if the legislature won’t abolish SB 52’s terms for letting counties ban solar and wind, Republicans will no longer be able to unilaterally override Acton if she vetoes bills to further restrict solar, wind, or energy efficiency.


“It would be fantastic to make sure we can’t go further down the path of promoting fossil fuels at the expense of different types of clean energy that could save Ohioans money and could do wonders for the impacts of climate change,” Leppla said.


However, there’s still the lame-duck session to get through.


One proposal, House Bill 1024, would shift authority for review of thousands of agency rules and processes from the governor to lawmakers — essentially letting them undo regulations without having to amend the law or risk Acton’s veto. Republican Rep. Jamie Callender introduced the bill last month, shortly before the election; he was also a primary sponsor of 2019’s House Bill 6, the coal and nuclear bailout law that gutted Ohio’s clean energy standards and is at the heart of the state’s ongoing utility-corruption saga.


Another gambit, House Joint Resolution 11, proposes making the governor’s veto power meaningless by letting simple majorities override it. Introduced days after Acton’s election, it would place the issue before voters as a constitutional amendment next year.


Meanwhile, lawmakers could try to ram through some energy bills before the new year. Senate Bill 294, which the Ohio Senate passed in June, may make building solar and wind even more difficult by specifying a minimum capacity factor of 50%. Capacity factor refers to the ratio between actual electricity production and maximum output if a source runs continuously. Federal data shows the average capacity factor is around 24% for U.S. solar farms and 34% for wind, meaning Ohio’s law could essentially force developers to add batteries — along with costs and complexity — to their projects to meet the 50% threshold


Another proposal, House Bill 862, would let utilities own nuclear plants — and possibly stick consumers with part of the costs. That would run counter to a 2025 law that generally bars regulated electric utilities from owning generation and passing costs on to customers in what is supposed to be a competitive market.


Other draft bill language circulated this week would also keep coal plants open, even if the owner has signed a contract agreeing to close a facility or convert it to natural gas. Most imminently, that could force a large unit at the Cardinal power plant in eastern Ohio to stay open, even though the group that runs it is bound to shutter the facility by 2028 under a 2015 settlement deal prior owner American Electric Power made with the Sierra Club.


Much then could depend not only on Acton’s plans for next year, but also on what happens between now and New Year’s Eve, when the legislative session ends. Nonetheless, Rader is optimistic that the election results will lead to more renewables coming online in Ohio.


“Let’s put all energy on an equal footing,” he said.

title: Sen. LaTonya Johnson and Rep. Tip McGuire tapped to lead powerful budget committee
description: Sen. LaTonya Johnson (D-Milwaukee) and Rep. Tip McGuire (D-Kenosha) were named as the co-chairs of the state’s powerful Joint Finance Committee on Tuesday.  The lawmakers will lead the 16-member committee, which is made up of eight senators  and eight Assembly members. It’s the latest announcement in Democratic leadership for the upcoming session.  Democrats[...]
text:
Rep. Tip McGuire (D-Kenosha) (left) and Sen. LaTonya Johnson (D-Milwaukee) (right) were named as the co-chairs of the state’s powerful Joint Finance Committee. (Wisconsin Examiner photos)Sen. LaTonya Johnson (D-Milwaukee) and Rep. Tip McGuire (D-Kenosha) were named as the co-chairs of the state’s powerful Joint Finance Committee on Tuesday. 
The lawmakers will lead the 16-member committee, which is made up of eight senators  and eight Assembly members. It’s the latest announcement in Democratic leadership for the upcoming session. 
Democrats will hold a majority in the state Legislature for the first time in 16 years, and that means being responsible for writing the state’s next two-year budget, a process that falls majorly to the Joint Finance Committee.
The last time the state budget was written by Democrats was the 2009-2011 legislative session, and lawmakers entered that situation in a much different financial position — the state had a $6 billion budget deficit. Wisconsin will enter 2027 with a $3 billion budget surplus. 
In a statement, incoming Senate Majority Leader Dianne Hesselbein (D-Middleton), who is responsible for deciding committee assignments, said Johnson had “demonstrated her ability to connect with people across the state and fight for their needs during her time on JFC.”
Johnson, who was first elected to the Senate in 2016 and previously operated an in-home childcare center, has served on the budget committee since the 2018 session. Hesselbein said that she has the “judgment and leadership to deliver a budget that reflects the needs of this moment in our state’s history.” 
Johnson said it’s been a privilege to listen to people from across the state  and she promises to “keep listening and to carry your stories with me into the Capitol as we write a responsible budget investing in the people because I know what having opportunity means to a family, and how much can change when people have a fair shot to build a better life.”
Incoming Assembly Speaker Greta Neubauer (D-Racine) named McGuire as the Assembly co-chair. She said in a statement that he has “spent his career fighting for working families” and has “deep experience in the budget process.”
“I know that he is going to make sure that the next state budget truly reflects the will of the people,” Neubauer said. “He understands that every appropriation and every line item affect people in communities across Wisconsin.”
McGuire, who previously worked as a Kenosha County special prosecutor and Milwaukee County assistant district attorney, was first elected to the state Assembly in an April 2019 special election. He has served on the state budget committee since the 2023-24 legislative session. 
McGuire said in a statement that he is “humbled” to have the chance to craft a budget. 
“For nearly fifty years in America, working men and women have struggled while the rich get richer and corporations get bigger. When I first ran for office, I made it my No. 1 priority to fight to restore the middle class and advocate for the working people of our state,” McGuire said. “I am more committed than ever to that mission.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: So many credentials, so little value — what states can learn from Ohio’s reboot
description: This story first appeared at The 74, a nonprofit news site covering education. Sign up for free newsletters from The 74 to get more like this in your inbox. The gap between workforce policy ambition and the infrastructure that’s needed to make it a reality is a defining story in American workforce policy. Ohio is […]
text:
Workers moving equipment and road signs on a highway. (Getty Images)  This story first appeared at The 74, a nonprofit news site covering education. Sign up for free newsletters from The 74 to get more like this in your inbox.
The gap between workforce policy ambition and the infrastructure that’s needed to make it a reality is a defining story in American workforce policy. Ohio is an example of this problem and the pathway to solving it.
Last year, about 9,000 Ohio high school students earned a retail sales and customer service credential. State records show employers were looking to fill exactly three jobs statewide that required it. Another 4,000 students earned a stack of emergency management credentials for a field with fewer than 300 openings.
These students didn’t do anything wrong. The problem belonged to a state that built an enormous credentialing system far before it had the tools and data infrastructure to know which credentials were worth earning.
Since 2019, Ohio has allowed high school students to earn a diploma by completing career and technical education coursework and receiving an industry-recognized credential rather than passing a state test. Students responded rationally, with credential attainment rising from 53,000 in 2019 to 170,000 in 2024.
On paper, that’s a career readiness success story. But beneath the topline number is anarchy. Some credentials, like welding certifications, open doors. Others, earned in a few hours, mainly satisfy a graduation requirement rather than signal a marketable skill.
The value of these credentials differs greatly by field, according to an analysis by The Ohio State University Workforce Development and Education program. For example, credentials tied to transportation, manufacturing and construction produced wage gains lasting into people’s mid-20s. Nurse’s aide or culinary arts training showed no meaningful income advantage.
The mismatch is not unique to Ohio. Research from ExcelinEd and Burning Glass Technologies found that roughly two-thirds of states collect the data needed to know whether their credentials align with employer demand. That same analysis found that just 18% of the credentials students earn nationally are actually sought by employers.
To its credit, Ohio spent the past year building the infrastructure it should have had from the start. ExcelinEd’s Adriana Harrington calls this story a “cautionary tale,” noting that Ohio’s approved list had over 700 credentials. Working with Ohio Excels, a nonprofit formed by the state’s major chambers of commerce, the state cut its approved list to 126. It also built a framework for screening credentials on job placement, pay, field growth and whether the coursework also counts toward a degree.
Emily Passias, deputy executive director of Advance CTE, who helped build Ohio’s original list, said states have mostly been identifying credentials “based on vibes,” letting them pile up. What Ohio is attempting, she said, is to right the ship.
The state also created an online high school outcomes dashboard. It tracks what students do after they graduate, including employment, college enrollment and completion, and earnings data from the Ohio Unemployment Insurance program. It includes specific information on outcomes for those who leave high school with a CTE concentration or at least two approved workforce development courses in a single CTE career pathway program.
Other states are undertaking similar approaches, though with some differences. For example, Michigan and New Hampshire use earnings data from an outside source called the Living Wage Calculator, created by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
An Advance CTE 2024 50-state survey reports that 27 states have processes for reviewing approved credentials on a regular schedule to ensure they are still meeting program goals, though only 14 incorporate wage information in that process. The report concludes, “too many states lack robust systems, policies and data to ensure true quality and value.”
Ohio’s credential anarchy isn’t only a K-12 education story. The same problem is showing up in the new federal Workforce Pell program that started July 1 and extends Pell Grant eligibility to short-term career training programs.
A month after Ohio launched its Workforce Pell initiative, the state hadn’t approved a single program. Nine applications were submitted, six were marked incomplete and three were rejected. According to Signal Ohio, the Ohio Department of Higher Education says postsecondary institutions are still determining “their internal capacity to administer” the program.
Governors and legislators working on credentialing and Workforce Pell implementation should recognize this as a problem similar to the one Ohio just fixed in its high schools. It involves building the data infrastructure to know which credentials are actually worth earning before students pay for them, not after.
Here are five lessons states can learn from Ohio’s experience.
• Don’t wait to build the data infrastructure for determining credential value. Ohio’s dashboards arrived after more than 170,000 students had earned credentials. The fix came years behind the boom it was meant to steer. Ohio’s own approved credential list didn’t get pruned until state numbers turned embarrassing enough to force the issue.
• Count credentials as career-ready only when paired with real coursework, not as standalone certificates. The Ohio State research shows what that pairing is worth: Students who combined a credential with a CTE concentration saw a 41% income premium in their first year out of high school. That’s more than double the standalone credential bump. The advantage held up seven years later, long after the credential-only advantage had faded.
• Anchor wage thresholds to independent, regional sources. A single statewide wage-earning calculation doesn’t take into account real differences in the cost of living and labor demand. A wage that counts as solid in Youngstown, Ohio, can be modest in Columbus. That’s why a regional or independently calculated threshold is better than a single figure an agency sets for the whole state.
• Build a scheduled revalidation process into policy from the start. This will ensure that lists shrink as often as they grow. Removing a credential creates political friction that adding one rarely does. That’s why states need to implement a regular review schedule rather than waiting for an embarrassing statistic to force a review.
• The problem applies well beyond Ohio’s K-12 credentials. Community college certificates, apprenticeships and now Workforce Pell-funded training programs all rest on the same premise: that a short-term credential can be trusted to signal real value in the job market. Without the data infrastructure to check that, states can’t actually tell which credentials keep that promise and which don’t. Students are left to guess — navigating a maze instead of following a map.
Ohio, like many states, let its credential system grow before building the infrastructure needed to govern it. Every state weighing a new credentialing incentive, and every K-12 school, college or training provider chasing it, faces the same choice. They must create that infrastructure first, updating it as needed, or spend years finding out why they should have.

 Catching Our Eye

• Education. Cleveland.com’s Laura Hancock is reporting, “Trump administration approves Ohio waiver critics say risks school privatization.”
U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon has approved an Ohio plan that gives the state more control over how it handles struggling public schools and greater flexibility in how it spends federal education money.
Critics say the changes could make it easier for Ohio to turn low-performing public schools into charter schools or close them, while allowing federal money intended to help students in high-poverty schools to be spent elsewhere.
McMahon formally signed off on the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce’s plan Oct. 30, granting the department’s request for a waiver from parts of a key federal education law.
• Communication. The Ohio Newsroom’s Kendall Crawford is reporting, “Amid plans to shut off landlines, rural Ohioans worry of isolation.”
Decades ago, before cell phones buzzed and beeped in everyone’s pockets, people relied on a network of copper wires to stay connected to loved ones. A landline phone’s chime was a familiar part of everyday life.
In some Appalachian Ohio homes, like Paul Feezel’s, those landlines are still ringing.
Feezel said the outdated tech is his only option. He lives in a valley, about a mile from the road on the outskirts of rural Carrollton. The beautiful hills he loves are also the obstacle to good cell service or satellite connection.
