FAYETTEVILLE, N.C.— North Carolina environmental regulators this week sent a scathing critique to Chemours, which is responsible for contaminating at least 10 counties with toxic “forever chemicals,” arguing that the company’s cleanup proposal violates the terms of a consent order.
The state Department of Environmental Quality detailed multiple inadequacies in the company’s plan to remediate widespread, decades-old groundwater and soil contamination from PFAS chemicals in southeastern North Carolina.
“Today’s direction to the company makes clear that DEQ expects Chemours to clean up all the areas they have polluted,” said DEQ Secretary Reid Wilson in a prepared statement. “DEQ will hold Chemours accountable no matter how long it takes.”
The company’s predecessor, DuPont, is responsible for some of the contamination emanating from the Fayetteville Works plant, but it shielded itself from liability when it spun off Chemours in 2015. An international company, Chemours manufactures chemicals used to make Teflon cookware, data center coolants and grease-, water- and stain-resistant consumer products.
DEQ’s letter said the agency also determined the company could not justify how it assessed the public health and environmental risk of PFAS exposure. The letter cited numerous instances of what DEQ described as missing data, substandard sampling methods and flawed analyses in Chemours’ reports. In some cases, these errors led the company to reach conclusions that lacked a factual, scientific or legal basis, according to the letter.
The groundwater and soil remediation must be detailed in a corrective action plan, a key component of a 2019 consent order between the company, DEQ and the nonprofit Cape Fear River Watch. The agency rejected the company’s draft corrective action plan in 2020, calling it “inadequate” and lacking a “thorough technical basis.”
Progress on the plan stalled for six years until September, when the state announced it had reached a half-billion dollar settlement with Chemours that included a provision accelerating progress on its completion. The settlement required DEQ to provide written feedback to Chemours.
A Chemours spokesperson told Inside Climate News that with DEQ’s formal feedback to its 2019 corrective action plan, risk assessment and other studies “now in hand, we can move forward. We are reviewing the comments in detail and will respond through the established process.”
Because of shortcomings in Chemours’ data and analysis, DEQ wrote, neither the company nor the agency knows the full extent of the PFAS contamination in the Lower Cape Fear River Basin, nearly 10 years after the public first learned of it through media reports.
Over 36 pages, DEQ rebutted the company’s conclusions about the extent of the contamination and the public health and ecological risks.
Chemours told DEQ that current concentrations of the PFAS chemical GenX near the Fayetteville Works plant were unlikely to harm human health even without treating the groundwater. However, the state said, Chemours failed to evaluate all PFAS originating from the plant, as legally required. DEQ said the company also used outdated toxicological data for GenX, one of 15,000 types of PFAS compounds.

What are forever chemicals?

There are more than 15,000 types of PFAS—per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, the so-called “forever chemicals.” They are found in many consumer products, such as microwave popcorn bags, pizza boxes, stain- and water-resistant clothing and furniture, and lithium-ion batteries, including those used in electric vehicles.
They’ve been linked to many serious health conditions, including several types of cancer.
PFAS also disrupt the ocean’s ability to sequester carbon, a driver of climate change. PFAS manufacturers emit thousands of tons of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere each year.
In 2022, the Chemours Fayetteville plant emitted 52,000 tons of greenhouse gases, according to EPA data.




Chemours’ health risk assessment excluded people who regularly fish in the Cape Fear River for food, and the company didn’t account for other ways people could become exposed, such as eating contaminated vegetables, touching water or soil that contains PFAS or inhaling the compounds, the state added.
Image: Adobe Stock
DEQ also requested that Chemours complete its investigation about biosolids—sewage sludge—that could have originated from the plant and have been applied to farm fields. The agency requested comprehensive information about where and when the biosolids were shipped offsite and their quantities.
Sewage sludge is often used to fertilize farm fields. When the sludge is contaminated, the PFAS can seep into the soil, groundwater and drinking water wells.
“The agency is asking the company to look into how their contamination is truly going to harm communities,” said Jean Zhuang, senior attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center, which represents Cape Fear River Watch. “It demands much more of Chemours than the company has ever done so far.”
Over the past six years, Chemours has spent about $1.2 billion on complying with some provisions of the consent order. The company installed a thermal oxidizer to remove 99.9 percent of all PFAS emissions from the air, offered free water filtration systems to more than 10,000 homes with contaminated wells and built a mile-long underground barrier wall to prevent contaminated groundwater seeping from the site and into the Cape Fear River.
These projects have reduced, although not eliminated, the amount of PFAS entering the environment. Contaminated groundwater continues to seep from the Fayetteville Works plant into the river and other surface waters; PFAS are still entering the air.
The magnitude of the contamination is so vast that Chemours has previously told DEQ it is “technologically and economically infeasible” to comply as closely as possible with the state’s groundwater rules.
However, DEQ told Chemours in the letter that the company has not provided sufficient evidence to support that conclusion. “While DEQ recognizes that the geographic scope of the contamination caused by Chemours is enormous and unprecedented in this state,” DEQ Deputy Secretary Sushma Masemore wrote, “the vast scope does not release Chemours of its obligation to thoroughly evaluate all remedial alternatives.”
Chemours’ sampling methods to determine health and ecological effects were also flawed, according to the letter. For example, contractors sampled soil along roadways, which is often trucked in from other areas. And instead of collecting earthworms to assess exposure risks in the soil, contractors evaluated grasshoppers, crickets and dragonflies—which don’t live in the dirt.
Contractors also wiped loose dirt off leaves before collecting them, which likely removed PFAS bound to the dust that was deposited through the air, the state said.
Chemours failed to sample aquatic plants and organisms and excluded animals from its studies due to time constraints, which DEQ called “an inadequate justification.”
Questions about air emissions 
Chemours has also failed to identify all of the PFAS compounds it is emitting into the air from the Fayetteville Works plant, which is continuing to contaminate the groundwater, Michael Abraczinskas, director of the state’s Division of Air Quality, wrote in a separate letter.
Nor do the company’s sampling and reporting methods meet quality control standards, Abraczinskas wrote, adding that “the issues identified in this letter require immediate attention and corrective actions.”
There is a direct link between air emissions that contain PFAS and contaminated groundwater. After the compounds enter the air, they can travel on the wind and fall to the earth, where they seep into soil and groundwater. PFAS traced to the Fayetteville plant, such as PFMOAA and GenX, have been detected in private drinking water wells as far as 25 miles away.
“Chemours has acted like it’s done everything it needs to do on air emissions, and even asked to expand its facility,” Zhuang said, “and DEQ is saying, ‘No, they are continuing to be an issue, and we’re going to take this really seriously.’”
NC AG Jackson calls on residents to weigh in on Chemours’ ‘backroom deal’ over PFAS

Chemours has underestimated its air emissions at least twice before, DEQ records show. In 2018, state regulators found Chemours was emitting 2,700 pounds of GenX into the air—amounts 40 times higher than the company had originally reported in early 2017, and four times higher than the company’s revised estimates.
In 2021, the company again underreported its GenX emissions by 40 percent. The next year, DEQ fined Chemours $305,000 for failing to maintain air pollution control equipment, which allowed excessive amounts of GenX to enter the air.
Chemours plans to expand its Fayetteville Works plant, which DuPont opened in the early 1980s. The company filed an air permit application with the state in 2022 and revised it last year. However, environmental advocates, including the Southern Environmental Law Center, objected to the application because it redacted key information that Chemours claimed was confidential, including emission rates from stack testing, hours of operation and production figures.
DEQ notified Chemours nearly a year ago that the application was on hold until the company could submit revised emission calculations necessary for the Division of Air Quality to conduct review. Chemours has yet to submit this information, an agency spokesman said.
Based on the new deficiencies identified in its letter, the division could request additional data.
Chemours has until February to file a plan to address the state’s air concerns listed in the letter. As for the groundwater and soil cleanup plan under the consent order, DEQ has asked Chemours to respond to the state’s critique within 60 days.
There still is no timeline for the work to be completed. Given the scope of the contamination, it could take decades.

name: Source New Mexico
title: ICE increases arrests at New Mexico home construction sites, putting workers on edge
description: New Mexico homebuilders are reporting a sharp increase of federal immigration raids at home construction sites across Albuquerque and Santa Fe in recent weeks, resulting in arrests and project delays across the industry during a statewide housing shortage.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcements agents targeted workers building these single-family Habitat for Humanity homes in Albuquerque on Nov. 10, 2026, according to the organization’s CEO, amid an apparent increase in ICE activity at home construction sites across the state. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico homebuilders are reporting a sharp increase of federal immigration raids at home construction sites across Albuquerque and Santa Fe in recent weeks, resulting in arrests and project delays across the industry during a statewide housing shortage.
Miles Dylan Conway, CEO of the New Mexico Home Builders Association, told Source NM that he’s received approximately 20 calls or texts from developers in the last week reporting that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have descended on home construction sites, often in unmarked SUVs, and have arrested multiple workers at a time.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The level of activity I’ve had on my phone, the calls from members who are sometimes calling on behalf of their subcontractors, are telling me that the pace and intensity of the immigration enforcement is significantly escalated,” he said.
ICE officials did not respond to Source NM’s emailed request for comment Tuesday about whether the agency is stepping up its activity at home construction sites and how many people it has detained.
But Source NM’s interviews with home developers, immigration advocacy groups and homebuilder organizations suggest at least five such operations netting more than a dozen arrests have occurred at construction sites over the last month. Social media video has also shown ICE agents leading handcuffed workers away from partially built homes in Santa Fe and Albuquerque in recent weeks. 
The raids have occurred at large, multi-family developments as well as at least one small project site in a low-income Albuquerque neighborhood.
On Tuesday morning, ICE agents arrived in Albuquerque’s San Jose neighborhood as workers were pouring concrete for driveways on two nearly complete, single-family Habitat for Humanity homes, Bill Bidal, CEO of the Greater Albuquerque Habitat for Humanity, told Source NM on Wednesday. 
“Out of the blue, the federal authorities showed up,” Bidal, who said he arrived at the site shortly after workers fled, relayed. “We’ve heard rumors all over town for the last couple weeks about activity, but to have it hit home like this was very, very sudden.”
ICE didn’t detain any Habitat for Humanity contractors, Bidal said, and the two low-income families the homes are built for will likely be able to move in after Thanksgiving. But he said he remains “in total shock.”
Sales employees from Twilight Homes, which is developing several large subdivisions in Albuquerque and Santa Fe, told Source NM on Wednesday that ICE targeted their subcontractors in recent weeks and those of other developers at adjacent sites. 
Pauline Hansen, a sales counselor for Twilight Homes in Mesa Del Sol, said ICE agents have been out “several times” in the last few weeks to hers and other companies’ sites in the subdivision south of Albuquerque. ICE detained four subcontractors doing concrete work for Twilight Homes several weeks ago, she said, and she witnessed an additional raid last week for another company during which ICE arrested an additional four workers on a different development. 
“They’re going everywhere, apparently,” she said. “It’s quite disturbing.”
Federal immigration agents have increased their arrests at New Mexico home construction sites in recent weeks, including at Los Brios in Santa, a Twilight Homes development pictured above Nov. 11, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)
Fear of ICE arrests has prompted workers not to show up to job sites, even in locations that ICE hasn’t targeted, Conway said. 
“A lot of projects this week are not operating,” he said. “It’s oftentimes even folks with documentation — visas and work permits — are not coming to work because the potential for them to get swept up in one of these actions is very real.”
Johanna Gilligan, the CEO of nonprofit developer Homewise, told Source NM on Wednesday that workers on Homewise projects, particularly those contracted for stucco work, have shown up at low rates over the last month or so. She said her organization is anticipating at least weeks of delays in projects being completed.
“It has the potential to have a knock-on effect, just out of people taking an abundance of precaution,” she said about workers afraid to show up to job sites. “So we are definitely concerned about how this could be exacerbating what’s already a hard process of building homes.”
The National Association of Home Builders estimates that the industry relies on a workforce that is approximately 30% foreign-born. In a state that lacks approximately 58,000 affordable housing units, Conway said he is hoping homebuilders will prevail upon President Donald Trump’s administration to stop the crackdown. 
The administration has revoked millions of immigrants’ work permits in the last two years, including in the construction industries. But Trump also said he was open to making a deal on work permits in certain industries in an interview shortly after the midterm elections last week in which Democrats reclaimed control over both chambers of Congress. 
Conway said he hopes New Mexico homebuilders will speak up more in the coming days to pressure Trump to make a deal. 
“When I get that many calls and texts, there just seems to be an overwhelming energy to try and find a strategy forward,” he said. “We just really need a strategy forward that’s different than what’s happening now.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Commentary: The fine art of constitution writing, and the continued lengthening of Tennessee’s Constitution
description: Tennessee voters this month grew our state’s constitution by 442 words.  Amendment One, expanding the number of crimes for which the accused can be held without bail, passed by better than a two-to-one margin. It added 152 words and deleted 53.  Amendment Two, banning a statewide property tax, also passed more than two-to-one. It added […]
text:
The U.S. Constitution is a model of brevity, but Tennessee lawmakers can't stop adding to that of the Volunteer State. (Illustration: Getty Images)Tennessee voters this month grew our state’s constitution by 442 words. 
Amendment One, expanding the number of crimes for which the accused can be held without bail, passed by better than a two-to-one margin. It added 152 words and deleted 53.  Amendment Two, banning a statewide property tax, also passed more than two-to-one. It added 36 words and deleted 20.  Amendment Three, a victim’s rights measure, passed by better than a three-to-one margin. It added 517 words and deleted 190.
Let’s put aside, for a moment, the merits of each of these public policy questions and instead ask ourselves what kind of things belong in state constitutions and which are better placed in statutes (laws) or left to judicial discretion (interpretation of laws)?
The U. S. Constitution is a model of brevity. The original draft contained just 4,543 words, including the signatures of the 39 signing delegates. It has 27 amendments, the first ten of which —the Bill of Rights — have been with our republic since the start. Add in those amendments and 17 subsequent ones and our Constitution grows to 7,591 words — still one of the shortest national constitutions in the world. The original handwritten text fit on just four large parchment sheets.
Tennessee voters will decide whether those accused of some felonies lose right to pretrial bail

By contrast, the average state constitution is about 26,000 words, more than three times as long. Alabama’s state constitution is a behemoth at an estimated 388,882 words. The recent additions send Tennessee’s state constitution over 14,000 words, still rather modest compared to many other states — Texas at nearly 87,000, Oklahoma’s topping 81,000, Louisiana and Missouri both clocking in at more than 69,000.
The impulse when crafting a constitution is to put a lot of things in there to be certain you get the kind of society you want. Some of these provisions don’t age well and look silly or worse in retrospect. We still have a provision, one hopes unnecessary, preventing those who fight in or challenge others to duels from holding public office in our state (Article IX, Section 3). In 2022 Tennessee voters quietly removed a provision that allowed slavery or involuntary servitude as a criminal punishment. That same year we also removed an obsolete (and long held unenforceable by federal courts) ban on the clergy serving in the General Assembly.
Several states have “zombie” provisions that remain on the books but are unenforceable, including literacy tests for voting, restricting certain offices only to men and disqualifying atheists from public office.
Amended: All four amendments to Tennessee’s Constitution pass overwhelmingly

Florida’s Constitution (Article X, Section 21) prohibits the cruel and inhumane confinement of pregnant pigs on farms. Now, before anyone squeals that I am for inhumane treatment of pigs, let me reiterate this column is not about the merits of the policy; it’s about what needs to be in a constitution and what works just fine as a statute.
Constitutions set out the basic functions of government (done at what level and by what body) and also protect against government overreach by delineating what rights exist, are held by the people, and cannot be abridged by the government. 
The U.S. Constitution is far from a perfect model, especially when one considers the democracy twisting potential of the Electoral College and some of the interpretation abuses by the current Supreme Court. Nevertheless, it remains a good work in progress and usually a coherent structure.
Elected officials, new members of the military, and naturalized citizens all take an oath to uphold the Constitution. Many groups give out pocket copies of it, and many Members of Congress repeatedly point out how they carry those pocket copies with them. This “less is more” approach works so long as some neutral court is given the task of interpreting constitutional application. The founders, for example, did not and could not envision video recorders, much less streaming services, but they did set out a provision, Article I, Section 8, Clause 8, for Congress “To Promote the Progress of Science and the Useful Arts, by securing for limited Times to Authors and Inventors the exclusive Right to their respective Writings and Discoveries.” Past precedent regarding copyrights and patents thus can guide courts in these matters.
In Tennessee, we could and should let judges weigh the merits of when to hold without bail those not yet convicted of anything. We could and should also pass laws about victim rights and the procedures to assure them. We probably do not need to doubly and triply assure our fidelity to no state income tax ever. We have made all of these constitutional matters, however, and just for a moment or two let us ask ourselves, what really requires constitutional amendment and what is pompous pandering.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV school officials ask Supreme Court to halt Logan court proceedings regarding school closure
description: West Virginia school officials are asking the state’s highest court to step in and stop a lower court’s decision temporarily preventing the closure of a Logan County elementary school.
text:
(Getty Images)West Virginia school officials are asking the state’s highest court to step in and stop a lower court’s decision temporarily preventing the closure of a Logan County elementary school.
The state Department of Education and the Logan County school board this week filed an emergency writ of prohibition with the state Supreme Court of Appeals. The legal action seeks to halt proceedings in Logan County Circuit Court, where Judge Sabrina Deskins last week granted a temporary restraining order preventing school officials from taking further action to close South Man Elementary School.
The Logan school board is considering consolidating the school into Man Elementary School, a decision that would require the approval of the state school board.
School officials are also considering closing Hugh Dingess Elementary and Justice Elementary, all of which have fewer than 100 students and need repairs to bring them up to code, school officials have said.
Deskins granted a temporary restraining order requested by parent Lauren Browning and community member Donna Thibault, who asked the judge to stop school officials from moving forward with closing South Man until the resolution of legal challenges over the state school aid formula and the 2027 legislative session, which is expected to focus on the school aid formula.
The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia filed a lawsuit in September over the funding formula, asking the the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals to require lawmakers to correct it.
Deskin’s order last week directed the Logan school board to cancel a public hearing on the school closure scheduled for Nov. 4, and not to move forward with a vote on the proposed closure that had been planned for Thursday.
In the emergency petition filed Thursday, attorneys for the school boards argued that they are empowered by law to close and consolidate schools in the state, and that Deskin’s order prevented them from complying with the laws.
“That result cannot stand — this Court should issue a writ of prohibition undoing the Circuit Court’s temporary restraining order and prohibiting it from blocking Petitioners from complying with West Virginia law governing school closure,” the petition said.
“This case implicates core separation of powers principles. The Legislature creates laws that govern the school system. The West Virginia Board of Education creates the policies and rules to manage the day-to-day operation of the school system, including ‘clos(ing) and consolidat(ing) schools when it deems necessary.’”
In their lawsuit, attorneys for Browning and Thibault argue that the judge should grant the restraining order until after the Legislature has time to address the school funding aid formula.
“It would be tragic to deny the (temporary restraining order) and South Man Elementary School closes, and then in six months the legislature fixes the funding formula solving the very funding issues the defendant publicly states are inadequate to keep SMES open and thriving,” attorneys wrote in the petition.
“Granting the relief of a temporary restraining order would permit the Supreme Court time to address the numerous legal challenges to the current school funding formula, as well as the Legislature time to allocate resources to counties that meet the mandate required by the West Virginia Constitution of providing a thorough and efficient system of free schools. If neither happens, the defendant is no worse off.”
School officials told lawmakers this week they would need an increase of $410 million in state aid for public schools to stabilize public school finances, which are in dire straits and have prompted a wave of school closures across the state.
The Logan County court has indicated it could not hold a hearing in the case until Dec. 8, a date the state school board said is too late
“If this Court does not issue a writ of prohibition now, Petitioners cannot follow the law and resolve whether to consolidate South Man Elementary School into Man Elementary School effective for the 2027-2028 school year,” the school boards wrote.
“Time is of the essence. School closure decisions must be made shortly, or it will be too late to issue a closure decision affecting the 2027-2028 school year,” the petition said. It added that if the decision to close the school is postponed, state taxpayers will pay an $1.3 million for each additional year the school remains open.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Outgoing DFL Rep. Dan Wolgamott arrested again on suspicion of driving while impaired
description: Rep. Dan Wolgamott, DFL-St. Cloud, was arrested by the St. Cloud Police Department on Wednesday on suspicion of driving while impaired. The fourth-term legislator was arrested just after 9 p.m. on Wednesday and booked into the Stearns County Jail. He was arrested on three DWI-related charges, including criminal vehicular operation, bodily harm under the infl[...]
text:
Then-House Speaker Pro-Tempore Dan Wolgamott, DFL-St. Cloud, hands the omnibus supplemental education finance and policy bill to Chief Clerk Pat Murphy on April 27. (Photo by Paul Battaglia/Minnesota House Information.)Rep. Dan Wolgamott, DFL-St. Cloud, was arrested by the St. Cloud Police Department on Wednesday on suspicion of driving while impaired.
The fourth-term legislator was arrested just after 9 p.m. on Wednesday and booked into the Stearns County Jail. He was arrested on three DWI-related charges, including criminal vehicular operation, bodily harm under the influence of alcohol; third-degree driving while impaired; and operating a vehicle under the influence of alcohol.
The circumstances surrounding Wolgamott’s arrest are unclear, but a charge for bodily harm criminal vehicular operation indicates police judged that someone was injured, according to state statute.
Wolgamott did not answer a Reformer call seeking comment, and his voice mail box was full. He did not immediately respond to a text message seeking comment. The Stearns County Jail roster indicates Wolgamott was still in jail as of Thursday morning.
Wolgamott is leaving the Legislature after an unsuccessful run for state auditor.
In 2023, Wolgamott was arrested by the state patrol on suspicion of DWI in Kanabec County. Wolgamott pleaded guilty to a 4th degree DWI charge after a Minnesota State Patrol trooper pulled him over and arrested him near Mora, Minnesota. In that incident, Wolgamott acknowledged that his blood alcohol concentration was above the .08 legal limit.
The 2023 arrest came after someone called in a complaint about a person drinking in a liquor store parking lot in Mora. The trooper later saw the car weaving within its own lane, according to the state patrol’s incident report, and the trooper pulled the car over. Wolgamott was identified as the driver.
In security camera footage of the liquor store parking lot, Wolgamott appeared to take a drink out of a bottle, put it in his trunk, get back in his car and drive away.
In a statement at the time, Wolgamott said he had undergone professional testing and received “an assessment that I do not have an alcohol-use disorder.” In addition, Wolgamott said he attended an eight-hour alcohol education class and a Mothers Against Drunk Driving victim panel.
A number of Minnesota lawmakers have been arrested on suspicion of drunk driving in recent years. Most recently, then-Rep. Elliott Engen, R-White Bear Lake Township, was arrested in March on suspicion of DWI. Rep. Walter Hudson, R-Albertville, was a passenger in his vehicle and he was not charged with a crime. Hudson was carrying a firearm while impaired, which is against the law, though he was never charged.
Other current lawmakers arrested include DFL Rep. Brion Curran, DFL-White Bear Lake, DFL Sen. Tou Xiong, DFL-Maplewood, and Sen. John Jasinski, R-Fairbault.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland environment secretary to step down, in latest shakeup to Moore’s Cabinet
description: Maryland Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain and Emergency Management Secretary Russell Strickland both announced their departures Thursday, as the Moore administration continues remaking its leadership ahead of a second term.
text:
Maryland Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain speaks at an Oct. 2, 2025, event at the Conowingo Dam. McIlwain announced Thursday she is stepping down, the latest Cabinet departure as Gov. Wes Moore prepares for his second term. (File photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Serena McIlwain, who has led Gov. Wes Moore’s (D) environmental department since shortly after his inauguration in 2023, will step down at the end of this year, she announced Thursday.
McIlwain, who came to the department from the California Environmental Protection Agency, said in an email to staff on Thursday morning that she would be resigning “after 38 rewarding years in public service and four incredible years serving as your Secretary.”
“When I returned home to Maryland to lead this agency, my priority was to support and empower the dedicated professionals who protect our state’s air, land, and water every single day. Thanks to your tireless efforts, we have accomplished extraordinary things,” McIlwain wrote.
Lee, Scruggs, Rothstein depart Moore’s Cabinet

Deputy Secretary Adam Ortiz will step in as acting secretary on Jan. 1, McIlwain said in her email. Ortiz previously served as a regional administrator for President Joe Biden’s (D) Environmental Protection Agency, overseeing the regional office for Maryland and four other states, plus the District of Columbia.
Also departing is Secretary of Emergency Management Russell Strickland, who will retire on Dec. 8. Moore announced he will appoint Montgomery County Assistant Chief Administrative Officer Earl Stoddard to serve as acting secretary, beginning Dec. 9.
Since winning a second term on Nov. 3, Moore has announced a new chief of staff as well as other changes to his Cabinet: Last week, the secretaries of State, Veterans and Military Affairs, and Public Safety and Correctional Services all cleaned out their desks and were replaced immediately by interim directors.
Additional changes are expected before the General Assembly reconvenes and Moore is sworn in for a second term in January. Such changes are not uncommon.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska education funding task force seeks input on plans to boost schools
description: After a nearly 18-month investigation, a joint legislative task force on education funding seeks not only to boost state spending on schools but to change the way Alaska allocates funding to support its troubled K-12 education system. Among the key recommendations in the draft report released Monday is the finding that annual education spending should […]
text:
Students begin their first day of school at the Tlingit Culture, Language and Literacy program at Harborview Elementary School in Juneau on Aug. 15, 2025 (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)After a nearly 18-month investigation, a joint legislative task force on education funding seeks not only to boost state spending on schools but to change the way Alaska allocates funding to support its troubled K-12 education system. 	

The Legislative Task Force on Education Funding will hear in-person public comment Thursday, Nov. 12 
9:00 am – noon: Anchorage LIO in-person testimony
1:00 pm – 3:00 pm: Fairbanks LIO in-person testimony
3:00 pm – 5:00 pm: Juneau in-person testimony at the Capitol Building in the Davis Committee Room (106)
5:00 pm – 7:00 pm: Kenai LIO in-person testimony
Those in the Anchorage area may call 907-563-9085, and those in the Juneau area may call 907-586-9085. From all other areas of Alaska, commenters may call 844-586-9085.
Written public comments are due by December 8 and can be emailed to TFEF@akleg.gov or edfundtaskforce@akleg.gov. 
Over the next two months, the draft report will be further refined, designed, and finalized prior to being officially submitted by the first day of the 2027 legislative session.


Among the key recommendations in the draft report released Monday is the finding that annual education spending should be adjusted with inflation, and that funding for school facilities maintenance and rising energy costs should be separate from dollars intended for student instruction. 
The task force also recommends that the question of how much the state should spend on education should be examined by a future independent “adequacy study” to see whether Alaska delivers adequate funding to schools. 
The Legislature’s task force was launched in July 2025 in the wake of Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s partial veto of an increase to per-student funding, which lawmakers overrode in a special session later that summer. Legislators agreed the task force would further examine funding for schools and ways to address rising costs of utilities, maintenance, transportation and insurance, as well as funding levels and accountability provisions.
The joint task force includes co-chairs Sen. Löki Tobin, D-Anchorage, and Rep. Rebecca Himschoot, I-Dillingham; Sens. Mike Cronk, R-Tok, and Jesse Kiehl, D-Juneau; and Reps. Justin Ruffridge, R-Soldotna, and Andi Story, D-Juneau. 
The task force held nine public meetings, and members made 19 school visits — in districts including the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, Anchorage, Fairbanks, Nenana, Kenai Peninsula, Juneau and Lower Kuskokwim. 
The task force released a nine page draft report of short, mid and long-term recommendations and will hear public comment in-person and call-in on Thursday and written comments until Dec. 8.  
The draft report references previous studies, expert recommendations and bills considered, as well as input from educators, district leaders and school visits and underscores where the incoming Legislature should take action, Tobin said.
“We really relied on all of those folks to give us quality information that we compiled into this document, and these recommendations don’t come from the task force as much as they come from Alaskans,” she said. 
“This is what our community is telling us needs to happen, and has told us this needs to happen for quite a while, and now is the time for us to actually act on these suggestions,” she said. 
Ruffridge, a Soldotna Republican, echoed the sentiment and the call for public input on the task force’s recommendations. “This is really the opportunity to hear from people statewide of what they consider to be some issues that they would like to see addressed,” he said.
How much the state should spend on education has been the focal point of ongoing political and financial debates among the Legislature and with the Dunleavy administration for years. The task force recommended an adequacy study examining the state’s funding formula.
Tobin said other states like Wyoming, Maryland and Massachusetts conduct regular adequacy studies, and an independent analysis is needed of Alaska’s complex education funding formula. The study would examine per student funding, known as the base student allocation, or BSA, and the multipliers added for factors like school size, special education services and correspondence schools, among others.  
“We knew if we wanted to take the politics out of the BSA, we needed this independent analysis,” Tobin said.     

Sen. Löki Tobin, D-Anchorage, speaks at a Senate press conference on Feb. 4, 2025 (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Ruffridge said he hopes the adequacy study will take a close look at the state’s funding formula and “whether or not the pieces of the foundation formula are actually built to fund the things that people want.”
Some of the areas Ruffridge said he’s heard about from constituents are smaller class sizes, access to extracurriculars like music and sports, and well-maintained buildings, “but our formula doesn’t really take that into account at all,” he said.
“I would really like to see study dollars go towards really analyzing the formula in ways that it could be changed to more comprehensively cover what it is that goes into offering you know a well rounded education system,” he said.
Tobin and Himschoot submitted a request for an estimated $500,000 to contract researchers to conduct the study, and encouraged a partnership with the University of Alaska’s Institute for Social and Economic Research, according to a letter to the Legislative Audit and Budget Committee. Lawmakers had approved $400,000 for such a study this year, but Dunleavy vetoed it.
“We would have hoped that we would have been part way through that process at this point,” said Tobin. “Unfortunately, once again, Mike Dunleavy has stymied that input, has stymied that science-based approach to analyzing our school formula, and that is really at the detriment of our public education system, because we’re going through another year at the very least of potentially not having adequately funded education because we don’t have the information we need to make informed policy decisions in those legislative roles.”
Short term recommendations
In the short-term, the task force recommended separate state dollars for funding school operations, facilities maintenance and repairs outside the pool of funds meant for instruction. 
It noted the state’s funding for capital projects has eligibility rules that excludes routine maintenance and operations and so a separate funding stream for school facilities would enable more funds dedicated to educating students.     

The Aniak Jr. Sr. High School is seen on Jan. 21, 2025. The Kuspuk School District evacuated around 50 students from pre-K to 12th grade, plus administrative offices, as the roof of the gymnasium of the Aniak Jr. Sr. High School was heard audibly cracking and breaking apart, due to a shifting foundation. The district is now planning for a controlled demolition to prevent total collapse of the building. (Photo courtesy of the Kuspuk School District)
 

Alaska has a major school maintenance backlog, estimated at $535 million in needed repairs, the report noted, and so the task force recommended the Legislature re-evaluate the regulatory process for how those repairs are funded. “Inaction will only increase the eventual costs of repair or replacement and continue to put children at risk,” it wrote.
Ruffridge called the current school maintenance system “appalling.” 
“I’ve never seen such a difficult scenario that faces, especially school districts with not a lot of staff or personnel, and the hundreds of pages of documentation that have to be produced, really for very low likelihood of getting any dollars, and sometimes (they) wait decades to have any sort of action taken on pretty significant maintenance needs,” he said. He said he thinks there will be the political appetite in the next Legislature to address those funding needs. 
Members also recommended the state fund rising energy costs for school districts. Last year, lawmakers approved a bill to reimburse districts’ energy costs based on a three-year average, but it requires future Legislatures to fund the program, which the task force recommended. 
“The process that we had created to deal with major maintenance and capital improvements has not been working. There needs to be a different approach that provides stable and consistent funding for every school across the state to ensure that that building is safe, it is warm, it’s well lit, and that it has the right technology in its facility,” Tobin said. “To ensure our young people are learning, and have tools and the skills they need to become future workers in our labor force.”
More broadly, members recommended several changes in the legislative budgeting process.
The task force recommended the base student allocation be adjusted with inflation each year, similar to how the state calculates an adjusted base budget for other state agencies in order to maintain services at a status quo level. “If the Base Student Allocation remains the same from year to year but the cost of delivering education increases, then the BSA is no longer sufficient to provide an adequate education,” it wrote. 
Additionally, the task force recommended the Legislature appropriate education funding earlier in the year, rather than in June or July, after school district budgets are finalized and layoff notices sent out. “This instability leads to unnecessary layoffs, delayed hiring, and loss of talented educators,” the report said. 
Instead of budgets based on annual student counts, the task force recommended state funding be based on a three-year average of student counts to allow more stable, predictable funding. The lawmakers recommended the Legislature adopt a bill to that effect similar to legislation introduced by Story, a Juneau Democrat and member of the task force, last year which passed the House but failed to advance in the Senate.
While Alaska law mandates the Legislature “establish and maintain” a public education system for all Alaskan students, members of the task force recommended an established definition of “adequate education.” That’s to ensure funding meets a standard so that all students have access to educational opportunities, qualified teachers with training and support, a safe learning environment, and well-maintained facilities, among others. 
Tobin said creating that definition in statute will help the Legislature make its budget decisions. 
Midterm recommendations
In the midterm, the task force recommended reevaluating the funding formula for transportation, to include accommodations for fluctuations in students with a hold-harmless provision. 
It recommended updating the funding formula for residential boarding schools, which has not changed since 2014, and updating the cap for school districts’ contribution to charter schools to more accurately reflect costs.
For homeschool programs, known as correspondence programs, the task force recommended a review of existing statutes to ensure those students are being provided an adequate education, noting currently the statutes “allow broad exemptions from statewide content standards, proficiency assessments, and fiscal audits.” 
Currently, state law allows homeschool parents and guardians to opt their student out of state testing. Last year, just 14.6% of homeschool students participated in the state’s standard assessment for math, while 80% of students in district schools participated, according to the Alaska Department of Education and Early Development. 
The task force also called for districts to look into methods for incorporating homeschool programs into district neighborhood schools because they say post-pandemic research shows that “in-person learning significantly outperforms online and distance learning.”
In order to boost teacher recruitment and retention, particularly to address high turnover in rural districts, members of the task force said they support the recommendations of a 2023 Teacher Retention and Recruitment survey of over 4,000 educators. 
Tobin said the task force’s final report will include more detailed recommendations for supporting teachers, including reviving a public pension system, increasing competitive pay and boosting professional development opportunities. 
Long-term recommendations 

Point Higgins Elementary School was one of the two elementary schools closed this year in Ketchikan due to budget cuts. Staff and volunteers helped move out the school in early June 2026. (Photo by Niki Suomala)

Many Alaska school districts faced steep budget shortfalls this year, resulting in the closure of 12 schools. Superintendents named the rising cost of health insurance as a major cost driver for districts. The task force recommended continuing to examine ways to reduce healthcare costs, including pooling insured workers and “exploring a publicly funded health insurance program.”
Other long-term recommendations include increasing the number of career and technical education instructors, creating a statewide absentee accounting system and creating incentives for districts to standardize equipment and create shared services agreements with regional partners. 
It also recommended identifying dedicated funding with local partners to enhance community and culture-based education opportunities. 
Tobin said the task force will continue to incorporate input from public comments in-person and by phone on Thursday, and those submitted in writing, into the final recommendations which will be delivered on the first day of the 35th Legislative session on Jan. 19.
“We wanted it to be a representative process, a democratic process…feedback is critical to the next steps forward,” she said. “At the end, the product is going to be one that we can all say, ‘Here’s what we do collectively believe is going to help improve education.’”

name: Mississippi Today
title: For Black trailblazers in Mississippi, Colom’s Senate win is personal
description: U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom waves to his supporters during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026.
text:
Mike Espy knows better than anyone what it takes to blaze trails in Mississippi politics. He did it in Congress, then again in a presidential cabinet, and came close to doing it again in the U.S. Senate. 
For Espy and many other Black Mississippians who were among the first to win elected office in the state, Scott Colom’s Wednesday night victory, which will make him the first Black person to represent Mississippi in the U.S. Senate since post-Civil War Reconstruction, is both a personal celebration and the culmination of decades of civil rights organizing.
READ MORE: Colom wins: Mississippi picks another senator
Espy, the first Black person to represent Mississippi in the U.S. House since Reconstruction and the first Black person to become U.S. agriculture secretary, also unsuccessfully ran against Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith twice, in a special election in 2018 and a regular election in 2020. 
Espy served as an adviser to Colom this year, handing over his donor and voter lists in the hope that his losses “paved the road” for the senator-elect, he said in an interview.
“There is a time and place for everything,” Espy said. “This is Scott Colom’s time, and his place is in the U.S. Senate. I’m so pleased with the way he ran his campaign, and I was happy to support him.”
Espy found ways around the old power structure
Espy and Colom share similar stories of how they were initially shut out of power by incumbent politicians but persevered to use that to their advantage.  
Democratic Senate hopeful Mike Espy concedes to incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith on Nov. 3, 2020, at the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Colom was blocked from getting a federal judgeship by Hyde-Smith. Espy was denied support from longtime Mississippi U.S. Rep. Jamie Whitten to gain congressional clout. Yet both would go on to secure other high-ranking positions. 
It’s a pattern that has played out through Mississippi’s political history. Politicians selfishly hold onto power and try to close the door on others seeking to gain it. But scrappy challengers, time and time again, jammed their foot in that door and, occasionally, yanked it open. 
Espy, in 1992, had served three terms on the House Budget Committee, steering money toward many parts of rural Mississippi. But internal rules of the Democratic caucus prevented him from serving another term on the committee. 
Still eager to divert money and projects to his impoverished district in the Mississippi Delta, Espy thought he could win Whitten’s support to secure a spot on the powerful House Appropriations Committee. 
Whitten was retiring from Congress and departing as chairman of the committee. If he had backed his fellow Mississippi Democrat, it would have given Espy a much-needed boost and likely secured him a spot on Appropriations. But the northeastern Mississippi congressman, who was initially elected as a segregationist in 1941 and had later suffered a stroke, ultimately declined to support Espy.
“After that, I began looking for a position in the government where I could have power and influence to provide for rural America,” Espy said. 
Espy asked newly elected President Bill Clinton to appoint him as agriculture secretary, a bold proposal for a young 39-year-old, three-term congressman. Espy pitched his proposal to the former Arkansas governor by scribbling on an envelope 10 reasons the president-elect should nominate him for the post. 
Asked about the historic nature of his win, Colom has said he only wants to ensure he won’t “be the last” Black person elected to the Senate from the Magnolia State. 
“I don’t want anybody to say that I did anything to hurt the next person that has the talent, the work ethic, the ability to be able to reach for their dreams,” Colom said recently. “That’s my focus.” 
Colom is focused on the next person ready to go through the door. 
Wright: ‘We struggled, we toiled, we kept moving’
Flonzie Brown Wright said Colom’s win also brings to mind those who never got the chance to walk through it.
Wright was the first Black woman elected to public office in Mississippi. She said Colom’s victory reminds her of how she felt in 1965, when the federal Voting Rights Act passed. 
“The same emotions, the same anticipation,” she said. “It’s a strange dichotomy because we were jubilant but sad in another sense, because there were so many we lost who couldn’t vote.”
Flonzie Brown Wright speaks with media after a press conference announcing a statewide voter registration day named in her honor, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, in Jackson.  Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Wright said she often thinks about the generations who didn’t live to see this. “Many of our ancestors brought us as far as they could bring us, but they couldn’t cast a vote,” she said.
“We got here not because somebody thought it was a nice idea to treat Blacks as equal,” Wright said. “We got here because we struggled, we toiled, we kept moving, we took the defeats, we cried. But we wiped those tears off and kept on marching.”
Wright’s own march began in the 1960s, when she became an election commissioner in Madison County on Nov. 5, 1968. She served one term before moving to Jackson. She later testified before a congressional subcommittee in support of the Voting Rights Act.
She views the U.S. Supreme Court’s recent Louisiana v. Callais decision that gutted key parts of the act as a major setback. But, Wright said, every journey of 1,000 miles begins with a single step. Every journey has setbacks, but she sees Colom’s win as one more step toward the end of that journey.
“The 1,000 miles was our goal,” Wright said. “But not everyone could walk the 1,000 miles. Some walked 50, and some walked 20. They walked as much as they could and kept stepping. They kept stepping, so we kept stepping.” 
When Colom goes to Washington soon to be sworn into office, he will become the first Black senator from Mississippi in nearly 150 years. He will climb the Capitol steps carrying all those miles with him.

title: Delaware State enrollment reaches record 7,407 as graduate programs, returning students drive growth
description: Fall enrollment rises nearly 12%; university reports its largest class of Delaware freshmen and a 56% increase in high school students earning college credit DOVER — Delaware State University’s fall enrollment has reached a record 7,407 students, with returning students, graduate programs and international partnerships helping push the total up nearly 12% fr[...]
text:
Photo Courtesy of Delaware State University
Fall enrollment rises nearly 12%; university reports its largest class of Delaware freshmen and a 56% increase in high school students earning college credit
DOVER — Delaware State University’s fall enrollment has reached a record 7,407 students, with returning students, graduate programs and international partnerships helping push the total up nearly 12% from last year.
The university announced Nov. 10 that its certified fall 2026 enrollment increased by 784 students from 6,623 a year earlier. Enrollment at the historically Black university has grown more than 47% since 2020, when it enrolled 5,027 students.
The total includes 5,959 students attending the university’s two Dover campuses or studying through its online programs, an increase of 7.8% from 5,528 last fall. Another 1,448 students are enrolled through international partnership programs in the Caribbean, Asia and Africa.
University officials attributed the growth partly to students continuing their studies and increased demand for graduate programs.
“This year’s growth came from a more intentional emphasis on students who were already here and decided to keep going, a central part of our work — and from a graduate school that working adults in Delaware and across the country are choosing in record numbers,” university President Tony Allen said in the announcement.
Delaware students and tuition support
The university reported its largest in-state freshman class, with more than 80% of new Delaware freshmen enrolled full time receiving INSPIRE Scholarships.
The four-year, full-tuition scholarship supports qualifying Delaware high school graduates who enter Delaware State the fall after graduation. The university said the program has brought more than 2,500 Delawareans to campus since its creation.
In-state undergraduate enrollment increased 8.4%, compared with 4.5% growth among out-of-state undergraduates. The incoming freshman class had an average high school GPA of 3.13.
The scholarship can make a significant difference for families weighing college costs, although full tuition does not mean all college expenses are covered. Prospective students should review eligibility requirements and costs beyond tuition with the university’s financial aid office.
Graduate programs lead growth
Graduate enrollment increased 27.1%, making it the university’s fastest-growing enrollment category. The number of continuing graduate students rose 34.1%, while online graduate enrollment increased 46.1%.
Gwendolyn Scott-Jones, dean of the School of Graduate, Adult and Extended Studies, said the programs are designed to serve students balancing education with other responsibilities.
“They are choosing Delaware State because our programs are built for people who are working, raising families and serving their communities while they earn the credential that moves them forward,” Scott-Jones said in the announcement.
High school students earn college credit
Dual enrollment — allowing high school students to take university courses for college credit — increased 56% to 684 students. That total includes 482 Delaware students and 199 students at HBCU Early College Prep in Queens, New York.
The university identified the Williams School as an important part of that pipeline. The early college school was dedicated in September in honor of former university President Harry L. Williams and Robin S. Williams.
Roughly two-thirds of the school’s graduates go on to Delaware State, according to the university.
Connecting enrollment to careers
The enrollment announcement also highlighted programs intended to help students complete degrees and prepare for employment.
More than 1,000 Delaware State students have completed the Braven Accelerator, a three-credit career preparation course taken during sophomore year. The university announced in October that it would expand that partnership through a Center for Economic Mobility intended to reach every undergraduate.
Its College of Business also hosted 720 students at its largest DEEP Day, while the College of Agriculture, Science and Technology welcomed 213 first-year pre-health students at a Sept. 29 White Coat Ceremony.
The final enrollment count exceeded an October projection that the university was approaching 7,000 students. Officials said additional online sessions and international semester starts were included before the Oct. 31 census.
To Go Box

Learn more: Delaware State University.
Admissions: Visit the university’s website and select Admissions for undergraduate, graduate and online program information.
INSPIRE Scholarship: Review eligibility, renewal requirements and covered costs on the scholarship webpage.
Dual enrollment: Contact the university or your high school counselor about courses, eligibility, costs and how credits may transfer.

title: Lawyers try to rehash anti-abortion law case by accusing Kansas judge of religious discrimination
description: OLATHE — Lawyers defending Kansas laws that imposed restrictions on abortion care accused the judge who struck down those restrictions of discriminating against anti-abortion witnesses for their religious beliefs. The accusation was one piece of attorneys’ argument to reopen, retry and dismiss a case that resulted in state-mandated restrictions on abortion c[...]
text:
Johnson County District Court Judge Christopher Jayaram listens to closing arguments on Oct. 17, 2025, in a courtroom in Olathe, Kansas, as proceedings in a consequential abortion trial challenging state restrictions came to a close. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)OLATHE — Lawyers defending Kansas laws that imposed restrictions on abortion care accused the judge who struck down those restrictions of discriminating against anti-abortion witnesses for their religious beliefs.
The accusation was one piece of attorneys’ argument to reopen, retry and dismiss a case that resulted in state-mandated restrictions on abortion care being voided earlier this year.
Attorneys for state and county officials made the argument at a hearing Tuesday in Johnson County Court before a new judge, Stephanie Goodenow, who will deliver a written decision on whether to reopen the case.
A group of abortion providers sued officials in 2023 for abortion restrictions that date to the 1990s. After a seven-day bench trial in October 2025, then-Johnson County District Judge Christopher Jayaram, who is now a Kansas Supreme Court justice, issued an 260-page opinion in August that found the restrictions violated Kansans’ right to bodily autonomy. 
At the time, anti-abortion advocates criticized the decision for its content and its timing. Jayaram issued the opinion just hours before he was sworn in as a state Supreme Court justice. State and county officials appealed the decision almost immediately.
Lincoln Wilson, a partner at the Colorado-based firm First and Fourteenth who argued on behalf of state and county officials, called Jayaram’s decision “one-sided,” and said there was “religious discrimination and animus” in his findings. 
Jayaram gave little to no weight to each of the state’s seven witnesses, pointing, in some cases, to the witnesses’ “personal or spiritual beliefs.”
Wilson likened Jayaram’s findings to a 2018 U.S. Supreme Court decision in a Colorado case involving a cake shop owner who declined to make a wedding cake for a same-sex couple on the basis of his religious beliefs. The U.S. Supreme Court found that state officials were hostile toward the owner’s religious beliefs when the couple filed a civil rights complaint.
Wilson also said Jayaram’s findings were analogous to racial discrimination.
When Goodenow pressed Wilson, asking him to confirm whether he thought the Kansas and Colorado cases were the same, Wilson said there were “enough ingredients here” that are like the Colorado case.
Alice Wang, an attorney for Kansas abortion providers from the New York-based group the Center for Reproductive Rights, said the state’s accusation of religious bias mischaracterized the trial and Jayaram’s judgment.
“The state had its day in court,” Wang said. “It can and has appealed the result, but it has offered no basis for this court to reopen its own judgment, much less dismiss the case.”
The state laws, which included the Women’s Right to Know Act, that were challenged and voided contained several requirements for abortion providers that plaintiffs argued at trial were harmful to patients.
Under state law, patients were subject to 24-hour waiting periods. Providers had to disclose state-sanctioned anti-abortion language, including false claims that abortion poses a risk to future pregnancies and increases the risk of breast cancer. Physicians had to present the information in a specific typeface, font size and color. Patients had to wait another 30 minutes after meeting with their provider before they could receive abortion care. Providers had to tell patients at least five times that medication abortions can be reversed, a method that is regarded by some as an experimental and potentially dangerous treatment. Physicians had to ask patients the most important factor they considered when deciding to obtain an abortion.
Jayaram temporarily blocked those restrictions in 2023, and his August decision made the block permanent.
Wilson challenged whether the abortion providers who brought the case should have been able to sue in the interest of their patients in the first place. He said they have a conflict of interest, which warrants reopening the case.
“If you are invoking someone else’s rights, you have to be aligned with their interests,” Wilson said, “and what we have here is a fundamental conflict because the Women’s Right to Know Act gives patients the right to sue their abortion provider if requirements are not met.”
At the close of Tuesday’s hearing, Goodenow noted the case includes almost 750 pleadings over more than three years. The social and political battles over abortion have gone on for much longer. 
Jayaram’s decision was an affirmation of the right to an abortion in Kansas, which came after voters rejected a 2022 constitutional amendment that could’ve led to further restrictions and a 2019 state Supreme Court decision that cemented Kansans’ right to bodily autonomy.
Whether Goodenow decides to reopen the case and allow a retrial isn’t determinative of the case’s outcome.

title: A New Chapter, a New Normal: Hockessin Author Finds Joy Beyond Illness
description: A New Chapter, a New Normal: Hockessin Author Finds Joy Beyond Illness By John Riddle Suzan Jackson’s audiobook recording studio was her son’s bedroom closet. Her writing desk might be a recliner or, on difficult days, a couch where she works lying flat. The surroundings change. Her purpose remains steady: helping people with chronic illness build lives that[...]
text:
Suzan Jackson’s book, Finding a New Normal: Living Your Best Life with Chronic Illness, brings together lessons learned through writing, raising children and navigating a condition that transformed her family’s life.
A New Chapter, a New Normal: Hockessin Author Finds Joy Beyond Illness
By John Riddle
Suzan Jackson’s audiobook recording studio was her son’s bedroom closet. Her writing desk might be a recliner or, on difficult days, a couch where she works lying flat.
The surroundings change. Her purpose remains steady: helping people with chronic illness build lives that include joy, connection and meaning.
For the longtime Hockessin resident, that message comes from experience. Her book, Finding a New Normal: Living Your Best Life with Chronic Illness, brings together lessons learned through writing, raising children and navigating a condition that transformed her family’s life.
Originally from Rochester, New York, Jackson met her husband while both were working as chemical engineers for DuPont in New Orleans. Marriage and a transfer brought them to the Wilmington area 36 years ago. They have lived in their Hockessin home for 32 years.
“We never expected to stay,” Jackson said.
Then, on March 1, 2002, her life changed abruptly.
“I suddenly became very ill with what felt like a severe flu … but it never went away,” she said.
A year later, Jackson received a diagnosis of myalgia encephalomyelitis, commonly called ME/CFS. She describes an illness that severely restricts her energy and stamina, with even modest activity potentially bringing prolonged symptoms.
Two years after she became ill, both sons developed the condition, too. Their experiences would eventually help shape her writing and her work supporting other families.
Jackson’s publishing career began before her illness. Her first book, The ISO 14001 Implementation Guide: Creating an Integrated Management System, was traditionally published in 1997 through Wiley.
Freelance writing later offered work she could do from home when consulting and corporate training became impossible. She wrote about chronic illness, family, travel, outdoor experiences and books, while developing her blog, Live with ME/CFS.
Around 2018, she began gathering articles into a book for readers facing many kinds of chronic health conditions.
Professional editing proved essential.
“I edited it myself several times and thought it was in good shape,” Jackson said. After hiring an editor, she discovered the manuscript still needed substantial work.
Independent publishing brought another education. Jackson researched distribution, hired help and learned unfamiliar production tasks. When a formatter quit after saying her requests were impossible, Jackson figured out the formatting herself.
Throughout the process, she had to respect her physical limits.
“Any kind of work, including writing, has to be done in tiny increments over a long period of time,” she said.
Her book addresses emotional coping, daily living and relationships. It draws on her family’s experiences and lessons shared through support groups she has established.
“The emphasis in this book is on LIVING your life, not just enduring it,” Jackson said.
Making that message accessible inspired an audiobook edition. Knowing some readers depend on listening, Jackson learned recording and audio editing, narrated the book herself and eventually hired a professional to polish the recordings.
The closet studio became another example of adapting a goal to the circumstances.
Her advice to aspiring authors includes investing in professional editing, preparing for ongoing marketing and understanding distribution beyond Amazon.
“While it is now easy for anyone to upload a book to KDP, quality still matters,” she said.
Jackson also runs a local support group for people with ME/CFS, long COVID and related conditions, along with caregivers. Meetings mostly take place through Zoom.
Across her books, blogs and support work, she returns to the possibility of finding a new normal: accepting today’s limits while leaving room for hope.
For Jackson, helping readers recognize that possibility gives her writing purpose. Each completed page offers another chance to share what her family and fellow patients have learned.
“Be prepared to learn!” she said.
