name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: What the midterm elections could mean for Missouri’s economy
description: Wall Street’s initial optimism following Tuesday’s midterm elections quickly turned into a sharp selloff, driven largely by concerns about the future of AI and data-center investments. But beyond the market’s volatility, the election results sent a message that leaders in Washington and Jefferson City should take seriously: Americans want relief from rising [...]
text:
President Donald Trump's unpopularity, due in part to an inability to execute his campaign promise to lower costs, is likely to hurt Republican congressional candidates in the midterms, according to political scientists and analysts (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images).Wall Street’s initial optimism following Tuesday’s midterm elections quickly turned into a sharp selloff, driven largely by concerns about the future of AI and data-center investments. But beyond the market’s volatility, the election results sent a message that leaders in Washington and Jefferson City should take seriously: Americans want relief from rising costs and a more stable future.
Democrats made major gains in Congress as many people voiced frustration about the cost of living, economic uncertainty, and national and foreign policies. Missouri’s results also showed a changing political landscape. Democrats gained seats in the state legislature, while Republicans lost their supermajorities in Jefferson City.
These results should not be seen only as a win for one party or a sign of political gridlock. They offer a chance to rethink policies that affect Missouri’s workers, farmers, families, and businesses. And the economic concerns behind that opportunity are real, not speculative.
Months before the election, an August 2026 Saint Louis University/YouGov survey of 900 likely Missouri voters documented widespread financial anxiety. 69% worried about affording health care, 66% about groceries and gasoline, 62% about utility bills, and 59% about property taxes. Only 25% rated Missouri’s economy as good or excellent, while just 21% gave the national economy similarly positive marks. The same survey found that 68% opposed construction of a new data center in their community.
The war with Iran added to economic pressures. As I discussed in my March analysis and June follow-up, the conflict’s effects on energy markets, transportation costs, and economic uncertainty extend well beyond the Middle East, reaching Missouri families, farmers, and businesses. Those economic consequences have since become part of the broader political debate, with even administration officials acknowledging the war’s role in the midterm backlash.
These findings do not establish why every Missourian voted as they did. But they show that economic dissatisfaction and concerns about the costs of technological development were already widespread before Election Day. The challenge now is to translate the demand for change into policies that deliver meaningful economic improvements.
 Tariffs: An opportunity to reconsider the costs

Few policies show the gap between promises and reality as clearly as tariffs. The Trump administration says tariffs protect American industries, support domestic production, and improve the country’s position in trade talks. These goals may appeal to manufacturing states like Missouri, but tariffs can also raise costs for businesses that rely on imported parts, materials, and equipment.
As I explained in my earlier analysis of Missouri’s trade relationship with Canada, these costs are particularly significant because Missouri’s manufacturers depend on deeply integrated North American supply chains.
The new Congress can review the effects of current tariffs, strengthen oversight, and help shape a clearer trade strategy. The president has broad authority over trade, but Congress can influence policy through laws, hearings, and budget decisions.
 Missouri farmers need markets, not just assistance

Trade is vital to Missouri farmers, who rely on global markets to sell soybeans, corn, and livestock. Trade disputes can prompt retaliation, costing farmers access to markets and putting them at a disadvantage compared with producers whose trade relationships are more stable.
Government assistance can provide temporary relief when markets are disrupted, but it cannot replace steady buyers and reliable export markets. Trade uncertainty also makes it harder for farmers to plan or make commitments extending well beyond a single growing season.
The new political balance in Washington offers a chance to rethink how trade policies affect agricultural competitiveness. Instead of relying mainly on assistance after disputes hurt farmers, policymakers should prioritize restoring predictable access to international markets.
For rural Missouri, that would represent a meaningful economic response to the frustrations surrounding the election.
 Data centers and AI: Missouri voters are asking who benefits and who pays

The August SLU/YouGov poll found that 68% of likely Missouri voters opposed construction of a new data center in their local community, compared with just 17% who supported it. Opposition had increased by 17 percentage points since February.
The concern also crossed partisan lines, with majorities of both Republican and Democratic respondents opposing a data center in their community.
Large data centers can attract substantial capital investment, create construction employment, and expand local tax revenues, but they require enormous amounts of electricity, significant water resources, and costly infrastructure improvements. Their permanent employment benefits may be modest relative to the size of the initial investment.
As I have argued previously, attracting technology investment should not require communities to accept financial obligations without adequate transparency and accountability.
The new Congress can examine the national implications of AI-related electricity demand, energy infrastructure, and investment incentives. Missouri lawmakers, meanwhile, have an opportunity to strengthen transparency surrounding utility costs, local incentives, and infrastructure commitments.
Beyond data centers, AI brings both opportunities and risks to Missouri’s economy. It can boost productivity and create new opportunities, but it also threatens to displace workers, eliminate certain jobs, and widen economic inequality. Policymakers, businesses, and educational institutions must work together to prepare students and workers for these changes, help displaced workers transition into new careers, and ensure that small businesses can benefit from emerging technologies. They should make sure that innovation creates better jobs, raises living standards, and benefits communities, not just a few companies.
 The voters have spoken. Economic policy must respond.

The midterm blue wave emerged against a backdrop of widespread economic dissatisfaction. Missouri’s own polling confirms that concerns about affordability, economic conditions, and the costs of technological development were firmly established before voters went to the polls.
These problems will not go away just because control of Congress has changed. But the election has created an opening for a different economic conversation, one focused less on political victories and more on measurable improvements in people’s lives. What matters most now is how policymakers respond to voters’ concerns and turn that response into economic progress.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Hidden taxes: User fees siphon money from Nebraskans’ pocketbooks
description: Many, too many, Nebraska households and small businesses, including farmers and ranchers, are struggling with affordability. Conservatively, one in two Nebraska households, or over 1 million Nebraskans, are economically insecure, meaning every month they are struggling to meet just their basic needs like housing, food and gasoline. While the other half of Ne[...]
text:
(Getty Images)Many, too many, Nebraska households and small businesses, including farmers and ranchers, are struggling with affordability. Conservatively, one in two Nebraska households, or over 1 million Nebraskans, are economically insecure, meaning every month they are struggling to meet just their basic needs like housing, food and gasoline. While the other half of Nebraskans are managing better, affordability in the home, business and on the farm is real. This affordability challenge is being made worse by hidden taxes reducing our spending power. 
We are familiar with obvious taxes like income, property and sales taxes. These taxes reduce our incomes and in turn reduce our ability to spend, invest, and make choices. For many, if not most of us, we understand these taxes are important, funding national defense, schools, safe roads, police and higher education.
Let’s stretch our minds a bit and define what I mean by “hidden taxes.” Beyond the obvious taxes, there are numerous government policies — federal, state and local — that reduce the disposable incomes of households, businesses and farmers. These policies are taking up a bigger bite of our income than we might expect, and they are not as obvious as when we pay our income taxes April 15 each year. 
Elected officials from the Congress to our governor to local mayors are sensitive to the cost of property, sales and income taxes. Over the decades there has been a movement to control obvious taxes, minimizing political blowback. However, a striking array of user fees exists to fund government services and programs that are less obvious, including everything from getting a driver’s license to buying a house to starting a business.  
Let me illustrate just how extensively government user fees are impacting Nebraskans. According to the Legislature’s Fiscal Office and its Directory of State Agency Programs and Funds, there are more than 300 government cash funds associated with 75 state agencies. These cash funds are supported by legislatively authorized user fees. These are just state user fees, of course; there are federal and local government user fees expanding this list significantly. 
Fiscal year 2024-25 documents show that Nebraska took in over $627 million, or over a half-billion dollars, in various user fees. This is real money with real impact on our pocketbooks.
On the surface, user fees are reasonable where beneficiaries of services are directly paying the cost for those services. The policy is if you need a certified birth certificate, the agency responsible calculates the cost of providing this service and sets fees to cover those costs. We can reasonably argue that those of us not needing a birth certificate should not be responsible for paying for those who do. 
Unfortunately, Gov. Jim Pillen and a majority of the members of the Legislature are engaging in games with user fees. First, they are pushing more of the cost of state government to user fees to moderate income and sales taxes. Second, they are not managing the cost of services, with the rate of fees often generating surplus balances or more fee income than is needed to cover actual costs of service. Third, they are now sweeping cash fund balances to fund unsustainable income and property tax relief. 
Drilling down, providing property and income tax relief is great politics. Who does not want such relief? However, balancing the state’s budget as required by our constitution by overcharging user fees and using surplus cash funds to cover tax relief is neither sound tax policy nor sustainable. Good tax policy would work to set user fees more precisely, generating sufficient income to cover actual service costs but no more. 
During the past legislative session (2024-2026), over $160 million of user fees (cash funds) were redirected from their intended purpose to fund income and property tax relief. Now we are taxing those using specific services to provide benefits to all Nebraskans. Reverse and perverse logic. 
Rooted in America’s Revolutionary War, the debate over the role of government and taxations is core to our 250 years of history. This debate will continue, but we must embrace a public discussion on the role of government and how we will pay for the government, and ensure our tax system is transparent and fair.

title: Idaho constitutional scholar creates ‘Toward A More Perfect Union’ civics course
description: An Idaho constitutional scholar is launching a new online civics 101 course to help Idahoans understand what the U.S. Constitution and the government means for them following the 2026 elections.  Alturas Institute President David Adler created a seven-week online civics education course called “Towards a More Perfect Union” that begins Jan. 7 through Zoom. T[...]
text:
The preamble to the United States Constitution begins  with the words "We the People." (Photo by Getty Images)An Idaho constitutional scholar is launching a new online civics 101 course to help Idahoans understand what the U.S. Constitution and the government means for them following the 2026 elections. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Alturas Institute President David Adler created a seven-week online civics education course called “Towards a More Perfect Union” that begins Jan. 7 through Zoom.
The course is open to anyone in Idaho who is interested, costs $17.76 to enroll and is designed to reintroduce, or even introduce, basic civics education to the public. 
Adler said he hopes the course helps students become more informed and empowered voters and citizens. 
“I want people to better understand that people really are the driving force of this constitutional democracy, and they only hurt themselves when they retreat to the sideless,” Adler said. “They are better off participating. They are better off understanding which branch of government has responsibility for what particular matters and exercises which powers. That is crucial to holding government accountable.” 
David Adler
The course will cover the constitutional principles of the American Revolution; the Declaration of Independence; the Constitutional Convention; Congress; the U.S. presidency; the judiciary and courts, the Bill of Rights, liberties and freedoms and the 14th Amendment and equal protection under the law.  
Specific topics will delve into issues including limitations on the power of the presidency.
“It’s an overview designed to familiarize, or refamiliarize, Americans with constitutional frameworks to empower them to participate in the system with a better base of knowledge,” Adler said. 
Adler has taught courses on government and the Constitution at all three of Idaho’s public universities and now heads up the Alturas Institute nonprofit organization in Idaho Falls.
He said he came up with the idea for the “Toward a More Perfect Union” course while giving public talks on the Constitution. Adler said attendees frequently told him they wished the public was more informed about government and civics. 
Each of the courses will last 90 minutes and include a 45-minute talk by Adler, followed by 45 minutes for questions from the course participants. 
Adler said the course is designed for many people, whether they are young people who are just turning 18 and able to vote for the first time, or they are adults who have not been to school in many years but would like a refresher on civics and the Constitution. 
 



  Find out more about civics education

More information about the “Toward a More Perfect Union” online civics courses is available online at www.alturasinstitute.com/civics-101. The online zoom course takes place at 6:30 p.m. Mountain time Thursday evenings beginning Jan. 7.

name: WyoFile
title: Inside Chuck Gray’s working relationship with election denier Cleta Mitchell
description:
Public records shared with WyoFile show Cleta Mitchell provided advice and support to Wyoming’s chief elections officer. 
The post Inside Chuck Gray’s working relationship with election denier Cleta Mitchell appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
After working to overturn President Donald Trump’s 2020 election defeat, Cleta Mitchell, a conservative attorney and former Oklahoma state lawmaker, began building a national movement aimed at remaking American elections. 
Mitchell — who was on the phone call with Trump when he pressed Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find” enough votes to recalculate the results in his favor — launched the Election Integrity Network in 2021. 
The network works as a coalition of activists, attorneys, Republican party officials, advocacy groups and right-wing media outlets. Mitchell has also provided assistance to Wyoming Secretary of State Chuck Gray. 
Under Mitchell’s leadership, the network has wielded its influence to change state laws, purge voter rolls and cast doubt on election security. In an extensive profile published in October, ProPublica reported that “no one besides Trump himself has done more than Mitchell, 76, to turn the mundane processes of how ballots are cast and counted in American elections into mortal combat.” 
While Mitchell has kept a direct line to Trump, she’s also worked closely with Gray, according to text and email records obtained by American Oversight through a public records request. American Oversight, a public interest watchdog based in Washington, D.C. shared those records with WyoFile. 
The records indicate Mitchell recommended Gray as a witness before the U.S. House Administration Committee, suggested edits to his congressional testimony, and asked Gray to press Wyoming’s federal delegation and other GOP secretaries of state to support the SAVE Act. The federal legislation, which ultimately stalled in August in the Republican-controlled Senate, would have required voters to provide documentary proof of citizenship to register and expanded the federal government’s involvement in election matters traditionally left to the states. 
“Huge win Cleta!” Gray texted Mitchell on July 1, 2025, records show, alongside a Facebook video of him discussing several election-related laws going into effect that day in Wyoming, as well as his signing of an agreement with the Department of Homeland Security to use the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements database.
“Thanks for all your help and support Cleta – – it means a great deal!” Gray wrote in the same text. 
Secretary of State Chuck Gray listens to testimony at the House Corporations, Elections and Political Subdivisions Committee on Jan. 15, 2025. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
While Gray collaborating with Mitchell is not necessarily surprising given his focus as secretary of state, the records lay bare the enthusiasm of Wyoming’s chief elections officer to work closely with one of the country’s most powerful pushers of the false claim that U.S. elections are rigged and stolen. 
In 2022, Gray, then a state lawmaker, ran for the position of chief elections officer on a platform of unverified claims of “tremendous problems” with Wyoming’s elections. As part of his campaign, Gray sponsored showings across the state of the debunked film “2,000 Mules,” which alleged that rampant “ballot harvesting” in swing states stole the 2020 election from Trump. (The nonprofit whose claims the film was based on later acknowledged in a court filing that it had no evidence to back its claims in the film.)
After voters elected him to the position, Gray ardently lobbied state lawmakers for a slate of election restrictions and racked up legislative wins that included a bill similar to the SAVE Act that added proof of both citizenship and state residency to Wyoming’s voter registration process. In 2025, he made Wyoming the first state to cooperate with the federal government’s demand that states hand over sensitive voter data. 
“Wyomingites deserve to know why Cleta Mitchell, who helped try to overturn the 2020 election, has so much access to their chief elections officer,” American Oversight Executive Director Chioma Chukwu told WyoFile in a statement. 
“These records show her working behind the scenes to shape his congressional testimony and enlist him to advance her national network’s agenda,” Chukwu said. “What does that agenda have to do with the needs of Wyoming voters? What else is Gray getting out of this relationship, and how does it benefit the people he serves? How has any of this made it easier for eligible voters to cast a ballot? Gray owes Wyomingites answers.”
In response to an emailed list of detailed questions from WyoFile, Gray responded with a statement.
“My tenure as a legislator and as Secretary of State has been one of collaboration, and I have worked with numerous individuals to advance meaningful election integrity legislation at the state and federal level. Our administration has been very successful in working for the people of Wyoming to strengthen the integrity of our elections,” Gray wrote in the statement. “The media’s obsession with attacking citizens like Cleta Mitchell who are advancing common sense election integrity measures shows how out of touch the media is. I will keep advocating for common sense election integrity measures, because the people of Wyoming support these common sense election integrity measures.”
Earlier this month, voters elected Gray to Wyoming’s lone congressional seat in the U.S. House of Representatives. He takes office in January.
Video calls
Records show that Mitchell responded to Gray’s Feb. 1, 2025 message regarding Wyoming’s newly enacted proof-of-citizenship election law and his agreement with DHS later that day.
“That’s just fabulous!!!” Mitchell wrote. “You have to talk about this on the Friday call this week!!! Woo hoo!!” Mitchell wrote. “Can you do that?” 
“Yes absolutely!” Gray said. 

This video recreation was made using screenshots of text messages between Cleta Mitchell and Chuck Gray, but is not a screen recording of the actual conversation. (WyoFile)
Since its inception, a hallmark of Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network has involved weekly videoconference meetings with participants from across the country. 
After obtaining recordings of more than 400 of those meetings, the New York Times reported in 2024 that the coordinated calls “allowed debunked theories to jump from state to state” and “nurtured a cast of amateur election sleuths and armchair experts who often see evidence of election fraud in processes that they misinterpret.”
Records show that on Oct.7, 2025, Mitchell texted Gray and asked if he could join another Friday call to discuss running Wyoming’s voter rolls “through the updated SAVE system at DHS?” 
“I’ve got you on the agenda for Friday to talk about the SAVE system / process and what your experience has been. Can you still do that? 15 minutes?” Mitchell wrote in a later message. 
“Yep!” Gray responded. 
Congressional testimony and delegation
Gray testified to the U.S. Committee on House Administration during a February hearing titled “Make Elections Great Again: How to Restore Trust and Integrity in Federal Elections.” 
Sometime in the days ahead of the hearing, records show that Gray texted Mitchell with a favor. 
“I’m testifying on Tuesday in House Admin on the MEGA Act! Really excited about it – – thank you for all of your help! Can I send you testimony – – just wanted to see any suggestions you have?” Gray wrote. 
“Yes of course. I suggested they ask you” Mitchell responded. “I’d be happy to go over your testimony. Plus I have one key paragraph I want to suggest.”
In this Feb. 6, 2014, photo, Cleta Mitchell testifies on Capitol Hill in Washington. Mitchell, who advised former President Donald Trump in his fight to overturn the 2020 election, played a central role advising and coordinating the movement to tighten voting laws across the country. (AP Photo/Pablo Martinez Monsivais, File)
Email records indicate that Gray sent his testimony to Mitchell on Feb. 9, the day before the hearing. Records show that Mitchell mostly suggested slight tweaks to Gray’s testimony and asked that he add a paragraph about Wyoming being exempt from the National Voter Registration Act and how the MEGA Act would “allow states to take the actions necessary to clean voter rolls on a real time basis.”
As seen in his testimony, Gray did not adopt most of Mitchell’s edits, including the added paragraph, largely sticking instead to his original draft. 
Letters
Records show Mitchell texted Gray on Feb. 24 about a letter sent to Senate Majority Leader John Thune from the SAVE America Act Coalition, a project of Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network. 
“Make sure Cynthia [Lummis], [John] Barrasso and Harriet [Hageman] see this letter and publicly support the talking filibuster. Particularly Barrasso,” she wrote. 
Mitchell also asked Gray to “create a similar letter to be signed from GOP Secretaries of State.”
“If you get one together, we can help get it hand-delivered to Sen Thune’s office,” Mitchel wrote. 
On March 26, Gray announced in a press release that he had sent a joint letter with Indiana Secretary of State Diego Morales to Thune, urging the Senate majority leader to “enforce the talking filibuster to ensure” the passage of the SAVE Act. 
The records do not indicate whether Gray pushed Wyoming’s federal delegation to support the bill and he did not answer that specific question in his statement to WyoFile. 
WyoFile contacted Sens. John Barrasso and Cynthia Lummis as well as Rep. Harriet Hageman to ask whether Gray had urged them to support the SAVE Act. 
“No one has ever needed to convince Harriet Hageman about the importance of requiring an ID to vote in American elections,” Tristan Justice, Hageman’s communications director, told WyoFile in a statement. 
Neither Barrasso nor Lummis responded to WyoFile’s request by publishing time.

name: WyoFile
title: Deep roots
description:
What does it mean to be a Wyomingite? Ask the grass, writes columnist Walt Gasson. 
The post Deep roots appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

My friends in New Mexico call it the Llano del Norte, the Northern Plains. For their Spanish ancestors, it was the “Northern Mystery” — the land far beyond the rivers and the missions. It was too vast, too cold and forbidding. The native people were fierce and the gold the Spaniards sought was too elusive. The Comanche, the Cheyenne and the Arapaho soon convinced them that it was in their best interest to return to the thick adobe walls and the warm pinon fires of Santa Fe. It was a good decision.
We live on the very western edge of the llano, in the basin between the Laramie Range on the east and the Medicine Bow mountains on the west. Native people hunted here, passed through here on their way to someplace else. The Laramie Plains were too high, too cold and too windy to stay very long. It was a good place for bison, not so much for human beings. It is the westernmost outpost of the great American grassland, an afterthought of creation in the image of the shortgrass country to the east. It is a hard place.
But like that shortgrass country off east, it was a small province in an empire of grass. From horizon to horizon, the greatest expanse of grassland on earth. From the Assiniboine in the north to the Rio Grande in the south, from the Father of All Waters to the Shining Mountains, the Great Plains dominated the face of America six centuries ago. Bison, antelope, elk, wolves and grizzly bears. Whooping cranes and prairie chickens. Tallgrass to midgrass to shortgrass from east to west, it was a wilderness of incomprehensible proportions. A wilderness of grass.
It’s a funny thing about grass — you can only see a small portion of the plant above ground. Most of it is hidden beneath the surface. The buffalo grass and blue grama that grew on the flanks of the Laramie Range where the Cheyenne camped still grows here today. It’s scrubby looking stuff, seldom more than four inches tall. But it’s thrifty. It doesn’t need much water. It can grow in these cold, hard places because it has deep roots. Those roots sink down through the decomposed granite and limestone soil to find the water and nutrients the plant needs to survive. Despite the short growing season and the ever-present wind, it thrives.
So it’s been with the people who came to the plains country. They too needed deep roots to survive, clinging to the cold, dry, windy edge of the American heartland. Some tried to put down roots here but failed. You can still see the forgotten cabins of the miners and the collapsed remains of the sod homes built by homesteaders in our corner of Wyoming. Long-forgotten people gave their names to the creeks, then died in obscurity. But others stuck. The Swedes came to work in the timber. The Irish came to work on the railroad. The Texans came north with the herds on the old Bozeman Trail. The Mexicans came to work the sugar beet fields. They came from all over the world, from different cultures and different backgrounds. But they stayed and against the odds they thrived, through good times and bad. 
They thrived because they put down roots — deep roots, like the tough prairie grasses that were here when they came. They put down roots of family, with a love of this wide open country and a pride in their own brand. They put down roots of community, where they might ride all day to help a neighbor brand his calves or take a meal to a friend. They put down roots of faith, simple faith that brought families together to give thanks for rain or a new colt or a real house of their own. These are our roots, the fibers of our being that sink into this hard place and sustain us all.
Those deep roots come with time. It’s not an overnight thing, and we shouldn’t try to make it one. A hat from Murdoch’s or a new pickup truck won’t help. You can’t buy your roots. But you can begin to grow them. If you’re new in the country, here are a few gentle suggestions, based on things we do: 

We wave. When you meet a neighbor on the road or street, it’s expected that you will wave. It’s not a big production — just a minimalist greeting. Maybe just a finger (no, not that finger!) raised in greeting. If you don’t do it, we think you’re stuck up. If you overdo it, we think you’re weird. Just do it.


We help. If I’m stuck in the snow and you just drive right past, I’m going to remember that to my dying day. Stop and ask if I need help. I’ll probably say, “Nah, I got this.” But at least ask. I’ll do the same for you.


We like some things that might or might not be a big deal where you came from. University of Wyoming sports, the Buffalo Bills, hunting and fishing and the outdoors in general, rodeo and the smell of rain. Just kinda feel your way along with this. You’ll be fine.


We don’t like some things, too. Politics, religion, how much you make or how much your home or car or cosmetic surgery cost are all on that list. Just listen and smile and don’t say too much. 

But all that said, welcome. We all started out new in the country. We hope you like it here on the northern plains. It isn’t for everyone, but we think it’s a good place to live and work and raise a family. It isn’t an easy place, but that’s ok. Most things worth having aren’t easy. They never were. And if you’ve been here a while, maybe next summer, after what we fervently hope will be a long, very snowy winter, it might be good to walk out on the prairie early some morning and give thanks for a place that requires deep roots.

name: WyoFile
title: Legislative panel advances Wyoming Game and Fish fund
description:
Legislature aims to bolster agency’s coffers with $500M trust as costs continue to rise.
The post Legislative panel advances Wyoming Game and Fish fund appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CHEYENNE—Wyoming’s fish and wildlife resources are a step closer to being bolstered by a dedicated Game and Fish trust fund, with an ultimate goal of its principal reaching $500 million.
The Legislature’s Joint Travel, Recreation, Wildlife and Cultural Resources Committee met Tuesday to hear from the Wyoming Game and Fish Department about what the money would be put toward, in addition to discussing potential funding options.
The department has faced a growing financial challenge to maintain the management and sustainability of Wyoming’s wildlife resources due to inflation. Its requests for additional funding have largely been rejected in the past, but department leadership has been optimistic regarding the work the legislative committee has been doing to address the funding shortfall.
In recent years, in an attempt to bridge the gap, hunting and fishing licenses have increased in price, but that is not expected to provide enough revenue to meet the department’s needs going forward.
The fund would require a two-thirds vote of each chamber to be enacted. During testimony, Game and Fish Chief Financial Officer Meredith Wood outlined the agency’s main sources of revenue and how that money is being used. The department’s three pots of revenue are license sales, which make up 60% of total revenue; taxes on fishing and hunting equipment, which make up 22%; and the remaining 18% comes from grants and other revenue streams.
Wood also noted that the uncertainty of those revenue streams make planning for the future difficult.
“We have some future opportunities that we’ve been unable to invest in just due to the unpredictability in long-term revenue sustainability,” she said. Wood stressed that the department has prided itself on being fiscally conservative, but the pressure of rising costs and inflation forces the department to make cuts somewhere.
To make ends meet, Game and Fish has put off facility infrastructure and renovation projects that are necessary to ensure continued use of those facilities, she said.
“We are at a crossroads where that is no longer an option,” she said. “We have to invest in these things … sacrificing the investment in habitat, in surveys, in population and wildlife management and investment into the state people for conservation of the resource, the culture,” she said. “We can’t do one and not the other.”
Wood displayed a graph which showed that the department’s expenditures will exceed its revenues by 2030.
She outlined a 10-year plan to address infrastructure priorities such as annual maintenance, hatcheries, Wildlife Habitat Management Area facilities, elk feedgrounds and warden houses and offices.
Regarding annual maintenance, the department plans to invest 1.5% of its $227 million in total assets, which equals $3.4 million a year, to prevent catastrophic rebuilds.
Hatcheries would fall under major construction, as the youngest one is 50 years old and the oldest is 100 years old, which would be a total cost of $31.2 million over 10 years.
Wildlife Habitat Management Area facilities would receive $3.3 million over 10 years to update water storage and management in addition to replacing deteriorating bridges.
For the elk feedgrounds, older wooden sheds would be replaced with metal sheds at a cost of almost $1.9 million over 10 years.
Warden houses and offices, along with regional Game and Fish offices, would be replaced or remodeled at an estimated cost of $22.9 million over 10 years.
Wood noted that the department has marked $66.2 million worth of projects as high-priority. The department has also identified programs that could be enhanced through investment, including improved infrastructure for aquatic invasive species at an annual cost of $2 million annually; connectivity regarding fencing and highway crossings at $7.5 million annually; treating invasive annual grasses at $3.8 million annually; habitat restoration projects costing $700,000 annually; and conducting research and surveys about sensitive species which would cost $1.5 million annually. During public comment, the bill received unanimous support.
Jess Johnson, government affairs director for the Wyoming Wildlife Federation, expressed her belief that this fund would allow the state to reinvest in its second most profitable revenue generator: tourism. She highlighted how wildlife was a part of the fabric of Wyoming, and today’s investment would yield returns for decades to come.
“This is more than wildlife,” Johnson said. “This is about our state, our youth, our communities, and what we want in the next 100 years.”
Alex Aguirre, the Wyoming community partnerships coordinator for the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership, shared Johnson’s feelings.
“I just think being proactive and getting ahead of it is kind of our duty,” he said.
Legislators’ discussion of the bill primarily concerned what the funding mechanisms would be and the ultimate monetary amount for the fund.
Rep. Steve Harshman, R-Casper, was in full support of the fund, but he questioned what type of funding model should be used — namely, whether the fund should be inviolate or an endowment. The bill currently sets up the fund as inviolate, meaning funding could not be altered or diverted.
Harshman noted that future legislators would likely face public pushback if they considered dismantling the fund.
Rep. Liz Storer, D-Jackson, acknowledged that two-thirds of both chambers was a high bar, but it could be met if committee members educated their colleagues about the importance of this bill.
Rep. Karlee Provenza, D-Laramie, suggested a fund goal of $500 million, which was passed by the committee.
Harshman then suggested three levers for the funding, the first being any over-the-cap severance tax money, the second being any over-the-cap federal mineral royalties and the last being putting one-third of 1% of the severance tax into the fund.
Of that one-third, the first $1 million would go to the 988 trust for the suicide prevention hotline, $1 million would go to the Outdoor Recreation and Tourism Trust Fund, and the remainder would go to the Game and Fish Trust Fund, with all three of these funding options continuing until the total goal of $500 million is reached.
The committee voted to approve those funding mechanisms, in addition to voting to advance the bill overall.
Co-chairman Sen. Bill Landen, R-Casper, who is retiring at the end of this year, expressed his belief in this legislation, in addition to his hope that it will reach the two-thirds required and be enacted to support Game and Fish.
“This one is just paramount,” he said. “That’s all there is to it. It represents who we are, and it’s why everybody wants to come and visit us.”
The 69th Wyoming Legislature’s general session is scheduled to begin Jan. 12.

title: Your Health Idaho is in open enrollment. Insurance premiums hikes might be tamped down.
description: For about the next month, Idahoans can enroll in health insurance plans on the state’s exchange. As health insurance premiums continue to grow, Idaho’s exchange, Your Health Idaho, is the only place that Idahoans can go to get private health insurance discounted by the federal government.  For some Idahoans, that discount — in the form […]
text:
Next year marks the second consecutive year of double digit premium rate increases across Your Health Idaho plans. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)For about the next month, Idahoans can enroll in health insurance plans on the state’s exchange.
As health insurance premiums continue to grow, Idaho’s exchange, Your Health Idaho, is the only place that Idahoans can go to get private health insurance discounted by the federal government. 
For some Idahoans, that discount — in the form of a tax credit — might shield them from the average of 12% premium rises for plans on the exchange, said Your Health Idaho Executive Director Pat Kelly. That’s because the tax credit is linked to the cost of one slate of plans, the silver, he said. 
“We’re actually seeing net premiums — which is the amount consumers pay after the tax credit is applied — we’re seeing those net premiums either flat or declining in 2027,” Kelly said in an interview.
He offered a few examples of how that could work. A single person in Ada County earning $36,000 a year might pay $8 less in premiums. If that person lived in the Magic Valley, they might pay $30 less in premiums, he said. 
“Health insurance, for those that receive a tax credit, is an incredible affordability story this year,” Kelly said. “They’re actually seeing plans that are either the same net premium cost from ‘26 to ‘27, or actually a decrease, which is just unheard of these days.”
But he stressed that the tax credit’s application depends on your family’s specifics: Where you live, how big your household is, and how much you make. So he encouraged Idahoans to use Your Health Idaho’s online tool to estimate how much of a tax credit they’d receive. 
Congress last year didn’t renew bigger discounts on federal and state exchanges, but there are still smaller discounts baked into the federal Affordable Care Act, which led to the exchanges’ creation. The end of the enhanced premium tax credits last year led about 25,000 Idahoans to cancel plans on the state exchange, Your Health Idaho estimated. 
Next year marks the second consecutive year of double digit premium rate increases across Your Health Idaho plans. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 When is open enrollment? And how do I sign up and shop around?

Open enrollment for Your Health Idaho lasts until Dec. 15. The cutoff that day is 11:59 p.m. Mountain time. Coverage for new plans starts Jan. 1.
On the exchange, Idahoans can pick from 143 medical plans and 32 dental plans from 12 insurance companies. 
At the state exchange’s website, you can shop for plans, see how much in a tax credit you could qualify for, use an affordability tool and find an agent or broker who can help you free of cost. Find pop-up enrollment centers hosted by Your Health Idaho online. 
Your Health Idaho officials say you shouldn’t wait until the last minute to enroll. For the most part, open enrollment is the last time that Idahoans can enroll in Your Health Idaho before next fall, unless they have a qualifying life event. 
“Start early, bring your questions, and let a local expert help you find coverage that fits your life and your budget,” Marcia Benton, a broker in Meridian, said in a written statement. 
 New immigration policies for federal, state exchanges

As part of President Donald Trump’s sweeping One Big Beautiful Bill Act, new restrictions will apply for immigrants who are legally in the United States. Even before the new regulations, undocumented immigrants were not eligible for federally funded health coverage, according to KFF, a health policy research group.
Starting next year, the new federal law will cut coverage for marketplace subsidies for many types of immigrants who are lawfully living in the U.S., including refugees and people who applied or were granted asylum or withheld deportation, according to the National Immigration Law Center. 
Under the law, the immigrants who aren’t U.S. citizens who can access subsidies for health insurance on exchanges include: lawful permanent residents or green card holders, entrants from Cuba or Haiti, and people who are living in the U.S. under Compacts of Free Association, which cover residents of certain South Pacific nations formerly under U.S. control, according to KFF.

title: Alabama college, university counties shift toward Democrats in midterms
description: While Democrats saw gains in every Alabama county last week, shifts in counties holding three of the state’s major universities were notable. In Tuscaloosa County, home of the University of Alabama, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones won 54%-45% over Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville, a reversal from 2022, when Republican Gov. Kay Iv[...]
text:
The Denny Chimes on the University of Alabama campus as seen on March 28, 2026. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones won Tuscaloosa County, the home of UA, 54% to 46% on Election Day, part of a broader shift toward Democrats in the state's college and university counties. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

The shift toward the Democratic Party was dramatic in counties with colleges and universities. Democrats flipped Tuscaloosa County toward Doug Jones and gained ground in places like Lee and Pike counties.
Local party leaders attributed the shift to increased engagement from younger voters because of economic concerns.
Republicans said that the gains made by Democrats were part of a natural political cycle, as the party in power typically loses ground during midterm elections.
Some also said the shift has to do with President Donald Trump remaking the Republican Party into one that is more focused on working-class voters.




While Democrats saw gains in every Alabama county last week, shifts in counties holding three of the state’s major universities were notable.
In Tuscaloosa County, home of the University of Alabama, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones won 54%-45% over Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville, a reversal from 2022, when Republican Gov. Kay Ivey won against Democratic nominee Yolanda Flowers, 62%-34%.
Tuberville won Lee County, home of Auburn University, and Pike County, home of Troy University, but by reduced margins over Ivey’s in 2022. Tuberville got 51% of the vote in Lee County, winning the county by about 1,800 votes out of 54,000 cast. Ivey got 67% of the vote in Lee in 2022.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In Pike County, Tuberville got 52% of the vote, down from Ivey’s 66% in 2022. Tuberville won by a margin of 370 votes out of over 10,000 cast.
Democratic Party chairs attributed the results to the policies of President Donald Trump.
“Local is national and the national is local,” said Jonathan Buchwalter, chair of the Tuscaloosa Democratic Party. “We see a country that elected Donald Trump, we see an Alabama that elected Donald Trump who promised affordability and no new wars. And what we got in the first two years was massive unaffordability and bombing in Iran.”
Republicans said the results are part of a natural political cycle.
“It seems to be the natural ebb and flow of politics,” said Cole Lawson, chair of the Republican Party in Lee County. “I don’t think it is particularly unusual if you look at the historical record of where the country has gone, whether it be a Republican or Democrat presidency. Generally, in a midterm the election swings toward the other party.”
Mitchell Brown, a political science professor at Auburn University, said the results were a statement of popular feeling against the current administration and about affordability issues.
“Things that college students are starting to see, ‘I am going to the grocery store and wait a minute, this costs how much?’ Gas, ‘I want to go to Atlanta and see a concert with my friends, but gas,’” Brown said. “For more recent graduates and who have jobs, ‘Can I afford to get a house?’”
The Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts University analyzed data from a survey conducted by the NORC Civic Health & Elections Project at the University of Chicago. The survey included more than 110,000 registered voters nationwide who were interviewed in the week leading up to the 2026 midterm elections.
Among young voters, 52% identified the economy and jobs as one of the three most important issues facing the country, followed by health care at 42% and the war in Iran at 27%.
Those issues mirrored the concerns of the electorate. According to a survey from Gallup, a firm that conducts polls, about 87% of registered voters identified the economy as either an extremely important or very important issue. That was followed by healthcare, with 77% saying that was either extremely important or very important. This was the same as the number of people who said the situation in Iran is important.
Alabama voters go to polls with affordability and national issues on their minds

Young voters also shifted toward Democrats compared with the 2024 presidential election.
“In that 2024 election, not only did Trump make serious inroads with nonwhite populations, which scared the heck out of the Democrats, he also made huge gains with young men,” said David A. Hughes, an associate professor of political science at the University of Louisiana Lafayette, who follows politics in Alabama. “Younger voters have, for many decades now, been the primary sources of Democratic votes.”
Tufts reported that Trump received about 47% of the votes of people between 18-29 versus former Vice President Kamala Harris who received the support of 51% of voters from that age bracket.
That estimate was based on a survey conducted by the Associated Press Vote Cast that included interviews with 139,000 registered voters in all 50 states between Oct. 28, 2024 and Nov. 5, 2024.
That was a smaller margin than former President Joe Biden’s 25-point advantage among young voters in 2020. Trump made dramatic gains in 2024 with young men, winning that group 56%-42%.
In last week’s election, according to an analysis based on data taken from NORC Civic Health & Elections Project, Tufts estimated that 66% of voters between 18-29 voted for a Democratic House candidate. Tufts also estimated that about 60% of young men, the demographic group where Trump made most of his gains among youth, voted for the Democratic candidate.
Hughes also noted that college-educated and suburban voters have started to shift toward the Democrats.
“We see the same thing in Alabama, the counties that are better educated, that make more money, those are the ones that swung hard toward the Democrats,” Hughes said.
Blue Huntsville: Democrats see major gains in Rocket City after years of effort

Madison County, where the University of Alabama in Huntsville is located, has a median household income of about $86,000 per year, and almost half the population has at least a college degree, according to the U.S. Census. The median income for Alabama overall is about $67,000. In 2022, almost 60% of voters in that county cast their ballots for Ivey. This year, Jones received almost 58% of the vote.
Local party leaders also said that the economy played an important role in the outcome of the races.
“Politics has morphed from this hypothetical, theoretical, thing to something that most people are living in, including our young people,” said Jamie Lowe, chair of the Lee County Democratic Party. “They are paying for gas just like the rest of us, they are paying for groceries just like the rest of us, they are buying a car and looking at inflation, they are looking at the possibility of homeownership and interest rates.”
Lawson also said that many people are upset about the economic climate.
“People generally vote with their pocketbooks, and I don’t think it is any secret right now that things are more expensive right now for most people, me included,” he said. “And you saw that at the ballot box.”
Lawson did not assign blame to Trump, however.
“There is no clear person who is responsible for that, and there is no clear party that is responsible for that, I think like all things, the world goes through phases and shifts, and various other powers that we don’t have any control over, like international affairs and things that are well above my paygrade, all contribute to it.”
Some also pointed to immigration.
“We had several ICE raids that disrupted our community, and on both sides of the aisle that was not attractive,” Lowe said. “Several of them were noticeable, in the middle of the day. That affected how people handled this election for sure.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: 40,000 WV Medicaid recipients not meeting work requirements, state estimates
description: About 40,000 Medicaid recipients in West Virginia are not meeting the new federal work requirements taking effect in January, meaning they could lose their health coverage next year, according to the latest estimate from the state Department of Human Services.
text:
The West Virginia Department of Human Services' website, wvmedicaidhelp.org, explains the changes coming to the program in January on Nov. 11, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)About 40,000 Medicaid recipients in West Virginia are not meeting the new federal work requirements taking effect in January, meaning they could lose their health coverage next year, according to the latest estimate from the state Department of Human Services. 
The new work requirements take effect Jan. 1 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or H.R. 1, which President Donald Trump signed into law last year. 
The new estimate is 7,000 more than an initial estimate from August, and represents the number of West Virginians on expanded Medicaid who have not been identified as meeting the work requirements and or qualifying for an exemption, Angel Hightower, a communications specialist for the Department of Human Services, wrote in an email to West Virginia Watch. 
“The original number of 33,000 was a preliminary estimate made prior to the release of additional federal guidance,” Hightower said. 
She added that the Department of Human Services is reviewing additional data to identify more people who qualify for exemptions, and expects to have updated estimates this month or in early December.
Under the new requirements, beginning Jan. 1, people aged 19 to 64 who are part of expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act will be required to work, volunteer or train at least 80 hours per month in order to keep their healthcare coverage. About 160,000 West Virginians are on expanded Medicaid.
There are exemptions to the work requirements, including households that include someone who gets the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, and already meet the work requirements for that program and those who are “medically frail,” among others.
Court blocks Trump administration’s narrow ‘medical frailty’ definition 
In June, the Trump administration issued an interim final rule that required that those who seek an exemption for medical frailty prove that their condition significantly limits their ability to comply with the work requirements. 
Late last month, a district court ruled that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid had overstepped its authority with the narrow definition, according to KFF, a nonprofit health policy research, polling, and news organization. 
Based on the court ruling, people will now only need to show they have a condition that falls into one of the five medical frailty categories listed in the law to qualify for an exemption, KFF said. 
The categories include: those who are blind or disabled; people who have a physical, intellectual or developmental disability that limits their ability to perform one or more activities of daily living, those with a substance use disorder or a “disabling” mental disorder; and those with “serious or complex” medical conditions.
Hightower said the department has done an assessment and determined that its current policies are in line with the ruling.
Kelly Allen, director of West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy, said the Trump administration complicated the already difficult process of implementing the work requirements with rules that go beyond H.R. 1, putting more people at risk of losing coverage. 
“Thankfully a court has halted those rules, but that too adds to the chaos and challenges state Medicaid agencies face in implementation and that Medicaid enrollees face in understanding how to comply with new eligibility rules,” Allen said.
“We urge West Virginia to ask CMS for a good faith waiver to delay implementing terminations for work reporting noncompliance while they work to ensure the entire work reporting requirements eligibility apparatus is working properly as a whole,” she said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ‘I got to tell him’: Ojeda wins NC-09 seat just days before father passes away
description: Richard Ojeda unseated GOP Rep. Richard Hudson in a surprise upset.
text:
WASHINGTON, DC - Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-NC) speaks during a Veterans Day Democracy on November 11, 2026 in Washington, DC. Veterans, military family members, advocates and civilian allies gathered at the U.S. Capitol to reaffirm the constitutional oath. (Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)ABERDEEN, N.C. — When he found out he’d won the race for North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District, the first thing Richard Ojeda did was head upstairs to his father’s room. 
Ojeda’s father, also named Richard Ojeda, had been fighting Parkinson’s disease for six years. Ojeda’s campaign team held a small gathering at Ojeda’s house in Aberdeen on election night to watch the results. 
“I got to wake him up. I got to tell him that his son made it to Congress,” Ojeda said. “He had the biggest smile on his face.”
Ojeda’s father passed away two days later. The younger Ojeda said he plans to carry a small bag of his father’s ashes around his neck when he’s sworn into the 120th Congress. 
Ojeda’s victory is part of a blue wave that swept the nation last week. Democrats appear to have flipped seven U.S. House seats in the Tar Heel State, leading to a 11-3 majority in the congressional delegation. 
In the 9th District, Ojeda unseated GOP Rep. Richard Hudson in a surprise upset. Hudson has held office since 2013 and serves as the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the party’s campaign arm. 
U.S. Reps.-elect Chuck Hubbard, Jamie Ager, and Richard Ojeda at freshman orientation in Washington on Nov. 8, 2026. (Photo: Richard Ojeda on X)
President Donald Trump won the south-central North Carolina district three times, most recently by 16 points during the 2024 election. Ojeda beat Hudson by 6,290 votes, or 2.3 points, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. 
“Hudson, under normal circumstances in a more neutral year, would hang onto the seat, but he got swept out,” said David Holian, a political science professor at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro. “I didn’t see much of him on the air until fairly late in the campaign when people started to realize that this might be an actual contest.”
Ojeda and his team spent 22 months on the campaign trail. They received national support — the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee placed the seat in its “Districts in Play” program in August. 
This cycle marks the second consecutive midterm election that hasn’t gone well for a chair of a party’s campaign arm. DCCC chair Sean Patrick Maloney lost his reelection bid for his New York seat in 2022. 
“Parties tend to confer this job every two years, or however often someone is willing to do it, to members who are in safe districts, precisely because they can spend more time concentrating on getting other folks elected and gaining seats or protecting seats than worrying about themselves,” Holian said. “The extent of the wave caught a lot of folks by surprise.”
Ojeda, 56, is a retired Army major who grew up in rural West Virginia. His grandfather was an immigrant from Mexico who changed the pronunciation of his last name — hard “J” — to better assimilate. 
Now, Ojeda will be the first Hispanic member of Congress from the Tar Heel State. 
Before running for Congress, Ojeda served in the West Virginia Senate from 2017 to 2019. There, he played a pivotal role in the 2018 statewide teacher strike. 
“He was one of the leaders of that effort to raise the pay of teachers and school service personnel,” said Mike Woelfel, a state senator who was Ojeda’s seatmate in Charleston. “He’s a character, and he has character, and that’s not always the case with politicians.”
Ojeda has garnered national attention for a social media post he made calling for the impeachments of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and border czar Tom Homan. He has also attracted criticism from conservatives for a 2022 podcast in which he said he’d be “happy to go to jail” to punch Stephen Miller.
From classroom to Congress, Cyril Jefferson is bringing his public service to Washington

Former West Virginia state senator Mitch Carmichael, a Republican, served as Senate president during Ojeda’s tenure. He described Ojeda as a “loose cannon,” but said they got along personally. 
“He is somewhat radical in his approaches to certain aspects of the decorum of a body and so forth,” Carmichael said. “He’s really enthusiastic, very excitable, and we just wanted to make sure he brought all that passion and he was stable in the manner in which he displayed it.”
North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District covers all or portions of Alamance, Chatham, Cumberland, Guilford, Hoke, Moore, and Randolph counties. 
It includes Fort Bragg, the largest U.S. Army military installation by population. Ojeda spent more than 15 years there during his Army career. 
He said one of his top priorities is joining the House Armed Services Committee, and he’s been a vocal critic of the war with Iran. 
“I’m going to do everything in my power to not just elevate soldiers, sailors, airmen, and marines, but I’m going to elevate their families,” Ojeda said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota unveils application process for first potential charter schools
description: North Dakota’s first charter schools are potentially on the horizon for fall 2027 as the Department of Public Instruction released application materials last week and a timeline to set the new schools in motion. North Dakota public charter schools were authorized by the Legislature in 2025 with the passage of Senate Bill 2241. “Opening a […]
text:
A North Dakota charter school academic performance framework packet is displayed on Nov. 11, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s first charter schools are potentially on the horizon for fall 2027 as the Department of Public Instruction released application materials last week and a timeline to set the new schools in motion.
North Dakota public charter schools were authorized by the Legislature in 2025 with the passage of Senate Bill 2241.
“Opening a public school is a serious responsibility, and North Dakota families deserve confidence that any new school has a clear plan to help students succeed,” said Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier in a statement.
The state will provide an average per student payment of about $8,300 to each charter school based on its enrollment. The new schools are not eligible to receive funding from property taxes, according to the department.
Applications for new charter schools under the ND ANCHOR program, Authorizing North Dakota Charters for High-Quality Outcomes and Results, can be submitted to the department beginning Dec. 2 and will continue until March 2, 2027, according to the DPI website. 
Under state law, public charter schools will operate within the state’s public education system and cannot charge students tuition. They also must enroll all students who apply and use a lottery system, if enrollment surpasses the school’s capacity. Public charter schools must not base admission criteria on ethnicity, national origin, religion, gender, income level, English proficiency or disabling conditions.
The schools are also prohibited from engaging in religious educational programming and operations, according to state law.
Arlene Wolf, director of school approval and opportunity for the department, said the application materials, process and timeline were the results of nearly two years of work looking into best practices.
House passes bill authorizing charter schools in North Dakota

“We’re ensuring that we’re really, truly opening those that are high quality schools with really good plans and have the best interests at heart,” Wolf said. She added the department consulted with national charter school organizations and other states.
A public charter school is not something that can be opened quickly, she said, and potential schools should take some time to weigh whether becoming a public charter school would be the best fit.
Wolf said the performance agreements with the department will be a key mechanism in setting the benchmarks for the new charter schools and evaluating their success.
As part of the application, prospective charter schools must enter into performance agreements that measure student academic proficiency and growth, attendance and recurrent enrollment, graduation readiness, financial and governance performance and community engagement. The school’s results in those areas will determine renewal eligibility and potential corrective action if performance goals are not met, according to the department.
“They are kind of held to that,” Wolf said. “It is a contract.”
Nick Archuleta, president of ND United, a union representing teachers and public employees, said the charter school performance agreements are an important guardrail to ensure quality education.
“If you are covering the academic, financial and governing structures of these things, that’s a very good place to start,” Archuleta said. “I think it is a sustainable path and I think it’s a good path because it does put those guardrails in right away so there isn’t any gray area.”
He also commended the department for requiring licensed teachers and staff members for the charter schools, as well as, an in-person learning requirement that would prevent online academies from sprouting up across the state.
“We know that education is predicated on relationships,” he said. “And it’s hard to form those relationships, if you are going to be constantly online.”
Each potential charter school must also submit to a public interview with department officials before any approval decision is made.
Established North Dakota schools are able to convert to public charter schools under the law.
Private schools that could potentially shift to a public charter school may already have a lot of the information needed for the application, she said. 
Dave Archambault Sr., of Fort Yates, speaks during an administrative rules hearing for the Department of Public Instruction on Dec. 2, 2025. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The department will release an informational video Monday to explain the application process.
“We wanted to get it out. We wanted people to look it over,” Wolf said. “It’s gonna take time.”
Dave Archambault Sr., a member of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe, a former principal and superintendent of tribal schools in South Dakota, told members of the department during a December administrative rules hearing that charter schools give opportunities for communities to try something new, which is needed in tribal education.
“I want a lot more for our children on these reservation schools to do better,” Archambault said. “It (charter schools) has such great possibilities for developing human potential and that’s what I want.”
He said having more options for Native American families choosing where to send their children to school could lead to more successful outcomes.
During the 2021-22 school year, the average graduation rate for students across the U.S. was 87% while the rate for Native American students was 74% during the same time period, according to the National Center for Education Statistics.
A few people and groups have reached out to the department since the application was posted last week, Wolf said, but interest has waned a little since the law went into effect in 2025.
The department also plans to open another application window for public charter schools next fall, she said, and hopes to have an annual application window opening every fall.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Morrisey administration will expand childcare subsidy eligibility to include parents with LLCs
description: West Virginia will soon allow eligible parents who operate small businesses through an LLC to qualify for the childcare assistance program.
text:
West Virginia will expand its childcare subsidy eligibility to include parents or caregivers who operate LLCs, removing a 2007 policy that barred their participation. An employee at Cubby’s Childcare Center in Bridgeport, West Virginia, plays with two infants on July 6, 2026. (Photo by Amelia Ferrell Knisely/West Virginia Watch)West Virginia will soon allow eligible parents who operate small businesses through an LLC to qualify for the childcare assistance program.
The Morrisey administration’s change to a long-standing policy comes after West Virginia Watch detailed how the rule prevented low-income mothers with LLCs from accessing childcare.
Parents operating LLCs have been barred from eligibility since 2007, predating the Morrisey administration.
“The policy is being revised to include LLCs as eligible forms of self-employment activity for the childcare subsidy. DoHS expects to complete this change in early December this year,” said Anne Moore, spokesperson for Gov. Patrick Morrisey. 
The state’s childcare assistance program helps working parents find and pay for childcare. Eligible parents — those who are working or furthering their education — pay anywhere from $0 to $13 per day; the state pays the rest of the assistance to participating childcare centers.
More than 11,000 children use the childcare assistance program in West Virginia. 
Del. Evan Worrell, R-Cabell, said he does not support any cuts to the state’s childcare subsidy program due to TANF funding shortfalls after lawmakers passed a landmark childcare bill during the 2026 legislative session. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
House Health Chair Evan Worrell, R-Cabell, raised questions about the LLC policy Monday at the state Capitol with Human Services officials. Worrell said constituents have brought the issue to him after losing eligibility due to their LLC under Morrisey. 
“I am just happy to see this being revised, and I think it is very important for working West Virginians. Sometimes people have some very creative minds, and they want to go out and start a business. And I applaud that,” Worrell said in a phone interview.
“The biggest thing I love about West Virginia is our entrepreneurial spirit. We have a lot of entrepreneurs, and so by saying you’re having an LLC, you can’t qualify for a subsidy, I feel like it is the exact opposite of what we should be saying,” he said.
LLCs offer business owners legal protections by separating personal assets from business. 
Families on average spend over $10,000 a year on childcare in West Virginia, making the state’s childcare assistance a lifeline for parents and caregivers.
“I think that the Legislature, the Chamber of Commerce and so many different organizations have said that childcare is a barrier to workforce. So, we shouldn’t then also provide a barrier to that workforce by not allowing you to have an LLC,” Worrell said. 
Worrell wants to review the final language of the childcare subsidy policy change; he hopes it includes some type of language to help parents who lost the childcare subsidy after moving their business into an LLC.
“I will have follow up questions,” Worrell said.
West Virginia’s childcare assistance program is primarily funded through federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families dollars and the Child Care and Development Block Grant.
Morrisey and Human Services officials are currently reviewing the state’s use of TANF funds due to a looming deficit in that federal funding. Issues with TANF funds were linked to Morrisey’s controversial handling of the state’s school clothing voucher program over the summer.
The scrutiny of TANF dollars could prompt changes to the childcare assistance program in 2027, including decreasing eligibility.

title: Grocery tax cut draws cautious response from Tennessee Senate speaker nominee
description: The Tennessee legislature will consider measures to cut grocery sales taxes in 2027, but the Senate’s nominee to be next speaker gave the idea a lukewarm reception, despite acknowledging that people are struggling with “affordability.” Sen. Jack Johnson of Franklin, selected Tuesday by the Senate Republican Caucus to be the new speaker, said afterward the […[...]
text:
For the last two legislative sessions, Democratic and Republican lawmakers have unsuccessfully sponsored bills to cut Tennessee's grocery tax. Similar moves are expected in the new session. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The Tennessee legislature will consider measures to cut grocery sales taxes in 2027, but the Senate’s nominee to be next speaker gave the idea a lukewarm reception, despite acknowledging that people are struggling with “affordability.”
Sen. Jack Johnson of Franklin, selected Tuesday by the Senate Republican Caucus to be the new speaker, said afterward the legislature has looked at sales tax breaks, including several bills to cut the 4% grocery tax, in recent years and he expects to “have that question again.” He did not say whether he endorses it.
Republican Sen. Jack Johnson of Franklin, who is likely to be the next Senate Speaker, has not said whether he endorses a plan to cut Tennessee’s grocery taxes. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
“Affordability is a real concern. It’s a real issue out there,” Johnson said. He added that despite limitations at the state level, the Senate will look at ways to make “incremental improvements to affordability issues.”
Johnson made the statement after outgoing Senate Speaker Randy McNally said during Tuesday’s caucus election that the Iran war and high gas prices led to a wave of Democratic wins nationally. Johnson said he heard those concerns on the campaign trail this fall.
Republicans such as Rep. Todd Warner of Chapel, now-former Rep. Elaine Davis of Knoxville and Sen. Bo Watson of Hamilton County, chairman of the Senate finance committee, sponsored bills in the 2026 session to reduce the state’s grocery tax, but they weren’t taken seriously. 
Democratic Rep. Aftyn Behn and Sen. Charlane Oliver, both of Nashville, carried a bill this year to remove the grocery sales tax and replace the lost revenue by collecting a corporate minimum tax generating $900 million. They said their argument was backed by a state report showing Tennessee’s most profitable companies are avoiding taxes.
Tennessee lawmakers renew push for grocery tax break

Republicans who hold supermajorities in the House and Senate didn’t give the Behn-Oliver bill a chance to pass.
House Speaker Cameron Sexton introduced a bill this week to cut the sales tax on milk, eggs and bread. It could see changes as the session progresses.
Behn said in a text message she plans to introduce another bill next week to remove the sales tax on groceries.
Cutting the state’s portion of the grocery tax would cost the state about $800 million, and eliminating it entirely would take about $1.2 billion of state and local tax revenue.
State officials, though, are projecting a billion-dollar surplus, on top of a $1.2 billion surplus in collections last year.
