text:
Sometimes you make a connection that floors you. This is one of them.
In July 2025 I was at a conference at the Turtle Bay Resort on the North Shore. Former Governor John Waiheʻe was speaking, and he did what he often does. He had the room leaning in as he wove together hard-won insights from decades of leadership. He is an incredible storyteller.
And then our phones buzzed, well, at least most of ours did. Mine didnʻt, but it became apparent something was going on. Then mine buzzed too.
Tsunami warning. Leave now. You are in a danger zone. This is not a drill. Or something like that.
I thought this might be another false alarm. Most of us remember the warning we got in January 2018 that a missile was on the way. You could see people Googling to verify the alert. This one was real.
After a few awkward minutes, the room settled and people started to talk story. A minority of the group decided to ride it out upstairs at the resort. I gave that a serious think over and felt it was a safe option, but decided to join my ʻohana back home and braved what was becoming some of the worst traffic of my life.
I am grateful no destructive wave came because I would not have made it out of the danger zone in time. I was also grateful that I had a self-driving car, at least for a bit. I used voice mode to make calls and talk to Google Gemini to figure out what I would do if I got stuck on the coast. 
I started toward the Kāneʻohe way, switched directions toward Wahiawā, found traffic was worse and switched back.
It didnʻt matter. Both sides were backed up for hours, and I started to estimate how much time I had before the wave came. Both ways home run right along the coastline, the worst possible place to be in a tsunami. 
I know this was wrong, but I swiped my phone more than a few times to switch between calls and Googleʻs Gemini while in self driving mode. I was looking for a place to ditch my car and hike to higher ground if I had to.




Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email  news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

My car warned me. Pay attention to the road. I think after the third warning, it banned me from self-driving for a day. I didnʻt know that was a thing, and I agree that kind of protection should be in place. I drove inch-by-inch the rest of the way myself.
About halfway home, now without Google Gemini, I started thinking about what I wrote in my upcoming book about Hawaiʻiʻs role in catalyzing the worldʻs scientific tsunami warning system. The first warning was triggered about a hundred years ago by a quake from the same region, Kamchatka. 
That also made me think about research I had read on the unusual bend in the chain of our underwater mauna. They march nearly 4,000 miles from their birthplace over our Hawaiian hotspot and end up diving under a plate at Kamchatka.
The Hawaiian and Emperor seamount chains. Map made from NASA Blue Marble imagery and SRTM15+. Olin Lagon/Civil Beat/2026
And then it hit me. The plate carrying our oldest mauna had just shaken Kamchatka and sent a tsunami back toward home. Our mauna can still send us messages millions of years after they have lost their fire.
Let me back up a bit.



Thomas Jaggar, founder of the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, at work in 1925.  (Courtesy: USGS)


Seismographs at the Thomas A. Jaggar Museum at Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park.  (Courtesy: Jaggar Museum)


Thomas Jaggar started an observatory on the rim of Kīlauea. He saw patterns on his seismographs that connected earthquakes and tsunamis. In late 1922 he detected an earthquake in Chile and ran the numbers. He predicted it would create a tsunami and he was right.
A few months later, in February 1923, he picked up an earthquake off Kamchatka. He ran the numbers and predicted that a tsunami would strike Hawaiʻi. He warned the Hilo harbormaster and told him when it would strike. The harbormaster did not take him seriously. 
The tsunami hit Hilo as predicted, and a fisherman died.
Hilo after the 1946 tsunami.  (Courtesy: USGS)
Ten years later, after a big quake off Japan, Hilo got another warning. This time people listened, and no one died.
Jaggar kicked off an era of scientific tsunami warnings. What Hawaiʻi built after Jaggar still influences how the world warns people today.
On April 1, 1946, a tsunami from Alaska killed 159 people across our islands. The observatory Jaggar founded detected the quake about five hours before the wave hit Hilo, but no one was there to read it. Three years later, the first U.S. tsunami warning center was founded here in ʻEwa Beach to watch the Pacific Ocean, so the next quakes would not go unread.
Innovations to save lives did not stop there. In 1960, a tsunami from Chile killed 61 people in Hilo even though the sirens sounded. Too many people did not know what the sirens meant. So Hawaiʻi invented and built Civ-Alert, a way for Civil Defense to interrupt every radio station at once, and later television.
What we catalyzed here was exported. Warning systems in the Indian Ocean, the Caribbean, and the Mediterranean were largely based on our Pacific model. Federal officials studied Civ-Alert before creating the national Emergency Broadcast System in 1963. 
Today that system lives on as the Emergency Alert System, still cutting into TV and radio when we need to be warned. These really are islands of innovation.
Back to our mauna and that bend.
Look at this annotated map. Most of us know about our long chain of Hawaiian islands. But it does not end there. For reasons still debated, our Hawaiian chain bends northward. 
There are a couple of leading theories. Iʻd recommend reading the papers. They are fascinating. Regardless of the reason, our oldest surviving mauna end up at Kamchatka, at the far end of a chain almost 4,000 miles long.
Right now, a massive old mauna called the Meiji Seamount sits at the edge of the trench off Kamchatka, next in line to dive under. It was born about 82 million years ago over the same hotspot that is building Hawaiʻi Island today, yet carries a Japanese emperorʻs name.
Olin Lagon at Cheboksary Electromechanical College in Russia, where he taught for two years in the early 2000s.  (Courtesy: Olin Lagon)
I studied Russian in Moscow. I was a volunteer teacher at the Cheboksary Electromechanical College from 2000 to 2002, an engineering college in the heartland of Russia. It was a special Peace Corps assignment where the Russian government opened up their borders for a few years to a limited number of volunteers. I was an oddball kanaka ʻōiwi, teaching in Cheboksary and deeply involved in community life there.
People there asked me a million questions about Hawaiʻi. I spent two years explaining where I came from. I never knew a piece of where I came from was already there in Russian waters, linked to us for millions of years.
Stay curious, folks. Some of our deepest connections sit quietly out of sight until we wander off to find them.
The post Olin Lagon: Credit Hawaiʻi’s Mauna For Teaching Us About Tsunamis appeared first on Honolulu Civil Beat.

title: Native Hawaiians ‘Take The Torch’ Of Big Island Council Majority
description:

text:
Native Hawaiians will hold a majority of the Hawaiʻi County Council seats when newly elected members take office next month — the first time in at least three decades. 
Maile David, who became the first Native Hawaiian woman to chair the Hawaiʻi County Council in 2020, called the incoming representation remarkable.
“It took a long time,” she told Civil Beat through tears. “I’m glad I’m still alive to see this happen.”
Between one and three Native Hawaiians have occupied seats on the council at the same time since at least 1992, the earliest publicly available election data online. 
But in that time, they have never held a majority on the nine-member lawmaking body. Maui is the only other county where Hawaiians hold a majority of council seats.
All four of the newly elected Big Island council members — Manu Powers, Ikaika Rodenhurst, Lloyd Enriquez and Zed Kaʻapana Aki — are Native Hawaiian, along with two incumbents, Holeka Inaba and James Hustace. 
The new Indigenous members say they plan to lead with their Hawaiian values as they make decisions on development and land and water use that will affect the future of the island, home to the state’s largest Native Hawaiian population. 

Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026

Provided: Zed Ka'apana Aki/2026

From top left the newly electeds: Lloyd Enriquez (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026), Ikaika Rodenhurst (Twilight Greenaway/Civil Beat/2026), Zed Kaʻapana Aki (Courtesy of Zed Kaʻapana Aki), Manu Powers (Twilight Greenaway/Civil Beat/2026)
They will hold firm control over the council’s direction as they step in to head up some of the most powerful committees for the next two-year term, which starts the first week of December. 
When the council selected its leadership and standing committee assignments earlier this week, they chose Inaba to continue as the overall council chair, Hustace to chair the finance committee, Powers to head government operations, Rodenhurst to lead planning and economic development, Aki as chair of public works and Enriquez to head the public safety and health committee. Committee chairs shepherd legislation, guiding public input and discussion on amendments, before it moves on to the full council for approval.
“We all was hoping that our young people will learn all the things that we fought so hard to learn and to implement,” David said. 
David grew up in Kona during an era of fast-paced development with few Hawaiians in elected positions. She watched as the shoreline from Kailua-Kona to Keauhou was developed with resorts, she said, with scant attention paid to Hawaiians’ rights or environmental health. 
“Our gathering places were restricted from access, and our families were forced to move further and further south,” she said. “It was just really a hard thing to see.”
She became an activist because of it, but never planned to become a politician. Then, she said, fellow activist and former Native Hawaiian councilman Angel Kaʻapikapika Palago told her it was time Native Hawaiians worked from inside the government.
Her dream of is beginning to be realized, she said, after seeing Hawaiians win a firm majority of the council seats: “Now they just can take the torch and follow it through.”
Working From Within
Powers, who will represent North Kona, also realized that working from the outside wasn’t enough to create the change she wanted to see. 
“We’re finally getting the memo that you have to come from the inside at this point,” Powers said.
Growing up, Powers didn’t feel represented by her government, she added.
“Native Hawaiians have always felt very outside of government,” Powers said. Many of her kūpuna, she added, had to combat a system that suppressed their rights to their language, culture and land.
The illegal overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom in 1893 and that history created a foundation of distrust in the government for many Hawaiians. For some, engaging in the American political system contradicts their belief that Hawaiʻi is a sovereign nation. 
“I’m hoping that this representation demonstrates to them that this government is their government,” Powers said. 
Powers said it was her family, which includes the likes of Haunani-Kay and Mililani Trask, that she looked up to growing up. The Trasks were leaders in the Hawaiian sovereignty movement. 
Six of the nine seats on the Hawai‘i County Council will be filled by Native Hawaiians following last week’s election. Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2025
Rodenhurst, a Kamehameha Schools Kapālama graduate who will represent Puna Makai, said it’s been a long, troubled history for Kanaka ʻŌiwi.
Native Hawaiians, who make up 21.8% of Hawaiʻi’s population, are less likely to graduate from high school or college than the average resident, census data shows. Hawaiians also face disproportionate rates of serious health issues and are over-represented in the prison and homeless populations.
“Finally (we are) making those steps forward to be in positions where we can make decisions,” Rodenhurst said, “and change our ʻāina, change our home for the better of not just kanaka, but all the people of Hawaiʻi.”
Making Hawai‘i More Hawaiian 
Native Hawaiians’ connection to ʻāina and wai make this change particularly notable. As Hawaiʻi faces a housing shortage, the Big Island’s council is juggling water, land and cultural conservation with a need for more housing and infrastructure to support development. 
Those issues came to head last month when the council heard a bill to rezone agricultural land for a housing development called Waikōloa Green. Worries over whether there was enough water for the homes made the council push the issue to July and into the hands of the new council members. The new council will also have to decide on amendments to the county’s general plan, which guides 20 years of future growth and development.
The task ahead for the first-year lawmakers is large, David said. They’ll carry the kuleana of representing Hawaiians while making decisions on difficult issues. They’ll also have to learn to navigate the political system, she added. 
“My only advice would be: learn the process and conduct yourself with aloha,” David said.
For Aki — who will represent South Kona, Volcano and Kaʻū, his family’s ancestral land — when it comes to future development, having Hawaiians as the majority of decision-makers will test whether the county can balance housing needs with environmental and cultural values.
A sign at Punaluʻu Black Sand Beach is seen May 23, 2025, in Pāhala, Akiʻs district. Locals have been fighting against development in the area for decades.  Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2025
It will also be a chance, he added, to find where the most appropriate place for development is and for people culturally tied to the islands to make that decision. 
“This is an opportunity for us,” Aki said, “to infuse our culture, our cultural values, these wonderful things, into policy to make this place more distinctly Hawaiian.”
Having leaders whose decision-making is rooted in Hawaiian ʻike and values — such as aloha ʻāina, mālama and kuleana — is good for all residents, Rodenhurst said, not just the Native Hawaiian population. 
“We want to really do what’s right,” Rodenhurst said.
People come to Hawaiʻi for its natural beauty, Aki said, adding that Hawaiʻi has been able to hold onto that because of the work of Native Hawaiians. 
“At the same time we have a large number of people who are coming in who don’t necessarily share these values,” he said, citing overdevelopment and overtaxation of natural resources.
In an era of climate change, rapid technological advancement and a growing wealth divide, this council will lead by example, Aki said, as they figure out how to ensure traditional beliefs are upheld in an unknown future. 
“How do you approach mālama ʻāina in an ever-shifting world,” Aki said, “especially one where money talks and economics often requires exploitation?”

Without us, the big question is what will this place look like?Zed Kaʻapana Aki

Keeping Hawaiians Home
While a majority of the council will be Native Hawaiians, most of the Indigenous population doesn’t live in Hawaiʻi. That’s a statistic that both worries and drives the new lawmakers. 
Aki is familiar with the pressures that move families away. His family moved from Kaʻū to Oʻahu in search of more economic opportunity two generations ago. They had always dreamed of moving back, he told Civil Beat last month. 
“Without us, the big question is: What will this place look like?” Aki said. “It adds an extra layer of kuleana.”
For Powers, keeping her grand-nephew, Wai, in Hawaiʻi is part of what led her to run for office. As a councilwoman, she wants to ensure he and other Hawaiians don’t have to leave Hawaiʻi to afford a home and basic necessities.
“Having six Native Hawaiians on the council who understand that pain of potentially having to leave the place you are so connected to,” Powers said, “is a heavily motivating factor for all of us.”
As the council makes decisions that will affect the future of the island, having Hawaiians at the helm will help, she added, but they’ll need the community’s buy-in.  
“I don’t think having a majority of Native Hawaiians on the council is going to solve all of our problems,” she said. “We need (the entire community) to understand exactly what it is we’re dealing with, what the possible solutions are, and how they can contribute.”

title: Simpson vs. Maggiore: The battle for New Hampshire House speaker heats up
description: After last week’s election results dramatically shifted power in the New Hampshire House, the new Democratic majority faces its first big task: picking leadership. Republicans held a 215-177 majority prior to Election Day. Once the new lawmakers elected last week are sworn in, that’ll become a 291-108 Democratic majority (including one independent), pending [...]
text:
Democratic Reps. Jim Maggiore and Alexis Simpson are vying to become the next speaker of the New Hampshire House. (Photo at left by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin. Photo at right by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)After last week’s election results dramatically shifted power in the New Hampshire House, the new Democratic majority faces its first big task: picking leadership.
Republicans held a 215-177 majority prior to Election Day. Once the new lawmakers elected last week are sworn in, that’ll become a 291-108 Democratic majority (including one independent), pending recounts. With their new majority, Democrats will have enough control to pick the speaker of the House for the first time in six years.
The speaker has an array of responsibilities. They make committee assignments, preside over voting sessions and control how bills move through the legislative process.
Rep. Alexis Simpson, who has led the caucus as minority leader since 2024, was instantly seen as a candidate for the role. But she now faces a challenge from Rep. Jim Maggiore, a five-term representative from New Hampton. On Thursday, the House Democratic Caucus is set to meet with the goal of coalescing around one candidate before Dec. 2, when the full House will convene to officially elect the position.
Democratic House Leader Alexis Simpson, of Exeter, addresses a crowd in opposition to the House Finance Committee’s proposed budget, Wednesday, April 9, 2025. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
The old guard
Simpson, who has represented Exeter for five terms, argues her time leading the caucus has prepared her for this moment. She said the affordability agenda she and her colleagues pushed for the past two years was what voters responded so well to.
“My team has spent years preparing for this opportunity to put the agenda into action and hold steadfast to our values,” she said. “We did that even in the minority with grit and perseverance and determination, and now we have the chance to really lead.”
That affordability agenda mirrored Democrats’ strategy nationwide this past election cycle as candidates from North Carolina to California focused on the cost of living in campaign messaging.
“The most important thing that a House Democratic speaker can do is make sure that the needs of Granite Staters are prioritized,” Simpson said.
She believes she’s proven in the last two years that she prioritizes those needs, specifically when it comes to housing, where Democrats pushed unsuccessfully to better fund the state’s Housing Champions program, as well as childcare, where they sought to create workforce programs.
Simpson said “1.3 million people are counting on us to address their basic day-to-day needs with integrity, and that’s what our House Democratic Caucus plans on doing.
“There are people who can’t find housing. There are people who need the government to do our job and to do it well,” she said. “And the House Democrats are ready to step up and to govern. And I don’t want that to be lost in the midst of this battle for the speaker nomination.”
State Rep. Jim Maggiore speaks to reporters and fellow lawmakers during a press conference announcing his candidacy for New Hampshire House speaker on Nov. 11, 2026, inside the Legislative Office Building in Concord. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
A challenger
On Friday, Maggiore, who represents North Hampton and sat on the House Municipal and County Government Committee, officially announced his candidacy for speaker at a Concord press conference.
“The residents of New Hampshire have sent a clear message with this historic election,” he said. “They demand better communication, better collaboration, greater transparency, respect, and most importantly, historic legislative results across New Hampshire.”
He echoed Simpson’s call for affordability. He said it “must be the organizing principle of our work and the foundation of the most important bill that we’re going to have to undertake on day one, which is the 2027 state biennial budget.” He said that means insisting on “at the very least” accountability for the state’s voucher-like education freedom account program, which Republicans expanded in 2025, and fully funding housing initiatives.
Most notably, Maggiore argued Simpson’s leadership of the caucus hasn’t been collaborative enough.
“We will change how our caucus works,” he said. “Members should help shape major decisions, not hear about them after the fact.”
That includes, he said, engaging committee expertise earlier, better educating members about caucus priorities and mentoring newer members.
Asked about these criticisms, Simpson pushed back, saying the caucus has relied on committee member expertise and has a process for when members disagree with a committee’s stance.
“Everyone has an opportunity to sway their caucus members,” she said, “but they’re not always going to win the caucus’ vote.”
A voting record and leadership style in question
The candidates voting records are likely to emerge in the debate ahead. Simpson has voted with the Democratic caucus 99% of the time in partisan votes (excluding votes that were overwhelmingly bipartisan), according to an analysis by Citizens Count, a New Hampshire-based political resource nonprofit. Maggiore, on the other hand, voted with the caucus 91% of the time on such votes. Only seven Democrats voted with their party less than Maggiore, and many of the votes he broke with the party on are ones likely to ruffle some feathers.
He was one of only nine Democrats to vote in favor of Medicaid work requirements. He was one of two Democrats to vote to cut the Office of the Child Advocate budget. He was one of 49 Democrats to vote against marijuana legalization. He was one of two Democrats to vote to table a minimum wage increase. He was one of two Democrats to vote for hard labor as a punishment for certain crimes. He also voted against multiple bills to loosen zoning laws with the goal of allowing more housing.

Asked about those votes, Maggiore said representatives must “serve their constituents,” “be responsible to their own conscience” and “be responsible to the caucus.” He said balancing those three factors is “why sometimes people are going to break” with the party.
On Friday, he criticized Republicans for cutting business taxes because “the estimated benefits of the repeal went overwhelmingly not to you and me, not to the small-business owners, not to the small individual sole proprietors” but “the highest-income earners and the biggest companies in our nation.” However, he voted for one of those cuts to the business profits tax. He said he didn’t regret the vote.
“I don’t think I’ve regretted any vote I’ve ever made,” he continued. “Although I haven’t reviewed every vote I’ve ever made.”
Maggiore has taken heat online for some of his views, including from Kayla Montgomery of Planned Parenthood of Northern New England, who pointed to a survey he completed. There, he said he was “undecided” on whether to ban abortion in the first trimester. She called it “disqualifying for a leadership position — of any party in NH” on social media.

Being “undecided” on banning abortion – at all – much less in the first trimester is disqualifying for a leadership position – of any party in NH. #NHpolitics https://t.co/InNx1ORlP3
— Kayla M. Montgomery (@KMontgomeryNH) November 11, 2026

However, to those who support him, Maggiore’s crossing the aisle represents a big tent view of the new Democratic majority.
Rep. Wendy Thomas, who represents Merrimack, described herself as “the poster child for progressive.” Still, she’s endorsed him, largely because she’s opposed to Simpson, echoing Maggiore’s complaints about her lack of collaboration. Thomas argued that the party can’t have “purity tests.”
“Alexis is a weak leader,” said Thomas, who was part of an informal group calling itself “Friends of Democracy” that sought an alternative to Simpson’s leadership. “She can’t hold the caucus together. She alienates people who challenge her. She’s not happy with rocking the boat.”
While vetting Maggiore, she said she and Rep. Eric Turer asked him about his vote to ban certain gender-affirming care, which concerned them as progressives.
“We were like, ‘Explain this one to us, please,’” she recalled. “And he said, ‘Well, I voted because I can’t endorse 9-year-olds having life-changing surgery. … And we said that never happens. That’s a Republican talking point. That just never happens, especially in New Hampshire.”
However, she said she doesn’t blame Maggiore, because in her mind, it was Simpson’s fault he wasn’t educated on the issue.
State Reps. Rosemary Rung (left) and Wendy Thomas (right) attend a press conference announcing Rep. Jim Maggiore’s candidacy for New Hampshire House speaker, on Nov. 11, 2026, inside the Legislative Office Building in Concord. Both representatives are endorsing Maggiore, despite the fact that he is ideologically dissimilar from their progressive beliefs. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Another Maggiore supporter, Rep. Lucius Parshall, added: “I’m supporting him because I feel right now we have a lot of people whose voices aren’t being heard.”
Behind Simpson is her leadership team. Rep. Lucy Weber, who has served as the Democratic floor leader under Simpson in the minority and was the House speaker pro tem the last time Democrats held the majority, said she “absolutely supports” Simpson.
“I think she has the temperament and the knowledge and is good at finding the right slot for each person,” Weber, who has represented Walpole for 18 years, said.
She said speakers need to ensure that even superminority party members get a chance to speak their minds before a vote. Otherwise, it creates dysfunction and affects decorum.
“Creating a culture of respect where people don’t feel like they need to act out because they’re being squashed is a high priority for me,” she said. “And I know it’s a high priority for Alexis, and I absolutely assume it’s a high priority for Jim Maggiore.”

title: Collections are coming for millions of student loans in default
description: A long-postponed reckoning could be coming soon for millions of student loan borrowers who are now faced with garnished wages and seized tax refunds as soon as next year.  Since pandemic forbearance finally expired last year, more than 9 million borrowers already are in default, owing a collective $234 billion, and millions more are late […]
text:
A soon-to-be college graduate tosses her cap for photos at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill in 2024. Student loan debt is crushing people across the country as pandemic forbearance ends, leaving some 9 million borrowers in default. (Photo by Sean Rayford/Getty Images)A long-postponed reckoning could be coming soon for millions of student loan borrowers who are now faced with garnished wages and seized tax refunds as soon as next year. 
Since pandemic forbearance finally expired last year, more than 9 million borrowers already are in default, owing a collective $234 billion, and millions more are late in their payments. Those borrowers are likely to face severe collection measures such as wage garnishment and seizure of tax refunds next year. Such collections have been repeatedly paused, most recently this past January.
Betsy Mayotte, president and founder of The Institute of Student Loan Advisors, a nonprofit that advises borrowers, schools and employers, said she expects collections to start next year. 
“It’s heartbreaking,” Mayotte said. “People tend to get caught off guard when their tax refund is taken and if they’re struggling financially, a lot of times they’re counting on that refund to catch up.”



Quotation







I fear that unless something miraculous happens, I will default and my wages will be garnished for life.


– Timothy Varro, a New York City attorney who owes $375,000 in student loans


The Washington Sun reported in October that collections plans would likely be announced after the midterm elections. The U.S. Department of Education did not respond to a Stateline question. 
States with the highest default rate, Mississippi, Louisiana and New Mexico, had more than a quarter of borrowers living there in default, but even the lowest state rates were 15% for Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Utah and Wisconsin. That’s according to a Stateline analysis of Education Department data from the second quarter of this year.  
Defaults began to start up again in late 2025 and early 2026. In those two quarters alone, 13% of student loans went into default in Louisiana and Mississippi, and at least 5% went into default in every state, according to data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York based on credit reports. 
Older borrowers seemed to be struggling more than they were before the pandemic, according to the bank’s analysis. 
As feds resume student loan collections, states try to catch borrowers before they sink

One of them is Timothy Varro, 40, who has made payments for the past 10 years but can’t keep up even with the interest on the roughly $120,000 he borrowed for college in New Jersey and law school in Rhode Island. 
Despite a good job as an attorney for a bank in New York City, the balance has ballooned to $375,000, and he can’t make the $2,000 minimum payment. It didn’t help that he graduated in a recession and took low-paying public service jobs at first. 
“I don’t have rich parents to pay this off for me,” Varro said in an interview. “This may be my conspiracy theory, but I think this is punishment. They’re trying to send a message that this is what’s going to happen if you’re lower or working class and you strive for upward mobility.” 
Varro said he worries about collection efforts because he’s supporting his fiancé in a small apartment in New York City and has been ill at times with epilepsy that requires breaks from work. 
“I fear that unless something miraculous happens, I will default and my wages will be garnished for life,” Varro said. “I don’t think it’s asking too much to just give us a payment plan that’s reasonable.” 
Even on a smaller scale student debt can be a burden when a college education doesn’t pay off as planned. 
Taylor Lewis, 26, owes $29,000 for her time at Kennesaw State University, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in media and entertainment. 
Taylor Lewis, 26, of Atlanta went into default on $29,000 in student loan for a degree in media and entertainment that didn’t help her get a job. (Photo courtesy of Taylor Lewis)
“I was young, I was just trying to chase my dreams. I wanted to be a talk show host. I wanted to work in the media world,” Lewis said. “I was just young and stupid, pulling out loans every semester and thinking, ‘Yeah I could pay that back. I don’t care about that.’  They prey on undergraduate students. They know we don’t have anything to lose at the time.“ 
After graduating in 2023 Lewis found that her degree did not get her into the media world without more experience, and she now works as an assistant manager for United Parcel Service in Atlanta.
After missing a payment by mistake, she said her loan went into default and she wasn’t allowed to rectify it without paying the full $29,000, which she can’t afford. She’s hoping to be offered a repayment plan and planning to go back to school, paying her own way this time, to get a degree in human resources. 
Some states, such as Maine, have initiatives to advise students on loans starting in high school. The state suffers too if young people fall into debt, said Mila Tappan, education affordability training manager at the Finance Authority of Maine, known as FAME.  Maine is among the states that offer a tax credit for student loan payments to help keep and recruit educated workers. Connecticut has similar credits for employers who help with student loans. 
Maine had one of the lowest rates of new defaults at the peak in late 2025 and early 2026, along with other New England states such as New Hampshire and Vermont, but also Kentucky and Wisconsin.
Maine’s finance authority offers student loan counseling through emails, webinars and in-person events. “We like to think that what we do makes a difference. Some of it is as simple as the mentality here in Maine, that you do what it takes to repay your debts,” Tappan said. 
Preston Cooper, a senior fellow at the conservative American Enterprise Institute, has written about the student loan crisis and lobbied for changes to benefit taxpayers, he said. He helped craft a process that could deny schools student loans if they can’t prove their degrees raise pay for graduates, for instance. 
New student loan rule could dissuade people from advanced nursing degrees

Some private vocational schools have very high rates of late payment on student loans, as high as two-thirds for some that are mostly in the South, according to a 2025 federal report. Schools of medicine and health, on the other hand, often have little or no default. 
The current crisis caught a lot of student borrowers by surprise because they were allowed to stop payments during the pandemic without being classified as delinquent or in default, and the pause was extended many times. 
“The government did not do a very good job of communicating the fact that repayment was starting again for real. There were a lot of false starts,” Cooper said. “They would say the student loan payments are about to resume, only to extend the pause. 
“You had heartbreaking stories where people only found out they were delinquent on their loans when they suddenly got dinged on their credit.” 
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

title: IHA legislative agenda focuses on Medicaid, insurance transparency
description: The Indiana Hospital Association will lobby in the coming legislative session for the elimination of duplicative reporting requirements, transparency from insurers and retroactive Medicaid coverage for Hoosiers booted from the Healthy Indiana Plan for procedural reasons. Lawmakers return to Indianapolis in January for what is expected to be a contentious bud[...]
text:
The Indiana Hospital Association released its legislative priorities for 2027. Retroactive Medicaid coverage, regulatory reforms, transparency and medical education funding topped the list. (Photo by Jack Forrest/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana Hospital Association will lobby in the coming legislative session for the elimination of duplicative reporting requirements, transparency from insurers and retroactive Medicaid coverage for Hoosiers booted from the Healthy Indiana Plan for procedural reasons.
Lawmakers return to Indianapolis in January for what is expected to be a contentious budget-writing session, with Democrats breaking the GOP’s supermajority in the House for the first time in 14 years.
The IHA’s legislative agenda, published Thursday morning, offers a glimpse into policy debates Hoosier lawmakers will entertain in the 2027 session.
The General Assembly will also have two new chairs for the House and Senate health committees. Republican Sen. Tyler Johnson, a physician, takes over the Senate panel while a new House chair hasn’t yet been announced. Former House leader Brad Barrett did not seek reelection and the vice chair was defeated.
Retroactive Medicaid coverage a priority for IHA
Lawmakers will return as federal Medicaid cuts mandated by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act begin to take effect. Those cuts include work reporting requirements for many working-age Hoosiers insured through the Healthy Indiana Plan starting in January.
“Mitigating the impacts of these cuts will be imperative to protecting long-term access, especially for rural communities,” IHA President Scott B. Tittle said in a news release Thursday.
In October, The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration estimated 58,000 Hoosiers were at risk of losing their coverage through HIP next year for failing to comply with work reporting rules. 
The agency has removed more than 500,000 Hoosiers from the state’s Medicaid rolls for unrelated reasons over the last two years, according to its Medicaid enrollment dashboard. AHA says Indiana hospitals are reporting a 30% surge in uncompensated care for uninsured patients at the same time.
‘Powerless’: Indiana families describe the toll of losing Medicaid access

The IHA is pushing to codify retroactive Medicaid coverage for Hoosiers who were eligible at the time of service, as well as those who were disenrolled for administrative reasons to prevent disruptions in care. This follows a decision by FSSA last month to provide 30-day retroactive coverage for some Hoosiers who enroll in HIP next year.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act also caps provider taxes like Indiana’s hospital assessment fee — one of two taxes the state uses to fund its share of HIP. 
The association wants to ensure revenue generated by the fee remains dedicated to HIP and Medicaid reimbursement for hospitals as the tax winds down, with any remaining funds directed to offset future Medicaid cuts. 
Outpatient drug discounts for hospitals
Lawmakers also may continue debating the merits of an obscure federal program known as 340B, which allows certain hospitals to purchase outpatient drugs at steep discounts while billing commercial insurance, Medicare or Medicaid for the full cost of the drug.
That controversial reimbursement model is the subject of intense debate: Supporters say 340B is critical to subsidizing services for low-income patients while critics allege the program is vulnerable to profiteering and abuse.
A proposed rule set to take effect in January will redirect any 340B savings Indiana hospitals once obtained through Medicaid to state coffers instead, while another law requires hospitals to report how 340B savings are used.
The program made IHA’s list of priorities for next year.
“340B was intended to be the pharmaceutical industry’s contribution to keep healthcare prices down,” Tittle said in the release. “These discounts represent just 3% of pharmaceutical companies’ global revenues — yet provide critical resources for patients and Indiana healthcare providers that struggle with sustainable operations as a result of government underfunding.”
Transparency from insurers
IHA is pushing for more transparency from insurers too, starting with a statewide review of claims submitted by insurers that administer benefits for the state’s Medicaid program.
The association also wants corporate insurers to share in-network rates directly with patients and report how many prior authorizations and patient claims are denied only to later be approved, which it said promotes “greater visibility into critical decisions that can delay and affect the care patients rely on.”
Both proposals are likely to meet resistance from insurers.
Ashton Eller, president of the Indiana Association of Health Plans, said insurers already share in-network rates with patients, while state-regulated plans report prior authorization, approval and denial statistics to the Indiana Department of Insurance and federal government each year.
He said insurers are under “rigorous, continuous” oversight and audits of managed-Medicaid plans too.
“When claims require additional review or recovery, it’s often to catch improper upcoming, duplicate billing or billing errors that would cost Hoosier taxpayers money,” Eller said. “If we weaken the ability of health plans to audit questionable claims, it only forces taxpayers to subsidize private billing mistakes and system waste.”
Steve Cooke, a spokesperson for the IHA, said consumers and employers continue to question what their premiums will ultimately cover — and what will they will be required to pay in copays, deductibles and coinsurance.
“Although certain information may be provided today, we regularly hear from both patients and employers that their health plan design is difficult to understand, and there is confusion about what will actually be covered after prior authorization requests and claim denials,” he said. “We look forward to working with the legislature to improve transparency in these areas.”
IHA estimates Indiana hospitals write off more than $1.6 billion each year in insurance claim denials and bad debt.
Meanwhile, the association says more than 80% of hospital claims are initially denied and overturned — amounting to $4.7 billion in delayed payments each year, which Indiana hospitals spend $400 million pursuing.
Still, Eller said premiums are a reflection of healthcare costs set by hospitals.
Insurers are “happy to be a partner in this focus on transparency as long as it leads to lower prices at the point of care,” he said. The group is expected to release its own legislative priorities in December.
Physician shortage, regulatory reform
IHA’s agenda also includes a call for more state funding for medical education to fend off a physician shortage, streamlined credentialing for newly hired physicians and elimination of duplicative hospital reporting requirements.
A report released by the Indiana Business Health Collaborative Thursday found there are just 239 active physicians per 100,000 Indiana residents — 6,380 physicians shy of demand.
Competition to recruit and retain physicians from other states is likely to worsen the shortage, according to the report, which recommends increased state funding for medical residency programs, particularly in primary care, specialty shortages and underserved communities.
“Without substantially increasing the number of physicians Indiana trains and retains, Hoosiers will face  increased limitations in access to medical services,” Beth Lock, chief executive officer and executive director of the IBHC, said in a news release Thursday. “The ripple effect is long-term consequences to community health outcomes, healthcare affordability and economic competitiveness.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: DeSoto County moved more voters to inactive in the leadup to Election Day than any other. Here’s what happened.
description: Kelly Jacobs, left, chair of the anti-Trump grassroots group Indivisible DeSoto MS, and Olive Branch resident Sheila Jackson wait for the start of the DeSoto County Election Commission's efforts to count affidavit ballots at the commission's office in downtown Hernando on November 11, 2026.
text:
This story was published by Votebeat in partnership with Mississippi Today. Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration. Mississippi Today is a nonprofit newsroom dedicated to covering justice, voting rights, politics, education, health and culture. Sign up for Votebeat’s free newsletters here and Mississippi Today’s free newsletters here.
HERNANDO – Dozens of people crowded into the old Trustmark Bank building in downtown on Wednesday afternoon to watch DeSoto County’s election officials pore over bins of ballots in a longtime Republican stronghold key to the political earthquake that has rattled Mississippi.
DeSoto, a Memphis suburb just below the Mississippi border, has been solid Trump country. Until now.
A jolt of Democratic enthusiasm and a slump in Republican voters appears to have delivered DeSoto County for Democrat Scott Colom, the Mississippi district attorney declared the winner Wednesday night over GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
DeSoto’s proximity to Memphis has established the county as a bright spot locally. It’s a center of economic development in America’s poorest state and the fastest-growing county amid statewide population decline, attracting Memphis suburbanites and Elon Musk-backed data centers alike.
From left, DeSoto County Election Commissioners Sissie Ferguson, Laura Edler, Tim Snyder and David Ross begin counting affidavit ballots in the 2026 midterms on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
But the county has drawn an uncomfortable spotlight since last week’s election as an epicenter of the election turmoil roiling Mississippi. This was the first federal general election in which officials across the state used unverified address data from the credit bureau Experian to render thousands of voters inactive, forcing them to cast affidavit ballots that are less certain to be counted. 
Voting rights advocates are concerned that errors in Experian’s data affected many voters who were already properly registered, forcing them to take additional steps in order to vote and blocking their access to the ballot box.
DeSoto moved more voters to inactive status than any of Mississippi’s 82 counties in the eight months between the primaries and the midterms. During that time, the county’s part-time election commissioners said, they moved to inactive nearly every voter flagged on the address lists that the secretary of state sourced from Experian’s data: more than 15,000 voters.
Over those months, DeSoto’s list of inactive voters more than doubled, leaving one in five of the county’s voters inactive by Election Day. Many didn’t find out until they came out to vote and found their names missing from the poll books in places where they had lived and voted for years.
Reports of hourslong voting lines, affidavit ballot shortages, and a now-dismissed Democratic lawsuit against DeSoto County followed soon after. 
Election protection hotlines sounded off with complaints of chaotic scenes at the polls. The state Democratic party’s lawsuit alleged that the line at one polling place got so long that someone waiting to vote passed out and had to be taken to the hospital. 


“The conditions were horrible,” said Ravonda Griffin, a local attorney hired by Colom after Election Day. “Having to stand in line for three and four hours in the rain, that is a form of voter suppression. It is, and that’s just not fair.”
In the week since, the five commissioners responsible for running the county’s elections have taken time off from their day jobs to verify and count an unexpected surge in affidavit ballots. DeSoto County reported roughly 275 affidavit ballots in 2022, during the last midterm election, according to data tracked by the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. 
This year, commissioners have reported more than seven times the number of affidavit ballots: about 2,100.
The commissioners’ long hours have been punctuated by charged exchanges with residents seeking answers and accountability for the dysfunction that they say plagued this year’s midterms. 
“There’s nothing normal about this,” Sheila Jackson, a resident wearing a “Drink Water. Love Hard. Fight Racism.” shirt, said on Monday to Tim Snyder, a Republican in his first term as a county election commissioner.
Standing in the old bank drive-through lane outside the commissioners’ office, Snyder defended the commission’s embrace of the Experian data to clean its voter rolls.
The DeSoto County Election Commission meets out of an old Trustmark Bank building in Hernando, pictured Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
“You get false positives, but it’s just part of life,” Snyder said. “You know, it’s hard to find perfect.”
Use of the Experian data has triggered fingerpointing. Experian blamed Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson’s office for misusing the data, which, the company wrote in a statement Tuesday, should not have been used to “validate voter records” — although the state’s $50,000 contract with the company specified the information would be used for voter roll maintenance.  
Watson’s office blamed county election commissioners for failing to verify the addresses before changing voters’ status, and some election commissioners are blaming the secretary of state’s office for directing them to use flawed information that caused more headaches than help.
A fateful decision to use credit bureau data to clean voter rolls
Before Watson, a Republican, handed down address lists sourced from Experian’s data to every county statewide last year, the state had solely relied on government information, including U.S. Postal Service data, to do the routine job of cleaning the rolls of voters suspected to have moved.
His office announced that Experian’s data would “strengthen the integrity of elections.” But in March, Mississippi Today first reported that errors in Experian’s information had gone unverified at every stage of the voter roll maintenance process, leading election officials to inactivate voters who were properly registered and hadn’t actually moved.
Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson speaks to reporters at a press conference in his Mississippi State Capitol office on Jan. 21, 2026, about strengthening Mississippi’s campaign finance laws. Credit: Katherine Lin/Mississippi Today
David Becker, a former Justice Department voting rights attorney who is now executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research, said Mississippi’s use of commercial data raised concerns that the state was improperly disenfranchising voters.
“You don’t have to be an expert on election law to be looking at Mississippi right now and thinking, ‘There must be a better way of doing this,’” Becker said. “I don’t know of any other state that uses commercial data as a single check and bases inactivation based, at best, on a flawed data set for voter maintenance purposes.”
In DeSoto, both Snyder and fellow Republican election commissioner Sissie Ferguson confirmed in separate interviews that the secretary of state’s office put pressure on county election officials to use the Experian data to clean the voter rolls. Ferguson said state officials specifically called out DeSoto County at an election commissioner conference in January. 
“We were told, ‘Y’all still have 15,000 that you haven’t worked,’” Ferguson said, referring to the number of voters flagged in the lists drawn from Experian’s data.
Watson’s office did not respond to a request for comment on Ferguson’s recollection of the conference.
Ferguson said she could tell the records were flawed, and in some cases didn’t change a voter’s status when she knew for sure they hadn’t moved. 
DeSoto County Election Commissioner Sissie Ferguson observes Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, at the commission’s office in downtown Hernando as affidavit ballots are counted in front of dozens of onlookers. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
 “I recognized two or three of mine, and I thought, ‘That’s not true. He didn’t move, his dad did,’ so I didn’t make him inactive,” she said.
Watson has defended his deployment of the Experian data as a tool that empowered election commissioners to better clean the voter rolls and said county officials are responsible for the actual work of inactivating voters in Mississippi.
“Their job is to make sure they verify the information,” Watson said on a talk radio show Monday. “And I’ve heard people say, ‘Well, you pass the buck.’ What I am doing is explaining how the law works. I cannot make an election commissioner do his or her job.”
State law requires election commissioners to use “reliable information” to clean the voter rolls. In the announcement of the Experian deal, Watson’s office said Experian’s information would “bring a new level of reliable data” to the process.
Other jurisdictions that have checked voter rolls using Experian data took steps to verify the data in ways that Mississippi didn’t. For example, in West Virginia, election officials mail voters a notice asking them to verify their address before changing their registration status. 
But in Mississippi, state law requires election officials to move voters to inactive status at the same time as they mail the notices. Mississippi Today confirmed cases in which the notice was mailed to the unverified address sourced from Experian’s data. When the address was incorrect, properly registered voters who were moved to inactive status never got a notice to correct their status.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks to his supporters during his election watch party at the Ice House in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
On Tuesday, Colom criticized Watson for relying on Experian, even though the company warned the secretary of state’s office in their contract that it couldn’t guarantee the “accuracy or reliability” of its data.
 “Experian told him they were not reliable, and he did it anyway,” Colom said at a news conference about the election. “This chaos is a result of that decision.”
Watson’s office has stopped deploying Experian data and shifted to what he told Mississippi Today was a better source, from the data broker IDI. 
“It’s not that we moved on because we didn’t like Experian,” Watson said. “We moved on because we’ve gone with what we thought was a better product.”
Watson has conceded that the Experian files weren’t perfect and that some legitimate voters might get improperly flagged.
“Now there’s an aggressive approach to cleaning the voter rolls,” he said in the radio interview. “Is there going to be a little bit of pain? Perhaps. Did people have to wait an extra 5-10 minutes to vote affidavit? Perhaps.”
A line snakes out of a polling place in DeSoto County to vote in the 2026 midterms on Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Courtesy of Deborah Williams
Experian wrote in a statement that election officials shouldn’t rely on its data as a basis to inactivate voters. 
“Our supplemental address information provided at that time was not designed or intended to validate voter records,” Experian spokesperson Scott Anderson said of the company’s deal with Mississippi. “Decisions regarding voter registration policies, procedures and record updates are made solely by election officials in accordance with applicable local, state and federal laws.”
A surge in affidavit ballots in DeSoto
Jennifer Morrell, a former Colorado elections official who now serves as CEO of The Elections Group, a consulting firm that advises elections leaders around the country, said that Mississippi’s election laws and processes had to be seen in the context of the state’s long history of using the voting process to disenfranchise Black residents.
“When you look at all the ways that Mississippi makes it harder for people to vote, it’s not hard to see a direct line from the Jim Crow era straight to the present day system,” Morrell said. 
Voters across DeSoto County reported lines as long as three hours to vote on Election Day, with folks arriving before dawn and people standing in chilly rain to cast their ballots. 
People wait in line to vote in the 2026 midterms at a polling place in DeSoto County on November 3, 2026, as storms roll in on election night. Credit: Courtesy of Deborah Williams
Poll workers, voters and the Democratic Party’s lawsuit alleged various polling places — including the high school serving the county’s most populous precinct — ran out of envelopes for affidavit ballots and that there weren’t enough voting machines in some places to handle the number of people who wanted to cast ballots. 
In her two decades of voting in Walls — a small town on the county outskirts bordering the Mississippi River — probation officer Heather Cavallo has become used to Election Day being an in-and-out affair. But during this month’s election, she said, it was a two-hour ordeal.
Throughout the day, a line snaked out of the town library that serves as the local polling place for more than 3,500 voters. By the time Cavallo’s son and husband came out to vote later that day, they were even more unlucky. The clouds that covered the skies when she came out to vote at lunchtime had morphed into showers and then thunderstorms by election night.
For three hours, the two men stood in the rain to cast their ballots, Cavallo said. Her husband, who had headed to the polls after a long shift at his construction job, didn’t get to vote until an hour-and-a-half after workers closed the polls to newcomers. By that point, the thunderstorms were raging so hard that they prompted flash flood warnings throughout the county. 
When her son got to the end of the line, he found out his name wasn’t even in the poll book.
He was among the one in five voters in the county who were inactive, so the 26-year-old cast an affidavit ballot. All there was left to do was wait and see if his vote would actually count.
DeSoto County Election Commissioners Laura Edler and David Ross prepare to start counting affidavit ballots in the 2026 midterms at the commission’s office in Hernando, Mississippi, on November 11, 2026. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
“I’m at a loss,” Cavallo said. “I have seen nothing like this.”
But for Cavallo, it was all worth it to get to be one of the voters who flipped the Republican stronghold blue for Colom.
Ferguson downplayed complaints about voting. 
“They stand in line every day at Walmart and Kroger, and they don’t complain,” she said. 
Mississippi Today reporter Taylor Vance contributed to this story.
Dion Nissenbaum is Votebeat’s senior national reporter and is based in Houston. Contact Dion at dnissenbaum@votebeat.org.
Madeline Nguyen is an investigative reporting fellow at Mississippi Today and is based in Jackson. Contact Madeline at mnguyen@mississippitoday.org.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Energy, PFAS and Knowles-Nelson on the environmental agenda as Democrats take control
description: Following a campaign in which Wisconsin voters frequently cited concerns about data centers and energy affordability as major issues and Democratic candidates for the Legislature touted plans to restart the state’s land conservation program, Wisconsin Democrats are signaling they’ll use their new control of state government to take action on a number of clim[...]
text:
Starkweather Creek empties into Lake Monona at Olbrich Park in Madison. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Following a campaign in which Wisconsin voters frequently cited concerns about data centers and energy affordability as major issues and Democratic candidates for the Legislature touted plans to restart the state’s land conservation program, Wisconsin Democrats are signaling they’ll use their new control of state government to take action on a number of climate and environmental issues. 
“We are going to deliver bold action for Wisconsinites. We are going to lower costs, support our public schools, protect our rights and freedoms, help working families, ensure safe and welcoming communities, hold big corporations accountable, fight back against federal overreach, ensure a clean environment for future generations, and much more,” Rep. Greta Neubauer (D-Racine) said in a statement after being elected to serve as the next speaker of the Assembly.  
Wisconsin Democrats will take over state government at a time when President Donald Trump’s administration has prioritized extractive industries and rolled back environmental protections. 
There are limits to what officials in one state can do to address a global problem like climate change, but state government’s purview over environmental issues includes regulating pollutants in the state’s air, land and water, purchasing and maintaining public land, overseeing the state’s electric utilities and funding efforts to protect the environment. 
As Democrats prepare to take majority control of the Legislature  in January, advocacy groups are pressing Democratic lawmakers to address their concerns both through standalone legislation and in the next state budget — which will dominate the agenda next summer. 
Clean Wisconsin has released a list of its policy priorities for 2027, which include increasing efforts to keep pollutants such as PFAS, nitrates, lead and phosphorus out of the state’s water; providing farmers with more tools to responsibly manage the land; investing in county-level initiatives; regulating data centers; changing how utility companies plan their energy development and expanding renewable energy.
“We’re really focused on pragmatic work, like a long list of on-the-ground programs that help protect our water systems, our groundwater, drinking water, our surface water, and help protect our climate and our air, and put some meaningful guardrails in place around AI data centers,” Amy Barilleaux, a spokesperson for Clean Wisconsin, told the Wisconsin Examiner. “I think people want to hear, ‘Oh, this big thing and that big thing,’ but it takes like a thousand little things to accomplish that big thing.
Barilleaux said that Gov.-elect David Crowley and whomever he appoints to run the state Department of Natural Resources can have a significant effect on environmental protection in the state simply by working to restore the agency’s muscle to what it was before Republicans slashed its staffing and budget under former Gov. Scott Walker. 
“I think it’s not that the DNR doesn’t recognize some authority, but you have to have people to do the work,” she said. “It’s been very difficult with understaffing at some agencies to really be able to do the work they are in statute being asked to do. So that’s a big one as well. We just need to improve the function of our government.”
Utility regulation 
In the days since their electoral victory, Wisconsin Democrats have signaled that their first priority in January will be addressing the affordability concerns that dominated the debate on the campaign trail. For environmental groups, that has led to a focus on how the state regulates its utility companies. 
In recent months, the Public Service Commission — the agency responsible for utility regulation — has taken some actions to prevent data center developments from increasing electric bills and to slow down requests to raise rates. But, Barilleaux said, the commission has also said in its recent decisions that if it’s going to do more, the Legislature needs to give it some help. 
Clean Wisconsin and a number of other groups are pushing for integrated resource planning. Under current law, the state’s utilities are not required to make long-term plans for where they’ll get the energy required to meet the state’s demand. This means that as hyperscale data centers have begun to pop up around the state, the utilities can do whatever they want to meet that increased demand. So far, that has meant extending the life of or planning to build new plants that rely on fossil fuels such as coal and natural gas. 
Moving to integrated resource planning would require that the utilities get their future plans approved by the PSC, which advocates say will encourage them to use energy from sources that are cheaper in the long term, largely solar and wind. 
“Our utilities don’t have to be transparent about what they’re doing, they don’t have to have a big picture where we look at different utilities together for a full statewide energy system in Wisconsin, and that leaves us very vulnerable in this moment, extremely vulnerable as we have these AI data center projects coming in and demanding just intense amounts of energy, historic amounts of energy,” Barilleaux said. “So we’re just sitting here flat-footed with no integrated resource plan. So the Public Service Commission … when it approved the latest two gas plants, it was almost a cry for help, saying, ‘We can’t, we don’t have any authority to do anything about this,’ and that should be alarming to everyone. Even though integrated resource planning does not sound like a super exciting topic, when you see how things are unfolding here in Wisconsin, when you see the Public Service Commission saying we need help from lawmakers right now — we’re expecting lawmakers to take that very seriously.”
PFAS
Barilleaux said that another big priority for Clean Wisconsin is doing more to clean up PFAS contamination in the state’s water. 
Over the last year, the Legislature and Gov. Tony Evers have finally passed legislation to spend $125 million set aside for PFAS mitigation after years of partisan deadlock. The Natural Resources Board recently established a standard for the amount of PFAS allowed to be in the state’s groundwater after years of failed efforts. 
Barilleaux said more money beyond that previous appropriation is needed to address the full scope of the problem statewide and added she’d like to see a total ban on the use of PFAS in the state. 
“We need to take this seriously. We can’t pretend like it’s not happening. We can’t pretend like groundwater standards and surface water standards and drinking water standards are it, because it’s not,” she said. “It is over $100 million a year in health harms that PFAS exposure is causing right here in Wisconsin, and so these are tremendous costs. I think sometimes things get characterized as, you know, cost versus environmental protection, or jobs versus environmental protection, but really, this is people’s health on the line. It is expensive to be sick from pollution and contamination. You know, this is about protecting the health of our communities.” 
Knowles-Nelson
Among the most divisive environmental issues during the last legislative session was the failure to reauthorize the Knowles-Nelson Stewardship Grant Program, which for nearly four decades had allowed the DNR to fund the purchase and maintenance of public land. 
A faction of Republicans in control of the Legislature had become hostile to the program — which had previously enjoyed bipartisan support — over broad objections to government land conservation and more specific complaints about the hit to local property tax revenues that can be caused by state land purchases. 
Multiple compromise bills were proposed, but nothing was able to pass and the program expired this summer. The reauthorization of the program was a campaign issue in some of the legislative races that helped Democrats win majority control. 
Charles Carlin, the director of strategic initiatives at the land conservation nonprofit Gathering Waters, told the Examiner that Democratic control opens up new possibilities for what the program can become, balancing how much money is spent purchasing new public land and how much is spent developing existing public land into both usable space for recreation and wildlife habitat. 
“It feels like everybody is sort of absorbing the ramifications of the elections, what’s possible,” Carlin said. “But I think that certainly one of the things that you know that we are looking at now is it feels like there is a real opportunity here to have a long-term authorization for Knowles Nelson, one that is appropriately funded, and I think the other thing we’re looking at is there’s an opportunity to rebalance the program between development projects and land acquisition.” 
He said it’s helpful not to have to negotiate with people who are hostile to the idea of public land conservation and added that the complaints about dwindling local government revenue on this issue tie in to coming debates about local government funding in general that are likely to play a major role in the work of the new government. 
“Local government revenue is likely to be a hot topic of conversation in the next legislative session on all kinds of issues,” Carlin said. “So public lands is one small one, but shared revenue, school funding, transportation — these are all going to be things that get talked about and considered a lot. But I do want to see a renewed emphasis on DNR soliciting input from local governments on projects that are happening in their jurisdiction and taking those viewpoints and that feedback into account. I also think that if the conversation in the Legislature can be more fact-based and less driven by an anti-conservation ideology, then I think that creates the space for us to have a really solution-focused conversation about how tax and land use policy really impacts local government revenues.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Will a new farm bill arrive in Kansas farmers’ stockings this holiday season? Don’t count on it.
description: During his reelection campaign, Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall trumpeted his role writing a new farm bill. It was minimal and apparently not enough. Democratic Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said he would have voted to advance the Senate’s bill. Kansas politics rewards farm largesse and punishes parsimony — Sunflower State bipartisanship. Our congressional de[...]
text:
Despite years of competing proposals, our columnist suggests that a new farm bill won't emerge from Congress before year's end. (Allison Kite/Kansas Reflector)During his reelection campaign, Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall trumpeted his role writing a new farm bill. It was minimal and apparently not enough. Democratic Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said he would have voted to advance the Senate’s bill.
Kansas politics rewards farm largesse and punishes parsimony — Sunflower State bipartisanship. Our congressional delegation fronts every pass-the-farm-bill parade.
Its members should prepare to be disappointed.
The lame-duck Congress must replenish the government’s coffers by mid-December. Defense Department activities await perdurance. The president’s war looms. Will Congress let him waste more money on it? The administration paired its request to increase war spending with $11 billion more in farmer bailouts. If the former fails, will the latter survive?
That’s a daunting agenda for a productive Congress in the best of times. This one isn’t, and they aren’t.
Is a new farm bill a must-do, too? No, it’s a can’t do, won’t do. The House bill dies when Congress adjourns, and the stalled Senate bill remains stalled — a double flop. Lawmakers will pass sheepishly a fourth extension of the 2018 act.
That actually is a good thing.
Incoming leaders of the agriculture committee should abandon — or at least curb — the recklessly out-of-control subsidies. They hit $54 billion this year.
Those same leaders need to jettison the failed policies that futilely masked 22 months of missteps strangling the farm economy and greedily fractured the farm-food alliance.
Neither of the proposals would rectify these mistakes. No bill is better than rushing to pass flawed legislation.
Policy quicksand began swallowing farm programs with former U.S. Sen. Pat Roberts’ Freedom to Farm bill. It manipulated congressional budget scorekeeping, ending the formerly foundational counter-cyclical farm policy philosophy that low prices trigger aid. Its touchstone: mandated, maximum payouts.
Supporters peddled the scheme as “transitional.” That’s aggie lingo — it translates to “until we come up with a new buzzword.” Perhaps “bridge payments,” the Trump administration’s label for its massive bailouts. Freedom to Farm, boosters claimed, would save the treasury $2 billion over seven years. Spending ballooned to $141 billion in just five.
Lawmakers and lobbyists were undeterred by the shocking underestimate of the bill’s cost. They vigorously labored to keep money flowing and shunned evaluating efficacy of the cash tidal wave.
Congress stopped asking simple, fundamental questions: Is this spending working? Have taxpayers gotten their money’s worth?
Their dereliction deepened when they capitulated to Trump-think and fell under the spell of don’t question Trump-think. Neither agriculture committee examined whether the Trump bailouts — in this term or his first — achieved their objective or whether the tariffs benefited or hurt farmers. They hurt.
The Kansas beef economy suffered some of the worst damage. Republican U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann of Kansas heads the House subcommittee with jurisdiction, but he didn’t convene it for a single minute to assess the carnage. A new leader will take over in January.
In the 2025 session, the House Agriculture Committee approved more than $1 trillion in new farm subsidies. Its chairman explained that Congress had not approved new commodity program payments since 2002, therefore it must approve the spending in his bill — spend more money for the sake of spending more money.
That was the sum of his rationale. Even if inadvertent, he succinctly stated three decades of farm policy — the apotheosis of Freedom to Farm.
Most congressional farm state lawmakers, including those from Kansans, and the farm lobby boasted they were “putting the farm back into the farm bill.” That’s more aggie lingo. It means raiding SNAP — the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — of nearly $300 billion to pump up farm spending.
To the 10,000 Kansas kids who lost access to SNAP, it means going without a meal.
That plunder ended food assistance to as many Kansans as the residents of Derby, Dodge City or Garden City. They have fewer resources to feed themselves and their families than before this avaricious transfer of income to well-heeled farmers and tax cuts for upper-class taxpayers. The number could swell ninefold when “putting the farm back into farm bill” fully takes effect.
Although Roberts engineered unprecedented spending, he didn’t raid feeding programs like the current Congress. He knew no food aid meant no farm spending. Rural lawmakers can’t pass farm bills alone — they rely on urban votes. While writing his bill, again in 2013 and 2018, he played a key role in keeping the coalition together. But there is no Roberts in the Republican conference today, or someone like U.S. Sen. Bob Dole, the Kansas Republican who likewise had the political sense and skill to preserve the farm-food alliance.
Today’s GOP farm lawmakers’ spending gluttony wrecked the alliance. Thus no new bill arrived in 2023, 2024, 2025 or 2026.
Marshall blamed Democrats, whitewashing the obvious: He and his fellow Republicans controlled Congress every year it failed to produce a farm bill. Their legislative malpractice was unquestionably due to misprizing the Dole-Roberts presumption.
The farm-food coalition has served both sides well, a bedrock that many lawmakers forgot, never learned or don’t understand. They need a refresher in farm bill politics 101, starting with this reading:
It is hereby declared to be the policy of Congress, in order to promote the general welfare, that the Nation’s abundance of food should be utilized to the maximum extent practicable to safeguard the health and well-being of the Nation’s population and raise levels of nutrition among low-income households. The Congress hereby finds that increased utilization of foods in establishing and maintaining adequate levels of nutrition will tend to cause the distribution in a beneficial manner of agricultural abundances and will strengthen our agricultural economy.
That’s not some woke, “socialist,” extremist manifesto. A bunch of aggies memorialized their commitment to the farm-food partnership into those first passages of the original Food Stamp Act.
Greg Frazier helped write several farm bills while staff director on the House Agriculture Committee and USDA chief of staff before serving as USTR chief agriculture negotiator. He lives in Kansas City. He lives In Kansas City.
