title: Delaware’s rural health funding nears $318 million, putting focus on access, costs and results
description: La Red Health Center says federal support will strengthen care teams, expand transportation and improve coordination as Delaware builds out rural health services. NEW CASTLE, Del. — Delaware will receive another $160.3 million in federal rural health funding, bringing its first two years of awards to nearly $317.7 million as the state works to expand access [...]
text:
La Red Health Center says federal support will strengthen care teams, expand transportation and improve coordination as Delaware builds out rural health services.
NEW CASTLE, Del. — Delaware will receive another $160.3 million in federal rural health funding, bringing its first two years of awards to nearly $317.7 million as the state works to expand access to care, particularly in Kent and Sussex counties.
The funding will support community health centers, medical education, technology and other initiatives. Measuring its return will require tracking whether those investments translate into more available appointments, a stronger health care workforce and more affordable care.
The Delaware Department of Health and Social Services announced the $160,294,521 second-year award Nov. 9. It is approximately $2.9 million more than Delaware’s first-year award of $157.4 million.
For Sussex County’s La Red Health Center, the support is intended to address practical barriers to receiving care, including transportation and coordination among providers.
What La Red plans for Sussex County
La Red was awarded approximately $10.1 million in first-year funding, according to the state’s September announcement of nearly $23 million for federally qualified health centers.
“This funding is an investment in the future of rural healthcare in our county,” said Rachel Hersh, president and CEO of La Red Health Center.
“It will allow us to strengthen La Red’s care teams, expand transportation support, and improve how we share information and coordinate care with hospitals and specialists,” she said. “For our patients, that means better-connected care, more support managing chronic conditions, and easier access to their own health information.”
Hersh said the funding also would strengthen prevention.
“It also means a stronger focus on prevention by helping patients get screenings, identify health problems early, and have the tools and support to take greater control of their wellness,” she said.
Along with La Red, the state announced approximately $11.3 million for Westside Family Healthcare and $1.29 million for Henrietta Johnson Medical Center. The three awards total approximately $22.7 million.
Committed dollars and completed services
As of July 31, Delaware had obligated approximately $76.9 million, or 49% of its first-year award, according to state-submitted information published by the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
Obligations generally represent commitments through contracts, grants or other agreements. They do not necessarily establish that money has been spent, facilities have opened or patients have received additional services.
The July figures also predate the September health center awards and November update. They cannot establish how much Delaware has committed or spent since then.
CMS describes the report as an incomplete view of state progress and says it will update the information following submission of the Nov. 30 quarterly report. RHTP Tracker
Where the first-year commitments are going
The July report listed approximately $26.4 million obligated for two Hope Centers in Kent and Sussex counties, intended to connect homeless residents with housing, primary care, behavioral health and other services.
Approximately $16.8 million was obligated for Delaware’s medical school initiative, while $6.55 million was committed to health information technology involving real-time insurance verification and prior authorization.
Those technology improvements are intended to reduce administrative barriers that can consume staff time and delay care. RHTP Tracker
In its November announcement, DHSS said Delaware had funded four new school-based health centers in Sussex County and advanced plans for medical education through Thomas Jefferson University, including clinical training in Kent and Sussex counties.
The announcement did not establish that all four school-based centers were operating.
DHSS also reported work on telehealth, remote patient monitoring, chronic disease management and workforce recruitment. Secretary Christen Linke Young described the funding as an opportunity to improve rural care while addressing the long-term drivers of rising health care spending. news.delaware.gov
Private-sector innovation tied to milestones
Delaware is also directing part of the federal funding toward health technology companies.
Delaware Prosperity Partnership and DHSS are developing the Delaware Rural Health Challenge, an accelerator expected to award up to $5 million in competitive, milestone-based grants to health technology startups.
The grants are non-dilutive, meaning companies receive funding without giving up an ownership stake.
The program will begin by identifying specific rural health care problems with providers, community organizations and other stakeholders, then recruiting companies to develop and deploy solutions.
Program materials call for selected companies to work with Delaware health care organizations and rural communities to test and measure their impact. They set a Sept. 30, 2027, deadline for disbursing all program funds.
For taxpayers, evaluating those awards will require examining both whether companies meet their milestones and whether their products deliver useful, affordable services for patients and providers.
Measuring results and sustaining services
As Delaware enters the second year of the five-year federal program, evaluating its performance will require distinguishing funding commitments from improvements in care.
Useful measures would include additional appointment capacity, providers recruited and retained, completed transportation trips, shorter waits for treatment and changes in avoidable emergency care. Cost reporting could help establish whether technology and care coordination reduce expenses or shift them elsewhere.
Long-term operating costs also warrant attention. Expanded facilities, transportation and care teams can require recurring spending on personnel, maintenance and technology after startup funding has been used.
The announcements reviewed for this story do not provide a comprehensive explanation of how every initiative will cover those continuing costs after the federal program ends, or whether additional state support will be needed.
For patients, the practical test will be whether they can obtain timely, affordable care closer to home. For taxpayers, it will also be whether those improvements can be sustained at a manageable cost.
To Go Box: Delaware Rural Health Transformation Program

What: A five-year federal program supporting rural health care access, workforce development, technology and changes in care delivery.
First-year award: Approximately $157.4 million.
Second-year award: Approximately $160.3 million.
Two-year total: Approximately $317.7 million.
First-year funding obligated by July 31: Approximately $76.9 million, or 49%. This is a dated measure of commitments, not a current spending total.
La Red award: Approximately $10.1 million, announced in September.
Primary focus: Rural communities in Kent and Sussex counties, with some statewide initiatives.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC children’s advocates push for more funding to improve student mental health
description: North Carolina’s Child Fatality Task Force is hopeful 2027 brings new attention and more financial resources to issues they have been urging the General Assembly to address for years. With Democrats taking control of the N.C. House and Republicans holding a slim majority in the N.C. Senate, members highlighted on Tuesday their priorities for the […]
text:
North Carolina needs four times the number of school social workers and psychologists that it currently has to meet nationally recommended ratios. (Photo: iStock)North Carolina’s Child Fatality Task Force is hopeful 2027 brings new attention and more financial resources to issues they have been urging the General Assembly to address for years. With Democrats taking control of the N.C. House and Republicans holding a slim majority in the N.C. Senate, members highlighted on Tuesday their priorities for the legislative session that begins in January.
While the state has recently recorded improvements in youth mental health, serious challenges remain for students who are struggling. Topping the list is the need for the state to invest in more school nurses, counselors, social workers and school psychologists.
North Carolina needs four times the number of school social workers and psychologists that it currently has to meet nationally recommended ratios,  according to Whitney Belich, co-chair of the Intentional Death Prevention Committee.
Because not enough state funding is available for those support personnel positions, they’re often paid for using a combination of state and local funds. Small and rural counties that don’t have those local funds often leave the positions unfilled.
School support personnel play a critical role in identifying students’ needs and preventing crises and tragedies, Belich said, but the unfortunate reality is that whether a child has access to a school nurse or a counselor depends on where they go to school.
“Many of our North Carolina schools go without any of these support personnel on a daily basis,” Belich explained. “It is very spotty.”
North Carolina earned an “F” in mental health in the 2025 N.C. Child Health Report Card. There was also no new funding for support personnel in the 2026 state budget.
Without dedicated personnel in the schools, Belich says the state is likely to see an increase in adverse outcomes for North Carolina youth.
According to the 2025 North Carolina High School Youth Risk Behavior Survey released in August, almost 30% of high schoolers said they felt sad or hopeless. More than 11% said they had seriously considered suicide.
In the 2024-25 school year, school nurses reported having 579,000 counseling sessions with students. Of those, 18,000 sessions were related to depression, suicide ideation or other mental health issues.
“Only 21% say that they’ve been able to get the kind of help that they need,” Belich said. “That is startling and disturbing.”
Annie Goldberg is a nationally board-certified school counselor who works in the Alamance-Burlington School System.  She said her own school district has gone from being fully staffed with support personnel to struggling as federal COVID stabilization money dried up.
This year, Goldberg, a finalist for the 2026 National School Counselor of the Year, finds herself stretched very thin.
“My district went through a really serious reduction in force, and I am now the only counselor at my middle school of about 730 students,” Goldberg said.
Goldberg said the needs keep increasing among students, but the funding for trained personnel to respond to serious situations has not followed.
One potential bright spot on the horizon in 2027 is the settlement of the Meta lawsuit. As part of a multistate settlement, the owners of Facebook and Instagram have agreed to pay North Carolina up to $645 million by 2035. The first $45.2 million payment was made to the state in October.
Meta to pay North Carolina up to $645 million in landmark settlement

The panel voted Tuesday to urge lawmakers to support recurring funding for school nurses, social workers, and counselors to support student mental health needs, using the Meta settlement as a possible funding stream.
“There are already bills being put together about ensuring that the Meta funding all goes to children — making sure that money is spent the way it was intended,” said Karen McLeod, co-chair of the task force.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: More money, more problems: RI leaders aren’t celebrating a $109M boost to revenue forecast
description: Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes will have an extra $109 million to work with when putting together her first tax and spending proposal for the upcoming fiscal 2028 budget. The nine-digit boost to the income side of the state ledger came at the conclusion of the biannual Revenue and Caseload Estimating Conference on Tuesday. State budget […]
text:
Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes said at a press conference on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026 that the upcoming fiscal 2028 budget process will be challenging, despite higher-than-expected revenue. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes will have an extra $109 million to work with when putting together her first tax and spending proposal for the upcoming fiscal 2028 budget.
The nine-digit boost to the income side of the state ledger came at the conclusion of the biannual Revenue and Caseload Estimating Conference on Tuesday. State budget analysts now expect $108.7 million more in general revenue to flow through state coffers in the current fiscal year that ends June 30, compared with the spring estimates lawmakers used to finalize the fiscal 2027 budget.
The updated projections will shape Foulkes’ inaugural budget proposal, which will be unveiled sometime in January, setting off the six-month review and editing process by the Rhode Island General Assembly. 
Despite the rosier-than-expected financial picture, Foulkes, a Democrat, remained cautious about the state’s long-term financial picture.
“We need to think about more than just one year,” she said at a press conference Tuesday. “One of the challenges will be to be really disciplined about this.”
The revenue estimates adopted Tuesday don’t account for the expense side of the balance sheet. In June of this year, at the time the fiscal 2027 budget was adopted, the House fiscal office projected a $240 million deficit in fiscal 2028, swelling to $540 million by fiscal 2031.
Federal funding cuts under H.R. 1, including massive overhauls of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Medicaid, the latter of which accounts for one-third of the state’s $15 billion budget.
Rhode Island legislative leaders, all of whom are Democrats, pointed to federal policy changes under the Trump administration and a Republican-controlled Congress as an ongoing challenge despite an increase in projected revenue.
“While revenue projections are higher than initially forecast, we must remain mindful that many Rhode Islanders continue to struggle with rising costs and economic uncertainty,” Senate President Valarie Lawson said in a statement Tuesday. “As the state budget is developed and considered, we must also account for the significant fiscal challenges posed by changes in federal policy and their potential impact on our state. Our approach must be measured and responsible, balancing this positive revenue news with the needs of Rhode Islanders and the long-term financial health of our state.”
House Speaker Christopher Blazejewski echoed this concern, referring to “punishing” federal policy choices and “ongoing harm and uncertainty” from the federal government in a separate statement Tuesday.
In contrast, outgoing Gov. Dan McKee, also a Democrat, took an optimistic tone, touting the stronger fiscal outlook from the revenue estimates as evidence of his administration’s fiscal responsibility.
“We are leaving Rhode Island in a better fiscal position than we found it, and I’m proud of the stronger foundation we’ve built for our state’s future,” McKee said in a statement.
McKee, who lost his reelection bid to Foulkes in the September primary, also said the upward revenue revisions “set the stage” for holding the line on taxes, while providing enough extra money to continue phasing out the state tax on Social Security income and increasing reimbursement rates for primary care providers.
Foulkes said Tuesday it was too early to say how she would spend the extra revenue, but reiterated her campaign priority to increase housing development. During the campaign, Foulkes pledged to build 20,000 homes over the next eight years using the state millionaire’s tax. The surtax on income over $1 million begins in January, with the expected $22 million boost to fiscal 2027 revenue already spent through the state’s general fund. 
The state’s 7% sales tax was the largest driver of the revenue boost, now $61 million higher than previous estimates. Business taxes also rose by $49 million, while personal income taxes fell $25 million, reflecting lower-than-expected revenue from income withholdings.
Lottery revenue is now expected to be $300,000 less, too, with losses in income from iGaming and video lottery terminals partially offset by boosts to sports betting and table games at casinos in Lincoln and Tiverton.
State budget analysts will meet again in May to revise financial projections based on updated revenue reports.

title: Recounts confirm ousting of SC majority leader, narrow win of Greenville County Republican
description: COLUMBIA — The Republican legislator recently chosen to lead the House GOP Caucus officially lost his re-election bid with recount results certified Wednesday, while a second House Republican held on by less than three dozen votes. Official results show Democrat Joe Madge, a 59-year-old engineer at tire manufacturer Continental, defeated House Majority Leade[...]
text:
Rep. David Vaughan talks to a fellow legislator during the first day of session in Columbia, S.C. on Tuesday, Jan. 9, 2024. He won re-election by just 32 votes, according to results certified Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — The Republican legislator recently chosen to lead the House GOP Caucus officially lost his re-election bid with recount results certified Wednesday, while a second House Republican held on by less than three dozen votes.
Official results show Democrat Joe Madge, a 59-year-old engineer at tire manufacturer Continental, defeated House Majority Leader Micah Caskey, an attorney, by 106 votes out of more than 14,400 ballots cast.
Of the 10 state House Republicans ousted as part of a blue tsunami that swept the nation, Caskey’s loss in a Lexington County district considered deep red was arguably the most surprising.
Four years ago, Caskey barely survived a challenge from his right flank, winning a GOP primary by just 25 votes over an opponent who accused the former prosecutor of not being conservative enough. No Democrat challenged him that November. Then, in 2024, Caskey trounced his Democratic challenger by nearly 21 percentage points.
Democrat Joe Madge, an engineer, won the 2026 election to represent District 89 in the state House. (Photo courtesy of Joe Madge)
The final tally this week declared Madge the winner with 50.3% of the vote.
Responding on social media, Caskey said he called Madge to congratulate him Wednesday.
“The people have made their choice, and I respect it fully,” the 10-year incumbent wrote on X. “The seat has never belonged to me. It belongs to the people of Cayce, Springdale, and West Columbia, and it has been the honor of my life to hold it in trust for you.”
The Marine veteran added, “I learned long ago in the Corps that service is not a title. It is a way of living, and it doesn’t end when the uniform comes off or when an election is over.”
His loss means the House GOP Caucus will need to choose a new leader. The caucus just elected him majority leader in August to replace Davey Hiott of Pickens, who didn’t seek re-election.
Madge, who grew up in Washington, D.C., and a tiny Upstate New York town on Oneida Lake, moved to Lexington County in 1995. It’s been his home since, other than a three-year stint in Puebla, Mexico, with his job starting in 2003.
Madge said he decided to challenge Caskey, a 45-year-old Columbia-area native, because he was “tired of being angry” about what legislators were doing.
“They just really weren’t focused on the things that would help people out in their daily lives, and instead of just being mad all the time, I said, ‘Well, let me see if I can run for office. Maybe I can help change things,’” he told the SC Daily Gazette.
Madge, chairman of the Lexington County Democratic Party from 2018 to 2022, said he figured a Democrat could get at least 45% of the vote in a blue wave midterm and went door-to-door in an effort to draw support from people who don’t normally vote.
He said he’ll advocate for finding consensus on issues that should be nonpartisan priorities.
“Now between Republicans and Democrats, we may have different approaches to those things, but that’s the appeal I want to try and make,” he said.
“Can we focus on the things that the voters want to see us work on — reducing healthcare costs, improving our education system, fixing our roads and bridges?” he continued. “I think everybody wants to do those things. So that’s what I would like to see us focus on.”

Rep. Micah Caskey talks to reporters following a House Ways and Means subcommittee meeting in Columbia, S.C. on Wednesday, Jan. 29, 2025. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)

He’ll likely find himself at odds with others in his delegation.
The district he’ll represent is entirely in Lexington County. The 10 other House members who represent pieces of what’s normally a reliably red county include members of the uber-conservative Freedom Caucus. The only other Democrat is Rep. Jerry Govan of Orangeburg, who was first elected to the chamber in 1992.
The same wave that ousted Caskey in District 89 came close to toppling U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson, who lives in Springdale, from the 2nd Congressional District he’s represented since 2001.
Wilson’s winning margin of 0.95 percentage points was also finalized Wednesday following an automatic recount.
Greenville County Republican
Also holding on in a mandatory recount was Rep. David Vaughan of Simpsonville, who won by just 32 votes out of almost 18,300 ballots cast.
Two years ago, Vaughan defeated Democrat John MacCarthy by more than 20 percentage points. This year, he won re-election to District 27, located entirely in Greenville County, against the same Democrat by a fraction of a percentage point.
“I feel very thankful,” Vaughan told the SC Daily Gazette. “I knew that people were angry. I know that everybody was hurting from gas prices and grocery prices, and I knew that voter apathy was going to be a big issue. But I really and truly had no idea that it would quite turn out the way that it would.”
Rep. Joe Wilson wins squeaker against 25-year-old first-time candidate

Vaughan, first elected in 2022, said the tight race made it clear to him that the Legislature should focus on helping people through tough economic times.
He believes this means focusing on spending less and reducing taxes so people keep more of their money.
“It was a good wake up call for us that that people are really hurting, and I think the whole trajectory of the state House as a whole, not just me in my district, but as a whole, I think we’re going to really have to focus on how much money we spend, and how much money we can save and how much money we can send back to the citizens of South Carolina,” Vaughan said.
MacCarthy, a physics professor at Spartanburg Community College and former engineer, said his Christian faith propelled him to run again after his unsuccessful bid two years ago.
“My message was that we can do better than we’ve been doing in the state,” he said.
His first election allowed him to establish a base for his second run. He then built up a group of volunteers who helped reach other voters, MacCarthy said.
With the recounts completed on Tuesday, all races in South Carolina are officially certified.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi startups showcase innovation and compete for funding
description: Ali Fatemi, SpinTecx founder and chief clinical physicist, makes a pitch for venture capital during the Innovate MS Accelerate Conference held in Flowood Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
At Innovate Mississippi’s annual conference, 10 Mississippi startups competed to win a $15,000 grant. 
The companies showcased products that included magnetic resonance imaging software, a basketball artificial intelligence training app and a new type of military drone. 
Innovate Mississippi is a nonprofit working to cultivate the state’s startup, innovation and tech economy. The annual conference included panels on investing, networking and two “pitch competitions.” 
A key part of Innovate’s work includes these pitch competitions, where founders try to attract funding by presenting their business idea to investors. The organization also invests directly in companies.
“We want to make sure the rainbow continues, and we can keep investing and building in Mississippi for future generations,” said Lindsey Benefield, the fund manager for Invest Mississippi.
“I want our state leaders to not forget about entrepreneurs,” said Jim Lowery, chief market strategist at mTrade, an Oxford-based software company. “It is important that we support our companies both big and small. You never know when the next small company will become big.”
Throughout the conference, founders pulled investors aside to talk about their companies and try to raise more capital.
All of the companies participating in Wednesday’s competition are trying to develop new products and aggressively grow their business. 
Julien Bourgeois, the CEO of Automatic AI, a first of its kind app that uses artificial intelligence to help athletes train, said that the company wants to expand its business from the current 8,000 users to over 25,000 in the next few years. 
OmniBus Co-founder and CEO Matthew Roberson, makes his pitch for funding during the Innovate MS Accelerate Conference on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in Flowood. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Omnibus, an integrated platform to manage and track school buses in real time, is operating in eight Mississippi school districts but hopes to expand throughout the Southeast. 
Each founder had three minutes to pitch his or her company to a panel of investors and two minutes to answer questions. The time crunch forced founders to get their pitch across quickly, and a few were cut short by the timer going off.
LOA Carbon was founded in New York but relocated to Mississippi this year. When the company’s founders were looking to relocate and expand their manufacturing capacity, Mississippi wasn’t on their radar. 
“We thought we were likely to land in either Texas or Alabama, and we didn’t really even pay attention to Mississippi,” said Ryan Shearman, the company’s CEO. 
The company liked the research and development at Mississippi’s universities, the state’s manufacturing sector, labor market and programs such as Innovate.
“We wanted to look into what state support programs would be available,” Shearman said. “Between Innovate Mississippi, Invest Mississippi, the Mississippi Development Authority, the overall package of different things we would have a shot on goal for was most attractive here, comparable to other states.”
The decision paid off. LOA Carbon won the $15,000 grant.

title: Oklahoma man accused of sending threats to election officials released with conditions
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — An Oklahoma City man accused of mailing more than 700 letters with threatening messages and white powder to election officials across the country has been released from custody.  U.S. Magistrate Judge Shon Erwin signed an order Monday allowing Robin Patrick Martin, 67, to be released as long as he complies with a […]
text:
A photo of a threatening letter sent to the Oklahoma State Election Board in Oklahoma City. (Provided by FBI affidavit)OKLAHOMA CITY — An Oklahoma City man accused of mailing more than 700 letters with threatening messages and white powder to election officials across the country has been released from custody. 
U.S. Magistrate Judge Shon Erwin signed an order Monday allowing Robin Patrick Martin, 67, to be released as long as he complies with a series of mandated conditions. Those include surrendering his passport, seeking employment, not owning a gun or similar weapons. He must seek a mental health assessment and receive the recommended treatment, according to court filings. 
He is charged with mailing threatening communications and with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes in the U.S. Western District of Oklahoma. 
Martin will also be monitored by GPS and may not travel outside of the federal court’s jurisdiction, which includes 40 of the state’s counties and covers the western half of Oklahoma. 
Federal public defenders representing Martin did not return messages seeking comment. 
A postal inspector testified Monday that after he was arrested, Martin in an interview admitted to mailing more than 700 letters and using advice from artificial intelligence tools on how to stay anonymous, according to The Oklahoman. 
The inspector testified that Martin also apologized for his actions, according to The Oklahoman. 
He’s accused of sending hundreds of mailings with white powder, threatening messages and letters about a “DECLARATION OF WAR” to election officials, members of Congress, pollsters, media organizations and the FBI in 2024 and 2026. Some mailings had a return address for the “United States Traitor Elimination Army,” while others were from “DSA NEW YORK NY,” according to an affidavit from an FBI agent. 
FBI field offices determined the mailings, sent both years, were associated with the same sender who they identified as Martin. This includes an October mailing sent to the Oklahoma State Election board that contained an unknown white powder. 
If Martin violates any of the conditions of his release, he’ll be subject to arrest, revocation of his release, revocation of his $5,000 bond and could be subject to further prosecution or imprisonment on top of his current charges, according to a court filing.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Commentary: Letlow campaigned on insurance accountability. Here’s what that should look like.
description: I spent five years living in a FEMA trailer. Not because I didn’t have insurance. I did. I paid my premiums and believed that if disaster struck, my insurance company would help me rebuild. I couldn’t have been more wrong. I spent years fighting to get paid. I went through adjuster after adjuster, submitted the […]
text:
Ceiling damage is visible in a section of Terra Hillman's home in Lake Charles that Hurricane Laura damaged in 2020. (Chris Vinn for Louisiana Illuminator)I spent five years living in a FEMA trailer. Not because I didn’t have insurance. I did. I paid my premiums and believed that if disaster struck, my insurance company would help me rebuild.
I couldn’t have been more wrong.
I spent years fighting to get paid. I went through adjuster after adjuster, submitted the same paperwork repeatedly and struggled to get straight answers. Even after mediation and reaching agreements, the payments didn’t come.
Then my insurance company went bankrupt.
For years, that company took our money when the skies were clear. When the storm came, and the bill came due, it folded. The people who ran it moved on. The people who trusted it were left in trailers.
Mine wasn’t the only one. After the 2020 and 2021 hurricanes, about a dozen homeowners insurers went under, holding nearly 185,000 policies. Some had been handed policies from the state’s own program, plus grant money. Yet they sold coverage in a hurricane state without enough money set aside for a hurricane.
That isn’t bad luck. That’s how the business was intended to run. 
Premiums got collected. Claims never got paid. Mine was FedNat. Its CEO collected nearly $10 million over five years, then resigned two months before the company was declared insolvent, with a $1.2 million payout to boot. 
Somebody made money. It wasn’t the families who were owed. 
When a company fails, the state is supposed to catch us. Make sure the market works. 
My claim went to the Louisiana Insurance Guaranty Association, LIGA. 
It sounds like a safety net. It wasn’t. 
LIGA doesn’t honor the bankrupt company’s promise. It pays only up to a cap set by law, and it pays none of the penalties and attorneys’ fees a homeowner would have won against an insurer that stalled in bad faith. 
The day FedNat went bankrupt, every consequence for the year it stalled me disappeared. I had to hire an attorney to keep fighting, this time against the state’s own guaranty fund. 
A policyholder shouldn’t have to fight LIGA in federal court just to get a business to honor (a portion of) the contract it signed. Isn’t LIGA supposed to be for policyholders?
And who pays for LIGA? Not the executives whose companies collapsed. LIGA assesses the insurers still standing, who recoup it through state tax credits. So the bill lands on Louisiana taxpayers and policyholders. The companies are gone, and tens of thousands of families ended up in the same line I stood in. 
So when Julia Letlow ran for the U.S. Senate promising to hold big insurance companies and FEMA accountable, I paid attention.
Letlow is right: Louisiana has an insurance crisis. But affordability is only half of it. What good is insurance you can afford if the company’s executives can run off with millions and deny paying when your home is destroyed? 
For survivors like me, accountability starts with homeowners insurance, and the state’s promise to deliver when a company fails. 
To start with, who let these companies run away with tens of millions in profit while homeowners were left with nothing? Why should Louisiana and its homeowners pay for their business malpractice? Those questions have never been asked under oath.
Secondly, a guaranty system that worked would give policyholders what they were promised: a full, adjusted claim on time with the same bad-faith penalties the company (and its executives) would have faced. That’s not what we have seen from LIGA.
Finally, we know federal flood insurance has been rigged against Louisianans for decades, with rates rising 18% a year even as the state invests billions in new flood works. 
Letlow knows it too. In 2022, she signed a letter asking FEMA whether the upgraded New Orleans levee system even counts in its pricing formula. She never got a straight answer. That question is still unanswered, and Louisiana families are still paying the rates.
I’ve met other survivors who’ve spent years fighting insurance companies to rebuild. We’re speaking out and organizing because we’ve been through too much to sit quietly and hope somebody else fixes this.
I can’t get back to the five years I spent in a FEMA trailer. But I can fight so other families don’t go through what I did.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Museum swap bring bones of hero dog back to Alaska
description: More than 100 years after he ran the longest stretches in a heroic dogsled mission to bring lifesaving medicine to snowbound Nome, Togo has returned to Alaska. Or, to be more precise, Togo’s bones have returned. The skeleton of the famous dog that led legendary musher Leonhard Seppala’s team for 261 miles of the 674-mile […]
text:
A mount of Togo, the lead dog in Leonhard Seppala's team that delivered life-saving medicine to Nome in the 1925 Serum Run, is seen on display behind plexiglass at the Iditarod Trail Committee headquarters in Wasilla on Feb. 25, 2022. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)More than 100 years after he ran the longest stretches in a heroic dogsled mission to bring lifesaving medicine to snowbound Nome, Togo has returned to Alaska.
Or, to be more precise, Togo’s bones have returned. The skeleton of the famous dog that led legendary musher Leonhard Seppala’s team for 261 miles of the 674-mile Serum Run in 1925, which delivered lifesaving medicine to a diphtheria-stricken Nome, is now at the University of Alaska Museum of the North in Fairbanks.
It is a fitting resting place for Togo’s remains, said Link Olson, the museum’s curator of mammals.
“He’s probably one of the most beloved dogs in the history of humankind,” Olson said.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Togo’s bones, which arrived at the museum on Sept. 1, were sent as part of a trade with the Peabody Museum at Yale University. While the Alaska museum gained the remains of the famous dog, the Peabody Museum gained more than 1,000 specimens of small mammals from Cambodia, including treeshrews, a bamboo rat and microbats.
The museum trade plan goes back two decades, when Link and his friend Eric Sargis, the Peabody Museum’s mammal curator, were collecting specimens in Cambodia. The idea was to split the specimens evenly, storing some at the Alaska museum and some at the Yale museum.
But until recently, the Yale museum lacked the technology to properly store and protect the specimens, so they all came to Alaska. “We had this world-class collection of Southeast Asian mammals, the biggest collection to this day of Cambodian mammals, including a bunch of tissues. And we had liquid nitrogen cryo facilities, and at that time Yale didn’t,” Olson said. “So I basically sat on them for 20 years.”
The Peabody Museum underwent a recent renovation and expansion, and now it has the proper facilities. Additionally, it is on what is considered a geographic museum corridor that gives researchers from different institutions who are interested in Cambodian mammals easier access. All that made it logical for the Peabody Museum to be the repository of rare Cambodian specimens.
Alaska was already home to other parts of Togo’s body. A mount made from his skin and face is on display at the Iditarod Trial Committee headquarters in Wasilla.
The return of Togo’s bones actually started as a quip while plans were being made for distributing the Cambodian specimens, Olson said. “I started joking, ‘Hey, we want Togo back,’” he said.
The joke became reality, though not quite in time for the centennial of the Serum Run, which was last year.
Not all the Cambodian specimens were sent back east. The Alaska museum is keeping a lot of them. Even though its official name is “University of Alaska Museum of the North,” it has a lot of non-Alaska and non-northern specimens in its collection — including the skeleton of an elephant that died in Cambodia after falling into a hole left by an explosive mine during the Vietnam War. The elephant skeleton is useful for comparison to the museum’s woolly mammoth and mastodon specimens, Olson said.
At the Peabody Museum, Togo’s bones were assembled — “articulated,” as museum experts put it — and displayed intermittently as a full skeleton. They arrived in Alaska still articulated, though the hind legs got a little detached during shipment, Olson said.
Eventually, they will be put on display in the Fairbanks museum, though details are yet to be determined, he said.
 

The Univesity of Alaska Museum of the North is seen on Sept. 18, 2022. The museum has an extensive collection of preserved animal specimens from Alaska and elsewhere. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	As a museum piece, Togo’s skeleton is both a natural history specimen and a cultural history specimen.
The cultural history is well known. Togo’s story is part of Alaska lore.
His life started without signs that he would be a star sled dog. As a puppy, he was small and sickly. Seppala, figuring Togo would not be fit for a team, gave him away to be kept as a pet.
But in a famous episode, Togo escaped his new home by breaking through a window and running back to Seppala’s kennel.
To calm the rambunctious Togo, Seppala later harnessed him as a wheel dog in a team embarking on a work trip in the Nome area. In that first run, Togo proved himself to be lead dog material. After that, he led Seppala’s teams to victories in the All-Alaska Sweepstakes, an important Alaska sled dog race based in Nome.
Then came the Serum Run.
Twenty dog teams traveled relay style from Nenana, where the medicine had been delivered on the Alaska Railroad, to Nome. Conditions in the middle of winter were particularly harsh. Togo, leading Seppala’s team, traveled the longest, including the stretch over treacherous Norton Sound that continues to challenge mushers and dogs in the modern Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race.
The medicine was delivered in time to save Nome, and some of the participants in the Serum Run became national celebrities.
Later, Togo retired in Maine. His health deteriorated, and four years after the Serum Run, he was euthanized. It was a significant enough event to warrant a New York Times obituary.
“The big, shaggy Siberian husky which four years ago raced across the Alaskan wastes at the head of a dog team with serum for the diphtheria-stricken inhabitants of Nome went painlessly across the Big Divide to the dog’s Valhalla on Thursday night,” said the Dec. 9, 2029, story, which mentioned that Togo’s body was donated to the Peabody Museum.
Many years later, the mount made from Togo’s skin and face was shipped to the Iditarod Trail Committee headquarters in Wasilla, where it remains on display.
Immediately after the Serum Run — and in the years and decades to follow — a different sled dog got much of the attention: Balto, the lead dog in the final team that pulled up to Nome.
There was prominent national news coverage. “The north country has written on the pages of its history in large letters the name of Balto, lead dog of Gunnar Kasson’s team,” the New York Times reported on Feb. 4, 2025.
There was a statute erected in New York’s Central Park. There were numerous children’s books about him. There was a hit animated movie released in 1995 with ties to reality that are somewhat loose; for example, the movie version of Balto has a love interest whose cartoon appearance was modeled after the face of Hollywood icon Audrey Hepburn.
Though some Alaskans still complain that Balto’s celebrity overshadowed Togo’s accomplishments, the latter also got recognition.
Fictional detective Nancy Drew, in the books chronicling her adventures, named her pet dog Togo. Statues of both Balto and Togo were erected at the Cleveland Metropark Zoo. There was a live-action movie released in 2019 titled, simply, Togo. Closer to home, Camp Togowoods, a 400-acre site near Wasilla operated by the Girl Scouts, is named for the hero dog.
In 2011, Time magazine named Togo the most heroic animal of all time for his role in the Serum Run.
“The sled dog who did the lion’s share of the work was Togo. His journey, fraught with white-out storms, was the longest by 200 miles and included a traverse across perilous Norton Sound — where he saved his team and driver in a courageous swim through ice floes. Togo, we salute you,” the magazine feature said.
Mounts of Andy, a lead dog in the team of five-time Iditarod champion Rick Swenson, and Togo, the lead dog in Leonhard Seppala’s team that delivered life-saving medicine to Nome in the 1925 Serum Run, are seen on display behind plexiglass at the Iditarod Trail Committee headquarters in Wasilla on Feb. 25, 2022. On the wall are portraits of past Iditarod champions and their lead dogs. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

title: Safe2Tell tip line reports from Colorado students declined slightly last year
description: The anonymous tip line for Colorado students to report safety concerns received over 29,000 submissions last school year, the second-highest yearly total in its history. There were 29,302 Safe2Tell reports in the 2025-26 school year, according to new data from the Colorado attorney general’s office. After rising for each of the previous four years, the […]
text:
A person holds a phone with the Colorado Safe2Tell mobile app pulled up on July 16, 2020. (Photo by Moe Clark/Colorado Newsline)The anonymous tip line for Colorado students to report safety concerns received over 29,000 submissions last school year, the second-highest yearly total in its history.
There were 29,302 Safe2Tell reports in the 2025-26 school year, according to new data from the Colorado attorney general’s office. After rising for each of the previous four years, the number of reports was down from a peak of 31,117 in the 2024-25 school year.
“When a student speaks up about a friend who is struggling or a threat to their school, they’re doing something that takes courage and compassion,” Attorney General Phil Weiser said in a statement. “Nearly 30,000 times last school year, someone chose to take that step. Behind those reports are thousands of examples of schools, law enforcement, and mental health professionals stepping in to help.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The top report categories were bullying, safety concerns over school staff, suicide threats and self harm. There were also 510 reports about guns — including a spike following the September 2025 Evergreen High School shooting — along with 37 about explosives and 210 about a planned school attack.
Around 2% of the reports were deliberately false and submitted by people who wanted to mislead officials, the new data shows.
“The fact that nearly 98% of reports are submitted in good faith tells us that students and community members are taking Safe2Tell seriously,” Director Stacey Scardino said in a statement.
Safe2Tell began in 2004 as a non-profit organization, but was incorporated into the attorney general’s office in 2014. Students and community members can anonymously share threats or concerns over the phone, online or through a phone app. Analysts then forward the information to local partners like schools, law enforcement and mental health professionals who then decide how to respond.
In the most recent school year, responses included notifying parents 10,774 times, providing mental health services 5,111 times and doing 3,621 welfare checks, according to the report.
In one high-profile instance, someone made a Safe2Tell report about a former Green Mountain High School psychologist. James Chevrier was eventually convicted and sentenced to five years in prison for sexually assaulting a minor.
People can use Safe2Tell by calling 1-877-542-7233, visiting Safe2Tell.org, texting S2TCO to 738477, or using the mobile app.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa universities seek approval for reduced-credit degrees, program eliminations
description: New, reduced-credit pathways to a degree are making their way to Iowa’s public universities with preliminary approval from their state governing body. The Iowa Board of Regents Academic Affairs Committee Wednesday recommended approval for the University of Iowa and University of Northern Iowa to establish bachelor of applied professional studies degrees, dev[...]
text:
The Iowa Board of Regents meets on Nov. 11, 2026 at Iowa State University. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)New, reduced-credit pathways to a degree are making their way to Iowa’s public universities with preliminary approval from their state governing body.
The Iowa Board of Regents Academic Affairs Committee Wednesday recommended approval for the University of Iowa and University of Northern Iowa to establish bachelor of applied professional studies degrees, developed in deference to state law and board urging, as well as program changes and eliminations.
Regent Steve Lacy said during the committee meeting universities should focus more on marketing their programs like those slated for approval Thursday, adding that “we have a marketing and communications problem” when he speaks to people who don’t know about programs like these. Regent Christine Hensley suggested marketing to the Iowa Business Council and companies with employee tuition reimbursement programs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
University of Northern Iowa Provost José Herrera said officials need to be careful about marketing programs that have yet to win board approval but agreed they need to do a better job of marketing other accelerated programs.
“We’ve been doing a little bit of that with accelerated nursing and accelerated programs in communication science disorders, but I think we need to do a better job with communication,” Herrera said.
University of Iowa
The UI only brought one new degree forward for approval, and requested no program changes or eliminations.
The Bachelor of Applied Professional Studies in Applied Health Studies will be offered by the UI’s University College and represent the first of its degree type at the university, board documents stated. The mainly online, reduced-credit program will target working adults, healthcare professionals, and those with some college credit but no degree or a shorter degree or certification.
UI Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education and University College Dean Tanya Uden-Holman told board members the major “responds to workforce needs in healthcare and the demand for more flexible bachelor’s degree completion opportunities,” and separates itself from the UI’s traditional bachelor’s degree in health studies with different learning objectives and different student group targets.
Students enrolling in the degree will have two pathways to choose from — a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) certificate, which will include in-person practicum work in Iowa City, and healthcare services. Enrollment is projected in the board document to reach 98 students in five years.
No additional funding or resources is necessary to launch the new degree, which with board approval would begin in August 2027. Uden-Holman said resources will be reallocated from University College when needed and tuition revenue will also support the program, expected to break even in its first year and bring in net revenues of around $140,000 by year five.
“The University of Iowa is particularly well positioned to offer this program, with five health sciences colleges on one campus and strong connections to a nationally recognized academic medical center,” Uden-Holman said. “The proposed major also builds on University College’s established experience serving working adults and students pursuing flexible degree options through its online BLS and BAS programs.”
University of Northern Iowa
UNI brought forward multiple proposals for new degrees, as well as program changes and eliminations.
The Cedar Falls university’s bachelor of applied professional studies focuses on professional development, communication, artificial intelligence and technology, Interim Associate Provost for Academic Affairs Deirdre Heistad said, with a 12-unit core curriculum and additional discipline-focused courses students can choose to complete the 90-credit degree.
Enrollment is expected to reach 75 students in year five of the program being offered, with targeted groups including adult learners, transfer students and working professionals. Heistad said the program will be offered entirely online through the College of Graduate Research and Online Education, and it won’t need any additional faculty, facilities or large equipment.
The new degree will expand access to higher education, support workforce needs and strengthen UNI’s commitment to these principles, Heistad said.
“Graduates will be prepared to analyze workplace challenges, communicate effectively in professional settings, and apply interdisciplinary knowledge to real-world situations,” Heistad said.
UNI also received initial approval from the committee to establish an online bachelor of arts in human services in August 2027, which Heistad said has already seen success as an exploratory program with 100 students enrolled. She said the program will prepare students to “support individuals and families, navigate service systems and understand policies governing human services.”
Interest in the program doubled between 2024 and 2025, Heistad said, and “enrollment is projected to grow to 110 majors within seven years.” No new resources are required to launch the program.
The new program would sit in the university’s department of family, aging and counseling and pull from family studies, lifespan development and social sciences to address “Iowa’s growing shortage of human and social services professionals,” she said.
For programs slated for consolidation and elimination, Heistad said they “represent a thoughtful restructuring to preserve educational opportunities while improving efficiency and alignment with student and workforce needs.”
The board committee gave preliminary approval for UNI to consolidate its family services, gerontology and long-term care administration into a renamed family and lifespan development degree. The university will also bring together geography, environmental resource management and geographic information science majors into a renamed geography and geospatial sciences degree.
“Together, these proposals streamline degree structures, improve workforce alignment, simplify student pathways, and generate approximately $89,000 in annual efficiencies while preserving student access and academic quality,” Heistad said.
UNI’s biomedical program and ecology, evolution and organismal biology degree will also be combined within the university’s biology major as concentrations.
Regent Peter Cownie asked whether the program changes will impact UNI’s gerontology clinic, which Heistad denied.
Iowa State University
ISU brought 11 programs to the board of regents for elimination Wednesday, the majority combined master’s and PhD pathways.
Provost Jason Keith told the board that each of the programs were previously identified through the university’s program vitality review as under-enrolled, and each went through university processes before being added onto a board of regents agenda.
“MS and PhD” degrees in astrophysics and applied, condensed matter, high energy, nuclear and bio-physics will be combined under an “umbrella program,” Keith said, and other graduate programs in earth science and toxicology will be eliminated. Additional programs approved for closure include a PhD in wind energy science, engineering and policy, a master of engineering in energy systems and a bachelor of arts in environmental studies as a secondary major.
“These actions are part of Iowa State’s continuous improvement effort to better streamline our curriculum for its student demand,” Keith said.
A new vitality review will take place in spring 2028, Keith said.
Board criticisms 
Board members were not satisfied with all of the projected cost differences and enrollment numbers for the programs requested for elimination or establishment, with Regent Kurt Tjaden issuing challenges to university officials to take a harder look at financials and more continuous reviews of academic programs.
Tjaden said he heard words like “no incremental costs, no additional staffing” from university officials about the programs they’re trying to establish, but nothing about the new students coming to campus and the incremental tuition funding they represent. He’s “surprised the dollars aren’t higher” since costs weren’t factored in and suggested meeting again “offline” to go over everything.
“I think that the numbers that you presented for enrollment are really on the conservative side, especially once you have an effective marketing program,” Hensley said.
Universities also need to be more consistent and quick in their review steps for programs potentially up for elimination, Tjaden said, comparing it to reduction processes in business environments where there is a watchlist and ongoing process. It should be known what programs are in danger of elimination, timelines to decide upon their fate and “constant review.”
Regent Greta Rouse suggested tracking the cost savings from program changes and closures for the board’s Revenue Enhancement and Productivity Study (REAPS), to which Tjaden said they will include in their presentation to the board Thursday.
“I would challenge you to accelerate the cadence on this,” Tjaden said. “I’m not saying to terminate more programs, I’m saying have a process, be much more diligent about it.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Commentary: New Hampshire’s kitchen-table issues carry the weight of the world
description: At any kitchen table in any small New Hampshire town, the challenges are immense and layered. In the most panoramic view, our kitchen-table family can see ancient and ever-present existential threats come into focus: war, famine and pestilence. Each looming catastrophe, however dormant or remote, holds the potential to dismantle not only a household but […]
text:
Voting booths at Webster Elementary School in Manchester on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)At any kitchen table in any small New Hampshire town, the challenges are immense and layered.
In the most panoramic view, our kitchen-table family can see ancient and ever-present existential threats come into focus: war, famine and pestilence. Each looming catastrophe, however dormant or remote, holds the potential to dismantle not only a household but entire societies, rapidly and irrevocably. 
In the 20th century, two new world-enders emerged — nuclear proliferation and climate change. And now comes the rise of artificial intelligence.
Every nation on the planet must contend with these threats, all while navigating challenges unique to their geography, politics, economy and levels of wealth inequality. So along with these various avenues for apocalypse, the United States faces internal threats to its existence. Chief among them is the influence of money in politics, which compromises the nation’s ability to place public servants in a position to serve the public good.
The greed of special interests leaves the people of New Hampshire and the nation vulnerable not only to the global existential threats outlined above but a host of issues of enormous national concern: the cost of healthcare, childcare, college, electricity, housing, groceries, gasoline, etc.; a system of taxation that is inequitable in both design and enforcement; disinvestment from social safety net programs that punishes not only poor people but seniors, children, veterans and people with disabilities; and, at the heart of all of it, rampant and unchecked political corruption at the highest levels of government. 
The weight of these global threats and national dysfunction presses down on every state and at every moment, as if New Hampshire didn’t have enough structural challenges of its own.
The property-tax burden on communities and families here has long since reached its crisis point. A consequence of that pressure was made clear on Election Day, when voters in dozens of school districts adopted new tax caps with hopes of reducing the squeeze. One way to read those results is that people believe their school boards and administrations need to do a better job of managing taxpayer money, and that tax caps are a guaranteed method of applying fiscal discipline. Another way to read the votes, however, is that the people were left with no choice.
No state invests less state funding in public education than New Hampshire, and that means no state relies more heavily on local property taxes than New Hampshire. That gives the lie to the idea that school districts are solely or even primarily to blame for this statewide predicament.
In just about every public system, business, organization and household, there are always going to be efficiencies to be found. And often finding and executing new efficiencies will mean the difference between sinking or swimming. But the tax caps aren’t simply a cry for efficiency or restraint; they are a cry for mercy — and the state is the one doing the twisting.
Back at our table in a small New Hampshire town, the struggle is immense and it is growing. It would almost be a luxury for our family to focus just on what they can do to help fend off the universal existential threats — the malignant tentacles of climate change, nuclear weapons, war, disease, extreme poverty, AI. Even a collective dedication to meaningful campaign finance reform would signal a type of luxury most Americans don’t have — time and energy to both pursue urgent systemic correction and fight for their own financial survival.
But here in the kitchen, the household budget numbers demand the lion’s share of every family’s effort and attention. Property taxes, rents, healthcare premiums, gasoline, heating oil, electricity, car repairs, groceries, college, internet and phone service, the countless day-to-day expenses of modern life — these rising costs reliably erase any wage growth a New Hampshire worker might experience from year to year. They push families backward, if not under. And when the bottom-line number turns from black to red, and our kitchen-table family is forced to drain their savings and retirement funds before finally and desperately adding to their high-interest credit card debt, a singular fact takes hold: It is punishingly expensive to have nothing.
That is the moment where we find ourselves, and it’s the impetus for what happened on Nov. 3. For most, the American dream has become the American plight.
Now, new Democratic majorities in Congress and the State House are being asked by a vocal and frustrated majority to do everything they can to relieve the pressure, to make life more manageable by degrees.
It is a monumental task, and there is only one way for our new lawmakers to take it on: Layer, by layer, by layer — and all at once.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Legislative rulemaking committee shoots down changes to Hope Scholarship
description: An attempt to require all participating schools in the Hope Scholarship program be located in the state was vehemently rejected by lawmakers this week.
text:
Sen. Patricia Rucker, R-Jefferson, listens at the Nov. 9 meeting of the Legislative Rule Making Review Committee in Charleston, West Virginia. 
(Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)An attempt to require all participating schools in the Hope Scholarship program be located in the state was vehemently rejected by lawmakers this week. 
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, offered up an amendment Monday in the Rulemaking Review Committee to regulations governing the program that would require all microschools, private schools or parochial schools, receiving money from it for tuition or fees, be located inside the state of West Virginia. 
The Hope Scholarship uses taxpayer dollars for families to pursue private or home education. 
In the 2025-2026 school year, the vast majority of the $45 million spent on tuition and fees at nonpublic schools stayed in the state of West Virginia. About $2.4 million went to the surrounding states of Kentucky, Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Virginia, mostly to schools located in border regions. 
Young’s amendment mimicked a similar proposal released by the House Finance Committee in February, which was part of a larger package to cap spending in the Hope Scholarship. Lawmakers killed the bill after pushback from homeschool families and school choice organizations. Big-money supporters of the school choice programs funded a successful primary challenge against the committee chair months later. 
Sen. Patricia Rucker, R-Jefferson, one of the chief architects of the Hope Scholarship program, accused Young of “legislating through rulemaking.” 
“This amendment clearly is trying to change what’s in the code, and I will have to say that any member of this committee can introduce legislation if they disagree with something in code, and they’re welcome to do so,” Rucker said. 
The powerful rulemaking review committee is composed of six state senators and six delegates. Most agencies — there are a few exceptions like the Department of Education — can write regulations in order to effectively enforce the law. Those rules can’t contradict or undermine the law it’s meant to enforce. 
Lamakers on the review committee can then have their say in the rule. Once they get done tinkering with it, they recommend it be passed and the two co-chairs of the committee will introduce it in the following legislative session. 
Prior to hurling the accusation at Young, Rucker conferred with legislative attorney Phillip Childs. 
“I don’t know if you’ve had a chance to look at the code, I’m pretty certain it says there that the funds can be used anywhere, it doesn’t restrict it to just the state of West Virginia?” Rucker asked. 
“That is correct, Madam Chairwoman. The code does not explicitly say that it can be used — I don’t recall where it says explicitly used anywhere. It does not say that it must explicitly be used in West Virginia,” Childs said. 
The following day, Young took issue with a number of changes to rules surrounding the Aboveground Storage Tank Act. In that case, some of the changes proposed by the Department of Environmental Protection were from tweaks stricken out by lawmakers working on a law to change the act. Legislative attorney Robert Akers told Young that the DEP was within its right to add these features into the rules, because the law didn’t explicitly forbid it. 
“Unless we specifically say that, it’s not the law,” Akers said. “We didn’t say ‘thou shalt not do this’ in the bill.” 
“Well, we didn’t say it is the law,” Young said. 
“We didn’t put it in the code specifically, but we did not forbid it either,” Akers said. 
The aboveground storage tanks rules ultimately passed. 
In the case of the Hope Scholarship, the law defines schools that receive Hope Scholarship as “any” elementary or secondary private school. Rucker, in a phone interview Wednesday, said the “any” protects the out-of-state schools in the rulemaking process. 
“The state legislature could decide to narrow it to be more specific at any time that they want,” Rucker said. 
Young said she figured it would happen that way. 
“When it happened on Hope, I was like, oh, the reverse is going to happen tomorrow,” Young said. “I do think they’re moving the goalposts.” 
Rucker said in the case of DEP, that department is given more latitude in its rules because it has to adjust to changes on the federal level. So even though those proposals were nixed in the legislative process, they could come back. But in the case of the Hope Scholarship and the Treasurer’s Office, who oversees the program, they can’t. 
“Unlike the Hope Scholarship, in that law, we do give the authority to the commissioner, to DEP, the ability to do what he needs to in order to ensure the safety of the citizens,” she said. 
Young said she didn’t believe her amendment overstepped the boundaries of rulemaking.  
“We can’t change what the law says, but we can clarify what it says,” Young said. “So, I can say any school in West Virginia — that’s a reasonable clarification. I can understand if the members don’t want to do that, but I think that I have full authority under the law to do so.” 
The committee also shot down two other amendments offered by Young. One would’ve required self-reported income information by families applying for the Hope Scholarship for demographic purposes. The other would’ve required participating schools to submit their attendance policies to the Hope Scholarship Board.
