name: North Carolina Newsline
title: GOP incumbent Britt maintains 228-vote lead in closely watched NC Senate race
description: Republican state Sen. Danny Britt maintained a narrow lead over Democratic challenger Catina Hamm in North Carolina’s 24th Senate District. The candidates were separated by just 228 votes Wednesday after officials counted provisional and cured ballots as the race moves toward its official canvass Friday.  Britt received 28,047 votes, or 50.2%, compared with [...]
text:
Republican Sen. Danny Britt (left) and Democrat Catina Hamm (right). (Photos: NCGA and Hamm campaign) Republican state Sen. Danny Britt maintained a narrow lead over Democratic challenger Catina Hamm in North Carolina’s 24th Senate District.
The candidates were separated by just 228 votes Wednesday after officials counted provisional and cured ballots as the race moves toward its official canvass Friday. 
Britt received 28,047 votes, or 50.2%, compared with 27,819 votes or 49.8% for Hamm, according to unofficial results from the North Carolina State Board of Elections. 
The margin leaves the contest in recount territory. Under North Carolina law, Hamm can request a recount if Britt’s lead remains less than 1% after the county canvasses Friday. 
The district includes Robeson, Hoke and Scotland counties. Britt has represented it since 2017.
The race could determine which party controls the state Senate when lawmakers convene in January. 
Republicans entered Election Day with a 30-20 majority in the chamber. Democrats picked up four seats in the Nov. 3 election, leaving them with 24 seats and Republicans with 26 if Britt holds his lead. 
If Britt wins, Republicans would retain a narrow majority and control of Senate leadership, committee assignments and the chamber’s legislative agenda.  But the party would still lose its veto-proof supermajority, meaning it would need Democratic support to override vetoes by Democratic Gov. Josh Stein. 
If Hamm were to win, the Senate would be evenly divided, with 25 Republicans and 25 Democrats. Lt. Gov. Rachel Hunt, a Democrat, would be the tie-breaking vote.
Democrats have already taken control of the state House of Representatives for the first time since 2010. 
The deadline to file a recount request is noon on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: ICE agent in fatal Biddeford shooting had expedited training, held anti-immigrant views, NYT reports
description: The immigration agent who allegedly shot and killed a Biddeford man was fast-tracked through training and had expressed anti-immigrant views, according to new reporting from The New York Times. Media reports identified David Brouillette as the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who fatally shot 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in July. [...]
text:
The site where Johan Sebastián, 25, was fatally shot by ICE agents is outlined in flowers on Wednesday, July 15, 2026,  in Biddeford, Maine. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)The immigration agent who allegedly shot and killed a Biddeford man was fast-tracked through training and had expressed anti-immigrant views, according to new reporting from The New York Times.
Media reports identified David Brouillette as the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who fatally shot 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in July. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has not officially released the agent’s name. Guerrero, who was from Colombia, was not the intended target of the ICE operation and had a pending asylum case and a valid work permit, according to his family and lawyer. 
The Times obtained a series of emails that Brouillette, a former U.S. Army sergeant, sent in 2021 criticizing his sister’s relationship with a Colombian man, with whom she had two children.
“He can takes his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries,” Brouillette wrote in an email riddled with typos. He continued that the man’s “bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers.”
The reporting also revealed new details about Brouillette’s ICE training, citing anonymous sources who were briefed on his work history with the agency.
Brouillette applied at ICE in the fall of 2025 and was cleared to start on Dec. 1 after being fast-tracked through preliminary vetting, according to the sources. That was amid a hiring surge after President Donald Trump’s administration called for doubling the number of deportation officers. 
Brouillette skipped ICE’s full training course in Georgia, in line with ICE’s practice of recruits with some law enforcement experience completing a shorter online training program, and his background check was done by an outside contractor. However, officials still hadn’t checked his background for red flags that could result in his termination at the time of the Biddeford shooting, an anonymous source with knowledge of his hiring told the Times. 
Brouillette declined to speak with the Times. He has not responded to Maine Morning Star’s repeated attempts to contact him through phone or email. When Maine Morning Star asked ICE in July about Brouillette’s alleged involvement, an unnamed spokesperson said, “The ICE officer in question has nearly a decade of federal law enforcement experience with required training,” but declined to share a name.  
The 911 calls made after ICE fatally shot Biddeford man

The new revelations about Brouillette’s background come after earlier reporting revealed complaints of domestic abuse. 
Court documents show that one of Brouillette’s ex-wives filed several requests for protection from harassment and protection from abuse orders against him, for herself and on behalf of their minor child. Most of those were denied, though a judge required him to temporarily relinquish his firearms. Brouillette also filed several requests for protection against an ex-wife, including on behalf of their children.
Benjamin Gideon, attorney for Guerrero’s wife, Karolina Rojas Alvarez, and estate, called Brouillette “the poster child for what happens when our government chooses to recruit agents to carry out a campaign of hate against immigrants, hires those agents without adequate screening and places them on the street without basic training.”
“Johan Sebastián’s death was not an inevitable accident,” Gideon said in a statement Wednesday. “It was a natural and predictable choices of the policies of our government and its political leadership.”
The federal government has yet to tell Guerrero’s family anything about a federal investigation, according to Gideon. U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine said the latest reporting makes the need for a full, independent investigation even more urgent.
“Who authorized his deployment? What would a thorough review have revealed?” Pingree questioned in a statement. “An agency whistleblower has already warned the DHS Inspector General of an ‘unprecedented lowering of standards.’ How many other agents are carrying guns in our communities without completed vetting?”
The state has its own investigation underway. Another lawyer for Guerrero’s family, Sean Murphy, told the Times that investigators said Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey, who terms out at the end of the year, plans to announce any decisions in the case before he leaves office.
Maine Morning Star’s requests for records of communications between federal agencies and the state attorney general’s office and the coroner’s report have been denied as they remain confidential while the investigation is ongoing.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: Without prairie dogs, endangered black-footed ferrets disappear
description: The black-footed ferret is among the planet’s most endangered species. A native of central North America, it was considered extinct until Sept. 26, 1981, when a Meeteetse, Wyoming, investigator named Shep rediscovered it. Shep was a ranch dog who delivered a carcass to his owners’ front steps. Black-footed ferrets need prairie dog towns as habitat. […]
text:
A prairie dog stands near its burrow on Oct. 6, 2024, in Wind Cave National Park. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)The black-footed ferret is among the planet’s most endangered species. A native of central North America, it was considered extinct until Sept. 26, 1981, when a Meeteetse, Wyoming, investigator named Shep rediscovered it. Shep was a ranch dog who delivered a carcass to his owners’ front steps.
Black-footed ferrets need prairie dog towns as habitat. They prey on the rodents there and use their tunnels for refuge.
Prairie dogs are Great Plains ground squirrels that sound and act a lot like dogs. They bark, sit erect, wag their tails, wrestle like puppies and exchange kiss-like greetings.
They are also maligned. Ranchers claim they compete with cattle for grass. They don’t. Cattle, bison, deer, elk and pronghorns gravitate to prairie dog towns because prairie dogs bring rich, moist soil to the surface, aerate and fertilize soil, and improve water retention — all of which encourages lush, nutritious vegetation. Prairie dog towns support at least 150 species.

A black-footed ferret. (Photo courtesy of National Park Service)

It’s still a crime to intentionally kill or harm individual black-footed ferrets or other creatures protected by the Endangered Species Act. But on Sept. 14, the Trump administration decreed that it’s perfectly OK to destroy the habitat these animals require for survival. It’s “common sense,” proclaims Trump’s Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.
We’ve already wiped out 98% of prairie dog towns. But now, developers can legally build shopping malls on top of prairie dog towns occupied by black-footed ferrets. These same prairie dog towns can also legally be eliminated by poison applied by ranchers and county, state and federal agencies.
“This rule guts the standard that has safeguarded imperiled wildlife (for 50 years),” says Defenders of Wildlife. Another nonprofit, Animal Wellness Action, likens Trump’s weakening of the Endangered Species Act to “stripping anti-discrimination provisions from the Civil Rights Act.” The Environmental Protection Information Center warns that the change “removes a key legal shield that keeps forests, rivers, and wild lands intact.”
Since Shep’s rediscovery, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and partners have undertaken an expensive and complicated black-footed ferret recovery program. They have protected and restored prairie dog habitat throughout the West, immunized prairie dogs against rampant sylvatic plague, bred ferrets in captivity and released them in prairie dog towns in Wyoming, South Dakota, Montana, Utah, Colorado, Kansas, New Mexico and, most recently, Arizona.
Black-footed ferret recovery is hailed as one of the most spectacular success stories of the Endangered Species Act. But it may be for naught, even if the Trump rule is vacated by challenges in the courts.
That’s because America remains at war with prairie dogs. County commissions, the U.S. Forest Service and USDA’s Wildlife Services poison them. “Varminters” shoot them for recreation, leaving them to rot, but not before raptors and other scavengers consume them along with bullet fragments, then die of lead poisoning.
This October, the Prairie Dog Coalition circulated a petition to ban prairie dog shooting in Colorado, where 500 black-footed ferrets have been released since 2001. The U.S. Forest Service permits and promotes prairie dog shooting on national grasslands. Game and fish agencies permit and promote it on state lands. The Sioux Nation permits and promotes it on reservations.
Because so many raptors were dying of lead poisoning, Audubon of Kansas has offered nontoxic copper bullets to prairie dog shooters at the same cost as cheaper lead rounds. According to game managers and even the National Rifle Association, copper kills more efficiently than lead. But varminters resist copper because they’ve always used lead. After four years, Kansas Audubon didn’t have one taker.

I accompanied famed prairie dog shooter Rich Grable to the Rosebud Sioux Reservation in South Dakota. “Mr. Dog,” as he’s known, eschews the standard tripod, preferring to rest his Remington .222-caliber rifle on foam rubber at the base of his truck window.
Crack. Mr. Dog cut a target in half, sending hindquarters spinning. “Dead,” he declared, punching his dashboard-mounted kill counter. Babies, with paws on siblings’ shoulders, exploded in red mist. Once he killed five with a single shot.
“Can ya hear it go plop?” he cackled. “Dissolved him! Ha. Ha.” Whenever a target dragged itself back into its burrow, minus body parts, Mr. Dog shouted: “I done something to him.” One year he killed 7,652 prairie dogs.
Mr. Dog appreciates most wildlife. Yet he’s part of a ranching and federal and state management culture that perceives prairie dogs as divine typos in need of Wite-Out.
Unfortunately, that blots out whole ecosystems, and it has a good chance of blotting out black-footed ferrets — even if the Trump rule is overturned.

title: Mississippi’s top general: Veterans Day time to remember sacrifices of America’s military members
description: A memorial to fallen veterans stands outside the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026.
text:

The sacrifices made by America’s military members were highlighted  during a Veterans Day ceremony at the Two Mississippi Museums.
The event, conducted Tuesday outside of Jackson’s Two Mississippi Museums, honored Mississippi’s service members, veterans and their families. It featured a musical performance from the 41st Star Army Band and remarks from military leaders, including Maj. Gen. Bobby M. Ginn Jr., the adjutant general of Mississippi.
“As we gather on Veterans Day, we are reminded that behind every name engraved on a memorial is a life that mattered, a family that loved them and a story that deserves to be told,” he said.
A veteran observes remarks of a Veterans Day ceremony on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026 at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi Today
Ginn’s speech told the story of Meridian native and Army National Guardsmen Sgt. Robert S. Pugh, a combat medic who died during the Iraq War. After an improvised explosive device left him and Sgt. First Class Ellis Martin with severe injuries, Pugh directed the soldiers around him to give Martin life-saving treatment.
Ellis survived, but Pugh died of his injuries. Pugh was posthumously awarded the Silver Star, the Bronze Star, the Purple Heart and Mississippi Medal of Valor. The Mississippi National Guard Readiness Center in Morton bears his name.
“In what would become the final moments of his own life, Sgt. Pugh’s concern was not for himself. It was for the soldier beside him,” said Ginn. “That is the very definition of selfless service.”
Ginn conducted the wreath-laying ceremony with Pugh’s mother, Wilma Allen, followed by a memorial volley.
Mississippi Air National Guard state Command Chief Master Sgt. Kevin Myers said that stories like Pugh’s are, “a somber reminder that once we put the uniform on, it is always the possibility that we will be called into harm and dangers’ way, and for that, some of us pay the ultimate sacrifice,” he said.
Chief Master Sergeant Kevin L. Myers, state Command Chief of the Mississippi Air National Guard, speaks on the importance of honoring those who have served in the armed forces on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026 at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi Today
Myers considers Veterans Day a time for him to reflect on his 30-year career. He said he is honored to serve alongside multiple generations of service members.
“For those who make the choice to join our services and join our formations, I take it as a privilege to serve with them, because they are the younger generation,” he said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: How SC veterans can access state and national parks for free year-round
description: Most of the Palmetto State's National Parks Service sites are already free, but veterans can get a lifetime pass.
text:
Congaree National Park is free for everyone to visit, though veterans can get free access to all 64 national parks and many other sites for free. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Veterans looking to explore the outdoors have the option to do so for free in many cases.
On Wednesday, everyone can enjoy national parks fee-free in honor of Veterans Day.
Military veterans and families of those killed in the line of duty can get free lifetime passes to national parks and other federally operated lands, according to the National Park Service.
“Veterans have given so much to our country,” Jessica Bowron, acting director of the National Park Service, said in a news release. “National parks offer places to find connection, enjoy time with family and friends, and bring their skills to another meaningful chapter of service.”
Nearly all of South Carolina’s nine National Park sites are already free. That includes the state’s only national park, the 27,000-acre Congaree swamp just south of Columbia.
State Museum debuts exhibit highlighting SC’s role in Revolutionary War

Only Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie in Charleston Harbor require a $10 payment. That covers the fee for the Revolutionary fort on Sullivans Island, where Patriots repelled the British Navy in 1776.
Visiting Fort Sumter, where the Civil War began, requires taking a ferry, which additionally costs $43 for adults or $39 for active military members. The free lifetime pass for veterans does not cover that cost.
South Carolina has other historic sites related to the military. Specifically, Cowpens National Battlefield, Kings Mountain National Military Park and Ninety Six National Historic Site all tell the stories of Revolutionary War battles.
A lifetime membership can get veterans access to parks in neighboring states that do come with an admission cost. Visiting Great Smoky Mountains National Park locations in North Carolina and Tennessee, for instance, costs $5 for a daily pass, $15 for a week, or $40 annually.
State parks also have deals for veterans, though only those with proof of a disability through the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Disabled veterans are allowed to enter any state park for free under state law. To skip the entrance fees, veterans must present an identification card from the local Veterans Affairs office saying they are disabled.
Active members of the South Carolina National Guard can get unlimited access to all state parks, which is usually $99, for half that price, according to the state parks department. South Carolina has 51 state parks, with more in the works.
A bill proposed in the Senate this year would have allowed all veterans to visit state parks for free, though it never got a committee hearing. The bill was sponsored by Sen. Jeff Zell, a Sumter Republican and Air Force veteran.
“This is a simple, meaningful way to recognize the men and women who’ve worn the uniform and to ensure consistent access across the state,” Zell wrote on social media.

text:
Rep. Aaron Bernstine, R-Beaver (Courtesy of Bernstine campaign Facebook)In a move before the end of the legislative session, the Pennsylvania state House Rules committee voted unanimously to censure Republican Aaron Bernstine over alleged homophobic remarks made at a Harrisburg bar this fall.
The committee’s action, which is largely a symbolic gesture of disapproval, could set up a final vote by the full House next week.
After a prolonged recess Tuesday afternoon, House Speaker Joanna McClinton introduced House Resolution 676 to formally censure Bernstine “for his continued actions which are unbecoming a member of this House of Representatives.” House Republican leader Jesse Topper raised no objections and all 33 members of the committee voted for the resolution.
“This is a standard that will be held to both caucuses and is one the Speaker has been very clear about that all members are to be held to at all times,” said House Democratic leader Matt Bradford just before the vote.
Attending the committee meeting, though not a member, was Philadelphia Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta, who Bernstine was reported to have targeted with the slurs at a Harrisburg Pub in September.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Democrats eye seeking recount in Republican Senate leader Chris Garten’s tight reelection race
description: Indiana Democratic officials say they are preparing to seek a recount of Republican state Senate leader Chris Garten’s narrow election lead.
text:
Sen. Chris Garten, R-Charlestown, speaks during a Senate session in February 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana Democratic officials say they are preparing to seek a recount of Republican state Senate leader Chris Garten’s narrow election lead.
That announcement came after the Clark County Election Board voted 2-1 Tuesday night against conducting a planned count of the physical ballots cast for four precincts that voted at Jeffersonville High School, where a ballot scanner malfunction was reported on Election Day.
Republicans who control the state Senate are poised to vote next week on confirming Garten for the chamber’s top position of president pro tem — and Garten says he is confident that his election lead will stand.
Preliminary results posted by the Indiana Election Division show Garten leading by 297 votes, or about two-thirds of a percentage point, with 21,817 to 21,520 for Democratic challenger Nick Marshall in the Senate District 45 race. Libertarian Larry Mahaney had 993 votes.
Garten said in a statement to the Capital Chronicle on Wednesday that records from the precincts involved show 1,640 ballots cast on Election Day compared to 1,612 voters recorded in the electronic pollbook.
Garten’s statement said the 28-vote “discrepancy appears to be related to a technical issue with the electronic pollbook.”
State Democratic officials said the discrepancy is “fundamentally wrong” and that a jammed voting machine might have resulted in “several hours of votes that were not counted.”
“We must continue to push for transparency, honesty, and to ensure that every legal vote is counted. We will pursue all available legal avenues, including a recount and/or contest of the results in Senate District 45 and Clark County,” said the statement from state Democratic Chair Karen Tallian and 9th Congressional District Democratic Chair Adam Dickey.
Clark County Clerk Ryan Lynch did not immediately reply to an email Wednesday asking whether he agreed with Garten’s figures and explanation for the discrepancy.
Indiana Republican senators endorse Garten as chamber’s next top leader

Lynch and fellow Republican Election Board member Tony Singleton voted Tuesday against moving ahead with recounting the ballots, according to news reports.
Lynch told reporters after the meeting that it was unclear whether state law allowed the Election Board to conduct such a ballot count.
“We had some malfunctions on election morning, but at this point, I didn’t see a statistical basis to move forward with,” Lynch said. “I don’t ever want to take the easy route if there’s a chance that it goes against the law. I couldn’t get a clear answer from the state.”
County election officials have a Nov. 16 deadline to submit certified vote tallies to the Indiana Election Division. 
Candidates have until Nov. 17 to file recount petitions, with county party chairs having until Nov. 20 to do so.
A recount for the Senate seat would be overseen by the State Recount Commission. Current Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales is the commission’s chair, along with one Republican and one Democratic member.
The commission just two months ago saw the Indiana Supreme Court overturn its decision in a contentious Republican primary between state Sen. Spencer Deery and a President Donald Trump-endorsed challenger.
The court declared Deery the winner as it ruled the commission’s Republican members wrongly disallowed votes for him.
Garten on Wednesday called the claims from Democrats over votes in his race “political theater.”
“The records we have reviewed simply do not support their allegations,” Garten’s statement said. “Election officials have examined these issues, and the Clark County Election Board voted to respect the legal protections surrounding sealed ballots.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. State Police report near-total compliance on skill games removal
description: More than 12,000 businesses and social clubs have removed skill games in the three weeks since Pennsylvania State Police started enforcing a court order that found the slot machine-like terminals fell under state gambling laws.  PSP reported that just 68 places held onto the devices after Oct. 14 out of the 12,202 establishments they visited. […]
text:
Karma, an LGBTQ+ bar near the Capitol in Harrisburg, calls for saving skill games on Nov. 2, 2026. Pennsylvania State Police report that most businesses removed that gaming terminals voluntarily. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)More than 12,000 businesses and social clubs have removed skill games in the three weeks since Pennsylvania State Police started enforcing a court order that found the slot machine-like terminals fell under state gambling laws. 
PSP reported that just 68 places held onto the devices after Oct. 14 out of the 12,202 establishments they visited. The agency said it had seized 14 machines and $1,913, but investigations are ongoing. 
The Attorney General’s Office previously estimated there were as many as 70,000 skill games machines around the state, many providing a vital stream of income to gas stations, grocery stores and laundromats. 
The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled in June that skill games must be regulated like other gaming, meaning the terminals could only be placed in businesses that are licensed by the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board.
 
The Pennsylvania State Police urge the public to report such devices by emailing tips@pa.gov or calling 1-888-292-1919.


Justices paused their ruling for 140 days, giving lawmakers time to craft legislation legalizing the machines, but no consensus was reached.
PSP emphasized that, contrary to “claims from manufacturers and operators,” machines that don’t accept money or operate like a “sweepstakes” still fall under the order and can be confiscated.
“No manufacturer or operator sought PSP’s input on the legality of these devices before placing them inside Pennsylvania businesses. Distributors of these devices and establishments hosting them could face criminal charges for unlawful gambling and other related offenses if they continue operating these machines,” the agency said.
Devices that accept “any form of compensation from a player to engage in slot-style games” that comes with a potential payout “is a slot machine and/or gambling device,” the statement continued. 
The agency directs businesses with these machines to discuss “immediate” removal with distributors and vendors, noting that criminal charges can be levied against the latter parties as well.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Department of Transportation asks Legislature for speed cameras in highway work zones
description: The New Mexico Department of Transportation’s acting secretary told state lawmakers on Tuesday that he has one big ask of them for the upcoming legislative session: authorizing speed enforcement cameras in highway construction zones.
text:
New Mexico Department of Transportation Acting Secretary David Quintana on Nov. 10, 2026, told lawmakers his top legislative priority for the 2027 session is getting authorization for speed enforcement cameras in highway construction zones. (Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)The New Mexico Department of Transportation’s acting secretary told state lawmakers on Tuesday that he has one big ask of them for the upcoming legislative session: authorizing speed enforcement cameras in highway construction zones.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Acting Secretary David Quintana spoke before the interim Transportation Infrastructure Revenue Subcommittee to present his department’s four legislative priorities for the lawmaking session beginning in January.
In addition to the speed cameras, he asked lawmakers to craft legislation that would increase the education needed for certain commercial licenses; rename one of the department’s bureaus to show that it’s no longer under Public Regulation Commission control; and transfer the responsibility of crafting ambulance safety standards to the state Department of Health.
“The safety of our workers at DOT…is No. 1,” he said in reference to the speed enforcement cameras. “If we do nothing else this legislative session, that’s the one thing I would love to see get passed.” 
While Quintana was crafting his department’s annual budget request in July, he recalled, a motorist struck a state Department of Transportation worker on a highway near Hobbs. While no one died as a result of the crash, he said one injured person required an airlift to Texas for medical treatment. Episodes like that illustrate the need to discourage speeding and reckless driving in work zones by using enforcement cameras, he said.
One state lawmaker, Rep. Raymundo Lara (D-Chamberino), cited recent controversies over automated license plate readers from companies like Flock, and said he would want to closely review a camera and its capabilities before pursuing any legislation to that effect.
“Will they only be identifying speeders, or anybody and everybody that goes through that zone?” Lara asked Quintana, who said he’d investigate the question and follow up with Lara.
Earlier this year the Legislature adopted a law known as the Driver Safety and Privacy Act, which prohibits law enforcement agencies from using the cameras for general surveillance.
“If it’s mainly targeting speeders, then that’s awesome because it’s so important for the safety of the workers,” Lara said Tuesday. “At the same time, I’m very curious as to whether it’s going to be collecting everybody’s information, taking pictures of everybody’s license plates.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Advocates explore ways to boost health affordability and food security in Mississippi
description: Moderator Candice Wilder of Mississippi Today, left, asks a question of panelists, Oleta Garrett Fitzgerald, Director of the Southern Regional Office, Children's Defense Fund, second from left, Dr. Adrian Hammitte, Superintendent of the Jefferson County School District, and Robert Langford, executive director, Operation Shoestring, right, as they engage in a[...]
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Despite outperforming most of the nation in education, Mississippi ranks last on overall child well-being, according to the Annie E. Casey Foundation’s latest KIDS COUNT Data Book, particularly in health and poverty. 
During a “Families Count in the Deep South” event hosted by Mississippi Today on Tuesday, the newsroom’s staff joined leaders from health, education and community engagement across the state to highlight gains, build momentum for a way forward and bring data from the report to life.
Voting rights affect children’s well-being 
“‘Families count’ must mean something beyond counting families in a report. It must mean their lives count when decisions are made,” said Rep. Zakiya Summers, a Democrat from Jackson, addressing about two dozen people in the Mississippi Public Broadcasting Auditorium in Jackson. 
Summers, the event’s keynote speaker, called on her colleagues in the Legislature to prioritize funding childcare, maternal health and education. 
Mississippi State Rep. Zakiya Summers, D-Jackson, speaks to attendees of the Families Count forum in Jackson, Miss., Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, in Jackson, Miss.  Credit: Rogelio V. Solis / Mississippi Today
She also gave a nod to problems that have arisen during the latest midterm elections, and said the chaos highlights the need for easier online voter registration, early voting and universal suffrage. Summers said voting rights are intertwined with children’s well-being because they determine who is given the power to make decisions that will affect future generations. 
Mississippi ranks 50th in health and 49th in economic well-being, but the state has secured 16th place in education – what many have dubbed “the Mississippi miracle.” Nationwide, Mississippi scored second-to-last in on issues of family and community, such as teen pregnancy, single-parent families, households lacking college degrees and high poverty areas. 
Summers urged stakeholders to bring the same urgency they brought to childhood literacy to alleviating childhood poverty. 
“Before we finish the story of Mississippi’s so-called miracle, we must make room for the children whose lives still demand a different ending,” Summers said. 
Families face food insecurity
During a panel that explored food insecurity across the state, speakers highlighted the fact that 1 in 4 children face hunger. In Jefferson County School District, where Adrian Hammitte serves as superintendent, that’s 1 in 3 children. Hammitte said a cafeteria worker in his district keeps four jobs to earn enough money to put food on the family table. One of his district’s best performing teachers, he said, holds perfect attendance but works three jobs to make ends meet. 
Dr. Adrian Hammitte, Superintendent of the Jefferson County School District, speaks of the need of lunch programs for children during the Families Count forum in Jackson, Miss., Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, in Jackson, Miss.  Credit: Rogelio V. Solis / Mississippi Today
The adults who can’t afford to put food on the table raise children who are hungry, don’t perform well in school and repeat the cycle of poverty, Hammitte said. He mentioned a little girl in his district who ran up to him during a Friday afternoon dismissal, hugged his leg and said, “‘Can I go home with you this weekend? Because I know I’m not gonna eat.’” 
Last summer, for the third year in a row, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves opted out of a state-federal partnership that would have given summer food benefits to roughly 320,000 Mississippi children who rely on free meals during the school year. In refusing those dollars, Reeves has called the summer food program “attempts to expand the welfare state.”  
Many Mississippians lack health insurance
His rejection of social safety net programs also extends to healthcare policy, including Medicaid expansion. Mississippi remains one of 10 states not to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act, leaving tens of thousands of working Mississippians without access to health insurance. 
Healthcare panelists spoke about the steep participation drop in marketplace insurance over the last year. In December 2025, enhanced subsidies expired that made insurance more affordable for more than 22 million Americans. Between February 2025 and February 2026, active enrollment in the plans fell by about 70,000 Mississippians. Panelists warned that will create a greater pressure on charitable organizations compelled to cover those gaps and will lead to sicker patients and higher costs for hospitals and the state. 
Khaylah Scott, program manager with the Mississippi Health Advocacy Program, speaks at the Families Count forum in Jackson, Miss., Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, in Jackson, Miss.  Credit: Rogelio V. Solis / Mississippi Today
Khaylah Scott, program manager for the Mississippi Health Advocacy Program, said she often hears people argue that those enhanced subsidies were part of a COVID-era policy.  But she said the policy worked, nearly tripling the number of enrollees, and it shouldn’t be forgotten after the pandemic. 
“When you make healthcare affordable for people, they’ll buy in,” Scott said. “I think that our state is safer and healthier when more people are covered.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Commentary: This Veterans Day, Pennsylvania is turning Its back on the veterans who served us
description: For months, veterans organizations warned Harrisburg that failing to pass legislation regulating skill games would devastate their finances.
text:
For months, veterans organizations warned Harrisburg that failing to pass legislation regulating skill games would devastate their finances. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Every Veterans Day, Pennsylvania comes together to honor the men and women who served our country in the military. Politicians deliver speeches, attend ceremonies, wave American flags and remind us of the sacrifices made by those who defended our freedoms.
But this Veterans Day, those words ring hollow for veterans like me and others across Pennsylvania.
That’s because some of the same lawmakers who attend events at American Legions and VFWs, to thank veterans for their service, failed to take action that could have helped keep their posts open.
For months, veterans organizations warned Harrisburg that failing to pass legislation regulating skill games would devastate their finances. They explained that revenue from these games helped pay utility bills, maintain aging buildings and equipment, support struggling veterans and fund charitable programs throughout their communities. Nothing happened. 
As a reminder, in June, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court gave lawmakers 120 days to regulate skill games, or they would be deemed illegal. That was an opportunity for the General Assembly to establish a regulatory framework that protected veterans organizations, volunteer fire companies, fraternal clubs and small businesses while generating at least $300 million a year in revenue for Pennsylvania.
Instead, lawmakers failed to reach an agreement. On October 13, skill games had to be shut down, taking away an important source of income for countless community organizations.
Now, less than a month later, Pennsylvania’s veterans are paying the price.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At American Legion and VFW posts across the Commonwealth, leaders are confronting difficult financial realities. Some are cutting charitable donations. Others are exploring ways to reduce expenses even though they already were operating on a shoestring. Some fear their organizations may close altogether.
These are places where veterans find friendship, understanding and support. They are places where someone struggling after military service can sit beside another veteran who understands what they’ve experienced without needing an explanation.
They are also pillars of their communities.
American Legions and VFWs help veterans facing financial hardship, sponsor youth activities, provide scholarships and assist families during difficult times. At our American Legion we used a portion of our skill money to boost community programs. 
When these organizations lose revenue, there is a trickle-down effect. The consequences extend far beyond our membership.
And for what?
Pennsylvania lawmakers had proposals before them that would have regulated skill games, established oversight and generated tax revenue while allowing veterans organizations, small businesses and others to continue benefiting from skill machines.
There were legitimate disagreements over tax rates, licensing requirements and how these games should be regulated. Those questions deserved serious debate and a workable compromise.
But disagreement should not have become an excuse for doing nothing.
The irony is impossible to ignore.
We ask our veterans to demonstrate courage, discipline and leadership in the most difficult circumstances imaginable. Yet when these same veterans needed leadership from their elected officials, Harrisburg couldn’t deliver.
Veterans didn’t ask for a government handout. We asked for a reasonable regulatory solution that would enable our organizations to remain financially sustainable and continue serving our communities.
Instead, we were left scrambling to replace revenue we had come to depend on, in some cases for over a decade. Who could go back and sustain themselves on the income they received a decade ago?
This Veterans Day should be about more than speeches, ceremonies and expressions of gratitude.
It should be a moment of accountability.
Pennsylvania’s elected leaders should recognize the consequences of their inaction and return to Harrisburg committed to finding a responsible legislative solution.
That means establishing clear rules, appropriate safeguards and a fair tax structure that recognizes the important role veterans organizations play in Pennsylvania.
Veterans are watching. As our posts face an uncertain future, we deserve more than another round of political promises.
We deserve action.
The best way to honor Pennsylvania’s veterans isn’t simply to thank us for our service one day a year. It’s to stand with us when we need help.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Ex-US attorney, Trump lawyer faces ethics complaint over sex harassment settlement
description: Officials allege Alina Habba Mildon, Trump's former personal lawyer and New Jersey's ex-U.S. attorney, failed to disclose conflicts while convincing a server who sued over sex harassment to settle.
text:
Officials allege Alina Habba Mildon, Trump's former personal lawyer and New Jersey's ex-U.S. attorney, failed to disclose conflicts while convincing a server who sued over sex harassment to settle.  (Photo by Gage Skidmore)The New Jersey Office of Attorney Ethics filed a complaint against Alina Habba Mildon, President Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer and at one time our state’s chief federal prosecutor, alleging a slew of ethics violations surrounding a nondisclosure agreement she brokered for a server at the Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster.
In the filing, ethics attorneys argued Mildon, while a dues-paying member at Trump’s club but not yet his attorney, failed to disclose conflicts of interest and induced Alice Bianco, a server at the golf club, to sign an agreement ceding her legal claims for a pittance at Trump’s request. Trump soon after hired Mildon.
Mildon engaged in a concurrent conflict of interest by representing Bianco “when there was a significant risk” that her representation would be “materially limited” by Mildon’s personal interests, the ethics office wrote in its complaint.
Mildon previously served as acting and interim U.S. attorney for the District of New Jersey, but she left that position when judges found she had remained in the position unlawfully after the U.S. Senate declined to take up her confirmation. She married Turhan Mildon earlier this year.
The ethics complaint stems from allegations that a manager at the club sexually harassed Bianco and coerced her into having sex with him for “protection” and under the threat of termination.
Ethics attorneys alleged Mildon befriended Bianco after a conversation with the club’s general counsel and eventually convinced her to cease contact with her attorney, who stopped representing her over the silence not long after, according to text messages included as exhibits in the case.
The case settled for $15,000 in August 2021, far less than the six-figure payout Bianco’s original attorney believed the case could yield. Bianco later sued the club for fraudulently inducing her to sign the agreement, winning a $400,000 settlement, the filing says.
Mildon in October 2024 told ethics investigators she viewed herself as a neutral third party between the server and the golf club, but she never told either party she was not their attorney — a requirement in rules of professional conduct for New Jersey attorneys — and failed to disclose her prior conversation with the club’s general counsel, the filing says.
Attorneys for Mildon did not immediately return a request for comment. The Washington Sun first reported the ethics complaint’s existence.
In a March 2023 letter, Mildon’s then-attorneys told ethics officials she interceded in the case at Trump’s request, though she later recanted, claiming the letter had been sent without being reviewed first.
Ethics officials reviewed Mildon’s business and attorney trust records to see when her financial relationship with Trump began. The records showed the earliest payment came in Sept. 2, 2021, less than a month after the settlement was entered on Aug. 11, 2021.
But the review also revealed a slew of recordkeeping violations, ethics officials alleged, including a failure to maintain records showing the flow of funds into and out of the accounts.

title: First detainees arrive at Appleton immigrant detention center
description: The first detainees have arrived at the Appleton Detention Facility, Minnesota’s only immigrant detention center, according to local activists.  Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed the facility opened on Monday in a statement provided to the Star Tribune.  “(The Department of Homeland Security) opened the Appleton Detention Facility on Nov. 9 to st[...]
text:
The watchtower of the Appleton Detention Facility, which began taking immigrant detainees this week. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)The first detainees have arrived at the Appleton Detention Facility, Minnesota’s only immigrant detention center, according to local activists. 
Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed the facility opened on Monday in a statement provided to the Star Tribune. 
“(The Department of Homeland Security) opened the Appleton Detention Facility on Nov. 9 to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations,” the statement read.
ICE did not respond to multiple emails from the Reformer. 
Local observers saw buses arrive at the detention center on Monday and a heightened security presence, according to Misty Butler of the Prairie Alliance for Human Dignity, an activist organization opposed to the opening of the detention center and President Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts. 
The Appleton detention center, formerly the Prairie Correctional Facility, is the first detention center in Minnesota. Until now, immigrant detainees have been held in local jails or shipped to out-of-state detention centers.
The Department of Homeland Security purchased the 1,600-bed former prison in August from the private prison company CoreCivic for $496 million — more than six times the property’s assessed value of $75 million, according to county records. 
KARE11 obtained emails from May 2025 between CoreCivic and officials with the Minnesota Department of Corrections, in which CoreCivic offered to sell the prison to the state for $75 million. The state declined the offer. 
Homeland Security is also paying CoreCivic $536 million over the next five years to operate the detention center. 
CoreCivic runs some of the country’s largest and most infamous immigrant detention centers, including the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas, which holds families with children, including, at one time, little Liam Conejo Ramos. Disease outbreaks, lack of medical care, inedible food and lack of outside time are common complaints of detainees.
The Prairie Alliance for Human Dignity, Appleton residents and a number of progressive organizations will hold a press conference, vigil and rally outside the detention center on Saturday afternoon.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Neighborhood sues Rhode Island over $100M claim in overdue Medicaid reimbursements
description: Rhode Island’s largest Medicaid insurer is suing the state, alleging $100 million in unpaid insurance reimbursements, some of which are more than a decade overdue. The 20-page complaint was filed by Neighborhood Health Plan of Rhode Island in Providence County Superior Court on Oct. 30, and first reported by The Providence Journal. The Rhode Island […]
text:
Neighborhood Health Plan of Rhode Island has filed a complaint against the state alleging $100 million in overdue Medicaid reimbursements. (Getty Images)Rhode Island’s largest Medicaid insurer is suing the state, alleging $100 million in unpaid insurance reimbursements, some of which are more than a decade overdue.
The 20-page complaint was filed by Neighborhood Health Plan of Rhode Island in Providence County Superior Court on Oct. 30, and first reported by The Providence Journal. The Rhode Island Executive Office of Health and Human Services and its interim director, Kristen Sousa, are named as defendants.
Neighborhood contends that the state failed to recalculate and reimburse the nonprofit health insurer for higher costs associated with covering more medically needy residents — primarily those in long-term care and nursing home facilities — breaching its obligations under two pairs of contracts which together spanned 2013 to 2025.
“Neighborhood relied on the State’s promises,” the complaint states. “It continued to cover and pay for these members’ care without waiting for the State’s systems to catch up, executed amendments to the Contracts, and continued to work with [the health and human services office] to reconcile and resolve the amounts owed rather than pursue other remedies. The State has not kept its promises.”
Kerri White, a spokesperson for the state’s umbrella health and human services agency, declined to comment.
As a managed care organization, Neighborhood contracts with the state to oversee services for roughly 60% of the 250,000 Rhode Islanders who qualify for the government-subsidized healthcare program for low-income residents, children and people with disabilities. 
The state pays Neighborhood an upfront, fixed rate for every person who qualifies for Medicaid services. Recognizing that some people require more medical attention — correlating to a higher cost — and that medical needs can change over time, the state is responsible for keeping track of the actual cost associated with each Medicaid-eligible member, any increases to that cost based on changes in health, and reimbursing the managed care organization for the difference in expenses from the upfront payment. 
The complaint lays out a 13-year history of underpayment to Neighborhood, starting with a five-year, long-term care contract that began in 2013, and continuing with a second agreement for dual Medicare-Medicaid eligible members that began in 2016 and ended in 2025.
Gail Leach Carvelli, a spokesperson for Neighborhood, declined to comment when asked about the timing of the complaint — 10 months after the second contract ended and more than a decade after the payment problems began. 
The complaint points to the botched rollout of the state’s online public benefits system — originally called UHIP but renamed RIBridges — as the root of the reimbursement problem.
From its 2016 launch, the system was riddled with problems: trouble verifying eligibility, a backlog of applications and payment delays, all of which affected the state’s ability to keep accurate records, and in turn, reimburse Neighborhood for Medicaid members’ care.
Before the system debuted, the state took an average of 90 days to process applications for long-term care. After, it took 12 to 18 months on average, a delay which continued through at least 2019, according to the complaint.
State officials openly acknowledged the initial failures, and continued mistakes, plaguing the online public benefits program, evidenced by multiple reports by the state auditor general and in a 2018 amendment to one of its contracts with Neighborhood. 
“In 2018, in the actuarial certification it wrote into Amendment No. 9 to the Unity Contract, the State acknowledged that it ‘has identified and is working to resolve reconciliation issues between its eligibility and enrollment systems,’” the complaint states. “Eight years later, the State still has not reconciled the payments.”
In addition to the $100 million in reimbursements owed, the insurer also claims additional financial losses from its repeated attempts to correct medical records on the state’s behalf. 
“Year after year, Neighborhood has had to dedicate staff to tracking members, building memberlevel files, trying to identify underpayments, and urging the State to correct its errors,” the complaint states. “Neighborhood has incurred millions in costs trying to address the State’s mistakes, errors, and delays.”
Neighborhood has asked a judge to order the state to repay the amount owed, plus damages, or to appoint a special master or independent auditor to determine the reimbursements, giving both sides an opportunity to review and challenge the calculations.

name: Delaware
title: What the Blue Zones Can Teach Us About Living Well By Harmony Senior Services
description: The Concept we call “Blue Zones” demonstrates that healthy aging isn’t the result of one habit but countless small choices that promote purpose, belonging, movement, and connection. By Harmony Senior Services HOCKESSIN, Del – Imagine a place where 100-year-olds still walk steep hills each day, gather around family tables for hours-long meals, and remain acti[...]
text:
Residents enjoying exercise, fresh air, and each other’s company at Harmony at Hockessin
The Concept we call “Blue Zones” demonstrates that healthy aging isn’t the result of one habit but countless small choices that promote purpose, belonging, movement, and connection.
By Harmony Senior Services
HOCKESSIN, Del – Imagine a place where 100-year-olds still walk steep hills each day, gather around family tables for hours-long meals, and remain active contributors to their communities. These places are known as Blue Zones, regions of the world where people live longer and healthier lives than average. While researchers have spent decades studying these communities, the lessons they offer may be less about secret diets or longevity hacks and more about something much simpler: living with purpose, connection, and belonging.
That lesson came to life for Amber Dahle, Vice President of Memory Care and Life Engagement for Harmony Senior Services during a recent study-abroad experience in Sardinia, Italy, one of the world’s original Blue Zones. The trip provided a firsthand look at how daily habits, relationships, and community culture influence health and aging.
The term “Blue Zone” originated when researchers studying longevity marked regions with unusually high concentrations of centenarians using blue circles on a map. Today, five locations are recognized as Blue Zones: Sardinia, Italy; Okinawa, Japan; Ikaria, Greece; the Nicoya Peninsula of Costa Rica; and Loma Linda, California.
Although separated by geography and culture, these communities share striking similarities. Residents move naturally throughout the day, maintain strong social networks, eat minimally processed foods, stay connected to a sense of purpose, and remain deeply engaged with family and community life.
In Sardinia, one of the first things Dahle noticed was that movement wasn’t treated as exercise. There were no fitness challenges or elaborate workout programs. Instead, physical activity was simply woven into daily living.
The villages are perched on steep hillsides, requiring residents to walk regularly to visit neighbors, shop, attend church, and participate in community life. Even some of the area’s oldest residents continue navigating those hills well into their 90s and beyond.
Researchers have long identified natural movement as one of the foundations of Blue Zone living. In Sardinia, that principle is built directly into the environment.
But longevity isn’t simply about living longer. For Dahle, whose work focuses on dementia care, one of the most compelling observations involved the relationship between lifestyle and cognitive health.
Historically, Blue Zone communities have experienced lower rates of dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. However, Dahle observed differences between traditional villages and more modernized areas where convenience, processed foods, and fast-paced lifestyles have become more common.
As communities move away from traditional habits, some of the protective factors associated with healthy aging appear to diminish. The observation reinforced a growing body of research suggesting that environment, lifestyle, and social connection all play significant roles in maintaining health as people age.
Nowhere was the importance of connection more evident than around the dinner table.
Dining – Sardinia, Italy provided by Amber Dahle, Harmony Senior Services
In Sardinia, meals are far more than opportunities to eat. They are opportunities to gather. Multi-course meals often stretch for hours as families and friends share stories, conversation, and companionship. Fresh breads, cheeses, pasta, and local ingredients are prepared with care, but the true centerpiece is the time spent together.
For many Americans accustomed to hurried lunches and dinners squeezed between obligations, the experience offers a powerful reminder that social connection itself may be one of the healthiest ingredients of all.
That theme surfaced repeatedly during conversations with Sardinian centenarians. When asked about the keys to a long life, they rarely pointed to specific diets, supplements, or exercise routines. Instead, they spoke about family gatherings, friendships, neighbors, traditions, and community.
Again and again, the answer came back to people.
In village squares, churches, and neighborhood gathering places, Dahle witnessed relationships flourishing through everyday interactions. Residents spent hours sharing meals, conversations, music, and stories. Community wasn’t something scheduled into calendars. It was simply part of life.
The experience also offered valuable insights into dementia care.
During a visit to the Don Orione Dementia Day Center in Sardinia, Dahle observed an approach that emphasized identity, purpose, and contribution rather than focusing solely on diagnosis or limitations.
Residents participated in meaningful activities that supported the life of the community, from gardening and cooking to music, art, and creative projects. The goal wasn’t simply keeping residents occupied. It was ensuring each person remained valued and connected.
The lesson was clear: purpose does not retire.
In many cultures, aging is often viewed through the lens of decline. Sardinia offered a different perspective. Older adults continued contributing, participating, and remaining connected for as long as possible. Age itself was not treated as a barrier.
Those observations are helping shape conversations throughout Harmony Senior Services, including within its Delaware communities at Harmony at Kent in Dover, Harmony at Hockessin in Hockessin, and Harmony at Glasgow in Newark. The company is exploring ways to further strengthen resident engagement, meaningful contribution, social connection, and person-centered wellness programming.
Ultimately, Dahle’s biggest takeaway from Sardinia wasn’t tied to longevity statistics or nutrition research.
It was a reminder that a meaningful life is built from everyday moments: sharing meals, maintaining relationships, staying active, contributing to others, and remaining connected to a larger community.
The Blue Zones demonstrate that healthy aging isn’t the result of one habit. It is the cumulative effect of countless small choices that promote purpose, belonging, movement, and connection. And while few of us may live on the hillsides of Sardinia, the lessons from those communities may help all of us add not just years to our lives, but life to our years.
Article provided by Harmony Senior Services

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas legislative panel seeks $100,000 payment to nurse caught in regulatory clash
description: A committee of the Kansas Legislature urges payment of $100,000 to nurse sanctioned by a state board for filing a late license renewal application.
text:
A committee of the Kansas Legislature recommends nurse practitioner Amy Siple receive $100,000 in compensation after the state Board of Nursing aggressively punished her for mistakenly allowing her nursing license to expire in 2024 while she cared for a family member diagnosed with cancer. Her experienced prompted the 2026 Legislature to enact sweeping reforms applicable to the Board of Nursing. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Kansas Legislature video)TOPEKA — A committee of the Kansas Legislature recommended the state Board of Nursing pay $100,000 in damages to a nurse sanctioned by the regulatory agency for “unprofessional conduct” after failing to pay a licensing fee on time.
Geriatrics nurse practitioner Amy Siple, who missed the deadline while caring for her husband during his cancer treatment, was ordered by the Board of Nursing to pay a $300 fine and have her name added to databases identifying wayward health professionals. The Board of Nursing’s decision undermined opportunities to return to work, she said, because information about her disciplinary case had to be disclosed to potential employers.
“I anticipated a late fee, but this board decided that I needed to be disciplined, and part of that discipline included giving me a red Scarlet Letter labeling me with unprofessional conduct. It was the same title you’d have given a nurse who sexually assaulted a client,” Siple said.
After rigorous debate Tuesday, House and Senate members of the Special Claims Against the State Committee voted 4-3 to recommend the 2027 Legislature direct the Board of Nursing to provide $100,000 in compensation to Siple. Her request for financial relief was associated with her loss of income during a 21-month period.
The committee’s decision followed the presentation by Jacob Schmidt, an attorney with Foulston Siefkin representing the Board of Nursing, suggesting the legislators deny Siple’s claim. He said the Board of Nursing’s regulatory decisions may have been unpopular, but he couldn’t “identify what the agency had done wrong with respect to the state of the law as it existed” in 2024 when Siple was sanctioned.
Schmidt said he was concerned the state would establish a precedent and open itself up to liability by granting Siple’s request for compensation. The action could trigger more than 500 comparable claims by nurses disciplined by the Board of Nursing, he said.
In 2026, the Legislature revised the definition of misconduct for nurse licensing. Lawmakers also directed the Board of Nursing to rescind punishments for approximately 525 current or former Kansas nurses subjected to aggressive sanctions for administrative infractions.
Sen. Brenda Dietrich, a Topeka Republican who chairs the claims committee, said she opposed the payment to Siple because it would set an expensive precedent.
“I worry we’ll open the floodgates,” she said.
Wichita Rep. Susan Humphries, a Republican and an attorney serving on the committee, said misconduct by administrators with the Board of Nursing required a meaningful response.
“There’s consequences to bad behavior,” said Humphries, who proposed an unsuccessful motion to pay Siple $104,000.
Sen. Stephen Owens, R-Hesston, said he had intended to recuse himself from voting on the issue because Siple was among his constituents. However, he said, the committee shouldn’t disregard financial consequences of egregious mistakes by government regulators.
“I can’t sit here and be quiet,” Owens said. “I think she has a very valid claim.”
Siple’s nightmare was among numerous reports from Kansans entangled in administrative investigations launched by the Board of Nursing. Some inquiries resulted from an individual simply checking the wrong box on a license application.
During the 2026 legislative session, lawmakers responded to the controversy by placing in statute a package, wrapped into House Bill 2528, compelling the Board of Nursing to rescind penalties imposed on nurses for nonpractice disciplinary violations dating back to 2005. The new law also established a 30-day license renewal grace period and prohibited retaliation against nurses by staff at the Board of Nursing.
Separate from the Legislature’s directive, a Shawnee County District Court judge directed the Board of Nursing to vacate disciplinary actions from Siple’s professional record. That preceded Siple’s request for compensation from the Legislature’s joint claims committee.
Siple, of Wichita, filed Kansas Open Records Act requests with the Board of Nursing for all written communications attached to her name. An initial review revealed 4,579 pages of material. A follow-up search found 417 additional pages. The Board of Nursing assessed, and Siple paid on Tuesday, a fee of $1,028 for copies of those records.
“There are 4,996 pages of internal communications involving me, just a lowly nurse in Kansas, in the past two years,” Siple said. “Tell me this wasn’t personal.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia lawmakers approve 69% capacity rule for coal-fired power plants
description: Lawmakers agreed with a Public Service Commission rule on Tuesday that would keep a requirement for electrical generation capacity on coal-fired plants as a goal, rather than a mandate.
text:
John E. Amos Power Plant, seen in June 2013, is a coal-fired plant owned and operated by Appalachian Power, a subsidiary of American Electric Power in Winfield, West Virginia. (Getty Images)Lawmakers agreed with a Public Service Commission rule on Tuesday that would keep a requirement for electrical generation capacity on coal-fired plants as a goal, rather than a mandate. 
The legislative Rule Making Review Committee, composed of six state senators and six delegates, approved a set of regulations for the state’s power plants, which were tucked away in the 2025 data center bill that contributed to the loss of a few seats in last week’s election. 
The regulations govern how much power plants generate and how electricity is bought off the energy market. State regulators will also be monitoring how plants perform, measuring for electrical output and cost. 
One sticking point — which caused environmentalists and consumer advocates to side with the power companies against King Coal — required power plants be maintained to pump out 69% of total output at all times. 
The Public Service Commission interpreted the law to be aspirational and only required plants be maintained to meet that capacity except when “if doing so will cause an increase in the charges for electric energy.”
In 2025, no plant in the state ran at 69% of their capacity, according to data from Emmett Pepper, policy director of Energy Efficient West Virginia. 
At Tuesday’s meeting, state Sen. Brian Helton, R-Fayette, called the rule “ratepayer protection.” 
“It says if 69% is best for the rate payer, you need to do that. If it’s not, you don’t have to,” Helton said. 
While coal is the most expensive fuel used in the market, it can still be cheaper than buying off the energy grid, according to Larry Ellis, an advisor for the PSC. 
Ellis told the committee that on average, the state’s coal-fired plants cost about $35 per megawatt hour, as opposed to $70 per megawatt hour seen recently on the energy market. 
By encouraging the plants to generate more, Ellis told lawmakers they can either use it to power homes and businesses in the state or make a profit on the energy market. 
“Just to be clear, when we generate at a lesser cost and sell out to the market at a higher cost, that goes to lower people’s utility bills?” Helton asked Ellis. 
“Absolutely,” Ellis said. 
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, said she was concerned that getting plants up to capacity could cost residents, who ultimately foot the bill for the maintenance on the plants. 
That could affect another metric the PSC will be overseeing — making sure the plants are producing electricity at the cheapest price possible.  
“I know our coal fleet is — we put a lot of money into it and it’s operating well, but it’s not very young,” Young said. 
Ellis said issues of age of plants and other factors would be weighed against the cost by the PSC. 
“We could say the plant is in the last year of its life, and we all agree to that,” Ellis said. “And you can bring it up to snuff to meet your capacity requirement for $100 million. We would say no.” 
The rules will be reviewed for passage by the entire Legislature in January.
