name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Ayotte says no ‘set time frame’ for when she’ll nominate new Supreme Court justice
description: Gov. Kelly Ayotte said she doesn’t know when she’ll nominate a new justice to the state Supreme Court. “That is an ongoing process,” she told reporters in her office Tuesday. “And I don’t have any set time frame for that. But when we get the best people to serve, that’s when I will nominate them […]
text:
Gov. Kelly Ayotte speaks with reporters in her office Nov. 11, 2026. The Republican governor said she didn't "have any set time frame" for nominating a new state Supreme Court justice. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Gov. Kelly Ayotte said she doesn’t know when she’ll nominate a new justice to the state Supreme Court.
“That is an ongoing process,” she told reporters in her office Tuesday. “And I don’t have any set time frame for that. But when we get the best people to serve, that’s when I will nominate them and work with the council.”
A seat opened on New Hampshire’s highest court in September after former Chief Justice Gordon MacDonald resigned. Reporting from NHPR and an investigation by the judicial branch revealed that MacDonald orchestrated a highly unusual personnel move that allowed a close ally to collect nearly $50,000 in state funding while other branches were facing budget cuts. As governor, Ayotte will be responsible for nominating his successor and the Executive Council will vet and confirm or reject her nominee.
Before last week’s elections, some Democrats called on Ayotte, a Republican, to wait until new councilors were seated to make her nomination — a move they said would respect the will of the voters. The “blue wave” that brought Democrats dramatic victories in Congress and the State House also turned the Executive Council from a 4-1 Republican majority to a 5-0 Democratic majority.
The Frank Roe Kenison Supreme Court Building in Concord on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Several of the incoming councilors, including Luz Bay, Melanie Levesque and Democratic incumbent Karen Liot Hill told the Bulletin that scrutinizing Ayotte’s judicial picks will be a top priority.
“I think that there’s going to be an appetite for true accountability on the Supreme Court,” Liot Hill said in an interview on election night.
The court has had multiple ethical scandals recently. In addition to MacDonald’s resignation, Anna Barbara Hantz Marconi, another justice, was convicted in late 2025 of criminal solicitation. Prosecutors said she attempted to wield her influence as a justice to convince former Gov. Chris Sununu to intervene in a criminal investigation into her husband, Geno Marconi, who served as the state’s port authority director. 
However, the new councilors will not be sworn in until January, and Ayotte has the ability to nominate someone before then while the council is still in Republican control. But the timeline would be tight. And even then, the governor has clashed with the current council, which has sought to flex its authority.
Ayotte said the development hasn’t changed how she’ll go about nominating the new justice.
“My standard is the same,” Ayotte said. “So, working with our judicial selection committee, working with them to just review when I want the best qualified candidates for the court.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Hubbard appears to have ousted Foxx in NC-05 as provisionals, cured ballots counted
description: In unofficial returns on election night, Hubbard held a razor-slim lead over Foxx of 99 votes.
text:
Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx and Democrat Chuck Hubbard. (Photos via House.gov and Hubbard campaign)It looks like North Carolina’s longest-serving congressional Republican has lost her seat.
Democratic challenger Chuck Hubbard expanded his slim lead over longtime Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx after provisional and cured ballots were counted Tuesday across the 5th Congressional District.
In unofficial returns on election night, Hubbard held a razor-slim lead of 99 votes.  
As provisional ballots trickled in Tuesday, Foxx pulled ahead at times. But in the end, she couldn’t catch Hubbard, who ended the night with a lead of 335. Those results won’t be official until counties complete their canvasses Nov. 13.
Libertarian candidate Robert Tuffman received 7,579 votes, many times the margin between the two frontrunners.
Hubbard’s apparent win gives Democrats an 11th seat in the North Carolina congressional delegation, with three Republicans, a huge switch from the current delegation of 10 Republicans and four Democrats.
Foxx has held the seat since 2005. It was considered a safe Republican district, but couldn’t withstand this year’s blue wave election.
The race is eligible for a recount if Foxx requests one after the counties complete their canvasses. 
US Rep. Virginia Foxx says vote count isn’t over as she trails Dem in NC’s 5th District

After trailing Hubbard in Election Day results, Foxx said the counting process wasn’t over, pointing to overseas and provisional ballots. 
“Free and fair elections are a cornerstone of our healthy republic,” Foxx said in a statement last week. “The voters exercised their American rights and cast their ballots. I am so grateful for all those who took the time to vote in this election.”
There could still be very minor changes to the final tallies. Military and overseas votes that were mailed by Election Day will still be counted if they’re received by 5 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 12. The ballots of voters whose eligibility has been successfully challenged could still be removed at the Nov. 13 county canvass meetings. 
Hubbard is in Washington this week for new member orientation.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New Haven police update policies after former chief’s financial scandal
description: New Haven police are updating policies governing confidential informant funds following a scandal involving former Chief Karl Jacobson.
text:
New Haven police are updating policies governing confidential informant funds following a scandal involving former Chief Karl Jacobson.
According to Mayor Justin Elicker, Jacobson stole more than $175,000 from the CI program, which is used to reward people for passing police information about crimes.
Jacobson used the money he stole to fuel his gambling addiction. He pleaded no contest to larceny last month, and will be sentenced and ordered to pay restitution in January.
According to Elicker, the city acted quickly when the fraud was exposed by the department’s assistant chiefs. Among the responses: the CI program was temporarily paused, more frequent audits were performed once it restarted, more oversight was built into the process, and cameras were installed in the room where CI funds are stored.
Additionally, the city paid more than $80,000 for outside firm Police Executive Research Forum (PERF) to review its policies.
“The goal was to identify where improvements are needed in our confidential informant program and ensure alignment with nationally recognized best practices to include strong policies and oversight, clear roles and responsibilities, and adherence to the highest of ethical standards,” Elicker said.
“While [the report] seems like a lot of money, I think it’s very important for us to make sure that all of our systems are tight, so that we don’t have this kind of issue. I mean, Chief Jacobson stole more than the cost of this report.”
The returned report came with 33 recommendations.
“The 33 recommendations from PERF were across 11 category areas, including audits and inspections, policies and procedures, duty to intervene, digital management systems and electronic payments, training, concurrent investigations, sentinel event reviews, employee wellness, organizational structure, civilianization, and overtime,” Police Chief David Zannelli said.
The full, 57-page report is expected to be posted on the city’s website.
Elicker and Zannelli both stressed their ongoing commitment to transparency for the community.
“When we do identify wrongdoing, even if it’s our own chief of police, we hold people accountable,” Elicker said. “We act quickly, and my hope is that people have more trust because they see that no one is above the law.”
This story was first published Nov. 10, 2026 by WSHU.

name: Delaware
title: Pete du Pont foundation helps 28 Delaware businesses move beyond the EDGE pitch
description: Partnership with the state pairs business assessments with funded professional services and ongoing guidance WILMINGTON — Twenty-eight Delaware businesses participating in the state’s EDGE 2.0 program have received help identifying operational challenges and connecting with professional services through a partnership with the Pete du Pont Freedom Foundation,[...]
text:
Caption: Winners of the Fall 2025 and the Spring 2026 (pictured here) Grant may work with the Pete duPont Foundation in this new collaboration. Photo Courtesy of the Delaware Division of Small Business.  Image created on 11/11 using AI. 
Partnership with the state pairs business assessments with funded professional services and ongoing guidance
WILMINGTON — Twenty-eight Delaware businesses participating in the state’s EDGE 2.0 program have received help identifying operational challenges and connecting with professional services through a partnership with the Pete du Pont Freedom Foundation, the foundation announced Nov. 11.
The work spans the fall 2025 and spring 2026 cohorts and extends support beyond the grant competition, helping entrepreneurs address financial management, marketing, legal and operational needs as they prepare to grow.
“Access to capital is an important part of growing a business, but entrepreneurs also need the right systems, expertise and support to turn that investment into sustainable growth,” said Stephanie Johnnie, the foundation’s executive director, in the announcement.
“Through our partnership with the Delaware Division of Small Business, we are helping entrepreneurs identify their priorities, connect with professional resources and build stronger foundations for the future.”
From assessment to implementation
The foundation’s process starts with a five-week assessment conducted with support from IA Business Advisors. It examines operations, financial practices, leadership, marketing and growth objectives.
Business owners receive individualized reports and action plans that identify priorities and recommended improvements.
Those findings guide access to the foundation’s Resource Wallet, which provides funded professional services aligned with each participating business’s needs. Services may include financial management, marketing, legal guidance, operational improvements and commercialization planning.
Client success managers provide ongoing guidance, help owners navigate challenges and connect them with service providers as the plans move forward.
The foundation said implementation support remains underway, with staff continuing to coordinate services and monitor progress.
Early feedback identifies priorities
The foundation reported that all respondents to its post-assessment survey identified one to three clear business priorities for the next six to 12 months. All also rated their reports positively for accuracy and said they would recommend the process.
Among respondents, 78% identified previously unrecognized barriers or capability gaps, while 89% developed or planned new relationships with service providers or consultants.
The announcement did not specify how many business owners answered the survey. The findings describe participants’ assessments of the process; the announcement did not report changes in revenue, hiring or profitability.
Participating companies span technology, professional services, retail, health care and hospitality, according to the foundation.
An earlier foundation update listed 14 businesses in the spring 2026 group, including Huxley and Hiro, Little Town, 3E’s Equestrian Education Program, HouseCall VR and Mother Nurture Composting Services. Pete du Pont Freedom Foundation
How EDGE works
EDGE stands for Encouraging Development, Growth and Expansion. The Division of Small Business launched the grant program in 2019 and introduced EDGE 2.0 in fall 2025, adding greater funding flexibility and support after businesses pitch their proposals. State of Delaware News
The competition has separate Entrepreneur and STEM tracks. The state’s program page lists funding pools of up to $400,000 for Entrepreneur businesses and $750,000 for STEM businesses, divided among selected recipients.
Generally, eligible businesses must be majority located in Delaware, have operated for less than seven years, employ 15 or fewer full-time employees and have less than $700,000 in assets. Grants require $1 in business matching funds for every $3 from the state.
Applications are currently closed, according to the division’s website. State of Delaware %
To Go Box

Who: Qualifying Delaware businesses; foundation support described in this announcement serves participating fall 2025 and spring 2026 businesses.
Application status: EDGE applications are currently closed. Check the state’s website for future rounds and full eligibility requirements.
EDGE information: business.delaware.gov/edge

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Four takeaways on Randall Weddle investigation after big FBI raid
description: The FBI searched – and removed an extensive amount of material – from a home owned by former London Mayor Randall Weddle Tuesday morning, and here are a few things that can be said about the status of the FBI investigation. A large number of FBI agents descended on a Laurel County home of former […]
text:
London Mayor Randall Weddle exits the courtroom at the Laurel County Judicial Center in London, Kentucky on   April 15, 2026. The FBI searched – and removed an extensive amount of material – from a home owned by former London Mayor Randall Weddle Tuesday morning, and here are a few things that can be said about the status of the FBI investigation.
The FBI raid was a big and unusual operation
A large number of FBI agents descended on a Laurel County home of former London Mayor Randall Weddle before dawn on Tuesday. WKYT in Lexington reported neighbors were taken aback by the number of agents. Throughout the day “dozens of FBI agents went in and out” of the house “while people stood and watched.” 
LEX18 reported that the action lasted more than six hours with agents carrying boxes from the house to a green tent set up by the FBI. Video aired by both Lexington stations and other news outlets showed numerous FBI agents and vehicles including a large black van labeled “Evidence Response Team.”
The FBI released only a short statement to Kentucky Lantern about the matter. “FBI Louisville conducted court-authorized activity today off of Highway 552 in the London, KY area. There is no threat to public safety. Due to the ongoing nature of the investigation, I cannot comment further at this time,” said Katie Anderson, a public affairs specialist for FBI Louisville.
Topic of the investigation remains confidential
The Kentucky Lantern and other news outlets have acknowledged in their reports that they have little, if any, idea about what the FBI is investigating. But the actions of the FBI indicate this has been a major and prolonged investigation. Recall that on July 23 London Mayor Tracie Handley released a statement that federal authorities had contacted the city regarding an ongoing investigation. Handley said the city cooperated with the investigation and closed city hall the next day “to allow authorities to complete their work.” Handley declined to elaborate because “this investigation has been going on for months and remains active.”
The ongoing investigation is separate from pending criminal charges
The raid is a separate matter from Weddle’s March indictment by the Laurel County grand jury on four counts of making excessive campaign contributions to help Gov. Andy Beshear win reelection in 2023.
At the time of those allegedly illegal contributions, state and federal laws limited a person from giving more than $2,000 per election to a candidate for state office and no more than $15,000 per year to a state political party.
The indictment charges that Weddle shattered those limits by giving $18,000 to Beshear’s campaign, and $130,000 to the Kentucky Democratic Party in the names of his family members, friends and employees in a series of credit card transactions made during the final days of 2022.
Each of the four counts is a Class D felony which carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $10,000 fine. Weddle has pleaded not guilty. That case is being prosecuted by Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman and is pending in Laurel Circuit Court.
Weddle has had no immediate comment
Guthrie True, a Frankfort attorney who represents Weddle, did not return phone messages from Kentucky Lantern on Tuesday or Wednesday. Carmine Iaccarino, a Lexington attorney who has represented Weddle in some civil lawsuits, said he knows nothing about the Tuesday raid beyond what he had seen in news reports and referred questions to True.
Weddle was elected mayor of London four years ago. His tenure was a tumultuous one that involved clashes with political critics and a city council that impeached him for allegedly exceeding his executive powers. The council voted to remove him from office last year. Weddle initially fought that action and won at the trial court level, but resigned as mayor in July when the Kentucky Court of Appeals reversed the trial court and reinstated the council’s decision.
That decision prompted Weddle to drop his combative tone. “While this is not the outcome I had hoped for, I respect the rule of law, the judge, and the decision of the court. …It is time to look ahead. My optimism for London’s future has never been stronger.”

title: Commentary: On Veterans Day, let’s remember the little toy soldier that went to war
description: Most of the paint is missing from the little lead soldier. Half of his right arm is gone.  He probably wouldn’t bring a quarter, even at a yard sale. But he’s priceless to Chester W. Hack Jr. of Paducah.  “Daddy carried him all through the war,” said Hack, who worked out of Paducah Ironworkers Local […]
text:
Bill Hack before his death with all his World War II medals. (Photo by Berry Craig for Kentucky Lantern)Most of the paint is missing from the little lead soldier. Half of his right arm is gone.
 He probably wouldn’t bring a quarter, even at a yard sale. But he’s priceless to Chester W. Hack Jr. of Paducah.
 “Daddy carried him all through the war,” said Hack, who worked out of Paducah Ironworkers Local 782, the late Chester W. Hack Sr.’s labor union.
The little toy soldier that went to World War II with Chester “Billy” Hack of Paducah. (Photo by Berry Craig for Kentucky Lantern)
 The little toy soldier that went to World War II with Chester “Billy” Hack of Paducah. 
Better known as “Bill” or “Billy,” Hack’s war was World War II. A left waist gunner on a long range, four-engine B-17 “Flying Fortress” heavy bomber, he fought the Nazis miles above enemy-occupied Europe in some of the global conflict’s most lethal air battles.
 He flew 28 missions between May 19, 1943, and Jan. 2, 1944. He flew two more in 1945, shortly before the war in Europe ended in Germany’s surrender.
 The little soldier was tucked in Army Air Force Staff Sgt. Hack’s pocket on every mission, including the one that nearly killed him.
 On May 29, 1943, Hack was firing at enemy fighters with a .50 caliber machine that poked through an open window on the left side of “Barrel House Bessie from Basin Street’s” fuselage. The bomber force’s target was the concrete-reinforced German submarine pens at St. Nazaire, France.
 Swarms of German fighters and exploding clouds of anti-aircraft fire, known as flak, tore into the American bombers.
 “Bessie” was flying in a three-plane formation. The other two were shot down, their crews killed or captured.
 The fighters’ machine gun and cannon fire ripped gaping holes in “Bessie.” A flak burst knocked out one of her engines, setting the B-17 on fire and sending her into a near vertical dive from 22,000 to about 800 feet when her pilots, straining at the controls, finally managed to level her off.
 All 10 of her crew were wounded, the tail gunner fatally.
 Bessie almost made it home, but with the big bomber losing unrecoverable altitude, the pilots had no choice but to ditch in the English Channel. Bessie hit the choppy sea hard, burst into flames and began sinking.
 Hack had just turned twenty-two. “I was dazed,” he told me. “But when I smelled my hair burning, it gave me the strength to live.”
 A British air-sea rescue boat pulled Hack and his eight buddies from the sea. It was too dangerous for the boat to stay around to retrieve the tail gunner’s body, which “floated away into oblivion,” Hack said.
 The toy soldier flew again with Hack in an even bloodier air battle—the massive Aug, 17, 1943, dual raid on Schweinfurt and Regensburg, Germany.
 Air gunner Hack was aboard “Me an’ My Gal,” another B-17. While that one made it back to England, 60 out of 376 B-17s sent against Schweinfurt and Regensburg fell to fighters and flak—a loss of 600 men killed, captured or listed as missing.
At age 77, Hack vividly remembered the carnage he witnessed. He never saw “so many planes getting shot down, blown up, bodies flying everywhere, parts of aircraft.”
Chester “Billy” Hack of Paducah (Photo provided)
 Fighting back tears, the still tough-as-boot-leather retired Ironworker continued, “The sky looked like a junkyard, motors over here and a wing out over there and a tail section over yonder.” He spoke of watching in helpless horror as “maybe a half a dozen men in chutes going by…some of them on fire.”
 Hack was sent stateside after VE day. When Japan surrendered in August, 1945, he was on a troop train heading to the West Coast where he was to join another bomber crew to fight the Japanese. Instead, he and the toy soldier went home to Paducah.
Hack died in 2016 at age 95. I had the honor of speaking at his funeral and I’m writing a book about him.
 Chester Hack has his father’s medals under glass in a frame. They include his Distinguished Flying Cross, Purple Heart, Air Medal with three oak leaf clusters and his Distinguished Unit Citation ribbon. The toy soldier is safely stowed.
 Hack was a boy when his father gave him the toy soldier. Thousands of other fathers have given miniature armies of toy soldiers to thousands of their sons, who deployed them in make believe battles.
 Hack’s tiny soldier went with him to the deadliest and most destructive war in history.

title: With 25,000 more votes counted, Peltola, JKT and Begich near victory in Alaska election
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Republican U.S. House Rep. Nick Begich III came closer to clinching victory in Alaska’s general election as the Alaska Division of Elections added almost 25,000 ballots to the state tally on Tuesday night. With 245,470 first-choice ballots counted, P[...]
text:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins shakes hands with a supporter at an election night party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the Broken Blender in downtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Republican U.S. House Rep. Nick Begich III came closer to clinching victory in Alaska’s general election as the Alaska Division of Elections added almost 25,000 ballots to the state tally on Tuesday night.
With 245,470 first-choice ballots counted, Peltola now leads incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan by 4,250 first-choice votes, or 48.8% to 47.1%. That’s an increase of more than 1,600 votes from Monday.
If the race goes to a ranked choice runoff between Peltola and Sullivan preliminary, partial data published by the Division of Elections and analyzed by the Beacon shows Peltola winning that matchup as well.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

The Associated Press estimates about 84% of all ballots have been counted. A separate, independent estimate posted on Twitter found at least 37,000 votes remaining to be added to the statewide tally.  
In the governor’s race, Kreiss-Tomkins has 49.7% of the first-choice votes, ahead of three Republican competitors. In the U.S. House race, Begich has 48.8% of the first-choice votes, leading an independent challenger by a significant margin. 
In Alaska general election races, voters rank up to four candidates in order of preference. If a candidate in a particular race has more than 50% of the first-choice votes, they win.
If no candidate reaches that threshold, the candidate with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated, and votes for them are transferred to their voters’ second choices.
The eliminations and redistributions continue until only two candidates are left. The person with the most votes wins.
Friday is the deadline for absentee ballots mailed from within the United States to arrive and be counted. Division officials have said to expect a significant update then. Additional updates are possible Wednesday and Thursday.
Preliminary ranked choice data indicates Senate lead won’t change
The Alaska Division of Elections is scheduled to perform its official ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18, after the deadline for absentee ballots to arrive and still be counted. 
In preliminary, partial ranked choice tabulations by the Alaska Beacon using data published by the division on Tuesday, Sen. Sullivan gains 3,066 redistributed votes and Peltola gains 2,160, a net gain of 906 for Sen. Sullivan but not enough to overcome Peltola’s lead in first-choice votes.
The ranking data does not yet include 9,909 ballots from rural Alaska precincts where ballots are initially hand-counted. 
Two-thirds of the first-choice votes on those ballots went to Peltola, according to summary data published separately by the division, indicating that even after the ranked choice tabulation, Peltola will lead.
In addition, further ballot counting may help Peltola’s margin. The Democratic candidate has repeatedly gained more first-choice votes than Sullivan in ballots counted after Election Day; on Monday, she led Sullivan by 2,517 votes out of 219,342 cast, and that was an improvement over her 636-vote lead at the end of Election Day. 
Governor and US House leaders appear unlikely to change either 
In the governor’s race, Kreiss-Tomkins’ closest competitor is Republican candidate Bernadette Wilson, with 28.7% of the first-choice votes, followed by Republican Dave Bronson with 13.9% and Republican Treg Taylor with 7.3%.
Preliminary, partial ranked choice tabulations by the Beacon show that if Kreiss-Tomkins fails to top the 50% threshold by Nov. 18, he will easily receive the needed votes once the ranked choice runoff is used.
For the U.S. House race, Begich has lost a small bit of first-choice vote share since Election Day, when he was almost exactly at the 50% threshold. That indicates a ranked choice runoff will be needed, but his closest challenger, independent Bill Hill, has 40.9% of first-choice votes. Democratic spoiler candidate Eric Hafner, a man imprisoned in New York state for threatening federal officials, has 7.5% of the first choice votes. Libertarian Jim McDermott has 2.7%.
Preliminary, partial ranked choice tabulations show Begich winning once McDermott and Hafner are eliminated.
Hill — the candidate endorsed by the Alaska Democratic Party — ran a campaign that attempted to label Hafner a sham candidate and not a real Democrat. Ranked choice tabulations show Hill winning less than half of the second-choice votes from Hafner supporters.

title: Kansas Guardsman worries about father’s immigration status, possible deportation
description: TOPEKA — Kansas Army National Guardsman Luis Martinez was called to active duty in August to help with Wyandotte County storm cleanup. His father, William Martinez, offered to drop him off at his unit so he would be well-rested and ready to help with the natural disaster, Luis Martinez said.  “He told me he was […]
text:
Immigrant William Martinez, who has lived in the United States since he was 17 years old, was held for a few weeks in the Midwest Regional Reception Center in Leavenworth, after being detained in August. While he has bonded out, his family is worried that he will be deported even though his application for a visa is in the works. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas Army National Guardsman Luis Martinez was called to active duty in August to help with Wyandotte County storm cleanup.
His father, William Martinez, offered to drop him off at his unit so he would be well-rested and ready to help with the natural disaster, Luis Martinez said. 
“He told me he was proud of me and that he’s proud that I’m serving the nation, I’m serving the state, and I’m making an impact,” Luis Martinez recalled weeks later. 
On the way home, an Anderson County sheriff’s officer stopped Martinez’s father.
William Martinez has been in the United States since he was 17 years old. He is applying for a special visa given to family members of military personnel. (Photo submitted by Luis Martinez)
“One of the lights was out for the display (license) plate, but the other one was still on, and (my wife) said she even checked it out,” Luis Martinez said. “You could still read the license plate.”
Reports from the sheriff’s office obtained by the Kansas Reflector confirmed the reason for the stop. 
The situation escalated when the officer found that William Martinez had failed to renew his driver’s license, Luis Martinez said. The officer then asked for visas and questioned his immigration status. 
“My father responded truthfully that they’re in process,” Luis Martinez said. “The sheriff asked my father to please step out, and for like 30 minutes there, he was just questioning him. My father gave all the information about his lawyers, paperwork, and whatnot. He even mentioned that he just went to drop me off with my unit and mentioned that his son’s in the National Guard, but I guess the sheriff didn’t care.”
The officer didn’t run his mother or wife’s paperwork and let them go, Luis Martinez said. 
William Martinez was held two days at the Anderson County Jail and then transferred to CoreCivic’s Leavenworth prison, the Midwest Regional Reception Center, Luis Martinez said. He was released on bond in mid-October, but faces further hearings and the threat of deportation.
He also wears an ankle monitor with a 150-mile radius, Luis Martinez said. 
The experience in CoreCivic had a long-term impact on William Martinez, his son said. 
When Luis Martinez spoke to his father while he was in detention, he found his mood varied. 
“Honestly, there’s some days where he’s just depressed,” Luis Martinez said. “There’s some days where he’s just frustrated, and some days where he’s just joyful and optimistic. It just goes up and down, up and down.”
When William Martinez was released, he struggled for the first few weeks. He met people in the CoreCivic facility who were in the country legally, who had unexpired visas and shouldn’t have been imprisoned, Luis Martinez said. 
“He came out kind of traumatized. He seen a lot of things in there that really disturbed him,” Luis Martinez said. “He overheard a lady cut her wrists twice, in the nighttime. People were frustrated, angry, screaming in the night. He said he didn’t sleep at night because of all the noise.”
CoreCivic didn’t respond to questions about conditions at the facility.
William Martinez has lived in the United States since he was 17 years old. He raised his family here and worked as a mason, Luis Martinez said. 
He has applied to be here legally and is in the process of getting a military parole in place, which is an immigration benefit for the spouses, children, parents and other relatives of a U.S. military member, Luis Martinez said. 
“My mother and father are doing everything legally. They’re doing everything step by step,” Luis Martinez, who is a U.S. citizen, said. “They went through immigration. They did this. They did that. We have immigration attorneys. We’re literally doing everything by the book.”
The Anderson County Sheriff’s Office signed a 287(g) agreement with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which means the agency will hold people who are suspected of being in the country illegally for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.  
The program offers money to law enforcement agencies that participate, including initial stipends of $100,000 for transportation and $7,500 per credentialed task force officer for equipment, according to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Additional stipends are available on a quarterly basis. 
Anderson County Sheriff Wesley McClain said he made the decision to participate in the 287(g) program and that the county has not received any stipends for participation. 
“I made this decision based on my responsibility to evaluate available law enforcement resources, strengthen investigative capabilities, and establish partnerships that can assist our agency in serving and protecting our community,” he said in an email to Kansas Reflector.
McClain said that cooperation between local, state and federal agencies is an important part of addressing criminal activity across jurisdictional boundaries. 
“This decision was made as a law enforcement operational decision, not a political statement,” McClain said. “My responsibility is to make decisions that I believe best serve the public safety interests of Anderson County that I stand by.”
McClain said the partnership isn’t only about immigration status. 
‘It’s about improving communication between local and federal law enforcement, enhancing public safety, and ensuring that our deputies have the training, oversight, and resources necessary to carry out their duties professionally and constitutionally,” he said. 
The American Civil Liberties Union of Kansas has spoken out against the 287(g) agreements, and launched a program called Opportunity Forward to limit focus on limiting their use in the state. 
“When our local police are weaponized by the federal government against their own townspeople, it erodes the opportunity for everyone to feel safe and have trust in our local government and law enforcement,” the organization said online.

title: CA overhauled a key conservatorship law. Has anything changed?

text:
A picture of Annis Pereyra’s son, Joaquin Anthony “Tony” Pereyra, in the garden of her home in Walnut Creek on Oct. 28, 2026. Photo by Pablo Unzueta for CalMatters




Today we honor all of you who served in the armed forces and give our sincere thanks for answering your country’s call. 🇺🇸
We had a breaking story last night on a lawsuit against Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara that alleges his office illegally approved rate hikes. Check it out here.
Today we’re publishing a special report on changes to a California mental health law that determines when someone can be forced into involuntary treatment.  It’s among several laws Gov. Gavin Newsom signed to overhaul the state’s mental health system.
But that’s not all. We also have a breakdown on veterans and military kids in the California State University system, and a look at how school bonds fared on the ballot last week. 
Thanks for reading and enjoy the holiday. 
It can be incredibly difficult in California to secure treatment for people who have severe mental illnesses. New legislation, signed three years ago, was supposed to help. 
The idea of Senate Bill 43 was to make more people eligible for involuntary, one-year mental health conservatorships. But a CalMatters analysis found that so far, it doesn’t seem to be getting many more people into long-term treatment. 

Toni Navarro, director of behavioral health for Santa Barbara County: “It was not at all as big an impact as we thought it could be.”

CalMatters requested data from the state’s 25 most populous counties. Of those that provided information, the majority showed no significant increase in the number of conservatorships after the new law took effect.
Behavioral health officials in multiple counties said the law still has done some good. For one thing, it forced mental health and substance abuse professionals to work closer together, which is key when helping the many Californians who have both a mental illness and an addiction. 
But some families of people with severe mental illnesses hoped the legislation would do more. Joaquin Anthony “Tony” Pereyra was shot by Walnut Creek police during a mental health crisis in February. His mother, Annis Pereyra, believes the new law could have saved his life, if the county had used it to compel him to take an antipsychotic medication.

Pereyra: “His needs were ignored at every turn that happened. Every single turn.”

Read more from CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall and Jocelyn Wiener.



Focus on Inland Empire: Each Wednesday, CalMatters Inland Empire reporter Aidan McGloin surveys the big stories from that part of California. Read his newsletter and sign up to receive the next one.

More veterans enrolled at Cal State


A group of Marine Corps second lieutenants during the Naval Reserve Officer Training Corps San Diego commissioning ceremony at the USS Midway Museum in San Diego on May 29, 2025. Photo by Claire M. Alfaro, U.S. Navy




From CalMatters higher education reporter Mikhail Zinshteyn:
Nearly 22,000 veterans or their children attend the California State University — a growth of 17% since 2022. That uptick far exceeds the system’s overall student growth of around 3%.Most of those students are the dependents of veterans, and Cal State — the nation’s largest public four-year university system — provides a veterans’ center on each of its 22 campuses. Children of veterans can use their educational benefits if their parents transferred the perks to them, have a service-related disability or died in service. 
Helping to fuel that growth is taxpayer aid. “Since fall 2022, the number of students using federal veterans’ education benefits has increased 36 percent and the number using the California Department of Veterans Affairs College Fee Waiver has increased 18 percent,” according to an agenda item for next week’s Cal State Board of Trustees meeting that aims to highlight the myriad academic and social benefits to veterans and their families. Those include dedicated counselors and outreach on military bases. 
There are eight federal veterans’ education aid programs and one state-run program. While most make use of these, not all do, for reasons related to their discharge status or whether they’ve exhausted their benefits in other education settings. Many students also receive general state financial aid. 
Statewide, some 84,000 veterans are enrolled in a college or university, according to the Department of Veterans Affairs.



Voters soured on school repairs


Construction sites in the hallways of Keyes Elementary School in Keyes on Nov. 15, 2023. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local




Nearly half of the 86 bond proposals California school districts placed on the November ballot to repair facilities are on track to fail, writes Calmatters’ Carolyn Jones.
The bonds totaled more than $12.4 billion of debt that taxpayers would have to pay down over time. Compared to other big election years this is a relatively low amount: Two years ago, school bonds totaled almost four times as much and most of them passed.
Their failure could be a sign that voters are wary of the economy, although three big statewide bond proposals for housing and medical research passed. 
Visalia Unified, near Fresno, has a $158 million bond that voters are poised to reject. More than 70% of the district’s buildings are 50 years old or older and need repair, said Superintendent Kirk Shrum. Without the bond money, the district will have to shift money around to pay for repairs, but “we’ll never be able to get ahead of it,” Shrum said.

name: Delaware
title: Cape Henlopen and Milford Field Hockey advance to 2026 DIAA Division One Field Hockey State Championship Game
description: The Milford Buccaneers defeated the Caesar Rodney Riders and the Cape Henlopen Vikings defeated the Smyrna Eagles to play for the 2026 DIAA Division One Field Hockey State Championship on November 13.   FREDERICA, Del. — The Milford Buccaneers and Cape Henlopen Vikings will battle it out for the 2026 Division One Field Hockey State Championship on Friday, No[...]
text:
Milford Field Hockey celebrates after advancing to the 2026 Division One Field Hockey State Championship game. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The Milford Buccaneers defeated the Caesar Rodney Riders and the Cape Henlopen Vikings defeated the Smyrna Eagles to play for the 2026 DIAA Division One Field Hockey State Championship on November 13.
 
FREDERICA, Del. — The Milford Buccaneers and Cape Henlopen Vikings will battle it out for the 2026 Division One Field Hockey State Championship on Friday, November 13, following their semifinal wins on Tuesday, November 10.
Milford defeats Caesar Rodney, 4-0
The Buccaneers set up for a penalty corner opportunity leading the Riders, 1-0, halfway through the second quarter. Caesar Rodney defended the corner well and regained possession ready to advance the ball past midfield into its offensive zone. The Riders didn’t make it near the midfield line.
Buccaneer senior Molly Masten tipped the Riders’ initial pass which allowed sophomore Bria Leyanna to jump in front of the receiving player and take possession back. Leyanna dribbled the ball just outside the top of the circle and wound up for what appeared to be a shot attempt, but was a pass instead. Leyanna’s rocketed pass hit the stick of Masten who was sitting right in front of the cage. Masten handled the pass perfectly and without hesitation spun her stick around and fired a shot past the Rider goalkeeper to the back right of the cage.
Masten’s first goal of the game gave Milford a 2-0 lead with less than seven minutes remaining in the half and helped provide momentum for the Buccaneers’, 4-0, win Tuesday evening.
“I just liked our fast pace, our connected passes. We were working together really well and it was just really great to see,” Masten said after the game.
Milford recorded an assist on each of its four goals, starting with an assist from Masten on the Buccaneers’ first goal. 
Masten’s pass came from the top of the circle and found the stick of senior attacker Katelyn Joseph waiting at the left corner of the goal. Joseph shot the ball through the legs of the Rider keeper giving Milford its first lead less than two minutes into the second quarter. Masten’s first goal followed and the Buccaneers led by two at halftime.
Masten’s impact carried into the second half adding to her day with a second assist on sophomore Aiyana Atkins’ first goal of the postseason and a second goal that completed Milford’s scoring with less than six minutes remaining in the game. Masten played a part in each goal scored.
“Molly brought it today,” Milford head coach Andrea McPike said postgame. “She really set the tempo for us offensively and, you know, she contributed on both sides of the field today so we were happy, you know, that our lead dog was leading.”
This is the first time Milford field hockey is appearing in the state championship game since 1996. The Buccaneers won the 1996 state championship, 2-1, over Tower Hill.
“It feels amazing,” Masten said. “I mean that was our goal from the beginning, is just take things step-by-step and get to where we are now, so this feeling is honestly unreal.”
Cape Henlopen defeats Smyrna, 4-0
Junior Kailey McMahon set up in her position outside the shooting circle ready to run toward the cage when senior Grace Heers passed the ball into play from her position along the goal line. The Vikings and Eagles were scoreless near the end of the first quarter, but the Vikings generated momentum with six straight penalty corner attempts. Cape Henlopen’s seventh penalty corner resulted in more than momentum. It provided a lead.
McMahon settled near the front right of the cage as the action unfolded in front of her. 
Heers’ entry pass found the stick of senior Atia Sabbagh and Sabbagh fired a shot toward the goal that was halted by Smyrna senior Nora O’Connell. The ricochet found the stick of senior Mairead Rishko and Rishko shot quickly, but O’Connell blocked the shot with her leg pads, sending the ball to McMahon. McMahon fielded the rebound, settled for a second while spinning away from nearby defenders and fired a low shot past the outstretched left leg of O’Connell and into the back left of the cage.
McMahon’s goal was the lone score of the first half and gave the Vikings a lead going into halftime. Cape Henlopen added to the lead with three goals in the second half beating Smyrna, 4-0, to advance to its tenth championship game in as many seasons.
“I think we deserve it completely. We worked really hard this season with our coach and everybody else here putting their all out on the field,” McMahon said about reaching the championship game.
McMahon scored Cape Henlopen’s second goal — and first of the second half — on a play similar to her first. McMahon’s score came on a penalty corner that bounced around a bit before it found her stick at the front left of the cage and she converted on the chance, placing this goal just over the arm of O’Connell. 
Goals from senior Emily Wells and junior Blair Chubb in the fourth quarter completed the Vikings’ offensive output. The Vikings finished the game with 19 penalty corner opportunities with all but one of their goals coming via those chances — Wells’ goal came on a penalty stroke.
“Our goal is to execute every single corner,” McMahon said.
Cape Henlopen and Smyrna are no strangers to each other. The Vikings and Eagles have met in the championship game the past five seasons and they play each other during the regular season consistently. Smyrna defeated Cape Henlopen last season, earning the program’s second state title since 2021. The Vikings won the other three in that time. 
“The environment can be crazy, I mean a semifinal game is always going to be a chaotic environment, but the rivalry between these two teams can be a bit heated so we just talked about the importance of digging in and being prepared for sixty minutes or more of hockey because that’s what we’ve seen the last few times that we’ve faced them,” Cape Henlopen head coach Kate Austin said postgame.
Cape Henlopen’s championship opponent is also a familiar foe having played them earlier this season. 
The Vikings and Buccaneers will play each other for the second time on Friday at 4:00 p.m. for the state championship. The Vikings beat Milford, 3-0, back in October and will be a presumable favorite in the rematch on November 13. The sixth seeded Buccaneers will act as the underdog as they’ve done all tournament and hope to end a 30-year championship drought with a win against the Vikings.
“That’s what I want, I like that,” McPike said after being asked about being an underdog against either Cape Henlopen or Smyrna (Milford’s game concluded before the events of the Smyrna and Cape Henlopen game). “No pressure for us, you know. This is a spot we have not been in since 1996. We’re going to enjoy every step of the way. We’re not even really looking to Friday, we’re looking to tomorrow. That’s the mentality that we’ve had the past two weeks is taking it step-by-step.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: On Veterans Day, Mississippi Today recognizes central Mississippians making their mark as lieutenant colonels
description: For Veterans Day, Mississippi Today Ideas  talks with three central Mississippians who have risen to the rank of lieutenant colonel and command medical squadrons in Europe.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippians have excelled nationally, even internationally, in multiple fields ranging from business and entrepreneurship, to arts, entertainment and athletics.
And multiple Mississippians have certainly been impactful in the United States military.
On this Veterans Day, Mississippi Today Ideas is proud to recognize three active members of the military from Mississippi who have excelled. They are all worthy of individual accolades, but Mississippi Today Ideas opted to interview them together because they have much more in common than just being from the Magnolia State.
Lt. Col. Scott McKeithen. Credit: Courtesy photo
First and foremost, all three have risen to the important rank of lieutenant colonel where they serve as squadron commanders in Europe – two in Germany and one in Italy. All three lead medical-related squadrons.
The similarities do not stop there. The lieutenant colonel squadron leaders are not only Mississippians, but are residents of central Mississippi or the metro Jackson area. Two are graduates of Pearl High School and the third is a graduate of Jackson’s Forest Hill High School.
Scott R. McKeithen and Jack P. Craven are graduates of Pearl High, and Jasmine D. Cook is a graduate of Forest Hill.
The three recently participated in an online interview with Mississippi Today Ideas – Craven from Italy, where he is based, and Cook and McKeithen from Germany, where they are located.
They talked about their Mississippi roots, the pride they have in their state and in their service to the United States Air Force.
“ That foundation of what got us here today was driven by how we were raised, who we were raised by in Mississippi,” McKeithen said.
McKeithen and Craven said they did not know each other in high school, but knew of each other. Craven, a 2005 graduate, is a little younger than McKeithen.
McKeithen said he knew Craven’s father, who was a principal at Pearl High School, because he got in trouble a lot.
Lt. Col. Jack Craven. Credit: Courtesy photo
Craven smiled as McKeithen provided that detail.
McKeithen commands the 852d Medical Squadron at Geilenkirchen NATO Air Base in Germany. According to his Air Force bio, among his duties are directing medical and dental services for more than 1,500 U.S. personnel and family members and providing healthcare services for other military-related events.
“I lived in the trailer park in front of the skating rink in Pearl that everybody knows about,” McKeithen said. ”So to be where I’m at in life, it’s because of the government, it’s because of the hard work and the dedication that’s there.”
Craven played sports at Pearl and played soccer and baseball at Hinds Community College. His grandfather, an Air Force pilot and lieutenant colonel, pointed him toward ROTC, which eventually led to his military career.
“One of the reasons I was excited to join was to see the world,” he said, adding he “Got to go through a lot of places and see a lot of things.”
Lt. Col. Jasmine Cook. Credit: Courtesy photo
Craven commands the 31st Medical Support Squadron and also oversees the 31st Medical Group, Aviano Air Base, Italy. According to his Air Force bio, he heads the 109-member team responsible for healthcare administration and ancillary clinical support activities supporting 8,400 people.
Cook says his military career started early.
“I joined in 1998 when I was still in high school at Forest Hill,” he recalled. “Imagine a senior in high school trying to tell his friends that they’re in the military. … I was telling my friends I was in the Mississippi Air National Guard, and they were like, ‘man, you’re crazy,’ but I was. So I enlisted in ’98, my parents signed for that, and I went to basic training that summer. And, I went to Alcorn State University. I had a scholarship.”
He commands the 52nd Healthcare Operations Squadron, 52nd Medical Group, 52nd Fighter Wing, Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany. According to his bio, he leads 128 members delivering $18 million in medical care and support services for 8,3000 beneficiaries. His squad provides “full-spectrum readiness and 24/7 medical response.”
While the trio said they could not get into specifics, part of what their squadrons do is respond to military events where there might be injuries.
Craven said of all three squadrons, “Getting patients from the X or the point of injury to higher echelons of care as quick as possible is kind of our bread and butter and what we try to do.”
By the way, the three were interviewed shortly after the much discussed LSU-Ole Miss football game earlier this season. The interview proves the game drew attention even in Europe.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: The story of Maj. James Capers, SC’s most recent Medal of Honor recipient
description: Maj. James Capers became the 34th South Carolina-born military member to receive the Congressional Medal of Honor.
text:
Maj. James Capers, born in Bishopville, became the 34th South Carolina-born Medal of Honor recipient in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of Maj. James Capers)U.S. Marine Corps Maj. James Capers led his nine-man reconnaissance team to safety following an ambush during the Vietnam War, even stepping off the overweight helicopter several times as it struggled to evacuate as his squad pulled him back on board.
Those actions led to Capers, in June of this year, becoming the 34th South Carolina-born military member to receive the Congressional Medal of Honor. It came more than 59 years after he was severely injured in the firefight and took nearly two decades of supporters fighting on his behalf for the recognition.
Capers, born in Bishopville, was the first Black man to command a Marine recon company and the first enlisted Black Marine officer to earn a battlefield commission. And in the fall of 1967, still recovering from his combat injuries, he was the first Black Marine to appear on a national recruiting poster, only six years after the corps became fully integrated.
Recruitment poster featuring Maj. James Capers, born in Bishopville. (Photo courtesy of Maj. James Capers)
He’s heavily decorated: a Silver Star, two Bronze Stars with combat “V” device (for valor), three Purple Hearts, Vietnam Cross of Gallantry and numerous other ribbons and medals. He’s written a memoir, held speaking tours and was the subject of a documentary.
A medal ‘long-overdue’
But it wasn’t until June 18, when President Donald Trump fastened the Medal of Honor around Capers’ neck, that the 88-year-old officially received the country’s highest military honor that hundreds felt he deserved.
That’s not to say there weren’t naysayers who thought he and his supporters should just give up after several denials. But that wasn’t in Capers’ DNA, and the Marine veterans who championed him weren’t giving up either, said retired Sgt. Maj. Bryan Battaglia, second senior enlisted adviser to the chairman of the joint chiefs.
Bishopville celebrated with a parade in Capers’ honor and a museum exhibit telling his story. The town in the Pee Dee region is raising money for a bronze monument to Capers and Army Cpl. James Davidson Heriot, another Medal of Honor recipient from Bishopville killed in World War I.
U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., who sponsored the legislation urging Capers’ award, in June called the moment “long-overdue for an American hero.”
“When I first learned Major Capers’ story, I was struck by the magnitude of his sacrifice and the extraordinary valor he displayed in service to our country. It became clear to me that his actions deserved the highest recognition our nation can bestow,” the 5th District congressman said in a statement. “Major Capers’ courage, devotion to his fellow Marines, and unwavering commitment to duty serve as an enduring example for future generations.”
On Veterans Day, there is “no better example of the warrior ethos” than Capers, retired Marine Sgt. Maj. Scott Frye, another Capers supporter, told the SC Daily Gazette.
Capers’ heroism
Capers, who lives in Jacksonville, N.C., near Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune where he served, has stepped back from giving interviews and public appearances. But his memoir still tells his story.
Maj. James Capers as a recon Marine in Vietnam. (Photo courtesy of Maj. James Capers)
His squad in Vietnam, Team Broadminded, was weeks away from returning home when it was sent on a mission to scout potential attack routes into a North Vietnamese base camp. April 3, 1967, marked the fourth and final day of their patrol.
Under an ill-advised order, they were sent to backtrack through trails they had already cleared and covered. North Vietnamese forces were lying in wait.
As the team headed down the fourth and final path of the day, a claymore mine went off, killing the lead scout instantly.
“The next thing I knew, I was on the ground, my back up against a tree trunk,” wrote in his memoir.
Shrapnel ripped through his stomach. The blast flung another of Capers’ men on top of him, the man’s back, torso and legs also torn. A third limped over with his foot nearly blown off and the others were equally injured. But the team returned fire immediately.
Capers said they were in “survival mode,” heavily outnumbered 3-to-1 and trying to prevent being overrun and captured.
Running out of ammo, Capers called in air support almost right on top of the team.
He ordered the men to carry out the fallen Marine as he hobbled along under fire, using his rifle as a crutch and leading them to the extraction site.
The helicopter, designed to carry seven or eight people, failed multiple times to take off with nine of them. Capers, then 29 years old, tried to step off and remain behind, despite having a wife and young son at home.
His team wouldn’t let him. They’d become close and respected his leadership on dangerous missions that had included a prisoner of war rescue ordered by President Lyndon Johnson, beach landings under fire in the enemy-heavy Demilitarized Zone and recovery of a B-57 bomber rumored to have a nuclear bomb.
“His story is one of a kind,” retired Lt. Col. Brooks Tucker, who lives in Beaufort, told the SC Daily Gazette. “It’s an American story, because only in America can a guy like this come from very little in life and then become really larger than life with his reputation, his charisma, his promotions, and just his strength as a person.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Capers’ younger years
Capers was not yet 4 years old when his family left South Carolina under the cover of darkness for Baltimore, fleeing persecution in the Jim Crow South.
The son of sharecroppers, Capers wrote in his memoir: “Blacks were no longer sold on the auction block, but they had no choice but to break their backs laboring in the cotton fields for the white farmers while they dreamed of a better future for themselves and their children.”
After Capers’ father got into an altercation with a family his mother washed laundry for, the sheriff in Lee County put out a warrant for his arrest.
“To this day, I am not sure if the crime was serious enough for him to be hung, but my father believed it was serious enough for him to leave South Carolina in order to survive,” Capers wrote.
But Capers fell seriously ill around that time, so his mom stayed behind with him and two older siblings. A white family in Bishopville took him in while his mother worked, scraping together enough money so they could join his father in Maryland. It’s unclear from his memoir how long they were separated.
While it wasn’t South Carolina, Baltimore was still largely segregated.
“All the people in the neighborhood had one thing in common. They had come from the South, looking for the ‘Promised Land,'” Capers wrote. “They were running from poverty, disease and discrimination.”
SC military-connected arts group helps veterans handle trauma through storytelling

He grew up and attended Carver High School, a Black vocational trade school, where the Marines recruited him and his best friend.
Capers’ career
Following graduation in 1956, Capers found himself on a train headed back to South Carolina to attend basic training in the swamps of Parris Island.
He made it through the brutal training and “for the first time in my life I felt like I really understood what brotherhood was all about.”
After training, Capers went on tours in the Mediterranean and saw fighting in Lebanon. And by 1963, he’d risen through the ranks and was under consideration as a drill instructor.
But his young son, Gary, was partially blind, and Parris Island didn’t have the special school he needed.
“Even if there had been, Gary would probably not have been welcome in it, as a Black child,” Capers wrote.
Maj. James Capers in Marine alpha uniform (Photo courtesy of Maj. James Capers)
So instead, Capers took a posting at Fort Meade in Maryland.
Then, about a year later, he heard the Marines were looking for experienced officers to lead troops in Vietnam. After talking it over with his wife, Dottie, he chose to give up his Maryland position, far from the horrors of war, and volunteered to deploy.
Following months of training, he boarded an aircraft carrier, the USS Boxer, in early 1966 to cross the Atlantic Ocean with the young Marines he had led. They landed in Nha Trang Harbor in mid-May, joining some 250,000 military members deployed in the war.
Even after his injuries in Vietnam, Capers continued his service, including in Cold War covert operations in Eastern Europe and Africa.
But it wasn’t until decades after his service that the military fully recognized Capers, despite the intentions of Capers’ commanding general in Vietnam to nominate him for the Medal of Honor, Battaglia said. The major general had died in a helicopter crash before fulfilling that pledge, and Capers instead received a Bronze Star.
In 2006, retired Maj. Gen. James Williams, the assistant division commander at Camp Lejeune, began the effort to have Capers’ medal upgraded. He had served under Capers in the 1970s, and in 2010, saw Capers awarded the Silver Star. He then continued the push through regulatory hurdles standing between Capers and the highest honor.
Capers’ wife and son, both of whom died in 2003 and are buried in Arlington National Cemetery, also advocated for him.
The work of the family, politicians and a small group of veterans who call themselves Team Capers paid off this year. It also inspired the group to look into other deserving soldiers who were passed over.
“There are others,” Frye said. “And there are a number of them, sadly, that laid it all on the line, that jumped on grenades, that did a number of things that heretofore we might have thought was the gold standard for receiving the Medal of Honor, but they haven’t. We’ve been digging into those to make sure we exhaust all efforts to make those things right, too.”
