title: Post-election changes start with ourselves
description:
The midterm elections signaled a desire for a new direction for government, both nationally and here in Wyoming, writes columnist Khale Lenhart.
The post Post-election changes start with ourselves appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Election Day ushered in many changes, both nationally and here in Wyoming. Nationally, we saw a Democratic landslide at a level that few expected. Democrats will take control of the U.S. Senate by winning in traditionally Republican strongholds. Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Ohio put Democrats in the Senate. As I write this, Democrats lead in Alaska and Mississippi. In the House of Representatives, Democrats have flipped control of the chamber and will see gains similar to the Republican Revolution in 1994, the post-Watergate election in 1974 and the Tea Party Wave in 2010. All elections are important, but this one was so dominant that it portends at reckoning in American politics. After each of the wave elections listed above, the losing party had to turn inward and examine itself to discern why the electorate rejected it so harshly. It is time for my Republican Party to carefully consider just those questions.

Opinion

Wyoming underwent its own reckoning in August with the primary election. Many incumbents were turned out in favor of new faces and new approaches. If you looked solely at the general election, it may appear at first glance that nothing has changed. Wyoming still has all Republicans in statewide offices, all Republicans in Congress and the Democratic Party only picked up a single house seat in the state Legislature. However, focusing on party identity obscures the real change that happened. That change occurred in the hearts and minds of the voters. There is no way to interpret the election results, both here in Wyoming and nationally, as anything other than a desire for a new direction in government.
That raises the question of what voters should expect from our new elected officials. Where should we focus to see the change we so clearly desire? Here in Wyoming, we should first look to see if our elected officials recognize the desire for a change in approach. Wyoming is a conservative state, and more fundamentally, we are pragmatic and respectful. Our elected officials should reflect this character. We should expect them to address real problems, receive input, and show each other and those they encounter in their duties the respect that they deserve. Our politics works better when everyone involved recognizes that they need help from those around them. Humility is the key to thoughtful governance.
We also should remember that results take time. Whether it be changes to the national economy or to our state regulations, if things are going to be done well, they are not going to be done overnight. Too often, we expect instant gratification, and this extends to politics, too. Good policy requires time for reflection, input and amendment. Complex problems seldom have simple solutions, which means that if we are to start meddling in our regulatory scheme or our government structure, we should be aware of those changes’ ripple effects. Changing something in one place may have impacts in entirely different areas, and we should expect our elected officials to do their best to anticipate and weigh those effects before taking action.  
Perhaps most importantly, we must all recognize that no single person or election is going to save us. We hope that our elected officials will act wisely and will put good policy in place, but it is up to us to build the lives we want to live. Government plays a role in making that easier or harder, but the true questions of a meaningful life are not answered in the Legislature of our county government buildings. They are answered in our homes and in our own selves.
As we expect new approaches and changes in our political leadership, let us also seek to take up the same burden ourselves. We should seek to be part of the solution, not just aware of the problem. Seek out ways to serve, whether that be in formal roles or in your everyday life. Volunteer to help your neighbor and learn about the complexities of the issues you care about.
We need to hold our leaders accountable, but we should also recognize that they are human and learning in a difficult, fast-paced and stressful environment. They will make mistakes, but most important is whether they exhibit the traits important for true leadership: humility, desire for service and a willingness to learn. Their work is important, and some of it is urgent, but it is a process and we need to have the patience to recognize that the process takes time.
Above all, we must be part of the solution ourselves. Just as we have high expectations of our public officials, we must hold ourselves to the same standards. Our future is bright, as long as we choose it.

description: Tennessee officials must continue to issue driver’s licenses to immigrants who possess valid federal work permits while a legal challenge to new state policy rejecting the documents as valid continues, a court order issued Tuesday said. The decision extends a temporary restraining order that has blocked the abrupt change in state policy since last week, […]
text:
A Nashville court extended a temporary injunction preventing Tennessee from denying driver's licenses to immigrants authorized to work and live in the country. Pictured: a Tennessee Highway Patrol officer and two Homeland Security Investigations officers search a vehicle during a traffic stop on Lamar Ave. in Memphis, Tennessee on Oct. 7, 2025.(Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee officials must continue to issue driver’s licenses to immigrants who possess valid federal work permits while a legal challenge to new state policy rejecting the documents as valid continues, a court order issued Tuesday said.
The decision extends a temporary restraining order that has blocked the abrupt change in state policy since last week, while a legal challenge brought by the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition and six immigrants continues in court. 
Tennessee blocks driver’s licenses for Dreamers, other immigrants with U.S. work permits

Employment cards issued by the federal government have long been accepted as acceptable proof of immigration status in order to obtain a temporary Tennessee driver’s license. (Immigrants without permanent status are only eligible for a temporary license.)  The cards establish that an immigrant is authorized to live and work in the United States. 
For many immigrants including so-called Dreamers, who are protected from deportation because they were brought to the country as children, the employment cards have served as the only proof of a valid immigration status accepted by Tennessee driver’s license officials for more than a decade. 
Hundreds of Tennessee residents have been denied temporary licenses and license renewals since the department first began implementing the new rules, according to immigrant advocates. Thousands more in Tennessee are at risk of losing the ability to legally drive to jobs, school, doctors and grocery stores if the new policy continues. 
“Regardless of where they were born, Tennesseans rely on the ability to drive in order to work, care for their families, and access the basic needs of life – groceries, medical appointments, their children’s education,” a statement by Spring Miller, senior legal strategy director at the Tennessee Coalition for Immigrant & Refugee Rights, said. 
A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security, which administers driver’s licenses, cited Tennessee law that requires applicants for the temporary licenses to provide documentation that establishes a specific period of lawful status in the United States. The employment authorization card, the spokesperson said, does not.
A hearing date in the case has been set on Dec. 7 in Davidson County Chancery Court.

title: Colorado doesn’t lack two strong parties. They’re just both squeezed into the same one.
description: The polls had hardly closed on election night before Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, fresh off his victory speech, told reporters his landslide win should be a “clarion call to the Colorado Republican Party.” “I want a serious Republican Party,” said Weiser, a two-term Democratic attorney general who trounced GOP nominee Victor Marx in the governor’s race, […]
text:
Incoming Colorado House Majority Leader Javier Mabrey, left, a Democrat from Denver, and incoming Senate Majority Leader Dylan Roberts, a Frisco Democrat, represent two different ends of their party's ideological spectrum. (Photos by Chase Woodruff and Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)The polls had hardly closed on election night before Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, fresh off his victory speech, told reporters his landslide win should be a “clarion call to the Colorado Republican Party.”
 
Connecting the news in Colorado to the big picture.

“I want a serious Republican Party,” said Weiser, a two-term Democratic attorney general who trounced GOP nominee Victor Marx in the governor’s race, winning 61% of the vote to Marx’s 33%. “I didn’t get that this election.”
It was a theme Weiser returned to repeatedly throughout the 2026 campaign: “Competition makes us stronger,” he said in July. “It’s not healthy for any state to have one party that’s dominant because another party is dysfunctional. … It makes my job harder, because I’ve got to look harder for that counterargument.”
Many pundits echoed the governor-elect’s view as Marx and his fellow Republicans down-ballot slid further into statewide political insignificance this year. Colorado “​​needs meaningful political competition,” wrote John L. Barry in The Colorado Sun; it “needs a sane, viable opposition party,” opined Colorado Politics’ Eric Sondermann; it “would be better off with two functional, competent political parties,” said 9News’ Kyle Clark.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Whether the Colorado GOP can regain the seriousness that Weiser and others are hoping for is a question only Colorado Republicans can answer. But in the meantime, Coloradans who value a robust dialogue between two opposing ideological points of view on how best to manage public policy are in luck: That’s exactly what’s been happening within Colorado’s ever-more-dominant Democratic Party, which will return to the statehouse in January with unprecedented dual legislative supermajorities — and deep internal divisions about exactly what to do with them.
Politics, after all, is the clash of interest groups, not teams of red and blue. And most of the major interest groups that shape public policy in Colorado have continued to clash energetically in the last eight years of one-party rule.
Industry groups and environmentalists have continued to fight the state’s long-running oil and gas wars. Landlords, renters, homeowners and local governments have battled over housing affordability and property tax rates. Law enforcement groups and criminal justice reform advocates feuded over how to respond to a post-pandemic spike in crime rates and drug overdose deaths. Labor and capital have squared off over wage laws, workplace protections and collective bargaining rights.
Once, these policy disputes may have mapped neatly onto Colorado’s two-party system. Today, they’re being contested by two factions of the party in power: a progressive movement seeking to push state policymaking to the left, and a moderate bloc that’s been solicitous of growing concerns about tax and regulatory burdens from Colorado’s conservative business lobby.
A database of thousands of roll-call votes maintained by LegiScan, a nonpartisan data service that tracks state legislatures across the country, confirms the basic shape of this intra-Democratic divide. Well-defined groups of centrists in both chambers, many of them members of the Colorado Opportunity Caucus, were more likely over the last two legislative sessions to break from their fellow Democrats and vote with Republicans — often to block more progressive bills, or advance more conservative ones, in key committee votes.


Last week’s legislative leadership elections put a spotlight on the party’s factional fault lines, with Democrats in the state Senate electing their caucus’ two most moderate members, Sens. Dylan Roberts of Frisco and Kyle Mullica of Thornton, to key leadership positions.
Roberts and Mullica are members of the Opportunity Caucus, a group that describes itself as “not focused on moving to the left or to the center, but on moving Colorado forward.” Since 2024, the emergence of the caucus and an associated campaign group, One Main Street Colorado, has led to a bitter transparency fight and formal ethics complaints at the Capitol — as well as a series of hotly contested Democratic primaries between moderates and overlapping slates of progressive candidates backed by the Colorado Working Families Party, the Democratic Socialists of America and other groups on the left.
Meanwhile, with lawmakers in the House electing to leadership two members of this more progressive bloc, incoming House Speaker Jennifer Bacon and Majority Leader Javier Mabrey, the party’s left flank is poised to exert a stronger influence on the lower chamber than ever before.


Democrats who embrace a big-tent philosophy tend to emphasize the shared goals that unite the party — to be sure, the data suggests both wings of Colorado Democrats’ supermajority have more in common with each other than with the Legislature’s shrinking Republican minority. And plenty of Democratic lawmakers at the statehouse don’t fit neatly into either faction. They may see themselves as mediators between the two, or hew more closely to one side on some issues but not others.
Still, at opposite ends of the party’s ideological spectrum lie some fundamental disagreements about what a state government should and shouldn’t guarantee to its citizens. In most other democracies around the world, few would expect a democratic socialist and tenants’ rights attorney from an urban district, like Mabrey, to belong to the same party as his soon-to-be Senate counterpart Roberts, a pro-business centrist and ex-prosecutor representing affluent mountain resort communities.
But even in the absence of a true multi-party system, this swing bloc of Democratic centrists has been one of the most important factors shaping Colorado lawmaking in recent years — second only, perhaps, to the frequent vetoes and veto threats issued by Democratic Gov. Jared Polis, who will depart office in January.
In the last two sessions alone, moderate Democratic lawmakers have joined Republicans to block environmental and ratepayer protections targeting data centers; multiple bills enacting new eviction protections; multiple bills aimed at cracking down on overreach by federal immigration agents; a measure allowing cities to enact vacancy taxes on vacation homes; and stricter greenhouse gas reporting requirements for large corporations. And they’ve joined Republicans (and Polis) to enact laws supporting nuclear energy; cracking down on retail theft and enhancing some criminal penalties for other offenses; allowing cities to roll back minimum wage laws for tipped workers; and easing some wage and workplace protections for farmworkers.
It may be cold comfort to Colorado Republicans to know that the interest groups that once backed their party now largely pin their hopes on a group of moderate Democrats instead. But the Colorado Chamber of Commerce itself called the most recent legislative term one “in which business concerns were heard,” noting that “nearly every bill opposed vociferously by the business community ended up being killed or scaled back.”
As for Democrats, different parts of the party’s coalition will continue to try to gain the upper hand as Weiser takes office and lawmakers return to a host of hot-button issues in January, from data centers and surveillance pricing to rent control and the Worker Protection Act. Neither side is likely to end up perfectly happy with the outcomes. But for those who believe competition and dialogue produce good policy, arguments and counterarguments won’t be hard to find.



The Trendline provides analysis on public policy in Colorado. Articles explore ways to think about the news based on research, history and other important context, helping Coloradans connect the headlines to the big picture.

text:
Tennessee received received $210.3 million for the second year of the federal Rural Health Transformation Program. (Photo: Tennessee Department of Health)Tennessee received $210.3 million for the second year of the federal Rural Health Transformation Program, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced Monday. 
The state could receive up to $1 billion over the program’s 5-year duration, with year-to-year grant amounts decided based on Tennessee’s progress toward implementing its federally approved plans. Tennessee received $206.9 million in the program’s first year.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is a $50 billion federal initiative part of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed in 2025. The program was created to fund rural healthcare and partially offset the more than $900 billion in Medicaid cuts over the next decade to pay for the tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill. The health care research group KFF estimated that Tennessee will lose about $6 billion in federal Medicaid funding over the decade under the legislation.
Tennessee legislators expressed skepticism earlier this year about state policy changes required to receive full funding from the program. Lawmakers questioned whether the state should commit to spending on projects when federal grant funds could potentially be clawed back if the desired policy changes don’t pass.
Under the program, each state is guaranteed to receive $100 million in baseline funds. Additional funding is awarded competitively based on the state’s rural population characteristics, promised policy changes and how well each state performs on its promises.
Tennessee lawmakers skeptical over strings attached to Trump rural health grant program

Federal funds from the program cannot be used for construction, clinician salaries, loan repayment, hospital operating deficits, historical debt or higher reimbursement rates. The program also restricts payments to providers.
Progress on Tennessee’s plan
Tennessee’s plan includes five focus areas:

Improving access to healthcare
Maternal and child health
Technology infrastructure
Preventative health and wellness
Workforce development

Initiatives proposed in the application include several competitive grants within each category, a Last Mile Initiative for emergency medical services, expanding Tennessee’s Safety Net program, creating a Memory Care Assessment Network, a dental pilot extension, technical assistance investments and a $100 million expansion of value-based payments led by TennCare for hospitals as well as maternity and dental care in rural areas.
Progress is tracked by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Tennessee has completed planning and project preparation for five of its 17 initiatives. The remaining initiatives are still in progress on the project preparation stage.
As of July 31, Tennessee spent $31.3 million of its first-year funds, including $20.7 million to design and implement value-based payment programs intended to focus on overall patient health across practices and doctors in hopes of avoiding trips to emergency departments and hospital stays. The total also includes $3.3 million for perinatal center trainings, emergency medical services supplies and care, according to a report filed by the state.
The state’s application for the Rural Health Transformation Program committed to passing several policy changes, including:

Eliminating Tennessee’s certificate of need law, a move that the Tennessee Hospital Association has resisted for years. (Tennessee enacted a partial certificate of need reform law removing restrictions for satellite emergency rooms in 2024).
Enabling “full scope of practice” for nurse practitioners, physicians’ assistants, pharmacists and dental hygienists
Reestablishing the Presidential Fitness Test in schools
Requiring physicians’ continuing medical education to include nutrition
Submitting a waiver to the U.S. Department of Agriculture to prohibit the purchase of “non-nutritious items” using SNAP dollars

A “state snapshot” published by CMS showed Tennessee received $6.36 million in year one of the program as part of its effort to restrict the use of SNAP dollars for Tennessee recipients. A federal judge blocked several states, including Tennessee, from implementing those restrictions in June.
The snapshot also shows $2.19 million associated with Tennessee’s efforts to ease certificate of need laws, and $2.04 million tied to expanding practice scopes.
Tennessee must spend its first tranche of funds by Sept. 30, 2027.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Next generation of military scans archives for clues to missing service members
description: Bella Hammer, a social work student and member of the North Dakota Air National Guard, regularly supports military-affiliated students as part of her work with the University of North Dakota’s Veteran & Military Services.  She recently found a new way to serve veterans when she played a role in an archival project. Hammer is one […]
text:
University of North Dakota students Bella Hammer and Trevor Taylor pose with historical documents at the University of North Dakota's Chester Fritz Library on Nov. 10, 2026. The students have been working to digitize records related to U.S. service members missing from the Korean and Vietnam wars. (Photo by Russell Hons/For the North Dakota Monitor)Bella Hammer, a social work student and member of the North Dakota Air National Guard, regularly supports military-affiliated students as part of her work with the University of North Dakota’s Veteran & Military Services. 
She recently found a new way to serve veterans when she played a role in an archival project.
Hammer is one of two UND students who digitized records that could help investigators search for missing U.S. service members and civilians in southeast Asia. She helped to scan 6,400 pages from the James Wold Papers, which are preserved in UND’s Chester Fritz Library.
“It was such a rewarding and unique opportunity,” she said. “I’m so honored to have been asked.”
Small North Dakota town creates ‘sacred place’ to honor veterans 

The records were requested by Tours of Duty, a nonprofit that works with veterans and families seeking answers about their missing loved ones. As part of its work, the organization collects information that could shed light on the past.
“In our world, data is gold,” said Mike Luehring, who works with Tours of Duty. “When I heard about the Wold Papers, I realized this is something that would be valuable to our pursuit. When you’re trying to help families, you cast as big of a net as possible.”
The Wold Papers date from 1943 to 2003, the year Wold died, and have been housed at UND since 2007.
Wold enlisted in the U.S. Air Force in 1951 and commanded units in Vietnam. He retired from the Air Force in 1977 and went on to earn his degree at the University of North Dakota School of Law. He established a law practice in Luverne, North Dakota.
In 1994, Wold was appointed as the deputy assistant secretary of defense for POW/MIA Affairs. His work included efforts to account for Americans missing from the Korean and Vietnam wars.
Some of his records contain detailed information about service members whose remains were never recovered, according to Curt Hanson, who works with special collections at the Chester Fritz Library.
“The collection is all the documents he had from that time,” Hanson said. “It’s unlike any other collection we have.”
When Luehring contacted the archives to receive copies of some of the papers, Hanson knew it would take more time to scan than he and other staff members could commit to the project. 
That’s how Hammer and Trevor Taylor got involved.
Like Hammer, Taylor works in the UND Veteran & Military Services as peer support for other military-affiliated students. He served as a combat medic in the U.S. Army from 2021-25. After completing his tour, he came to UND to study commercial aviation. 
When he was asked if he would help scan documents from the Wold collection. Taylor didn’t hesitate. For him, it was an opportunity to honor those who served before him and to play a small role in bringing a forgotten generation of veterans back home.
“I served during the post-War on Terror when we had community support. This Vietnam generation didn’t have that,” Taylor said. “We left a lot of people behind, and a lot of people wanted to clean their hands of the conflict.”
More than 80,000 service personnel are missing from previous conflicts, according to the U.S. Department of Defense. About 38,000 are estimated to be recoverable.
It’s uncertain whether the Wold Papers will lead directly to any new discoveries, Luehring said. When trying to reconstruct events that occurred decades ago, any detail can become a needed piece of a much larger puzzle. Tours of Duty uses artificial intelligence tools to find connections, but investigators still conduct in-person interviews and study archival records to generate leads.
Luehring said he is grateful that UND students have been part of this project. Tours of Duty wants younger veterans to become involved in efforts to account for those who served before them.
“We emphasize this idea that no person can be left behind,” Luehring said. “When we have young veterans and service members participating in our work, we know they’re experiencing that message.”
For Hammer and Taylor, this has meant spending hours at a scanner. 
Taylor spent most of his volunteer hours scanning Wold’s personal journals and correspondence between the general and Vietnam military officials in the ’90s.
While doing so, Taylor couldn’t help but speculate.
“I imagine Gen. Wold talking to his former enemies in a combined effort to bring home our fallen service members,” Taylor said. “They deserve respect no matter what side they were on.”
Hammer scanned more professional documents. She saw maps of different areas and invitations from dignitaries.
As she did the work, she considered all the people and volunteers working toward a common purpose.
“I kept thinking about all the families we might be able to help,” she said. “If we can give even one family closure, that is important. I’m glad to do my part.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Commentary: Disabled vet honors ‘gold star’ teacher, families
description: CEDAR FALLS — Kelly Sullivan is a ‘gold star” teacher in many ways, but she and other families who lost loved ones in war received a ‘‘gold star” tribute from one of her star pupils this week ahead of Veterans Day. Disabled veteran Taylor Morris, who lost parts of all four limbs in a May […]
text:
Kelly Sullivan, left, reaches to embrace Taylor Morris before her remarks at the dedication of the Gold Star Families Memorial at Veterans Park in Cedar Falls. (Photo by Pat Kinney)CEDAR FALLS — Kelly Sullivan is a ‘gold star” teacher in many ways, but she and other families who lost loved ones in war received a ‘‘gold star” tribute from one of her star pupils this week ahead of Veterans Day.
Disabled veteran Taylor Morris, who lost parts of all four limbs in a May 2012 bomb blast in Afghanistan, and a cadre of volunteers dedicated a Gold Star Families Memorial at Veterans Memorial Park in Cedar Falls.
Kelly Sullivan was Taylor Morris’s third grade teacher. She is the granddaughter and grandniece of Waterloo’s five Sullivan brothers, who were killed in World War II.
Sullivan not only attended Monday’s dedication, she and staff brought third graders from Lincoln Elementary School in Cedar Falls to the ceremony.
“I am so proud of my former third grader Taylor,” she said.
Not only is Sullivan a member of a Gold Star family which lost loved ones in combat, in 2022 she was among a group of local educators nominated for a Gold Star Teachers award by the R.J. McElroy Trust, a local philanthropic foundation named for the founder of Waterloo television station KWWL.
Sullivan made the dedication a “teaching moment” for her students as well as the public in attendance — many of whom were veterans who already knew the lesson of service and sacrifice.
“To the 52 third graders here today, I want you to look at this hero. Taylor Morris has always been my hero,” an emotional Kelly Sullivan said at the dedication. “Ever since he was eight years old. And it is so wonderful to see him work so hard on this project to make it happen.”
Veterans and students from Lincoln Elementary School as well as the general public, attended the dedication of the Gold Star Families Memorial at Veterans Park in Cedar Falls on Nov. 9, 2026. (Photo by Pat Kinney)
Sullivan has taught the lessons of military service and sacrifice to her students practically throughout her teaching career. She is also the official sponsor of the currently serving Navy destroyer named for her grandfather and great uncles, the USS The Sullivans, hull number DDG-68.
The lessons stuck with Morris.
“Talk about full circle,” Morris said. “She was my third grade teacher; it was her first year too at Lincoln, I think. We asked her to come and speak on behalf of the Gold Star families. And she said, ‘I’ll come, and I’ll speak and I’ll bring 52 third graders!’ Awesome.”
Morris said he talked to her class. “We did a couple of times since we started this project. Seems like it really makes an impact on them. And it’s cool to get kids that age involved.” Some Lincoln fourth graders who heard him speak last school year also attended.
Morris, a U.S. Navy explosive ordnance disposal expert, was injured May 3, 2012 in Kandahar Province, Afghanistan, as he was trying to clear an area of improvised explosive devices for a unit of U.S. Army Special Forces soldiers. He began a rigorous rehabilitation and was fitted with prosthetics at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Washington, D.C. His wife and then-fiancée Danielle, then Danielle Kelly, supported him and served as his primary caregiver.
Taylor Morris speaks while an honor guard stands at attention at the Gold Star Families Memorial dedication Nov. 9, 2026 in Cedar Falls. (Photo by Pat Kinney)
“This is the latest project in Veterans Park,” Morris said. Several were conducted over the past 30 years, including relocating a replica Statue of Liberty to the park from Overman Park downtown, construction of a shelter, sales of commemorative bricks honoring individual veterans for their service to pay for park improvements and upkeep, and location of the official Black Hawk County Freedom Rock at the park by Greenfield artist Ray “Bubba” Sorenson II in 2015.
“This was a special project to me because it was something my grandfather had started on,” Morris said.
Vilas “Sid” Morris was a Korean War veteran, longtime local educator, Cedar Falls City Council member and Black Hawk County Veteran Affairs commissioner who spearheaded many projects at the park over the past three decades. Morris, U.S. Navy Vietnam veteran Mike Butler of the Cedar Falls Veterans of Foreign Wars post and local construction contractor Wayne Magee conceived the idea in 2019.
Sid Morris passed away in 2021, “and did not get to see this through to completion,” Taylor Morris said. “Mike asked me to join the team with him and Wayne Magee. And I was more than happy to do it. It’s been such a blessing and an honor to pick up where he left off, and do that on a project that has this level of significance.”
“I was here six months ago, with Taylor and (wife) Danielle and the kids, early morning Memorial Day, and he was telling me his plans,” Sullivan said, her voice quivering with emotion. “And it’s so wonderful to see someone when they’re so excited about something. It was beautiful. He was so passionate about it. I just admire all that.”
Disabled Afghanistan veteran Taylor Morris, left, is shown here with his third grade teacher at Lincoln Elementary School in Cedar Falls, Kelly Sullivan, granddaughter and grandniece of Waterloo’s five Sullivan Brothers killed during World War II. Sullivan is wearing the Navy Seabees jacket of her father, Jim Sullivan. (Photo by Pat Kinney)
Sullivan noted she was wearing the U.S. Navy Seabees coat of her father, Jim Sullivan, the only child of the five brothers. He is in an assisted living facility. “Unfortunately he couldn’t come today but he’s here with us in spirit,” she said pausing to gather her emotions.
“To be a Gold Star family member, it’s a club you never want to be in,” she said. She and her brother John, who lives in the Kansas City area, attended a reception for Gold Star families in Washington, D.C., a year ago and met and shared experiences with others who have lost loved once in military service.
“When you lose someone, your Christmases are never the same; the holidays, the birthdays,” she said. “Everything is changed forever. And I know my dad, Jim Sullivan, always felt that — not having his dad, his uncles and the big Irish Catholic family we would have had if one of the boys had survived.
“This memorial here is for the over 600 Gold Star families we have registered here in Iowa,” Sullivan said. “This memorial is dedicated to all Gold Star families who have paid the ultimate sacrifice for our freedoms.
“We have 52 patriots here today — these third graders, who are going to go on and do great things like Taylor did,” Sullivan said. “They’re going to bring their kids to this memorial. And they’re going to bring their grandkids here. Let’s make sure we utilize this space,” for Memorial Day, Veterans Day, “or just a beautiful morning like we have today,” she said.
Taylor Morris received the Bronze Star as well as the Purple Heart for his service. He and Danielle, a Cedar Falls real estate agent, have three children. He returned to a hero’s welcome in Cedar Falls following his rehabilitation. A massive fundraising effort spearheaded by the Stephen Siller Tunnel to Towers Foundation and the namesake foundation of actor Gary Sinise resulted in the construction of an iPad-operated “smart home” to accommodate Danielle and Taylor and Taylor’s disabilities. The effort included a 2013 concert at Gateway Park in Cedar Falls by Sinise’s “Lt. Dan Band,” named for Sinise’s Oscar-winning role as a disabled Vietnam vet in the movie “Forrest Gump” with Tom Hanks.
A video interview with Taylor Morris and Kelly Sullivan is attached here.
The memorial consists in part of a 7-foot-tall silhouette of a saluting service member, set in black granite, with a three-foot gold limestone star situated behind it. It’s positioned so that when the sun rises to a certain part of the sky on or around Memorial Day, the sunlight will be focused through the silhouette and illuminate the gold star. More details on the project can be found at a project website.
The front of the Gold Star Families Memorial at Veterans Park in Cedar Falls. The memorial is positioned in relation to the sun so that on May, around Memorial Day, an illuminated silhouette of the saluting solder will extend out to the gold star. (Photo by Pat Kinney)
The gold star is designed to be illuminated by the sun in May, around Memorial Day. (Photo by Pat Kinney)
“The monument will have a specific solar alignment so that every year the Memorial Day sunrise will create a ‘golden salute,’ saluting the Golden Star within the Memorial,” according to a project description. The silhouette will be positioned directly between the memorial and the gold star, like a sundial.
“The Golden Star will be flanked by six granite Armed Service Tribute benches, with three on each side defining the perimeter,” the project description says. The memorial “will be fully accessible with ample room for groups and individuals to easily navigate around the monument while admiring its beauty and paying their respects.”
Morris has said even the memorial’s measurements have patriotic significance. “The soldier silhouette itself is 7 feet tall,” with three panels. “So that represents your seven-man firing team, with three volleys, That represents a 21-gun salute” by an honor guard, he explained.
The memorial dimensions also symbolize the date of the commissioning of the Continental Army, the first branch of armed forces, on June 14, 1775 during the American Revolution. The two shortest heights on the outside are 3 foot, 6 inches; the middle height is 7 foot 6 inches. “When you add those together you get 14 feet, 6 inches — the 14th day, the sixth month,” Morris has said. “The width of the base in 17.75 feet. It gives the reasoning behind the size, the shape and the form.”
Taylor Morris, the Sullivan Brothers and late Medal of Honor recipient Robert J. Hibbs of Cedar Falls, a graduate of the University of Northern Iowa ROTC program who was killed in Vietnam in March 1966, all are featured on the Black Hawk County Freedom Rock at Veterans Park.
The image of Afghanistan war quad-amputee Taylor Morris on the Black Hawk County Freedom Rock at Veterans Park in Cedar Falls. (Photo by Pat Kinney)
George, Francis, Joseph, Madson and Albert Sullivan, the five sons of Thomas and Alleta Sullivan of Waterloo, died along with all but 14 of their nearly 700 shipmates when the Navy cruiser USS Juneau was torpedoed by a Japanese submarine and sunk following the naval Battle of Guadalcanal on Nov. 13, 1941 — 85 years ago this Friday. The five brothers’ deaths a considered the greatest combat-related loss of life by one family at one time in U.S. history.
Kelly Sullivan, the granddaughter of Albert Sullivan, youngest of the brothers and the only one who married, has been a very active sponsor of the USS The Sullivans, attending many events related to the ship and has hosted a number of its sailors and commanders on visits to Waterloo-Cedar Falls.
About $190,000 in cash and in-kind donations have been raised to make the Gold Star Families Memorial possible, Mike Butler said, and another $100,000 is needed to finish off the project, which Morris said will be illuminated with footlights at night.
Donations to the Gold Star Families Memorial project in Cedar Falls may be made online at the link here. Donations also may be made by check. Checks may be made out to “Veterans Memorial Fund” and mailed to the Cedar Falls Community Foundation, P.O. Box 546, Cedar Falls, Iowa 50613. Questions may be directed to project contact Mike Butler at (319) 239-6214 or Mike.Butler052@gmail.com

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Commentary: Arlington Cemetery is a national treasure. It should not be debased.
description: Arlington National Cemetery, the nation’s largest resting place for America’s heroes, is sacred ground for our veterans. As we commemorate Veterans Day this year, we should turn our thoughts and pay our respects to the many Idahoans who have been laid to rest in that hallowed ground.  They include two Congressional Medal of Honor winners. […]
text:
A replica of the proposed 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., is seen on June 30, 2026, on the National Mall at the Great American State Fair to celebrate America's 250 birthday. (Photo by Christophe Paul/U.S. Department of Agriculture)Arlington National Cemetery, the nation’s largest resting place for America’s heroes, is sacred ground for our veterans. As we commemorate Veterans Day this year, we should turn our thoughts and pay our respects to the many Idahoans who have been laid to rest in that hallowed ground. 
They include two Congressional Medal of Honor winners. Col. Reginald Rodney Myers, who was born in Boise, earned the Medal of Honor for valor in the vicious Battle of Chosin Reservoir in Korea in November of 1950. First Lt. Vernon J. Baker, who was born in Wyoming, but lived his last 15 years in Idaho, received the Medal of HOnor for conspicuous valor near Viareggio, Italy, in April of 1945. His award came 52 years late because of his black skin. 
A number of Idahoans from Vietnam and subsequent wars are interred in the peaceful environs of Arlington. In July of 2012, the remains of Chief Master Sgt. Larry Thornton of Idaho Falls were buried at Arlington, 45 years after his AC-47D took off from Vietnam on Christmas Eve of 1965 and disappeared over Laos.
I’ve been to Arlington many times since my Vietnam service. Every time I saw the grave marker of a Vietnam comrade, I was flooded with profound grief and anger for the 58,220 American lives taken by that ill-fated war, including 251 with Idaho connections. Those emotions were always somewhat assuaged by the quiet, dignified atmosphere of the cemetery. 
That calming atmosphere is currently facing a serious threat from another Donald Trump vanity project.
Trump’s 250-foot-tall triumphal arch will sit smack dab in front of Arlington Cemetery, destroying its peace and tranquility, as well as the symmetry and symbolism of its location. The National Park Service dared to report that the arch “would break alignment between the Lincoln Memorial, Memorial Bridge and Arlington House that was Robert E. Lee’s home.” 
It continued: “The bridge alignment and associated ceremonial landscape were intended to physically and symbolically unite North and South through a coordinated monumental composition extending across the Potomac River.” It has also been noted that the arch requires an act of Congress. It does not have congressional approval, but that has never stopped Trump from bullying ahead.
Trump is not the first president to propose construction that would have severely interfered with that alignment, as well as the pastoral atmosphere of the cemetery. President Franklin D. Roosevelt proposed building the Pentagon in that location. He changed his mind after being convinced that it would obliterate the backdrop of tiered headstones and Arlington House. 
Why build an arch in the first place? The Romans were among the first of the ancients to construct triumphal arches. They made an art of building arches to recognize victorious generals returning from battle. 
It is not clear why Trump would be entitled to an arch on that basis because his Iran War has been an unmitigated disaster for our country. The Iranians have kept what remains of their nuclear material. The war has caused skyrocketing prices for gas, diesel, fertilizer, and most consumer goods that need to be transported. The explanation for the arch must lie elsewhere.
Trump admitted last October that the monument was intended to honor “me” but later claimed it was to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary. As he has continued to take flak for the project, Trump and his lackeys now contend it is required for the national defense. 
We already have a national defense project in the grand ballroom adjacent to the White House, but that does not seem to be sufficient in the president’s mind. In a shameful attempt to get around building restrictions, he now claims the arch will be laden with drones, snipers and machine guns so as to protect Washington from attack. If he had the slightest understanding of military tactics, he would understand that his arch would make an indefensible sitting-duck target.
Not everyone is keen for Trump’s vanity arch. Three Vietnam War veterans have filed suit in federal court to stop construction. One of the veterans said his opposition is an act of loyalty to the country and our fallen service members. Another stated the arch is disrespectful to those who did not return and those buried at Arlington. 
Well said, brothers! The District of Columbia and Virginia have also brought suit against the arch.
The courts will likely rule against this vanity project, but that may not be enough. Citizens and veterans must raise their voices and demand that the cemetery not be debased just to satisfy the vanity of a failed president. 
Perhaps the congressmen and senators still standing after the midterm elections will find the courage to speak out against this slap in the face to the nation’s veterans that we honor on Nov. 11.

title: TN’s 4th district U.S. House race could be called after Nashville counts provisional ballots Monday
description: The Davidson County Election Commission will count the remaining provisional ballots in Tennessee’s 4th U.S. Congressional race at a Nov. 16 meeting, potentially allowing the outcome to be called in favor of a Democratic upstart.  After election night last week, Democrat Victoria Broderick led veteran Republican U.S. Rep. Scott DeJarlais by 285 votes in the [...]
text:
Tennessee’s 4th U.S. Congressional District likely can’t be officially called until after Nashville finishes counting its provisional ballots on Monday. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The Davidson County Election Commission will count the remaining provisional ballots in Tennessee’s 4th U.S. Congressional race at a Nov. 16 meeting, potentially allowing the outcome to be called in favor of a Democratic upstart. 
After election night last week, Democrat Victoria Broderick led veteran Republican U.S. Rep. Scott DeJarlais by 285 votes in the 4th District.
Broderick has not officially been declared the winner because the multi-county congressional district still has about 700 provisional ballots to count. The district includes the eastern third of Nashville-Davidson County, Rutherford County and nine more rural counties in middle and east Tennessee. 
John Richardson, administrator of elections with the Davidson County Election Commission, said about 600 of those remaining provisional ballots are in the part of the district that includes Nashville-Davidson County. 
“We have a process, and it takes time,” Richardson said. 
The commission will determine this week which ballots are valid, and those will be put into voting machines to be counted at an 8 a.m. meeting on Monday, Nov. 16, Richardson said. Voters are allowed to cast provisional ballots when questions are raised about their eligibility to cast a regular ballot. Davidson County plans to certify its election results Nov. 19. 
DeJarlais has not conceded the race because the remaining votes exceed Broderick’s current lead. 
Democrats won heavily in Nashville during this election cycle, and Broderick has won 75% of the vote in the part of the district in Nashville where provisional votes remain to be counted.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Survey shows broad agreement on school screen time limits, value of devices
description: A survey of over 3,400 Alabama parents and school employees found broad agreement about time limits on screen use by students, though several instructors also noted that the devices could be useful in classrooms. The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, formed by Gov. Kay Ivey, reviewed preliminary results of the survey on Tuesday, ahead of sending […]
text:
A child with a finger on a tablet. The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, formed by Gov. Kay Ivey, reviewed preliminary results of a survey on attitudes about screen usage in classroom, ahead of filing a final report to the governor next month. (Oscar Lopez Rogado via Getty Images)A survey of over 3,400 Alabama parents and school employees found broad agreement about time limits on screen use by students, though several instructors also noted that the devices could be useful in classrooms.
The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, formed by Gov. Kay Ivey, reviewed preliminary results of the survey on Tuesday, ahead of sending a final report to the governor next month.
Over 3,000 teachers and parents; nearly 400 school leaders and roughly 30 IT directors and staff participated in the survey. The survey was self-selecting, meaning people volunteered to take the survey.
Teachers who responded said they used screens in classrooms for assessment or progress monitoring, independent work, review skills, research and core instruction, among other tasks.
“What was interesting to the research team is that all of these activities are used (at least) sometimes or more (frequently in the classroom). So everything from passive practice review types of things to student creation work,” said Stefani Wind, a professor at The University of Alabama who worked on the survey.
Of the respondents, 50% of parents, teachers and school leaders strongly agreed that students are distracted by non-instructional content, or content that doesn’t directly involve teaching or coursework, and at least 30% of teachers, school leaders and parents agreed or strongly agreed that it’s difficult to bring attention back to instructional material after using devices.
Over 80% of teachers, parents and school leaders agreed that regular screen-free periods would benefit students.
The survey also took open-ended responses from teachers, parents and school leaders.
“Screen use interferes with the way the brain works and prevent(s) retention and transfer of information,” one school leader said. “Learning apps ‘gamify’ education to promote ‘engagement,’ but engagement does not mean learning.”
One parent said that while devices can be useful in classrooms, they shouldn’t be used across all grade levels.
“We need to be cognizant of how much time students are spending on screens. In my opinion, my five-year-old kindergartener should not know how to use a Chromebook and sign into Google Classroom,” the parent wrote.
One teacher wrote that they liked the access to information devices in the classroom provided and said there should be guidance.
“Sometimes, a kid might have 30 minutes on a screen, but during a research project,” the teacher said. “It might be more like an hour just because that’s the most efficient (and relevant) research tool.”
Brandy White, superintendent of Houston County Schools and a member of the commission, said in an interview after the meeting that the survey results were encouraging. 
“There were times where they may have their Chromebook open, but it’s actually guided instruction where the teacher is up at the board, and she’s going over certain questions,” White said. “So that looks like screen time, if you just calculate the amount of time that they were on it, but it’s actually guided instruction where they’re communicating back and forth.”
Rep. Jeana Ross, R-Guntersville, said after the meeting that filing legislation is a “possibility.”
“I think first you got to look at the recommendations and see exactly what’s in there, and also I want to talk some more to teachers and local school districts because that teacher autonomy I think is very important. But sometimes it helps, you know, to have some kind of guidance for them to be able to fall back on,” she said.
The committee will deliver its final report to Ivey on Dec. 1.

text:
Alabama Public Service Commission President Cynthia Almond (center) speaks during a meeting of the commission on Oct. 6, 2026 in Montgomery, Alabama. Commissioners Jeremy Oden (left) and Chip Beeker (right) listen. Alabama Power said Monday it would follow a request from the PSC to not pass on most advertising costs to its customers, though it was not immediately clear what effect if any that would have on power rates. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)Alabama Power said this week it would stop charging customers for advertising costs except those related to public safety, following a request from the Alabama Public Service Commission, the state utility regulator.
A state law passed in the spring will require the utility to stop using customer money for advertising by 2029. But PSC President Cynthia Almond moved to ask the utility to implement it on an interim basis at the commission’s meeting on Nov. 3.
“I don’t see any reason that we shouldn’t take steps now to begin that process rather than waiting Jan. 1, 2029,” she said during the meeting.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The move passed unanimously. Alabama Power said in a statement Monday it planned to comply with the request.
“While the commission’s written order has not yet been issued, based on the motion approved at the November meeting, Alabama Power plans to comply by removing advertising expenses from customer rates in 2027 and 2028,” the company said in a statement Monday. “We will evaluate the order once it is released.”
The agenda did not list advertising cost as one of the items on the agenda of the Nov. 3 meeting. Almond did not say how much rates would decrease because of the decision or if it was in response to any advertising from Alabama Power.
Alabama residents pay higher than average utility rates compared to other states in the Southeast. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration website, Alabama residents paid an average of 16.33 cents per kilowatt-hour. By comparison, Tennessee residents paid an average of 13.42 cents per kilowatt-hour; Mississippi residents paid 14.43 cents; Florida residents paid 14.99 cents and Georgia residents paid 15.90 cents.
Messages were sent to Alabama Power and the Public Service Commission Tuesday seeking clarification on potential rate impacts.
The company also said in its statement it has followed Alabama law and previous orders from the PSC that “half of advertising costs are excluded from customer rates.” The statement also said that advertising costs that are part of its rates deal with “electrical safety, energy efficiency, storm preparedness and scam prevention.”
Gov. Kay Ivey in April signed HB 475, sponsored by Rep. Mack Butler, R-Rainbow City, that made several changes to the PSC, including expanding the number of members; creating a secretary of energy to oversee the commission and placing limits on when a commission can call a rate hearing.
The law also prevents utilities from charging customers for advertising, lobbying and expenses that pertain to grants offered by a company.
In October, the PSC required Alabama Power to make summaries of agreements it makes with the data center publicly available, as well as information about the project and expected power consumption.
Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, a nonprofit that advocates for renewable energy in Alabama, praised the decision at its November meeting.
“It is great news,” he said in an interview Monday. “We were really excited by the commission President Almond’s leadership to get these costs out of rates immediately. There is no reason why customers should be paying for any advertising that Alabama Power is doing.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: ‘I don’t know if we’ve seen the worst of what’s coming.’ Medicaid changes loom for Kentuckians.
description: Cara Ellis was 27 when she got health insurance — which she’d gone without most of her life — through an expansion of Medicaid that allowed more, low-income adults to enroll in the government plan. Now Ellis, 39, a Pikeville native and senior at Morehead State University, said she’s worried she could lose coverage under […]
text:
Cara Ellis says Medicaid has been a lifeline for her. (Photo provided)Cara Ellis was 27 when she got health insurance — which she’d gone without most of her life — through an expansion of Medicaid that allowed more, low-income adults to enroll in the government plan.
Now Ellis, 39, a Pikeville native and senior at Morehead State University, said she’s worried she could lose coverage under pending, major changes in Medicaid required by federal and state law.
She credits Medicaid with saving her life after she was diagnosed in 2019 with thyroid cancer—four years after she qualified for health coverage.
“I have a lifetime of care ahead of me,” Ellis said. “This is something I worry about every single day.”
Significant changes enacted by Congress and the Kentucky General Assembly are coming to Kentucky’s $22 billion-a-year Medicaid program that provides health coverage for 1.3 million people including more than 600,000 children – making it the state’s single largest health plan. The federal government provides about 75% of the funding.
Kentucky officials worry that many beneficiaries don’t understand the changes or don’t realize they may have to follow new rules in an already complex program.
“I think the unfortunate reality is that it will catch people off guard,” said Dr. Steven Stack, secretary of the Cabinet for Health and Family Services, which oversees Medicaid in Kentucky. “No matter how hard you try to communicate, it’s hard to reach everybody.”
Key changes require most adults 19-64 to show they are working, in school or volunteering to keep coverage. And they will have to prove every six months they are eligible.
The changes take effect Jan. 1, and will be phased in with people allowed to “attest,” or self-report compliance with new rules over the first year. But that changes in 2028.
“Come Jan. 1, 2028, we are going to have to have all these systems operational and if people can’t demonstrate compliance, they unfortunately and very sadly are going to lose Medicaid benefits,” Stack said.
At the national level, 5 to 10 million people could lose Medicaid coverage in 2028 because of the changes, according to a study by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. Many will be people who qualify because they already are working or in school but don’t provide adequate documentation or who don’t realize they are exempt for health or other reasons.
In Kentucky, “tens of thousands” could lose coverage for similar reasons, Stack said.
Still, Stack said the administration of Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat,  is working to notify as many people as possible to try to ensure they retain coverage.
“It is a fact that people without health insurance live sicker and die younger,” Stack said.
The ‘Big, Beautiful Bill’
Most changes were included in federal HR 1 of 2025, dubbed by the Trump Administration as the One Big Beautiful Bill. It’s estimated to cut Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over 10 years.
The Republican-controlled Kentucky General Assembly enacted further changes to Medicaid through House Bill 2, including adding small-copays for some health services and tightening requirements for reporting work, school or volunteering.
Most changes begin Jan. 1, 2027. Newly elected Democrats, part of the recent blue wave, have vowed to make changes to the cuts, but it’s not clear if those could happen before the new rules go into effect in Kentucky.
Largely unaffected are the nearly 900,000 Kentuckians enrolled in “traditional” Medicaid—including low-income pregnant women, individuals below 100% of the federal poverty level, those with disabilities, and poor, elderly people in nursing homes.
Rather, most changes apply to those who gained Medicaid coverage through the 2014 expansion under the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare, that allowed adults earning up to 138% of the federal poverty level—about $22,000 a year—to enroll.
In Kentucky, that’s about 450,000 people ages 19-64—though some will be exempt for medical or other reasons.
Growth ‘unsustainable’
That includes Ellis, who said she already meets requirements through working and attending college full-time. But she worries that one missed deadline or piece of misplaced paperwork could cost her health coverage—and says she’s not alone.
“I think a lot of people are going to lose coverage,” Ellis said. “I think we’re going to see a lot of people across the state like me – who got health coverage for the first time – are going to lose coverage.”
Ellis is among people who spoke at a series of recent “listening sessions” House and Senate Democrats held in Louisville, Lexington, Morehead and Prestonsburg to hear people’s questions and comments about upcoming changes to Medicaid.
“It’s something I’m very passionate about,” she said. “I speak out frequently.
Rep. Lindsey Burke, D-Lexington and House minority caucus chair, attended the sessions and said she was impressed by the scope and importance of Medicaid in Kentucky.
“I would say by and large what we heard is Medicaid is a stabilizing force in the lives of Kentuckians,” Burke said. “Whether it’s the birth of a new child, helping new parents get on their feet, issues at the end of life or all the issues in between, Medicaid does a lot for the lives of Kentuckians.”
But Republicans have criticized the rapid growth and cost of Medicaid even as they express support for the health services it provides.
“What we have is a Medicaid budget (that) has nearly doubled, in fact, over doubled, over the past five years to an unsustainable level that we’ve got to do something (about) in terms of addressing the cost of this,” Rep. Ken Fleming, R-Louisville, said in February, speaking in support of HB2, which he sponsored. Fleming lost his election on Nov. 3 to Democrat Suhas Kulkarni.
What are the changes?
Changes include a requirement that individuals work, attend school or volunteer at least 80 hours a month and provide proof to the state. They also must “recertify,” or prove that they are eligible for Medicaid every six months instead of once a year.
During the first year, starting January 2027, individuals will be allowed to “attest” or report to the state they meet requirements.
But it gets more complicated in 2028 when individuals will be required to submit documents to verify employment, hours worked, income or other activities.
Stack, the cabinet secretary, said the state will use available sources, such as tax filings or public university enrollment records, to try to collect as much information as possible.
But state officials anticipate many will begin to lose Medicaid at that point.
“It will cause people to lose their coverage,” Stack said. “Not because they are ineligible . . . but because it’s a lot to keep up with.”
Who’s exempt?
The federal law cites a number of reasons individuals are exempt from the new rules including parents or caregivers of children under 14, pregnant women, foster youth or former foster youth up to age 26, those undergoing substance use treatment and disabled veterans.
It also exempts people considered “medically frail” with health conditions that prevent them from working.
For the first year, 2027, individuals will be able to attest that they can’t work, attend school or volunteer for health reasons.
But starting in 2028, they must provide proof of a health condition that counts as “medically frail.”
Stack said the state is working to come up with guidelines that define “medically frail” and how to verify it before 2028.


For more information:
The Kentucky Health Benefit Exchange, a state site that provides online information about changes coming to Medicaid as well as how to enroll or obtain other health coverage.
Also, the state is offering a site dedicated to the new, Medicaid work requirements.
Information is available through the local Department of Community Based Services office, with one in each of Kentucky’s 120 counties.
And Kentuckians whose Medicaid coverage is through one of five managed care insurance companies—Aetna, Humana, Passport, United and WellCare—can seek information through those providers. They are listed on the cabinet website.


Waivers not affected, mostly
“Waivers,” a handful of Medicaid programs that provide services to specific individuals with physical or intellectual disabilities, are not affected by reporting or work requirements, Stack said.
Cheri Kulik (right) with her daughter, Charlotte, at a T-shirt business they operate from their home in Oldham County. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Deborah Yetter)
But Cheri Kulik, an Oldham County mother whose daughter, Charlotte, 18, has autism and gets services through a program known as the Michelle P. Waiver, said even small changes can catch families unaware.
For example, the Michelle P.  program serves more than 10,000 individuals but has nearly that many on a waiting list – a wait that can last months or years because the state limits the number of slots it funds.
Previously, individuals could remain on the waiting list indefinitely.
Under a change in HB 2, families or guardians must prove they are still eligible once a year to remain on the waiting list, Kulik said.
“If you’re on that list and you miss this form you have to send back, they can take you off,” said Kulik, who attended the listening session in Louisville.
Kulik, who works with a support group for parents in Oldham County, said she’s trying to alert them to the change the state has begun notifying people about by mail.
“I said, ‘Watch for this letter. It’s coming,” she said.
Kulik, who said getting and keeping Medicaid coverage already is difficult enough, worries families may miss the waiting list renewal notice or other possible changes ahead.
“For a parent with a child with a disability, it is already ridiculously hard,” she said. “I cannot emphasize that enough.”
She added: “I don’t know if we’ve seen the worst of what’s going to happen.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Spanberger, Va. Democrats pitch medical debt relief, data center limits for 2027
description: Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Virginia’s top Democrats unveiled their 2027 legislative agenda Tuesday, proposing medical debt relief, limits on classroom screen time and tougher oversight of data centers and artificial intelligence as they seek to address rising costs for Virginia families.  Announced on the South Portico of the state Capitol in Richmond, the [...]
text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday unveiled Virginia Democrats' slate of legislative priorities ahead of the General Assembly session that starts in January 2027. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Virginia’s top Democrats unveiled their 2027 legislative agenda Tuesday, proposing medical debt relief, limits on classroom screen time and tougher oversight of data centers and artificial intelligence as they seek to address rising costs for Virginia families. 
Announced on the South Portico of the state Capitol in Richmond, the Moving Virginia Forward Agenda builds on Spanberger’s first-year affordability initiatives while adding proposals to address workers, help small businesses and crack down on AI-generated child sexual abuse material. 
Spanberger said healthcare, housing and energy costs remain priorities for her administration, warning that high living expenses could make Virginia less attractive to workers and businesses. 
“If the cost of living is too high, it impacts where talented people choose to live and work, where they choose to build their lives and their businesses,” she said. 
The lawmakers presented several data center proposals, including requirements for local approval of facilities using more than 25 megawatts, a ban on nondisclosure agreements with local officials and stronger oversight of cooling water use. 
Democrats also want to encourage solar development on previously developed land and working farms and create a new disaster preparedness declaration. 
The leaders repeatedly criticized President Donald Trump’s administration, blaming federal policies for adding to families’ financial uncertainty. 
Tuesday’s announcement comes ahead of another legislative election year. Democrats won 64 of the House of Delegates’ 100 seats in November 2025, a net gain of 13 that gave them a 64-36 majority. All 40 seats of the state Senate will be on the ballot in November 2027, along with the House. 
Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, the Senate’s president pro tempore, did not attend Tuesday’s event. She was indicted on federal corruption charges last month, a situation the governor declined to comment on Tuesday. 
Spanberger said the Democratic agenda is not yet complete, with more proposals to be announced around Virginia in the coming weeks. 
House Speaker Don Scott, D-Portsmouth, invited Republicans to work with Democrats on the legislation, saying affordability concerns extend across party lines. Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, said lawmakers could take steps to help Virginia families even when federal policies are beyond their control. 
 Healthcare: Debt relief and upfront prices

State Democrats want to create a medical debt forgiveness program that would work with a national nonprofit to buy outstanding debt from Virginia healthcare providers at steep discounts and cancel it. 
North Carolina, Michigan, Illinois and Arizona have established similar programs. Spanberger said the goal is to eliminate millions of dollars in medical debt. 
The package would also require healthcare providers and insurers to give patients good-faith cost estimates before non-emergency treatment. Hospitals would face new financial assistance requirements, including offering payment plans. 
“No one should walk into a doctor’s office with no idea what they’ll owe when they walk out,” Spanberger said. 
Scott said medical bills should not push families into financial hardship. Sen. Lashrecse Aird, D-Henrico, described hearing from a Virginian who was left with debt after an ambulance ride and treatment following an accident. 
The proposals follow legislation Spanberger signed earlier this year to address prescription costs, including restrictions on pharmacy benefit managers, which negotiate prices among insurers, drug manufacturers and pharmacies. 
The 2027 agenda, however, does not specify how the medical debt forgiveness program would be funded or who would qualify.
 Data centers and energy: Greater oversight, expanded solar

Spanberger highlighted some of her previously announced Data Center Accountability Framework, which outlines potential legislation that would tighten regulations on the data facilities growth and oversight as public pressure to rein in their growth intensifies.
Among those proposals is a move to ban nondisclosure agreements between data center companies and local governments. Del. Kathy Tran, D-Fairfax, said at Tuesday’s event that the controversial documents have left local residents in the dark as their elected officials make these development decisions.
“Communities deserve transparency, and a meaningful opportunity to weigh in on projects that will have lasting consequences for their neighborhoods,” Tran said. 
The governor’s priority list also includes a proposal to eliminate by-right approval for data centers using more than 25 megawatts of power and require local approval regardless of prior project approvals. 
By-right permitting is often allowed in specific zones deemed “technology overlay districts” or growth zones of counties. Projects can proceed under existing zoning without a project-specific rezoning or special-use vote in view of the public. 
Also in the governor’s plan are ways to protect “water scarcity” areas from evaporative cooling methods for the centers, putting more costs of transmission infrastructure onto those companies, and several other ideas. Official bills have not yet been filed.
Legislators also promised an increased investment in solar power on brownfields and in agrivoltaics — the method of putting solar panels on active farms that can maintain their crops concurrently. 
“That means expanding solar without paving over Virginia’s working families, working farms, and forests,” Scott said. “Through agrivoltaics, the former keeps forming, and the land produces food, and power at the same.”
 Housing: Building near transit 

Spanberger wants to increase housing near public transportation and give priority to affordable housing and transit-related infrastructure when the state sells or leases land.
She said building homes near transit could help residents save on both housing and transportation. Scott called for more walkable neighborhoods where people can reach jobs and businesses without relying as heavily on cars.
Surovell said additional housing near transit stations and above retail spaces could make it easier for younger workers to live near growing employment centers. 
The proposals follow this year’s debate over “housing near jobs” legislation, which would allow apartments, townhomes and mixed-use developments in certain commercial corridors. Republicans raised concerns about the state overriding local zoning decisions. 
Spanberger also signed legislation this year using Virginia’s bonding authority to support affordable housing and expanding efforts to reduce evictions. 
 Education: Less screen time, more career pathways 

Under a Democratic proposal lawmakers previewed Tuesday, Virginia school divisions would have to limit unnecessary student screen time, prioritize teacher-led instruction and regularly evaluate the technology used in classrooms.
Districts would also be required to develop plans to reduce excessive or ineffective use of digital learning tools.
The proposal goes beyond restrictions on students’ personal cellphones to address technology used during instruction.
Parents and former educators urged state officials in August to strengthen classroom technology guidelines, calling for greater use of physical books, handwriting and face-to-face learning. 
Senate Democratic Caucus Chair Mamie Locke, D-Hampton, said Tuesday technology can help students learn but should also not distract them or interfere with instruction. 
Locke also called for additional investments in early childhood education, teachers, literacy, mathematics and school facilities. 
Meanwhile, lawmakers are also considering changes to how Virginia funds public education. A legislative subcommittee approved hiring an expert last month to examine alternatives to the state’s decades-old K-12 funding formula. 
Democrats also want to expand pre-apprenticeship and youth apprenticeship programs, improve access to career training for underserved populations and establish quality standards. 
Transportation and childcare assistance would help more Virginians participate. 
 AI regulation: Child protection and worker pay 

Democrats proposed banning the creation, possession and distribution of AI-generated child sexual abuse material and holding AI companies accountable when their platforms or models produce such content for users.
House Majority Leader Charniele Herring, D-Alexandria, said the legislation would establish civil penalties for companies whose technology allows the material to be created.
She warned that advances in artificial intelligence could give predators new ways to exploit children while making it harder to identify victims and prevent abuse.
“The risks to our children and our communities are real, and they are growing,” Herring said. 
Another proposal would restrict employers from using AI and machine learning to determine the lowest wage or salary a job applicant might accept based on surveillance data and assumptions about their personal finances. 
Spanberger said employers should not be allowed to use the technology to take advantage of applicants’ financial circumstances. 
 Small businesses: A central source of help

The administration wants to expand the Department of Small Business and Supplier Diversity’s role in helping entrepreneurs find financing, technical assistance and other resources. 
Spanberger said small business owners often struggle to navigate the various programs offering capital, counseling and government contracting assistance. 
Under the proposal, the department would serve as a central point of contact, directing businesses to programs that fit their needs. 
Aird said workforce development is another challenge, particularly for businesses looking to expand and hire local workers who have the necessary skills. 
 Republican lawmakers respond, as legislature stares down January return 

In a statement Tuesday afternoon, House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, R-Scott, dismissed the Democrats’ affordability message. 
“If there was anything ‘affordable’ in that press event, I didn’t hear it. There was nothing that will bring down power bills, nothing that will end the car tax, nothing that will end the grocery tax, nothing that will help young people get started in life.”
Kilgore said House Republicans would put forward their own proposals to cut taxes for working families, lower electricity bills and expand economic opportunities. 
The bills lawmakers described Tuesday don’t yet appear in Virginia’s Legislative Informative System. Drafts of all bills must be available for public review by Dec. 31, according to state law. The 2027 General Assembly session is slated to convene on Jan. 13.
