title: Is the Florida GOP in denial about an immigration backlash in South Florida?
description: Some of Florida’s highest-ranking Republicans have attributed last week’s electoral results mostly to concerns about affordability and the Iran war, and not as much to the reaction —specifically in South Florida — to the Trump administration’s mass deportation policies. Policies that Gov. Ron DeSantis has done much to facilitate. “I don’t think that was a […[...]
text:
In a survey of Florida Latino voters last month, 81% said ICE had gone over the line and 50% were angry at its aggressive actions and lack of accountability. Among Cuban Americans, 78% said ICE had gone over the line. (Photo by Ben Ackman/New Jersey Monitor)Some of Florida’s highest-ranking Republicans have attributed last week’s electoral results mostly to concerns about affordability and the Iran war, and not as much to the reaction —specifically in South Florida — to the Trump administration’s mass deportation policies.
Policies that Gov. Ron DeSantis has done much to facilitate.
“I don’t think that was a major issue,” the governor said during a press conference in Tallahassee last week. “I don’t think it was a driving factor in South Florida, even though you did have some people that were concerned about it.”
Miami-Dade County Republican U.S. Rep. Maria Salazar certainly seemed worried when she aired an ad in September telling Trump his deportation policies had gone “too far” (Salazar officially was declared the winner in her race against Democrat Eliot Rodriguez after the machine recounted ended on Tuesday afternoon).
In Florida’s 26th Congressional District, which encompasses communities near Hialeah and Doral where 70% of residents are foreign-born, Republican incumbent Jose Diaz-Balart narrowly survived a challenge from Democrat Nicole Locklin. The race was not called for Diaz-Balart until Monday.
Miami immigration advocate Thomas Kennedy argues the reaction to Trump’s immigration policies has been“radioactive.”
“This is a community where you have hundreds of thousands of people — Nicaraguans, Venezuelans, Hondurans — being stripped of their temporary protected status,” he said. “You’re having people discriminately being denied their asylum claims. UCIS (United States Citizenship and Immigration Services) is not processing applications for really any immigration process. You have people getting arrested during their marriage petition interviews. And people are getting hunted down like animals.”
Survey results
A survey from UnidosUS and BSP Research released Tuesday of 516 Latino Florida voters taken last month showed 57% looking unfavorably at Trump. Although affordability was the defining issue for Florida Latinos, 81% said ICE had gone over the line and 50% were angry at the agency’s aggressive tactics and lack of accountability. Among Cuban Americans, 78% said ICE had gone over the line. (The survey had a +/- 4.3% margin of error.)
Meanwhile, Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, won Hispanic-rich Miami Dade County over Republican U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody by nearly 56,000 votes. Nixon narrowly won in Doral, the city Trump won overwhelmingly in 2024, carrying half of its precincts by more than 20 points, according to the Latin Times. Moody won over Nixon statewide by nearly 3%.
“That massive swing really spoke to the way that people were seeing on the ground when it came to the economy and immigration policies,” Jared Nordlund, Florida state director with UnidosUS, said Tuesday. “For months, ICE raids have been all over Doral and targeting Venezuelan families, asylum seekers with work permits, and then the end of TPS really shook that community hard.”
Another survey showed that 67% of Cuban Americans in Miami disapproved of the Trump administration’s increased deportations of Cubans with no criminal records. That was from a Florida International University poll of 1,004 Cuban Americans in South Florida conducted in September.
In recent months, community leaders in Doral have asked city officials to rescind their 287(g) agreement with ICE, and Kennedy said Tuesday that City Councilwoman Maureen Porras had submitted an agenda item to revisit the decision to sign that agreement.
ICE tactics were a huge factor in Texas last week, Kennedy said, but it was equally powerful in South Florida. “It really motivated a lot of Hispanics to go out and be like, ‘You’re not going to treat us like this.’”
Opinion shift
Cracking down on illegal immigration was a winning issue for President Trump in his election over Kamala Harris in 2024. But public opinion has shifted dramatically since then, with many Americans saying they disapprove of ICE’s enforcement of immigration laws.
Speaking Sunday night on CBS’ 60 Minutes, Trump acknowledged his crackdown had both “helped and hurt” him in the midterm elections.
“Now, there is a large part of the country that think they should be put out,” he said of undocumented immigrants. “And there’s a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscape company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes. And there’s a large group of people who think that they should be allowed to stay.”
Appearing on Fox News’ “Fox and Friends” Monday from Jacksonville Beach, Moody was asked whether she agreed with the president that his deportations of undocumented immigrants who have not committed any criminal offense may have gone too far.
She replied, “At all times, I worked with law enforcement to make sure that we were getting criminals off our streets so that we were the most pro-law enforcement, safest state in the nation,” she said.
“I know, but do you believe the president?” Fox’s Brian Kilmeade interrupted. “He says, ‘I regret a little of that.’”
“I can tell you, in Florida, we led the nation,” Moody responded. “Every single one of our sheriff’s departments signed up to work with the federal government to immediately go in and start removing people who were here illegally committing crimes.”
She did not note that although many Florida sheriffs had already signed 287(g) agreements pledging them to work with ICE in detaining undocumented immigrants arrested for crimes, it became state law in 2025 that all 67 sheriffs were required to do so.
On NPR’s “Here and Now” program Monday, host Indira Lakshmanan interviewed Republican Party of Florida Chair Evan Power, who said the lesson he took from last week’s elections was that “when we lead boldly, like we have here in Florida, the voters have backed us up. I think in a lot of other places, especially Washington, D.C., Republicans haven’t led as boldly as they could.”
Lakshmanan countered, “There was a whole slate of things that voters said that they did not like about President Trump, including by the way, his immigration policy, which affects Florida heavily.”
Power declined to address the issue.
Elaborating further last week during his press conference in Tallahassee, DeSantis acknowledged, “You did have some people that had been here for a lot longer than just when [President Joe] Biden let everybody in in. So, it was an issue, but it was not the overriding issue.”
The governor has shown little concern for undocumented immigrants who have lived in the United States without committing crimes. Earlier this year, a group of Florida sheriffs and police chiefs said they planned to urge the Trump administration to create a citizenship path for crime-free undocumented immigrants. “Some came here inappropriately only to do better for themselves and their family,” said Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd.
But the governor would have none of that.
“[To say] you come illegally and then you stay until you commit a really violent crime — that just doesn’t work. It’s incoherent, and it’s not what the president ran on,” he said during an event in Bradenton a few days later.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Veterans in their fields
description: More than, “thank you for your service,” we need to ask ourselves “what is our collective obligation” to our veterans, gay and trans veterans alike.
text:
When the War for American Independence came to an end in 1783, American soldier and sailor Elisha Fisher was finally free. He had spent the better part of seven years enlisted in the patriot cause, ending his service aboard an infamous British prison ship in New York Harbor. 
Now he ambled the city’s streets with no money and no food, asking passersby for assistance. Some gave him a few coins, others, he said “less than nothing but frowns.” Fisher, writes historian John Ruddiman in his book about Revolutionary soldiers Becoming Men of Some Consequence, “began his postwar life as a homeless beggar.”

Jason Smith

I often find myself thinking about Elisha Fisher and others like him. I remember them on Veterans Day, yes, but also on many others. He comes to mind whenever I encounter a weather-beaten man on some well-trod street corner of New Haven, grasping a cardboard placard with the words “homeless” and “veteran.” 
Fisher returned to me again a few days ago while I was driving home from Southern Connecticut State University where I teach American history, my car radio tuned to a report of rising VA mortgage rates. Many of us already know the egregious statistics on veterans’ suicide and their broader struggles to get jobs or to receive basic healthcare.
At my university, I regularly encounter the bureaucracy of GI Bill educational benefits that a surprising number of my students are trying to access and then to navigate, and I see the unwavering lengths to which campus veterans’ advocates go to support our students, their comrades. Many of these students are justly proud of their military service, but they are also left cynical –—some even embittered—- at their service and its fraught aftermath. Not a few turn to history for answers.
Some of those student-veterans join me and others in an annual Veterans Day tombstone cleaning at a New Haven cemetery just a short walk from our campus. There, we tend to 87 uniform headstones in the so-called “Grand Army of the Republic Plot.” The GAR was an enormous organization for Civil War veterans of the Union Army. In the first decades of the last century, the GAR and the city purchased burial plots for veterans who died too poor to pay for their own. Many of these men served in so-called “colored” regiments, all-Black units in an army that fought to destroy slavery, but not segregation.

A volunteer cleans the headstone of Civil War veteran Willoughby Tribble during a cleanup at New Haven’s Westville Cemetery, helping preserve the memory of those who served. Credit: Isabel Chenoweth / SCSU

In 1865, the American artist Winslow Homer painted “The Veteran in a New Field.” It depicts a man just home from the Civil War, his back turned to the viewer, a scythe in hand, reaping a field of golden wheat. The painting, on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, evokes the oft-repeated turning of swords into ploughshares, the gratitude and relief that comes with the end of war and the embrace of peace. Awaiting Homer’s soldier-turned-farmer is an unbroken field of gilded grain in all its amber waves, stretching ever on toward the future. Tranquility and a modicum of prosperity would be gold enough, the artist seems to imply, a rich reward for service and sacrifice on behalf of one’s nation. 
When we put Elisha Fisher or the men and women at attention on our streetcorners or those buried in the GAR plot or the ones who study in our college classrooms next to Homer’s veteran in his field, the disparities sometimes appear quite stark. 
On this Veterans Day -—and, indeed, every day until the next-— as those of us who have never put on uniforms in service to the nation offer our gratitude, we would do well to remember these veterans past and present—that is, not only those depicted in the triumphal poses of so many iconic paintings and photographs and ceremonial arches. 
More than, “thank you for your service,” we need to ask ourselves “what is our collective obligation” to these men and women, to gay and trans veterans alike, to Black sailors, Hispanic soldiers, and women pilots —some of whom are now being redacted from our national histories not long after belatedly being put there in the first place. 
These are extraordinary, ordinary people, trying to make it in America. Many are simply attempting to access what is best about the prosperity and equity embedded in so many American Dreams, dreams that our ancestors fought, died, and struggled to make and then to preserve. More than anything, however, we must wonder and remember what becomes of those who served and fought —and of those who are still fighting — in our country’s seemingly endless wars. 
Jason W. Smith is a Professor of History at Southern Connecticut State University in New Haven where he teaches and writes about American military history and the convergence of war and American society.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Honoring our veterans takes more than gratitude
authors: State Sen. Paul Honig, State Rep. Jaime Foster and State Rep. Hubert Delany
description: When individuals enlist in the military, they make a commitment whose demands can extend far beyond their years in uniform.
text:
When individuals enlist in the military, they make a commitment whose demands can extend far beyond their years in uniform. In return, our government promises that support will continue after military service ends.
The promise should mean something practical: help navigating benefits, access to care, and support for families managing the lasting effects of service. Speeches and ceremonies matter, but gratitude must be matched by action.
In Connecticut, our HERO Acts (a series of laws supporting veterans, service members, and military families) put that responsibility into practice. Together, these measures address the financial, health care, and administrative challenges that can follow military service. Each builds on a straightforward principle: benefits are only meaningful when veterans can access them.
For many veterans, that begins with having someone who can help them navigate a complicated system.
We increased the required staffing at Connecticut’s Office of Advocacy and Assistance from 10 to 19 employees, including an increase from eight to 14 veterans’ service officers. These officers help veterans understand their eligibility and pursue the benefits they have earned.
Requiring more positions, however, is only the first step. We must ensure those positions are filled and that veterans can receive the assistance they need.
We also expanded protections so that certain federal veterans’ pension benefits are not counted as income when determining eligibility for specified state assistance programs, to the extent federal law allows. Those programs include help with energy bills, health coverage, Medicare costs, temporary family assistance, and home care for older adults.
For a veteran on a fixed income, that distinction matters. A pension intended to provide financial stability should not unnecessarily make it harder to qualify for help heating a home or receiving care. Eligibility still depends on the rules of each program, but these protections address a barrier that can leave families struggling despite the benefits they receive.
Our work on dental care shows how one law can lay the groundwork for the next.
The first HERO Act required an examination of gaps in veterans’ dental care. This year, we followed through by establishing a Veterans Dental Care Access Program, with applications scheduled to begin in January 2027.
The program is intended to help eligible veterans who do not receive VA dental care access services such as examinations, fillings, crowns, dentures, and oral surgery. It is an upcoming source of assistance, and making sure veterans understand how and when to apply will be essential.
We have investigated actions to improve access to nursing home care for qualifying veterans and begun examining ways to expand long-term care options.
These commitments extend to military families. Spouses manage households during deployments. Children change schools because of military orders. Families adjust together to the long-term effects of service.
The HERO Acts help military-connected children maintain educational support when they move, including children receiving special education services. They also support children transitioning into Connecticut’s early intervention programs. We expanded higher education fee waivers for eligible veterans and National Guard members.
These measures address everyday concerns: continuing an education, maintaining a child’s services, and managing household expenses.
Veterans and families seeking help understanding benefits and eligibility can contact Connecticut’s Office of Advocacy and Assistance at 1-866-928-8387.
Passing legislation is only the beginning. Our responsibility is to ensure that programs are implemented, services reach those who need them, and families know where to turn. Veterans and their loved ones should not have to navigate the lasting burdens of service alone.
Honoring our veterans takes more than gratitude. It takes leadership, legislation, and the commitment to follow through.
State Rep. Jaime Foster (D-57) is House Chair; State Sen. Paul Honig (D-8) is Senate Chair; and Rep. Hubert Delany (D-144) is Vice Chair of the Connecticut General Assembly’s Veterans and Military Affairs Committee.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Boise City Council approves 6-month moratorium on large data center construction
description: A standing-room-only crowd of more than 100 people applauded after the Boise City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to place a six-month moratorium on the construction of large new data centers. The moratorium went into effect immediately, and applies to all data center projects that are 100,000 square-feet or larger, or use 20 megawatts of […]
text:
More than 100 people attended a public hearing on a six-month data center moratorium on Nov. 10, 2026 at Boise City Hall. After the hearing, the Boise City Council voted unanimously to approve a six-month moratorium in new large data center projects. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)A standing-room-only crowd of more than 100 people applauded after the Boise City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to place a six-month moratorium on the construction of large new data centers.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The moratorium went into effect immediately, and applies to all data center projects that are 100,000 square-feet or larger, or use 20 megawatts of power. 
Passing the moratorium means Boise will not accept or process any applications for large data centers that fall within the moratorium’s parameters.
“It’s a six-month moratorium that will put the brakes on hyperscale data centers in Boise, so it gives us the time to better determine and understand the impacts that these will have,” said Boise Mayor Lauren McLean, who proposed the moratorium Friday. 
McLean said the city does not currently have any large data center applications pending.
“I’m doing this now before we have an application so that we can be sure that we get it right,” McLean said. 
Boise city officials will use the moratorium to review code and policies, study the impact on water, energy use, wastewater, noise and public safety, and gather public feedback.
Chief of Staff Hannah Brass Greer said Boise’s existing code does not address data centers.
“One of the things we would be doing is looking at our code and where it would fit and what restrictions or guidelines we want to put in place,” Brass Greer said. 
The Boise City Council approved the emergency moratorium following an approximately one-hour public hearing during its meeting Tuesday at Boise City Hall. 
 ‘Don’t sell off our future to the highest bidder’: Public testimony supported the pause




Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Everyone who spoke during the public hearing either supported the data center moratorium or asked city leaders to go even farther. 
“Just please don’t sell off our future to the highest bidder,” Sydney Hair told the Boise City Council. “I am very concerned about this. AI has taken so much from my generation and it is taking so much from the planet.”
Mia Benson, a junior at Marsing High School and a fellow at the Idaho Climate Justice League, urged council members to approve the moratorium and develop strict permanent regulations around data center construction. 
“I encourage the city of Boise to collaborate with the local community to develop accountability policies within the next coming months that require future data center projects to cover 100% of their power costs, use 100% clean energy, pay 100% of their taxes and be 100% transparent on anything that impacts the public,” Benson said. “Data centers are not worth the intense pollution and depletion of our water resources.”
Officials from several groups including the Golden Eagle Audubon Society, Conservation Voters for Idaho, the Idaho Conservation League, the Wilderness Society and Idaho Data Center Reform, added their support to the moratorium.
“Given the potential long-term and irreversible impacts these centers may have on our landscapes and lives, we applaud the foresight this ordinance provides,” Cynthia Wallace of the Golden Eagle Audubon Society said. “Voting to approve this ordinance could also inspire other governments to preemptively evaluate and regulate data center permit requests.”
Nobody spoke in favor of data centers or urged the Boise City Council to reconsider the moratorium. 
Lisa Young, director of the Idaho Chapter of the Sierra Club, applauded McLean and the Boise City Council for taking on data centers.  
“We commend Mayor McLean for hearing the growing concerns of Boiseans and proposing a moratorium on data centers within Idaho’s largest municipality, and we hope this will encourage other neighboring cities and Ada County to do the same,” Young said in a written statement. 
Data centers – and their energy use, water use and impact on wildlife – have become hot-button public issues in Idaho.
Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, recently turned on a new data center south of Kuna.
Meanwhile, Conservation Voters for Idaho Executive Director Ryan McGoldrick told the Idaho Capital Sun he is monitoring multiple data center proposals across Idaho. That includes a proposed 4-million-square-foot Rhea Data data center proposed south of Boise that the Washington Sun broke the news of and another data center proposed outside of Twin Falls. 
The Boise City Council is not the first local government entity in Idaho to place a moratorium on data center construction.
In July, the Bannock County Board of Commissioners in eastern Idaho signed a 180-day moratorium on accepting or processing data center permit applications to give officials time to study and draft a comprehensive data center ordinance.

name: Mississippi Today
title: More than a dozen key races remain too early to call one week after Election Day
description: Deputy clerk Devin Black, right, assists Cheryl McGee and Johnny McGee Sr., who came to verify their identification after voting by affidavit on Election Day, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, at the Hinds County Courthouse in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
WASHINGTON — The strength of Democrats’ majorities in the House and Senate remains undetermined one week after Election Day as more than a dozen races are still too early to call Tuesday.
Democrats are on track to hold 54 Senate seats in January, but could pick up one or two more from Republicans as votes are counted in Alaska and Mississippi. With 255 seats in the House, Democrats will have their largest majority elected to the chamber since the 2008, with the potential to pick up several more seats as the remaining races are called.
Here’s a look at where things stand in some of the uncalled races:
Mississippi’s Senate seat too early to call
Late in the afternoon Tuesday, Democrat Scott Colom was about 2,600 votes ahead of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the race for Senate in Mississippi.
There are two key deadlines in the vote-counting process in Mississippi this week: Mail-in absentee ballots must be received by Tuesday, and counties are required to submit their certified election results — including tallies of provisional ballots — to the state by Friday.
Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde-Smith.
It is unclear exactly how many ballots are left to count.
Unlike in some other states, there is no central vote reporting system for Mississippi, and few counties release election results online. Instead, Associated Press journalists and analysts communicate with each of the state’s 82 counties directly for the latest available information on vote counts.
The state will certify its results on Dec. 3.
On Monday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said about 14,200 provisional ballots had been processed, of which about 80% were accepted, and about 2,700 mail-in absentee ballots had not yet been returned.
Mississippi does not have automatic recounts or permit candidates to request a recount. Recounts in the state are held only in the event of a court order. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is eligible for a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
Vote count is ongoing in Alaska Senate race
Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 2,500 votes in Alaska’s Senate race on Tuesday afternoon, with an estimated 76% of the vote counted. The results of some absentee ballots are expected to be released late Tuesday, though the final absentee ballots mailed back from outside the U.S. are accepted as late as Nov. 18, 15 days after Election Day.
Ranked choice voting could also affect the timeline. Peltola is just over 1 percentage point short of the majority needed to win outright. If neither candidate wins a majority, the race will proceed to ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18. The state’s “target date” for certifying the election results is Nov. 25.
Recounts in Alaska are automatic only in the event of a tie vote. Candidates may also request a recount within five days of the state’s certification.
More than a dozen House races are still up in the air
In most of the House races that have not been called, the margin between the leading candidates was less than 1 percentage point among votes counted as of late Tuesday afternoon.
In North Carolina, four races remain undecided, the most of any state, and Republican incumbents were being challenged in all. There are no automatic recounts in North Carolina, but candidates may request a recount if the margin between candidates is 1% or less of the total votes. The state must receive the recount request by noon Eastern time Nov. 17, two business days after the county canvass in the state. The state is scheduled to certify its results Nov. 24.
In California, only one of the remaining House races, in the 23rd District, will affect the chamber’s balance of power. The other uncalled race is between two Democrats. Mail ballots must be received by Tuesday and counties must certify their results Dec. 3. The state will certify its results Dec. 11.
In South Carolina’s 2nd District, a recount is ongoing in the race between Republican incumbent Joe Wilson and Democrat Zyon Khalia. Wilson led Khalia by only about 3,000 votes in the original tally by late Tuesday afternoon, when 99% of the votes had been counted.
In Minnesota’s 1st District, the race was still undecided late in the afternoon Tuesday, with about 300 votes separating the top two candidates and an estimated 99% of votes counted. Recounts are not automatic in Minnesota, but a candidate can request a publicly-funded recount if the margin between the winning and losing candidates is less than 0.25% of the vote.
In Tennessee’s 4th District, about 300 votes lay between Democrat Victoria Broderick and Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais as of late afternoon Tuesday. In that state, recounts are held only as part of a legal challenge in the courts. There are no automatic recounts, and losing candidates may not request recounts.
Two governorships remain undecided
Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher led state Republican Senate President Ty Masterson in the race for governor of Kansas by less than 1 percentage point late Tuesday afternoon. On Nov. 4, the state announced that a close-race audit of election results requiring a hand count of selected ballots had been triggered in six close Kansas races, including the gubernatorial race. The audit must be completed before Nov. 16, the day by which counties must certify their results.
In the race for governor of Alaska, only about 76% of votes were estimated to have been counted late Tuesday afternoon, and the Democratic candidate, Jonathan S. Kreiss‑Tomkins was leading Bernadette M. Wilson by about 45,000 votes, 49.6% to 28.9%. The race will advance to ranked choice tabulation if no candidate receives more than 50% of votes.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Feds consider next steps after losing challenge to Montgomery County gun law
description: The U.S. Department of Justice will contemplate how to proceed after a federal judge this week dismissed its challenge of a Montgomery County restriction on firearms in public places that the administration claims is unconstitutional.
text:
Montgomery County police were named as defendants in an unsuccessful U.S. Justice Department against a Montgomery County restriction on firearms in public places. A court Monday dismissed the suit. (Photo by WTOP)The U.S. Department of Justice will contemplate how to proceed after a federal judge this week dismissed its challenge of a Montgomery County restriction on firearms in public places that the administration claims is unconstitutional.
“The Department is assessing the decision and next steps, but remains committed to protecting the Second Amendment rights of law abiding citizens in Maryland,” Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels said in email Tuesday.
Judge Theodore Chuang of the U.S. District Court for Maryland wrote in a 33-page opinion Monday that the federal government was not likely to prevail in its challenge of the law, which was passed as an emergency measure in July.
That law prohibits firearms within 100 yards of public locations like government buildings, parks and schools. It actually narrows the scope of prohibited areas, removing hospitals, healthcare and childcare facilities and others, to comply with a separate court ruling, Chuang wrote.
County Executive Marc Elrich (D) released a statement on welcoming Chuang’s ruling on the law that was approved July 27.
“I am pleased that this legal challenge has been resolved in the County’s favor,” Elrich wrote
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“We will continue to stand by our responsibility to keep Montgomery County safe and to ensure that our public spaces remain places where residents can gather with confidence,” his statement said. “Our commitment remains unchanged: protecting our residents, supporting our communities, and using every lawful tool available to promote public safety.”
The federal government filed suit Aug. 3, a week after Elrich signed the bill into law, challenging the law and naming, the county, the coulnty police department and Sheriff Maxwell Cornelius Uy as defendants.
The Justice Department charged that the law violated the Second Amendment right to bear arms as well as the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994. That law allows the attorney general to file civil action to “obtain appropriate equitable and declaratory relief to eliminate the pattern or practice” that “deprives persons of rights, privileges, or immunities” protected in this country. It came into place after the police beating of Rodney King in Los Angeles in 1991.
The county argued that Justice had not provided any evidence that county police were engaged in a “pattern or practice” of prohibited behavior over the week-old law. Chuang agreed, writing that the suit was “devoid of any allegations of any actual conduct by law enforcement officers relating in any way” to the new law.
In fact, he wrote, there was “no claim or record of actual enforcement actions taken by Montgomery County law enforcement officers” not only on the new law, but on its predecessor or any “earlier Montgomery County laws relating to possession or transportation of firearms in or near places of public assembly.”
Appeals court upholds most of Maryland ban on weapons in schools, parks, other public places

Chuang, who held a hearing on the case Oct. 1, ruled that the Justice Department had never used the law enforcement act to “challenge solely to invalidate a state or local law absent any police misconduct.”
That left the government challenging the constitutionality of the law on its face, and not on any action of officer, which Chuang said would be a “breathtakingly broad expansion of federal power in advancing civil enforcement actions by the federal government against state and local governments.”
“The federal government should not have unfettered authority to intrude on the actions of state and local governments,” Chuang wrote. “And Congress, not the Executive Branch, must decide on when such intrusions are warranted by the need to protect individual rights.”
The county’s law is similar to a state law approved more than three years ago, that was immediately challenged in separate suits: One by Susannah Warner Kipke, the wife of Del. Nic Kipke (R-Anne Arundel), and the Maryland State Rifle and Pistol Association, on First, Second and 14th amendment grounds; and another by Katherine Novotny and Maryland Shall Issue, along with the Second Amendment Foundation.
U.S. District Judge George L. Russell III combined the complaints into one case, before ruling in August 2024 to uphold most of the Gun Safety Act of 2023.
A federal appeals court in January upheld most of that law that bans guns within 1,000 feet of a public demonstration or at places such as parks, sports venues and schools. The court said an exception to “sensitive places” did not apply on “private property held open to the public,” where the law prohibits guns without specific permission from the property owner.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Microplastics in the Chesapeake: Report finds contaminants in Maryland waterways
description: A small-scale study of water samples taken from 15 different sites in the Chesapeake Bay watershed found microplastics at every site, whether in the form of plastic fiber, film, beads or fragments, environmental groups announced Tuesday.
text:
Nina Harbison, right, an associate with Maryland PIRG, speaks in Baltimore on Tuesday about a report showing microplastic contamination is present in Chesapeake Bay waterways, beside Baltimore Harbor waterkeeper Alice Volpitta. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)A small-scale study from the advocacy group Environment America found evidence of microplastics throughout the Chesapeake Bay watershed, the group announced Tuesday.
Using citizen scientists, the group collected several water samples at 15 different places throughout the watershed, including five sites in Maryland waterways. They found microplastics at every site, whether in the form of plastic fiber, film, beads or fragments.
“Plastic pollution is pervasive, and it’s a danger that’s not just out there in some patch across the ocean. It’s right here. It’s knocking at our front door,” said Baltimore Harbor waterkeeper Alice Volpitta during a news conference Tuesday along the Baltimore waterfront.
The results, according to several local environmental groups, are strong evidence that Maryland lawmakers should move forward with legislation this year to curb plastic pollution, including a bottle return program that would reimburse Marylanders who drop off plastic drink containers for recycling.
Mr. Trash Wheel, the first trash wheel to be installed by Baltimore’s Waterfront Partnership in 2014, is pictured Tuesday. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
The environmental groups unveiled the report Tuesday beside Mr. Trash Wheel, one of the four anthropomorphized trash-collecting machines installed around the Baltimore Harbor by the city’s Waterfront Partnership.
In 2025 alone, the four wheels collected 768,000 pounds of garage and debris from the city’s waterways, said Allison Blood, senior manager of environmental projects and advocacy at the Waterfront Partnership.
“While that’s an impressive accomplishment, we know that cleaning up the pollution downstream is not a long-term solution. We need to turn off the tap upstream,” Blood said.
Microplastics are particularly insidious because their small size — less than 5 millimeters, or about the size of a sesame seed — means they aren’t easily collected by the wheels.
“Unlike an apple or piece of paper that will decompose gradually over time, plastic breaks down into smaller and smaller pieces of plastic,” said Nina Harbison, an associate at Maryland PIRG, a sister organization to Environment America.
Once they enter the ecosystem, these microplastics are often consumed by fish and other wildlife, causing a host of health issues. Microplastics can attract and carry pollutants found in the water, and release chemical pollutants of their own, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Plastics and their associated chemicals can delay developmental stages, hinder reproduction and make it more difficult for animals to fight disease, according to the agency.
Microplastics have also been found in the human body, and some studies have associated them with a greater risk of human health problems. For instance, in a study of patients with plaque buildup in their arteries, patients with microplastics in plaque had a higher risk of heart attack, stroke, or death.
The study from Environment America tracked microplastics at Maryland sites along the Patapsco, Choptank, Nanticoke and Susquehanna rivers — and in the Chesapeake Bay itself near Talbot County. Lab researchers also analyzed samples from sites in Washington, D.C., Virginia, Pennsylvania and New York.
All of the sites contained plastic microfibers, 93% of them contained microfragments, 47% had microfilm and 27% had microbeads.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
There is no “silver bullet solution” for addressing the “mini menace” of microplastics, Harbison said. But PIRG is among the groups that think a bottle return system would go a long way in Maryland.
Maryland’s “bottle bill,” as it’s known, has been introduced repeatedly in the Maryland General Assembly. The current iteration has been introduced in each of the past four years, but has yet to receive approval from the full House or Senate.
Under the bill, plastic producers would contribute funds to operate the program, which would be overseen by the Maryland Department of the Environment.
Meanwhile, environmental groups point to other wins, including 2025’s passage of broader “extended producer responsibility” in Maryland, requiring various packaging producers to pay fees that help cover the cost of recycling the materials.
In 2015, Maryland enacted a ban on “synthetic plastic microbeads,” in personal care products and over-the-counter drugs, which were added to rinse-off personal care products for exfoliation or cleansing purposes.
Maryland has also taken action on other harmful packaging materials. Beginning in 2020, Maryland banned most uses of polystyrene, also known by the brand name Styrofoam.
Since the ban took effect, Baltimore’s Waterfront Partnership has seen an 83% reduction in polystyrene collected by its trash wheels, Blood said. Similarly, the partnership has noted a 55% reduction in plastic bag pollution collected by the wheels, after a local plastic bag ban.
“These reductions demonstrate that policies can prevent plastic pollution from reaching our waterways in the first place,” Blood said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Children’s Mercy reaches agreement, will be covered by ACA marketplace insurance
description: TOPEKA — Children’s Mercy patients will have an insurance option on the Affordable Care Act Marketplace after the hospital reached agreement with UnitedHealthcare. “Beginning Jan. 1, Children’s Mercy will be in-network with UnitedHealthcare ACA Marketplace plans, expanding access to specialized pediatric care for children and families across the Kansas City [...]
text:
Children's Mercy's logos and locations are found throughout the Kansas City area, including greeting people arriving at the Kansas City International Airport. The hospital announced that it reached agreement with UnitedHealthcare to accept its Affordable Care Act marketplace plan, so that patients would have an ACA option. A previous announcement that it wouldn't be in-network for any ACA plans upset parents reliant on the facility's care. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Children’s Mercy patients will have an insurance option on the Affordable Care Act Marketplace after the hospital reached agreement with UnitedHealthcare.
“Beginning Jan. 1, Children’s Mercy will be in-network with UnitedHealthcare ACA Marketplace plans, expanding access to specialized pediatric care for children and families across the Kansas City region,” a Children’s Mercy news release said.
The hospital announced in late October that it would not be covered by any ACA Marketplace insurance plans after Medica, which it had accepted in the past, decided to exit the market in Johnson and Wyandotte counties in Kansas, and in Clay, Jackson, Johnson, Lafayette, and Platte counties in Missouri.
Upset parents, concerned about losing insurance for their children, posted on social media when they learned about the lack of ACA Marketplace insurance.
“We are pleased to work with UnitedHealthcare and provide an in-network option for families who rely on ACA Marketplace coverage,” the hospital news release said. “This announcement reflects a shared commitment to helping children access the specialized care they need, while providing greater choice for families selecting coverage for 2027.”
ACA open enrollment is open through Jan. 15 and families must select a plan by Dec. 15 for coverage to begin Jan. 1, the release said. 
The hospital is also in discussions with other ACA marketplace health plans about in-network access, the news release said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Democratic wave in NC flips a sixth Congressional seat as counting wraps up
description: Last Tuesday was a good night for North Carolina Democrats, who rode a blue wave to upset five Republican congressional incumbents. As counting continues, one more seat appears to have been added to that list. After provisional and cured absentee ballots were counted Tuesday, in unofficial results, Democratic former state lawmaker Raymond Smith appears to […[...]
text:
Republican Rep. Greg Murphy faced Democrat Dr. Raymond E. Smith, Jr. in North Carolina's third congressional district. (Photo: U.S. House and Smith's campaign website) Last Tuesday was a good night for North Carolina Democrats, who rode a blue wave to upset five Republican congressional incumbents. As counting continues, one more seat appears to have been added to that list.
After provisional and cured absentee ballots were counted Tuesday, in unofficial results, Democratic former state lawmaker Raymond Smith appears to have defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Greg Murphy in the race for the state’s 3rd Congressional District. 
In unofficial returns on election night, Murphy held a slim lead of 233 votes over Smith. But as provisional ballots were added to the unofficial totals, Smith overtook Murphy with a net gain of 526 votes. With all counties reporting, Smith now leads by 293 votes. 
Libertarian candidate Daniel Cavender received 3,007 votes, many times the difference between the two frontrunners. 
If the tally holds in official results, Murphy’s will be the sixth Republican seat Democrats flipped in North Carolina this midterm election, changing the makeup of the state’s congressional delegation from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to 11 Democrats and three Republicans. 
Murphy has held the 3rd District, considered a safe Republican seat, since 2019.
Last year, at the urging of President Donald Trump, Republican state lawmakers sought to unseat Democrat Don Davis in the 1st Congressional District by making the district more Republican-leaning. They did that by swapping some Democratic voters out of Davis’ 1st District into Murphy’s 3rd District.
Republicans went on to lose both the 1st and the 3rd Districts, an outcome sometimes called a “dummymander.”
There could still be very minor changes to the final tallies. Military and overseas votes that were mailed by Election Day will still be counted if they’re received by 5 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 12. The ballots of voters whose eligibility has been successfully challenged could still be removed. 
The counties will hold their canvasses Friday, Nov, 13. The race is subject to a recount if requested by the second-place candidate once the canvass is completed.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Wildfire season officially ends in Washington – state Lands Commissioner seeks future funding
description: The wildfire season in Washington state is officially over.  In 2026, “more than 1,500 fires ignited and nearly 1 million acres burned across the state,” Public Lands Commissioner Dave Upthegrove said Tuesday.  “We saw nearly a thousand homes destroyed from the Colville Reservation to Okanogan and most notably, here in Spokane. We saw 65,000 people […]
text:
By clearing out brush, needles and dead limbs, prescribed fires reduce the "ladder fuels" that can cause wildfires to spread into tree canopies and devastate forests. (Photo by Alex Brown/Stateline)The wildfire season in Washington state is officially over. 
In 2026, “more than 1,500 fires ignited and nearly 1 million acres burned across the state,” Public Lands Commissioner Dave Upthegrove said Tuesday. 
“We saw nearly a thousand homes destroyed from the Colville Reservation to Okanogan and most notably, here in Spokane. We saw 65,000 people in our state’s second largest city have to evacuate.”
At its peak, more than 8,500 people were on the ground fighting Washington’s fires, Upthegrove said. They came from everywhere: 27 states and four countries. Gov. Bob Ferguson called in the National Guard. Troops from Joint Base Lewis-McChord joined too. 
The destructive wildfire season coincided with the fourth year in a row that Washington state has faced a drought. 
“There’s no signs the scientists tell us that that’s going to change anytime soon,” Upthegrove said.
Earlier this year, the Legislature fulfilled a 2021 commitment to put $60 million into wildfire prevention and forest health, using revenue from the Climate Commitment Act. Upthegrove is asking them to fund it again next year, amid a budget shortfall. 
“Public safety is a core basic function of government, even in tough fiscal times,” he said. “Without that funding, we are likely to see more fires … and more risks to life and property.”
The department uses about half the funding to prepare for the season. That includes training personnel, buying equipment and supplies, Upthegrove said. About $15 million is used for forest health work such as thinning trees and prescribed fire. Another $15 million helps communities develop wildfire defense plans and carry out fuels reduction work, he added.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Voting rights group flags thousands of NC provisional ballots for review
description: A North Carolina voting rights organization is urging state election officials to closely review thousands of provisional ballots cast in last week’s general election.  The group says its team found voters who may have been eligible to vote in their counties but were required to cast provisional ballots instead.  The Southern Coalition for Social Justice […]
text:
Voters in line at the Durham County South Regional Library for the last day of early voting on Oct. 31, 2026 contributed to North Carolina's record-breaking midterm early voting turnout. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)A North Carolina voting rights organization is urging state election officials to closely review thousands of provisional ballots cast in last week’s general election. 
The group says its team found voters who may have been eligible to vote in their counties but were required to cast provisional ballots instead. 
The Southern Coalition for Social Justice said in a letter to the State Board of Elections that it identified 2,504 potential matches between provisional ballot records and the state’s voter registration files. 
The organization said some voters were listed as having no record of registration or as having previously been removed from the rolls, despite having matching records in the voter files. 
The North Carolina Board of Elections didn’t respond to NC Newsline’s request for comment on the group’s allegations. 
The findings come as county boards of elections review provisional ballots before the counties hold their canvasses Friday. These boards must determine whether those voters were eligible to vote and whether their votes can be counted. 
Hillary Harris Klein, senior counsel for voting rights at the SCSJ, said the organization reviews ballot data after elections to examine who had to vote provisionally, why they did so, and whether their ballots are counted.  
Hillary Harris Klein, senior counsel for voting rights at the SCSJ. (Photo: Courtesy SCSJ)
This year, this group raised its concerns before the canvass because it found what it described as troubling patterns in the provisional ballot records. 
“This time we’re raising alarm bells during the election because we were concerned about all this purported messaging about something being wrong with our voter rolls, and that they have too many ineligible folks,” she said. 
The organization’s analysis identified two broad groups of voters. 
The first includes 1,562 voters whose provisional ballot records listed them as having no record of registration or as previously removed, but whom the organization matched to active or inactive voter registration records in the same county. 
The second group includes 942 voters the organization said had been removed through the state’s voter list maintenance process but later attempted to vote in the same county where they had previously been registered. 
SCSJ said it sent letters and county-specific lists to election officials in 46 counties where it identified potential matches. They said election workers could have made errors, like misspelling voters’ names, which can make voter records difficult to match. 
Klein said the first group includes voters with active and inactive registrations. Voters with inactive registrations are still eligible to vote, she said, though some may have had other reasons to cast a provisional ballot, such as moving within their county.
She said the group has found similar issues in previous election cycles. 
“We’ve consistently seen folks showing up to vote and learning that they’ve been kicked off the voter rolls,” she said. “The list maintenance is very aggressive in North Carolina.”
Voters can be removed from voter registration rolls for a variety of reasons. Those can include moving out of the state or moving to a different county, duplicate registration elsewhere, new conviction for a felony, or being considered inactive. 
Inactive voters are voters who did not cast ballots in at least two general elections and did not contact their county board of elections to verify eligibility. 
Last year, the state removed more than 400,000 inactive registrations from its voting base. 
North Carolina law provides a process for reinstating certain voters removed through the list maintenance process. Under state law, a voter who appears to vote and confirms they’ve continuously lived in the county may be reinstated.
The State Board of Elections says provisional ballots are used when questioning a voter’s eligibility to vote a particular ballot. 
Reasons can include a voter’s name not appearing on the registration rolls at their voting location, voting at the wrong precinct Election Day, or being unable to show a form of photo ID. Eligible provisional ballots are added to election results during the canvass period.
The state board’s canvass is scheduled for Nov. 24.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Shifting counts leave Second Plymouth race unresolved as recounts loom
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: Until the outstanding ballots are resolved, results are certified, and any requested recounts are completed, the Second Plymouth District race remains without a definitive winner.
text:
ONE WEEK AFTER Election Day, the race for the Second Plymouth District seat in the Massachusetts House of Representatives remains unsettled.
Republican incumbent Rep. John Gaskey and Democratic challenger Sarah Hewins both at different points have declared victory or claimed to be winning in the district that includes all of Wareham and Carver and part of Middleborough.
Gaskey, a Republican from Carver, won the seat in 2024 after defeating incumbent Rep. Susan Williams Gifford in the Republican primary. Hewins, a Carver Select Board member, previously ran for the seat as a Democrat in 2016 and 2018, losing to Gifford both times. In 2024, she ran as a write-in candidate.
Republicans entered the election with 25 seats in the Massachusetts House, already a small minority against a Democratic supermajority. Democrats flipped a handful of Republican-held seats on November 3, and the Second Plymouth race could determine whether the Republican caucus loses three or four seats.
The unofficial totals in the Second Plymouth race have shifted, candidates have relied on different sets of figures to support competing claims, and questions remain about how preliminary numbers were reported and corrected in Wareham.
As of Tuesday afternoon, November 10, the local clerks did not provide vote totals when asked.
Both candidates are pursuing recount options, according to Secretary of State William Galvin spokesperson Deb O’Malley.
How the race has unfolded
Tuesday, November 3 — Election Day: According to the Wareham Week, Gaskey declared victory after results from Carver and Middleborough became available, before Wareham’s full results were included. The newspaper later reported that he declared victory based on those two towns’ numbers. At that point, the district-wide outcome remained dependent on Wareham, which accounts for a substantial share of the district’s voters.
Wednesday, November 4 — No official call: By approximately 4:30 p.m., Gaskey told the News Service that the race remained uncalled. The Wareham Week reported that Hewins “appeared” to have narrowly defeated him with an 89-vote margin. That same day, Speaker Ron Mariano announced that Democrats had gained four House seats, with his spokesperson confirming Gaskey’s seat was included in that tally but offering no figures to explain the calculation.
Thursday, November 5 — Hewins acknowledges an apparent lead: Preliminary town results showed Hewins ahead. Reached Thursday morning, Hewins told the News Service, “So far we’ve won. We’ll see what happens when they certify the vote.” She added, “Talk about every vote counts.” She also noted that Gaskey “can ask for a recount.” Gaskey, meanwhile, told the News Service that his campaign remained committed to the process and would allow the results to be determined without interference or pressure. He did not directly answer whether he intended to seek a recount.
Friday, November 6, morning — Hewins leads by 89 votes: Unofficial totals posted online by town clerks showed Hewins with 9,264 votes to Gaskey’s 9,175, an 89-vote advantage. Those figures did not include hand-counted ballots. The breakdown showed Gaskey winning Carver, his hometown, 2,787 to 2,573, and Middleborough, 1,840 to 1,417. Hewins was winning Wareham, 5,274 to 4,548, per the unofficial tally. Her advantage in Wareham outweighed Gaskey’s leads in the other two communities. At the time, the margin fell within the half-of-one-percent threshold required for a district-wide recount.
Friday, November 6, afternoon — Gaskey’s campaign declares victory: The figures appeared to shift again. Gaskey’s campaign manager, Jason Ross, provided the News Service with what he said was an updated preliminary results spreadsheet emailed by Wareham Town Clerk Lisa Johnson to both candidates. The email listed 4,719 votes for Gaskey and 5,305 for Hewins in Wareham, a different breakdown from the earlier figures. Ross announced that Gaskey had won reelection by 64 votes. The campaign combined the new Wareham figures with Carver’s previously posted results and updated Middleborough numbers of 1,889 for Gaskey and 1,453 for Hewins. Ross said Gaskey had obtained the Middleborough and Carver figures in person from the town clerks.
Gaskey also issued a statement thanking voters for returning him to the State House. “This is a reminder of just how important it is to listen to the concerns of every voter, to never take their support for granted, and to continue to work to make their lives better and our government more accountable to them,” he said. The News Service could not independently confirm the updated Middleborough figures with its town clerk, nor did it receive confirmation from either the Carver or Middleborough clerk that the numbers supplied by the campaign were accurate.
Monday, November 9 — Wareham corrects its spreadsheet: Gaskey said in a statement posted online that Wareham Town Clerk Lisa Johnson had emailed both candidates a corrected spreadsheet Monday, explaining that Friday’s version “was incorrect and contained typographical errors.” According to Gaskey’s statement, the replacement spreadsheet listed 4,588 votes for Gaskey and 5,306 for Hewins in Wareham. Gaskey said the corrections reduced his reported total by 131 votes and increased Hewins’s by one, a 132-vote swing that reversed the apparent district-wide victory his campaign announced Friday. According to his statement, the changes included a 100-vote reduction in his Precinct 6 Election Day tabulator count, a 30-vote reduction in his Precinct 3 early-processing count, and the removal of one hand-counted vote in Precinct 4. Hewins gained one vote in the Precinct 6 tabulator count.
Gaskey called on Galvin’s Elections Division to investigate, review the underlying tabulator tapes and hand-count records, and independently verify Wareham’s revised totals. He said “voters deserve an accurate count and a full explanation when the numbers provided by election officials inexplicably changed enough to reverse the apparent outcome.”
Tuesday, November 10 — Recount petitions and unanswered questions: Asked about Gaskey’s request for an investigation, Galvin spokesperson Deb O’Malley said, “If a candidate believes that the unofficial results that have been posted are not accurate, the appropriate remedy is to request a hand recount. Rep. Gaskey has obtained petitions for a precinct-level recount and a districtwide recount. I believe that Sarah Hewins is also circulating districtwide recount petitions.”
The News Service contacted Wareham Town Clerk Lisa Johnson on Tuesday afternoon seeking updated totals, copies of the spreadsheets shared with the campaigns, and information about outstanding ballots. Johnson said over the phone, “Everything is still preliminary,” and directed further questions to email. She did not respond to the subsequent questions. The Carver and Middleborough clerks also did not respond to requests for updated totals, outstanding ballot counts or information about recount petitions. Neither campaign returned calls seeking an update Tuesday afternoon. O’Malley did not directly address whether any review beyond the recount process was planned.
What happens next
Recount petitions must be submitted to town clerks by Friday, November 13, at 5 p.m., then certified district-wide recount petitions are to be filed with the secretary of state’s office by Wednesday, November 18, at 5 p.m.
Until the outstanding ballots are resolved, results are certified, and any requested recounts are completed, the Second Plymouth District race remains without a definitive winner.

name: California
title: Fired judge’s lawsuit alleges California was illegally approving insurance rate hikes
description: The lawsuit also accuses Ricardo Lara and top Insurance Department officials of undermining administrative law judges’ authority.
text:
In summary
The lawsuit also accuses Ricardo Lara and top Insurance Department officials of undermining administrative law judges’ authority.




An administrative judge in California’s Insurance Department who was fired last year is suing  Commissioner Ricardo Lara and his former special counsel, accusing them of illegally approving insurance rate increases and undermining the judicial branch of the department. 
Kristin Rosi, former chief administrative law judge for the department, filed the lawsuit in Alameda County Superior Court in late September. She alleges that Lucy Wang — the former special counsel who was also a deputy insurance commissioner — and other top officials at the department retaliated against her for calling out their practices and refusing to comply with orders to revoke or change her rulings.
“When Judge Rosi was making rulings consistent with the law she was informed improperly that she ought to rule certain ways, and that she ought not to hold hearings,” said Rosi’s lawyer, Wendy Musell. Rosi will not be giving interviews about the lawsuit, Musell said.
Gabriel Sanchez, an Insurance Department spokesperson, did not address CalMatters’ questions about the lawsuit or a request to interview Lara. “We have no comment,” he said in an email. 
Rosi’s lawsuit paints a picture of an Insurance Department that regularly breached the separation of its executive, legal and judicial branches — including in rate reviews in which the department approved how much insurers can charge homeowners for their policies. The allegations come at the end of Lara’s eight years at the helm, which have been beset with controversy that included him accepting insurance-industry donations and making decisions that allegedly benefited those contributors; criticism about his overseas travels; and major wildfires that affected insurance availability and affordability. 
“The judges observed that the underlying rate processes included settlement agreements for unprecedented rate increases, and it was relatively apparent that the Department was using prior rate approval procedures that are neither codified by insurance law, nor found in the regulations,” the lawsuit alleges.
Californians’ home insurance premiums have increased 23% since 2023, according to comparison website Bankrate.com.
Rosi also filed complaints last year against four people from the department, including Wang, with the California State Bar. Those cases are pending and have not been made public, but CalMatters obtained copies of the complaints. 
They give more detailed accounts of the judge’s allegations, which are related to rate reviews. That process involves insurance companies requesting rate increases and “intervenors” who are ratepayers or advocacy groups such as Consumer Watchdog that can object and get compensated for doing so, under California law. The department’s legal branch reviews those requests, and the executive branch has the final say, in some cases after the judicial branch has weighed in. The judicial branch provides a “neutral forum for conducting fair and independent evidentiary hearings and mediations,” according to the Insurance Department’s website.
The complaints say that Wang, and in at least one case Lara, as the people deciding on the rate reviews, should not have been meeting with the legal team about cases being reviewed by that same team without including all stakeholders, such as insurance companies and intervenors. It’s similar to how in lawsuits, a judge cannot meet with one side without the other also being present. 
In October 2024, in approving Consumer Watchdog requests for compensation, Rosi said in her ruling that she found that the department was approving rate requests without following the law. 
Wang and other members of the department — some of whom may later be named in Rosi’s lawsuit — then began to wrest away power from the administrative law judges, according to the suit. At one point, Lara emailed Rosi and asked her to “get on board” with the department’s plan dictating what’s in the judges’ jurisdiction, including “instruction to review settlements in rate proceedings only when a notice of hearing has (been) issued,” the lawsuit said.
Wang declined to comment on the lawsuit. She said, “I was sued in my official capacity as Special Counsel and am being represented by the (attorney general’s) office, so I can’t comment on the present litigation.” She now works for a San Francisco law firm and represents insurance companies. 
When CalMatters asked Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office about representing Lara and Wang, the office deferred to the Insurance Department. 
Dave Jones, Lara’s predecessor who appointed Rosi as chief administrative law judge, called the allegations in Rosi’s lawsuit “shocking and disturbing.” 
“The way it’s supposed to work is that the commissioner gets walled off from the rest of the department when there is a hearing in a matter where the commissioner is the ultimate decider, by law,” Jones said. 
There is now only one administrative law judge left in the Insurance Department; that judge in a ruling in August alluded to an understaffed and underresourced judicial branch.
Harvey Rosenfield, founder of Consumer Watchdog, called the allegations “really dirty and scandalous.” He said Californians need to know that “people who engage in this conduct will be held accountable.”
Robert Herrell is executive director of Consumer Federation of California, which sometimes intervenes in the department’s rate reviews. He was a deputy commissioner under Jones. 
Herrell said that because of the separation between the branches in the Insurance Department, he did not have a lot of interaction with Rosi, but that he knew her to be smart, serious and well-respected. She had been an administrative law judge in the department since 2007, and was appointed chief in 2016.
“An (administrative law judge) calls balls and strikes… they wanted the (insurance) industry to win almost all the time,” Herrell said. “Too bad it took this long for some of this stuff to come out.”
Jones and Herrell both said Commissioner-elect Jane Kim should make it clear the department needs to follow the rule of law when she takes the reins in January.
“Jane Kim as soon as she’s sworn in ought to initiate an investigation of these allegations and not wait for a superior court to make a decision,” Jones said. The first case management conference in Rosi’s lawsuit is scheduled for Feb. 16.
Kim sent a statement via a spokesperson: “While I can’t comment on pending litigation against the Department, I am committed to transparency and accountability — in rate decisions, and in general.” She added that she plans to investigate the claims as soon as she takes office.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: The real emergency in Alaska is keeping the public in public lands
description: Alaska is facing a public lands emergency. Some of our best and wildest places are being handed over to private, usually foreign, industry — and Alaskans and U.S. taxpayers are footing the bill in order to do it. The latest example is the proposed West Susitna Industrial Access Road, which the Alaska Industrial Development and […]
text:
Denali looms over the west Susitna region. (Photo courtesy of Andrew Esola)Alaska is facing a public lands emergency. Some of our best and wildest places are being handed over to private, usually foreign, industry — and Alaskans and U.S. taxpayers are footing the bill in order to do it. The latest example is the proposed West Susitna Industrial Access Road, which the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority, or AIDEA, has convinced the Army Corps is an “emergency” to permit. Nothing could be further from the truth.
At the end of September, the day the Army Corps announced this “emergency” and an incredibly short three-week comment period, I was returning from a trip doing one of my favorite things in the world — floating and fishing the Talachulitna River in the West Susitna region. 
The trip was bittersweet. Years ago, my first cast on the Tal, I landed a 50-pound king salmon. It was once a place you and some buddies could triple up on massive kings. At least for now, in a story that’s all too common, those days are gone and Alaskans have fewer opportunities to fish. Still, the river is one of the most beautiful places on the planet, and we were able to get out after rainbows and grayling. 
When I got back to Anchorage, I heard the news and read over the 16-page application. As an Alaskan, a father, a business owner, a fisherman and a public land owner, I was enraged. Since when is it an emergency for U.S. taxpayers and Alaskans to spend hundreds of millions of dollars of our money destroying one of our best, most accessible wild places to build an industrial road for Outside and foreign-owned gold mining claims? The comment period for this decision, which started September 25, ended on October 13. 
This is AIDEA’s portion of the more than 100-mile West Susitna Industrial Access Road, which the State of Alaska has broken into segments, avoiding transparency for the entire project. AIDEA’s section alone is 78.5 miles. It would cross 148 streams, build 10 bridges and 140 culverts, and fill in 65 acres of wetlands with zero proposed mitigation. 
The real emergencies are already here, including the decline of our salmon — especially our kings — which this industrial road will accelerate. Another emergency is the way we are being cut out of the future of our own public lands. 
AIDEA has played a big role in that process. At the end of the summer Alaskans became outraged over AIDEA’s request for a 20,000 acre public land giveaway in the Houston area. AIDEA wants the land for free, claiming that handing the land over to them for an industrial park including potential data centers is a “public and charitable” use. 
Nothing about that is charitable. What AIDEA is proposing is taking public lands out of public hands and handing them over to industry, the vast majority of which is located outside the country or the state. In both instances, AIDEA claims it will all pencil out economically, but this is the same state-owned corporation whose poor financial decisions have cost Alaskans $10 billion since the early 1980s. AIDEA has failed project after failed project on the record books.
The West Susitna Industrial Access Road has also already cost Alaskans tens of millions of limited state dollars. This past August, on a weekday morning when most Alaskans were hard at work, the AIDEA board approved another $25 million Alaska dollars for the project. AIDEA is meant to be subjected to legislative oversight, but over the years, that oversight has eroded.
What is happening in the West Su right now is AIDEA’s playbook of handing over our public dollars and lands to foreign corporations, now with federal help. 
There is indeed an emergency. But the real emergency is forcing taxpayer-funded projects like this for Outside and foreign companies while everyday Alaskans struggle with grocery bills, high fuel costs, closing schools and neglected everyday needs. 
Alaska’s public lands, and public dollars, don’t belong to a small cabal of industry insiders. 
They belong to us all. 
Keeping the public in public lands is the real emergency.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Supreme Court hears Stein’s appeals of laws stripping governors’ powers
description: The North Carolina Supreme Court Tuesday heard two cases concerning Gov. Josh Stein’s powers to make appellate court appointments and fill state commission vacancies.  The Republican-led legislature has worked for years to limit governors’ appointment powers to various boards and commissions. The state Supreme Court’s opinions on these attempts have been mix[...]
text:
The North Carolina Justice Building, which houses the Supreme Court of North Carolina, pictured on June 2, 2026. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) The North Carolina Supreme Court Tuesday heard two cases concerning Gov. Josh Stein’s powers to make appellate court appointments and fill state commission vacancies. 
The Republican-led legislature has worked for years to limit governors’ appointment powers to various boards and commissions. The state Supreme Court’s opinions on these attempts have been mixed. 
One case heard Tuesday was Stein’s challenge of a law requiring that the governor’s appointments to vacant Court of Appeals and state Supreme Court seats be taken from lists compiled by the state Democratic or Republican Party executive committees. The law also requires the appointee to be from the same party as the person who vacated the seat. 
Sarah Boyce, Stein’s general counsel, said the state constitution leaves decisions about those appointments to the governor alone. 
“Once you permit the legislature to insert itself into the process by imposing qualifications, you have taken what the constitution specifically grants the governor and given it to other actors,” she said.
Boyce pointed out that Republican lawmakers themselves said in 2018 that that power rests with the governor. 
In 2018, voters rejected a proposed constitutional amendment to change how judicial vacancies are filled. The wording of the amendment said it would “change the process in which the Governor has sole appointment power,” she noted. 
If the legislature believed that the governor had the sole constitutional authority, what changed between 2018 and now to make legislators think they had the authority to do it on their own, asked  Democratic Justice Allison Riggs. 
Martin Warf, an attorney for the legislature, said there’s no way to know why voters rejected the proposed constitutional amendment because it included other changes. 
The law preserves the voters’ partisan choices for judicial seats, Warf said, and there’s no language in the state constitution prohibiting the legislature from creating a nominating pool. 
In the other case, Stein is appealing a law that cuts his appointments on the Environmental Management Commission, the Coastal Resources Commission, the Wildlife Resources Commission, and the Utilities Commission.
Appeals Court sides with NC General Assembly in latest lawsuit over appointment powers

The governor no longer appoints the chairs of the Environmental Management, Coastal Resources, and Utilities commissions. They are elected by commission members. 
Diminishing the governor’s role inhibits his ability as the state’s chief executive to ensure laws are faithfully executed, as required in the constitution, Stein’s lawyer Eric Fletcher argued. 
Lawyers for legislators and Treasurer Brad Briner, who was given a Utilities Commission appointment, said legislators have the option to take appointments from the governor and distribute them to other members of the Council of State, who are all also members of the executive branch.
Every statutory official swears an oath to follow the law, said Matthew Tilley, the lawyer representing legislators. 
The justices did not indicate when they would rule on the cases. 
Stein is also appealing a recent Court of Appeals decision upholding the law allowing the transfer of Board of Elections appointments from the governor to the state auditor.  The Supreme Court has not yet scheduled that case for oral arguments.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Trump withdraws Rudofsky nomination for federal judge post in Arkansas
description: President Donald Trump nominated Arkansas Supreme Court Justice and former state Republican Party chairman Cody Hiland to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals Tuesday, withdrawing his nomination of a federal judge he originally named for the post. Trump nominated U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky to the appeals court in August. The federal judge previously [[...]
text:
The exterior of the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse in St. Louis, Missouri on Friday, June 5, 2026. The courthouse includes the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas Supreme Court Justice Cody Hiland (Photo courtesy of Arkansas Secretary of State)
President Donald Trump nominated Arkansas Supreme Court Justice and former state Republican Party chairman Cody Hiland to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals Tuesday, withdrawing his nomination of a federal judge he originally named for the post.
Trump nominated U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky to the appeals court in August. The federal judge previously issued rulings narrowing the Voting Rights Act and in favor of a state ban on “indoctrination” in the classroom.
Hiland was nominated to the Arkansas Supreme Court to fill a vacancy by Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders in 2023, and was elected to a full term in March.
The nominee swap comes a week after Democrats won control of Congress, raising the odds that Trump nominees will have a more difficult time being confirmed in the Senate next year. If Rudofsky was confirmed to the 8th Circuit bench, it would have created a vacancy in the Eastern District of Arkansas.
Trump previously praised Rudofsky as someone who would be a “rock solid defender of the Constitution,” in a post on Truth Social announcing the nomination. 
Republicans rammed through Supreme Court nominees. Now Democrats will have the votes to stop them

Hiland served as the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas during Trump’s first term in office, and was the prosecuting attorney for Faulkner, Van Buren and Searcy counties prior to that. After leaving the federal prosecutor’s office, he worked for the Arkansas Department of Public Safety and for Sanders’ 2022 campaign. He became chairman of the Republican Party of Arkansas the same year.
Since joining the Arkansas Supreme Court in 2023, Hiland authored an opinion striking down a state law that changed which state courts could hear constitutional challenges.
If confirmed, Hiland would replace retiring Judge Bobby Shepherd, a nominee of former President George W. Bush and father of Republican state Rep. Matthew Shepherd and U.S. District Judge Thomas Shepherd.
Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin said on the social media platform X that Hiland’s experience made him an “excellent choice” for the appeals court.
