name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey names new climate chief after Hoffer’s departure
description: Aladdine Joroff, an attorney who has held roles teaching at Harvard and served as Boston’s climate policy director, assumes the post as Healey heads into a second term fraught with complicated climate and energy issues.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY didn’t wind up looking far for her next climate czar, elevating a top deputy to a role she created on her first day in office in 2023 to marshal a whole-of-government response to climate change.  
Aladdine Joroff, who has been serving as the deputy climate chief since 2024, will take over as climate chief, Healey announced Tuesday. She replaces Melissa Hoffer, who started in the role as the nation’s first ever Cabinet-level climate chief when Healey took office nearly four years ago. 
Hoffer is set to become president of Vermont Law and Graduate School in December, leaving just days after a midterm election that saw a decisive reelection victory for Healey and a nationwide blue wave that catapulted Democrats back to power in Congress. 
“I’m excited to continue the transformative work Chief Hoffer has led to implement the Healey-Driscoll administration’s vision of a government wide approach to climate change,” Joroff said in a statement.  
Joroff, an attorney who has held roles teaching at Harvard and served as Boston’s climate policy director, assumes the post as Healey heads into a second term fraught with complicated climate and energy issues.  
Bay Staters are grappling with an energy affordability crisis that has left lawmakers frozen as a legislative remedy stalls, and the state is barreling toward a legal requirement to cut greenhouse gas emissions in half by 2030 from 1990 levels. Plus, Massachusetts has been hit hard by President Trump’s cancellation of new offshore wind projects that were poised to deliver a jolt of clean power.  
The federal hostility paired with soaring energy costs has raised fresh questions about whether the state can meet its targets or should slow its green transition.  
Healey has embraced natural gas as part of her all-of-the-above approach to bring in more energy supply, slow the growth of skyrocketing utility bills, and meet growing power demand. 
She highlighted that support on the debate stage last month with GOP challenger Mike Minogue.  
She also urged the Trump administration to speed up federal approvals of one planned gas expansion that she supports — and opened the door to a potentially much larger one in the works. 
Hoffer, though, appeared to back away from that position in a “farewell address” she gave Monday to environmental advocates when an attendee asked what her “magic wand” change would be.  
“We should be putting in place a hard stop on natural gas infrastructure,” said Hoffer, who previously served as a top lawyer at the US Environmental Protection Agency under President Biden, worked with Healey at the state attorney general’s office, and held top roles at Conservation Law Foundation. “It should be phased out by 2050. That is the rational thing to do.” 
In a wide-ranging interview with CommonWealth Beacon earlier this year, Hoffer, who has known the governor since their Northeastern law school days and ascent up Mt. Washington in the 1990s, praised the pace of the Healey administration’s climate agenda.  
At the time, Hoffer defended the climate chief role and ticked off accomplishments, from compelling hospitals track their emissions to establishing nation-leading biodiversity goals.  
Yet in the face of skepticism from some advocates and energy industry and public officials, she acknowledged the structural challenges she faced in getting a sprawling state bureaucracy to collaborate with someone who isn’t in their direct chain of command and has no regulatory authority and a modest budget. 
“We are asking people to do things differently, and that can be quite threatening sometimes,” Hoffer said in June. 
With Hoffer’s last day on Monday, it will now be Joroff making that entreaty.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa set to receive $216 million in second year of federal rural healthcare program
description: Iowa was awarded $216 million from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for the second year of the state’s rural health care improvement plan, “Healthy Hometowns.” This funding comes as part of the Rural Health Transformation Program, the federal grant program created as part of the 2025 “One, Big, Beautiful Bill” Act in an […]
text:
(Stock photo by Getty Images)Iowa was awarded $216 million from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for the second year of the state’s rural health care improvement plan, “Healthy Hometowns.”
This funding comes as part of the Rural Health Transformation Program, the federal grant program created as part of the 2025 “One, Big, Beautiful Bill” Act in an effort to offset losses for healthcare providers caused by Medicaid cuts. The 2025 law is set to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion over ten years, according to Congressional Budget Office estimates.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is set to offer states a total of $50 billion in grants over five years. This will not be enough to offset the estimated funding losses, but Republican leaders have said these investments offer targeted funding to help address specific needs in states like Iowa, such as funding for cancer prevention services and expansion of rural healthcare access.
Iowa’s “Healthy Hometowns” received $209 million for Fiscal Year 2026 through the federal funding program, which was fully distributed by the end of October 2026. That yearly funding total grew by $7 million for the second year of funding, which a news release from the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services stated “reflects continued confidence in Iowa’s implementation of Healthy Hometowns and the state’s leadership in transforming rural health care delivery, expanding access to essential services including cancer treatment and prevention, and build long‑term sustainability for hospitals and clinics across rural Iowa.”
In the program’s second year, the state department stated in plans to continue working on projects that started in the first year of funding. This includes funding for cancer screening and treatment, improving the state’s system for sharing health records, and expanding the “hub-and-spoke” model of healthcare delivery in rural areas through the existing Centers of Excellence system.
Other efforts to increase rural healthcare access include investments in mobile Emergency Medical Services (EMS) care services that can go into communities without a nearby healthcare facility, as well as providing funding to allow multiple healthcare providers with different specialties to share space and coordinate services within a community.
“Year 2 is about building on the foundation we’ve established and continuing to turn this investment into meaningful results for rural communities,” Iowa HHS Principal Deputy Director Larry Johnson said in a statement. “We’re focused on working with health care providers and community partners to strengthen services, support the rural workforce, and ensure these investments deliver lasting benefits for Iowans.”
Overall, the federal program is distributing $10 billion across all 50 states for the upcoming fiscal year. Iowa is ranked 11th in how much money it is set to receive — Texas was granted the largest award of almost $282 million for FY 2027, while New Jersey is set to receive the lowest amount at $142 billion.
CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said in a statement the program “gives states the resources and flexibility to bring care closer to home and build stronger, more sustainable health care systems for their rural communities.”
“As the program enters its second year, this next round of funding will help Iowa build on the progress made in year one and continue working toward lasting improvements in access, quality, and health outcomes for rural communities,” Oz said in a news release.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Lawmakers OK rules that could weaken West Virginia’s Aboveground Storage Tank Act
description: The Rulemaking Review Committee on Tuesday put its stamp of approval on a regulatory change that loosens how aboveground storage tanks are governed.
text:
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, is the only member of the Rulemaking Review Committee who on Tuesday who voted against making regulatory changes that loosens how aboveground storage tanks are governed. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)The Rulemaking Review Committee on Tuesday put its stamp of approval on a regulatory change that loosens how aboveground storage tanks are governed. 
The committee voted 8 to 1 to move forward with a rewrite of the regulations that accompany the Aboveground Storage Tank Act, which was passed in the wake of the Freedom Industries spill that left 300,000 people without water in the Kanawha Valley in 2014. 
“This is without a doubt the most egregious rule we’re going to pass,” Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, warned prior to the vote. 
The Department of Environmental Protection commenced a rewrite of the rule after lawmakers passed a bill earlier this year to exempt tanks that hold brine — frequently a byproduct of natural gas drilling — if it holds less than 210 barrels. 
Proposed to help “mom and pop” gas companies, lawmakers watered the bill down as it worked its way through the chambers of the Legislature. 
The West Virginia Rivers Coalition, during the public comments period on the rule changes, flagged that many provisions nixed in this year’s bill are now written into the regulations.  
Young asked legislative staff attorney Robert Akers why this happened. 
“Because the executive branch has decided they want them in,” Akers said. 
“So even though the Legislature said, ‘We don’t want these things,’ they can say, ‘Well, we’re going to do them anyways,’” Young said. 
Akers pointed out that the proposals weren’t explicitly forbidden in the law, so they could move through rules. 
The changes include allowing inspections on tanks with the highest risk of contaminating water to be inspected monthly, rather than every 14 days, if those tanks meet certain national standards, and gives the secretary of DEP the ability to extend a nine-month window for a newly designated tank. 
The DEP agreed to nix that last rule, but the committee did not amend it. So it was passed as is. 
Other changes included adding definitions to what constitutes a “leak,” “discharge” and “release.” Del. Bob Ferenbacher, R-Wood, lauded the definitions, saying in his experience the agency was using them interchangeably. 
He also defended the change in frequency of inspection. 
“The state of West Virginia, by adoption of this rule, this modification of this rule, are basically adopting national standards, as opposed to something more conservative, perhaps depending on the inspector’s perspective, more onerous than what this national standard requirement is,” Ferenbacher said. 
Ferenbacher’s county is home to Chemours, which has settled recently for releasing chemicals into the Ohio River. In that case, the contamination came from a landfill, not an aboveground storage tank. The company is now the target of a class action lawsuit. 
Prior to adoption of the rule, Young asked for the votes to be recorded individually. While Young is just one of two Democrats on the committee, there were only nine members present, giving her enough votes to successfully make the motion. 
Sen. Patricia Rucker, R-Jefferson, Sen. Brian Helton, R-Fayette, Sen. Darren Thorne, R-Hampshire, Del. Jonathan Kyle, R-Randolph, Del. Sarah Drennan, R-Putnam, Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanwaha, Del. Mike Hornby, R-Berkeley and Fehrenbacher voted in support of the rule. 
Young was the sole dissenting vote. 
The rule will now go to consideration of the whole Legislature in January.

name: National
title: Young, diverse voters showed up for midterms as older, Trump voters stayed home
description: Much of the midterm “blue tsunami” came from diverse, enthusiastic young voters with financial struggles who flocked to the polls, and also Trump voters sitting out the election, according to two experts analyzing turnout in a handful of states with detailed results.  The results, they say, could mean a mandate for bringing costs down and […]
text:
Sioux Falls residents vote in South Dakota's general election on Nov. 3.Turnout fell to a historic low in the state as Democrats gained in the Republican-dominated legislature. Democratic gains in many states could be explained more by the turnout gap than by voters switching their allegiance. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight) Much of the midterm “blue tsunami” came from diverse, enthusiastic young voters with financial struggles who flocked to the polls, and also Trump voters sitting out the election, according to two experts analyzing turnout in a handful of states with detailed results. 
The results, they say, could mean a mandate for bringing costs down and more power for young Latinos, but also a danger for Democrats if Republicans rally back to the polls in 2028. 
“It looks like more Trump voters who didn’t vote Republican stayed home rather than switching (to Democrats),” said Lenny Bronner, founder of Broome Street Labs and a data scientist formerly with the Washington Post, based on his analysis of 13 states with detailed results. 
“Those voters are easier for the GOP to win back than those who chose a Democratic candidate,” Bronner said. 
Bronner estimated 75% of Democratic gains came from a turnout gap and about 20% from Republicans switching sides and voting for Democrats.
His analysis included turnout data for Texas, Georgia, South Carolina, Colorado, New Mexico, Virginia, North Carolina, Arkansas, Iowa, Florida, West Virginia, Minnesota and Michigan. The share of Democrats’ gain that came from a turnout gap ranged from 40% for Texas to 133% for Michigan among the states he studied; some states had only partial detailed results.
Bronner wrote on X (formerly Twitter) that partial results in Texas showed that voters flipped their ballots more than expected; 45% of Democratic gains there came from voters switching away from Republicans. “So far, Texas is the only state where our model indicates that persuasion explains more of Democrats net gain than turnout does!” he wrote.
A University of Florida political science professor, Michael McDonald, also saw a turnout surge for young voters faced with high grocery bills, student loan debt and sluggish wages, based on detailed results from Georgia and Colorado. Trump’s older voter constituency was more likely to stay home, he wrote in a Substack post. 
In both Colorado and Georgia, 18- to 25-year-olds had the biggest jump in turnout compared with the 2022 midterms, he wrote, while it fell for voters older than 40. 
“This all makes sense when you realize that we just witnessed the most diverse electorate for a midterm election in U.S. history, with big increases over 2022 in Latino turnout,” McDonald wrote. “Latinos are markedly younger than whites, so if their turnout increases it means more younger voters are in the mix.”
Democrats romped in state elections. What will they do with their newfound power?

Even in Florida, where Republicans continued to dominate elections, GOP turnout was lower than in 2022 despite a registration drive that increased Republican registration by 400,000, McDonald wrote in another Substack post. Republican Gov. Rick DeSantis’ drive to purge voter rolls, affecting mostly Democratic and unaffiliated voters, may have played a role, he wrote. 
“DeSantis’ shrewd politics appears in part due to suppressing Democrat and unaffiliated votes through a massive voter registration purge that pushed Florida red, rather than rallying Florida Republicans to vote,” McDonald wrote.
On a statewide basis, midterm turnout increased almost 13 points in Mississippi since the last midterms, as the state appears close to electing its first Black senator since Reconstruction. Turnout fell to a historic low in South Dakota, where Republicans still dominate voting.
The University of Florida’s turnout calculations provide a window into overall turnout, which it measures as a share of voter-eligible population, excluding noncitizens and ineligible felons. McDonald did the calculations for the University of Florida’s Election Lab, and Stateline compared them to 2024 and 2022 turnouts for a state-by-state map.
The analysis shows the highest turnout for 2026 in Maine, Minnesota and Michigan, all at more than 63%, and lowest in West Virginia (33.3%), Oklahoma (37.1%)  and Hawaii, Indiana and Tennessee (all 38.2%).
South Dakota’s midterm vote remained heavily Republican, though Democrats gained legislative seats for the first time in 18 years. They took four new seats, for a total of 12 in the 105-seat legislature. 
South Dakota had higher turnout in 2022, possibly in part because of contentious statewide ballot measures for Medicaid expansion, which passed, and marijuana legalization, which failed. 
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Nurse’s license is revoked for financial exploitation of home-health patient
description: State regulators have revoked the license of a home-health nurse due to the financial exploitation of an elderly patient with dementia. Earlier this year, the Iowa Board of Nursing charged 51-year-old licensed practical nurse Danielle Renee Wilson, also known as Danielle Rainey, with committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare; committi[...]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)State regulators have revoked the license of a home-health nurse due to the financial exploitation of an elderly patient with dementia.
Earlier this year, the Iowa Board of Nursing charged 51-year-old licensed practical nurse Danielle Renee Wilson, also known as Danielle Rainey, with committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare; committing an act that causes injury to a patient; misappropriating the property of a patient; misappropriating money from a patient; and engaging in a relationship with a former patient when there is a risk of exploitation or harm to the patient.
The board alleges Wilson, who has lived in Altoona and Carlisle, worked for Angels Care Home Health and provided nursing services for an elderly woman named Patricia from December 2023 through May 2024. At the time, Patricia’s diagnoses included diabetes, chronic pain syndrome, obesity, congestive heart failure, arthritis, anxiety, atrial fibrillation and major depressive disorder.
In June 2025, the board received a complaint alleging Wilson had maintained contact with Patricia after home health services were discontinued and that Wilson had engaged in a personal relationship that resulted in financial exploitation.
According to the board, an investigation revealed that on June 12, 2024, Wilson became Patricia’s power of attorney, and was also executor of the woman’s will, and was named trustee of a trust that was created in Patricia’s name, and was nominated as the woman’s conservator and guardian.
According to the board, in January 2025, Wilson persuaded Patricia to sell her home in Pleasant Hill and purchase a new home in Mitchellville. Patricia paid $240,000 for the new home, after which Wilson, along with her spouse and two children, moved into the new home with Patricia, the board alleges.
The board asserts that Patricia’s financial information and resources were repeatedly used by Wilson and her husband, Chad, to acquire items unrelated to Patricia’s care. The transactions included nearly $40,000 in purchases related to a lawn care business owned by Danielle Wilson and operated by Chad Wilson, as well as a small, $400 motorbike that was utilized by one of the Wilsons’ children, and multiple transactions – some made out of state — at TopGolf, Menards, restaurants and gas stations.
The board alleges that medical records show that on May 1, 2025, Patricia, then age 78, completed a mental-competency examination that was indicative of dementia or severe cognitive impairment.
When interviewed by state officials and law enforcement officers, Patricia allegedly indicated she was unaware that she owned the home in Mitchellville and thought it belonged to Wilson. When asked about some of the transactions on her account, Patricia indicated she had not been to TopGolf but knew Wilson and her spouse went there.
Criminal charges lead to plea deal
State records indicate U.S. Postal Inspector Nicholas Kuehn investigated the matter and obtained multiple search warrants for Patricia’s financial records, saw the motorbike at the Mitchellville home, and later testified before the board that Patricia was not physically capable of playing golf or operating lawn equipment or the motorbike.
In August 2025, a Polk County judge determined dependent adult abuse had occurred and that Patricia was in need of protection. Her financial accounts were frozen at that time, and state officials were authorized to pay expenses on her behalf as needed.
On Aug. 29, 2025, Patricia was moved into an assisted living facility, and on Nov. 7, 2025, a dependent adult protective services assessment was completed by the state, which resulted in a determination that the complaint of dependent adult abuse through financial exploitation had been deemed to be founded.
Board records indicate that when interviewed by investigators, Wilson said it was Patricia’s idea to buy a new home so she could live with the Wilsons, and she denied asking Patricia to update her will or power of attorney. Regarding the purchases, Wilson allegedly stated her husband had purchased a lot of things with Patricia’s money without either woman’s knowledge.
When interviewed by investigators, Danielle Wilson allegedly admitted she was still in contact with Patricia and was regularly visiting her at the assisted living center.
In its recent, written ruling revoking Danielle Wilson’s nursing license, the board stated that Patricia’s “money was repeatedly used for items she clearly had no ability to use, including approximately $40,000 in lawn care equipment, a mini motorbike, and multiple visits to TopGolf. (Wilson’s) testimony that (Patricia) was the driver of their personal relationship and living arrangement, if true, does not excuse the clear boundary violation under the board’s rules. (Wilson) continued an inappropriate personal relationship with a client, which caused them significant financial harm.”
According to the board, Danielle Wilson is now on the state’s registry of abusers of dependent adults.
Court records show Danielle and Chad Wilson were each criminally charged with dependent adult abuse and financial exploitation of an older individual. As part of plea deals with Polk County prosecutors, the state agreed to dismiss the charges of financial exploitation of an older individual in exchange for guilty pleas on the dependent adult abuse charges, with the understanding they would seek deferred judgments on the latter charge.
In October, the two were awarded the deferred judgments, which will result in the convictions being expunged from their records after the successful completion of two years’ probation and the payment of civil penalties of $1,025 each.
Prosecutors on Tuesday asked the court to amend its sentencing orders in both criminal cases to require the payment of victim restitution in the amount of $50,000.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Danielle or Chad Wilson regarding the board action and criminal cases.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho judge orders release of police employment records to InvestigateWest, Invisible Institute
description: This article originally published in InvestigateWest on Nov. 10. Idaho State Police and the Idaho Department of Correction improperly withheld police employment records and other information from two news organizations, according to a state court ruling ordering the information be released.  InvestigateWest and the Invisible Institute sued the state agencies[...]
text:
After InvestigateWest and Invisible Institute filed a lawsuit seeking the records, Ada County District Judge Patrick J. Miller ordered Idaho State Police and Idaho Department of Correction to release information about officers’ employment history, including the dates of their employment and the reason for their separation. (InvestigateWest illustration)This article originally published in InvestigateWest on Nov. 10.
Idaho State Police and the Idaho Department of Correction improperly withheld police employment records and other information from two news organizations, according to a state court ruling ordering the information be released. 
InvestigateWest and the Invisible Institute sued the state agencies on June 16 for allegedly concealing information about officers’ employment histories that were previously disclosed to the news outlets. InvestigateWest used officer employment records to expose alleged sexual misconduct by dozens of Idaho prison guards in an October 2025 series, and to show how many were allowed to resign without facing other disciplinary action or criminal prosecution. The reporting prompted Idaho lawmakers to remove a loophole in a sexual abuse law that made it more difficult for prosecutors to charge prison staff, and to order an independent review of how the women’s prison system handles reports of sexual abuse.
After those stories were published, reporters from InvestigateWest and the Invisible Institute sought updated officer employment records, but the Department of Correction and state police denied those requests, stating that they would no longer disclose whether an officer retired, resigned or was fired. A records clerk also told the Invisible Institute that Idaho State Police leadership decided to “disable” a tool that allowed them to search an internal employment database. 
In a Nov. 5 ruling, Ada County District Judge Patrick J. Miller ordered the state agencies to release information about officers’ employment history, including the dates of their employment and the reason for their separation. That includes information about two former prison guards accused of sexually assaulting an inmate, who described the assaults and the mental toll it took on her to an InvestigateWest reporter. 
“This ruling is a win for government transparency — and accountability — in Idaho,” said Jacob Fries, InvestigateWest’s executive director. “These public records had been essential to our reporter’s work, which led directly to a new state law helping protect incarcerated people from abuses of power.”
State law broadly defines “employment history” to include the entire course of a person’s employment, from when it started to the nature of how it ended, Judge Miller wrote, concluding that whether someone was terminated, retired or resigned is public information.
The agencies argued that disclosing an officer was terminated, for example, would suggest potential disciplinary action against the individual, and that legislators specifically exempted disciplinary details from disclosure. Idaho State Police also claimed the requested employment history information was contained in confidential decertification files that it said are exempt. 
Judge Miller said disclosing the reason for separation doesn’t amount to revealing the underlying details behind an employee’s departure. And just because an officer’s employment history and dates of service are in the same file as confidential details doesn’t mean they “lose their character” as disclosable records, the judge wrote. 
The Idaho Public Records Act “does not categorically shield every piece of information contained within an otherwise exempt file. To hold otherwise would permit an agency to withhold nonexempt employment-history information based solely upon the location in which it is maintained,” according to the ruling.
The judge also ordered the prison system and state police to go back and search for database records requested by the news organizations. 
The Invisible Institute had previously obtained a database of all officers who had been certified in Idaho to date, and later requested updated information. The nonprofit public accountability journalism organization, which is based in Chicago, uses the data for its National Police Index, a searchable database of certified police and correctional officers by state and where they’ve worked.  
Idaho State Police responded that the tool it used to generate those reports was no longer in use because it was unreliable and was generating different results for the same queries. The agency said it had no records in response to the public records request. 
The state’s Public Records Act doesn’t require agencies create new records when one doesn’t already exist. But Miller said Idaho State Police’s decision to deactivate a tool doesn’t eliminate those records or “transform them into nonexistent information.” 
A public-facing search tool on the state Peace Officer Standards and Training website that allows people to search and retrieve similar information about officers is also “inconsistent” with ISP’s claim that it doesn’t have records, Miller said.
“An agency may not defeat the public’s statutory right of access by choosing to maintain public records in a system from which the agency claims it cannot retrieve them, by disabling a retrieval function, or by shifting to the requester the burden of identifying each responsive record by a name or identifier already contained within the agency’s records,” according to the ruling.
The court said Idaho State Police hasn’t shown that it properly searched for records and ordered it to go back and look for the information. 
Miller also ordered the disclosure of the names of several state employees accused of misconduct, finding they were improperly redacted from records. 
This litigation was supported by the National Freedom of Information Coalition through a grant from the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation, by the Society of Professional Journalists through a grant from the SPJ Legal Defense Fund, and a grant from the Idaho Press Club.

title: Powell says she’ll be ‘proud’ to vote for Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker
description: Nebraska 2nd Congressional District Rep-elected Denise Powell is ready to make history with her vote for leader.
text:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries hugs Denise Powell in North Omaha on Oct, 29. 2026. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — While some newly elected Democrats are debating whether Hakeem Jeffries should be House Speaker, the new House Democrat from Nebraska is ready to make history with her vote for leader.  
Denise Powell told States Newsroom in Washington, D.C., that she knows “how big a deal firsts are.” 
“I’m the first Latina to ever be in Congress for my state,” Powell said. “So I’m proud to vote for the first Black Speaker of the House.” 
Powell is coming off a historic victory in Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District, where she won by 15 points. Her answer about Jeffries has been consistent throughout the campaign. She told CBS News in October she would vote for him as leader.

Jeffries also campaigned for Powell in the last few days before Election Day. Democrats are coming into the next congressional session with a huge majority. name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina challenges public school students to read 10 million books in 2027
description: Can North Carolina public school students read 10 million books in one year? State Superintendent Maurice “Mo” Green thinks they can. Green announced the 10 Million Book Challenge on Tuesday, asking the state’s 1.5 million public school students to collectively read 10 million books in 2027. The campaign is intended to encourage children to read […]
text:
State Superintendent Mo Green speaks to the media about the 10 Million Book Challenge initiative, Nov. 10, 2026. ( Photo: Ahmed Jallow/NC Newsline)Can North Carolina public school students read 10 million books in one year? State Superintendent Maurice “Mo” Green thinks they can.
Green announced the 10 Million Book Challenge on Tuesday, asking the state’s 1.5 million public school students to collectively read 10 million books in 2027. The campaign is intended to encourage children to read for fun, at a time when fewer are choosing to pick up a book outside school.
“Learning to read and loving to read are not the same thing,” Green said. “We are teaching more children how to read. Now we want to be sure that they learn to love to read.”
The challenge begins Jan. 1. Students can log the books they read through an online platform, with each book counting toward the statewide goal. Picture books, graphic novels, audiobooks and books read aloud by parents or teachers will all count.
Participation is voluntary and students will not be tested on what they read.
Green said the challenge is meant to complement the state’s efforts to improve reading instruction.
Reading proficiency among students in grades three through eight rose to 55.7% in 2025-26, up from 50.1% two years earlier, Green noted.
Third-grade reading proficiency also increased, from 48.6% in 2023-24 to 55.3% last school year. Still, about 45% of third graders were not yet reading on grade, he said.
“We’re not declaring victory,” Green said. “We know that there is more work to be done, and we will do it.”
The book challenge is focused on getting children to read outside the classroom. Green cited national figures showing that the share of 9-year-olds who read for fun almost every day fell from 53% in 2012 to 37% in 2025. Among 13-year-olds, the share dropped from 27% to 14% over the same period.
The idea comes from a similar reading challenge Green led when he was superintendent of Guilford County Schools. The district initially set a goal of having students read 1 million books in a year. They read 1.1 million, Green said. The following year, the district raised the goal to 2 million. Students read 2.6 million.
Green said he believes students statewide can meet the 10 million target.
“I have amazing confidence in our students,” he said.
More than 170 public school units, including traditional school districts and charter schools, have signed on to help coordinate the challenge, according to Green. Businesses, nonprofits and community organizations are also supporting the effort.
The State Employees Credit Union and the Bojangles Foundation are serving as the campaign’s main sponsors. Other sponsors include First Citizens Bank, Book Harvest, Healthy Blue and Benchmark Education.
Green said sponsors have provided six-figure financial contributions, along with other support. The money will help pay for promotional materials and advertising, including billboards and social media campaigns.
The Department of Public Instruction has also built an online platform where students, families and educators can log books. The system will use automated checks to flag unusually high submissions, followed by reviews from school-level coordinators.
Molly McGowan Gorsuch, DPI’s strategic partnerships manager and a project lead for the challenge, said schools will have a month to review and verify their numbers before they are publicly released.
NC students show gains in testing, graduation rate reaches record high

DPI also plans to hold celebrations as students reach reading milestones, including 1 million, 2 million, 5 million and 10 million books.
School and public libraries will play a role in the effort, too. North Carolina has 90 public library systems and more than 400 library locations where students can find print books, e-books and audiobooks.
Ginger Young, founder and CEO of Durham-based Book Harvest, said giving children the freedom to choose what they read can help them develop an interest in books.
Book Harvest has distributed 3.4 million books to North Carolina children and families since 2011, she said.
“When kids get to choose what they read, and when they have someone cheering them on, they keep going,” Young said.
The statewide launch celebration is scheduled for Jan. 7.

title: Nonprofit celebrates personal finance and economic literacy
description: Jacqueline Brown speaks after being presented with the teacher of the year award during the Mississippi Council on Economic Education’s 2026 Forum on American Enterprise at the Jackson Convention Complex on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Business leaders, politicians and educators learned about the importance of financial and economic literacy at the Mississippi Council on Economic Education’s annual fundraiser. 
“If we all begin making decisions from a place of being better informed, we can make a meaningful impact on our families, schools, communities and society,” said Jaqueline Brown, a teacher from Okolona High School who received the award for economics teacher of the year at the Tuesday event.
The nonprofit works to increase economic and financial literacy by providing training and resources to students, adults and K-12 teachers in the state. Brown has completed all of the council’s certifications for teachers in subjects such as economics and entrepreneurship.
“You take teachers such as myself who come from rural communities,” Brown said. “We’re able to take those courses to become teachers of personal finance, economics, entrepreneurship and college and career readiness. And we’re better informed to bring that information back to our students.”
During this year’s legislative session, the lawmakers passed a bill expanding the requirement for financial literacy education for public school students. This is part of an expanding national effort to require financial education. 
“You’re going to see so much financial literacy coming forward from this where our children have a future because they will be more educated,” said Secretary of State Michael Watson, who was inducted into the council’s hall of fame during the event. 
“So only by understanding that by having financial literacy, and raising your economic intelligence, will we be able to be full participants in this economy and thus in the broader civil system,” said Kai Ryssdal, the host and senior editor of the public radio news program “Marketplace.”
Kai Ryssdal, host and senior editor of public radio show ‘Marketplace,’ speaks during the Mississippi Council on Economic Education’s 2026 Forum on American Enterprise at the Jackson Convention Complex on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026 Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Ryssdal talked with Bridget Bodnar, director of podcasts and co-host of his program’s kids podcast “Million Bazillion,” about the larger economic forces at play and how that impacts the lives of everyday people.
“We use business and the economy as a lens to tell stories about this society, and we do it in a way that we hope is accessible,” Ryssdal said. 
“You can tell someone how to manage a budget, but if they don’t understand the broader forces at play, why it matters what (Federal Reserve Chair) Kevin Warsh is doing and what that will mean to them, they don’t have the full picture,” Bodnar said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Sen. Rob Sampson to lead smallest GOP caucus in CT history
description: State Sen. Rob Sampson of Wolcott will lead the GOP Senate caucus of just three members, including Sens. Eric Berthel and Henri Martin.
text:
Sen. Rob Sampson was selected this week as the next Republican minority leader in the Connecticut Senate, setting him up to lead the smallest caucus in the chamber’s history with just three members. 
Sampson, a Wolcott resident who has served in the legislature since 2011, was already one of the most recognizable Republicans in the General Assembly because of his frequent appearances on the Senate floor, where he has filibustered many of the Democratic leaders’ bills in recent years.
In his newly elected leadership position, Sampson will become one of the most prominent figures in the Connecticut Republican Party, which is seeking to rebuild after devastating electoral losses across the state during this year’s midterm elections.
Sampson, by default, will become the highest-ranking Republican office holder in the state, given the party doesn’t hold any statewide constitutional offices and hasn’t held a seat in the state’s congressional delegation since 2008.
This week, Sampson and Sen. Eric Berthel, who was chosen as the Senate’s No. 2 Republican, issued a statement about their ascendence to the leadership posts, which were left empty after eight Republican-held seats were lost Nov. 3.
In the press release this week, the two Republican lawmakers vowed to rebuild their party’s numbers in the General Assembly, which have steadily declined since President Donald Trump’s first term, and they took a passing shot at some of the outgoing members of their own party.
The statement referred to “Republicans in positions of authority who were satisfied simply to remain in the minority.” And it accused those unnamed individuals of setting aside Republican principles when it was convenient. 
That stands in contrast to what Sampson is known for in the upper chamber: regularly speaking for hours on legislation he opposes.
[RELATED: Which Senators talked the most during CT’s legislative session?]
In an interview on Tuesday, Sampson said he did not want to frame the incoming Senate Republican caucus as the opposition party, and he suggested he was willing to work with his Democratic colleagues on bills he agrees with.
But he said he intended to use what little power the caucus maintains to highlight what makes Republicans different from the Democratic supermajority.
“If there is a failure among the Connecticut Republican Party as far as the legislature goes, it’s our inability to give a clear contrast and choice to voters,” Sampson said. 
Sen. Bob Duff, who was just elected as the Senate’s new president, said the three Republicans who remain in the Senate were duly elected by their constituents, and he respects the authority that those voters entrusted to those senators.
But Duff, who represents Norwalk and part of Darien, also emphasized that Democrats now hold a 30-seat advantage in the Senate, and he said he and his Democratic colleagues intend to use those numbers to advance their agenda, which includes addressing the high cost of living in Connecticut and challenging the policies of President Donald Trump.
He said it is up to the Republicans to decide how much of that agenda they want to support. 
The trio of Republicans who remain in the Senate — Sampson, Berthel and Sen. Henri Martin — received votes from roughly 65,000 people across their three districts, which cover parts of Southington, Bristol, Watertown and 19 other municipalities in the Naugatuck Valley region.
Sampson said he believes it is their job to represent every voter in the state who cast a ballot for a Republican this year. “We still represent 40% of the people across Connecticut who voted for Republicans,” he said.
Still, the senator recognized the physical and mathematical limitations to what Republicans can hope to accomplish over the next two years, considering they face a 33-3 disadvantage in the Senate.
Engaging in extended debate, Sampson said, will be more difficult in 2027 with only three Republicans available to hold the floor. 
“That’s diminished to the point where I don’t know it will be effective at all,” he said. “Even if we are putting in every last bit of effort, it will be so grueling and demanding that I don’t know how long we could keep it up for.”
The lopsided makeup of the Senate, Sampson said, will also make it next to impossible for the three Republican senators to participate in all of the more than 20 legislative committees. 
Sampson said his small caucus is going to have to rely on their Republican colleagues in the House, who also suffered losses this year, to keep them informed about what bills are working their way through those committees.
Given all of those constraints, Sampson said, the most effective tool that he and his Republican colleagues may have are Connecticut residents. And he said Republicans need to harness that power by organizing protests at the State Capitol.
During Gov. Ned Lamont’s first term, Republicans helped to organize protests, which contributed to lawmakers dropping a proposal to implement tolls on Connecticut highways. And in recent sessions, Republicans helped to rally large groups of parents who were opposed to Democratic proposals to increase regulations over homeschooling in the state.
“I think the No. 1 thing that we will utilize as a small three-person Senate Republican caucus is the public,” Sampson said. “We’re going to work very hard to make sure that when there are bills that are onerous to the benefit of Connecticut, we are going to invest our time and energy to make sure the public is engaged.”
Sampson is also banking on the Democrats encountering divisions within their own caucus over what policies to prioritize and which direction to take the party.
“I think trying to wrangle a very large caucus of members in both chambers is just as difficult as trying to figure out what to do when you have very few,” Sampson said. “Because they’re going to run the gamut. There is going to be a wide spectrum of Democrats, from people who are pretty darn moderate to people that I would consider extreme.”

title: Legislative priorities could focus on mental health diversion, Oklahoma lawmaker says
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma needs to focus on policies that divert people seeking mental and behavioral healthcare from emergency rooms and jails, a state lawmaker said Tuesday.  State Rep. Mark Lawson, R-Sapulpa, who chairs a special legislative committee on mental health funding, said that Oklahoma’s jails have become de facto mental health clinics even thoug[...]
text:
Rep. Mark Lawson, R-Sapulpa, left, is pictured speaking with reporters May 5, 2025, at the Oklahoma state Capitol. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma needs to focus on policies that divert people seeking mental and behavioral healthcare from emergency rooms and jails, a state lawmaker said Tuesday. 
State Rep. Mark Lawson, R-Sapulpa, who chairs a special legislative committee on mental health funding, said that Oklahoma’s jails have become de facto mental health clinics even though the people working in those facilities are not trained clinicians. 
Diverting people to the proper treatment venues is important as Oklahoma remains under the terms of a consent decree, Lawson told the crowd of about 100 people who were attending an event in Oklahoma City focused on the state of mental health in Oklahoma. The event was hosted by the Healthy Minds Policy Initiative, an Oklahoma City-based nonprofit focused on policy changes for mental illness and addiction in the state. 
The court-ordered decree requires the Oklahoma Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services to reduce the wait time for competency restoration services for jailed people with severe mental illness. 
“In the Legislature, it continues to be a priority for us to have a very healthy and robust mental health service array available to Oklahomans who need it,” Lawson said.
Lawmakers will also have many unknowns to deal with in the upcoming session, Lawson said. Gov.-elect Mike Mazzei will appoint a new leader for the Mental Health Department when he takes office in January, and there could be changing priorities in Congress after the midterm elections, he said. 
Zack Stoycoff speaks Oct. 23, 2024 at the Oklahoma Contemporary Arts Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Zack Stoycoff, president and CEO of Healthy Minds Policy Initiative, said programs that divert away from emergency rooms and jails are critical as the cost of treating people in these places is much higher than the cost of investing in proper treatment would be. 
In 2025, there were about 45,000 mental health-related emergency room visits in Oklahoma which carries a cost of about $266 million, he said. A large share of these visits were related to suicide, which Stoycoff said made up about a quarter of this cost. 
“The emergency room is the most expensive possible place to treat a mental health crisis,” Stoycoff said. “And until we have a healthcare or mental healthcare system that can adequately get upstream of the ER, we will continue to feel the burden of rising healthcare costs at the state Capitol for employers, for health plans, for providers, and everyday Oklahomans.” 
The cost of admission to an emergency room for behavioral and mental health-related visits is also rising, he said. 
In 2025, the average cost for a behavioral health-related admission was about $4,960. It cost an average of $6,450 for substance use disorder, and about $7,050 for suicidality, Stoycoff said. 
Strategic investment in mental health can produce long-term savings across public spending and economic activity, Stoycoff said. 
“We will all be waiting to see what changes happen federally after the recent elections, as they could dramatically alter the outlook for healthcare in 2027 and beyond,” he said. “But no matter what happens, we believe the path forward must recognize mental health not just as another line item, but as a solution.”

title: Hawaiʻi Supreme Court Weighs Who Is Worthy Of Freedom From Captivity
description:
State Supreme Court justices considered the case of unlawful detention Monday of Mari, 51 and Vaigai, 41, who have been detained for decades in Honolulu. Their attorney described the trials of their captivity — a dirt floor hard on their joints, and they are unable to bathe. A petition to the court on their behalf […]
The post Hawaiʻi Supreme Court Weighs Wh[...]
text:
State Supreme Court justices considered the case of unlawful detention Monday of Mari, 51 and Vaigai, 41, who have been detained for decades in Honolulu.
Their attorney described the trials of their captivity — a dirt floor hard on their joints, and they are unable to bathe. A petition to the court on their behalf said: “Mari and Vaigai’s lives are nothing but a succession of boring and frustrating days, damaging to their bodies and minds.”
But neither plaintiff was able to plead her own case.
For starters, both are nonverbal. Beyond that, both are too large to fit in the courtroom set up inside Punahou School’s expansive theater — or most any room for that matter.
That’s because both are elephants at the Honolulu Zoo.
Nonhuman Rights Project attorney Jake Davis presents oral arguments to the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court at Punahou School, part of the Supreme Court’s program Courts in the Community. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
The zoo is “a world away from the serene forests of their native homes,” Nonhuman Rights Project attorney Jake Davis said during Monday’s hearing. His plea to the court: Declare the elephants eligible for a hearing to determine whether they can go free. 
His organization says that the zoo’s 1.5-acre enclosure overly restricts Mari’s and Vaigai’s liberty, and that they should be released to a sanctuary closer in size to the 6,400 acres they would be able to roam in the wild. 
The Nonhuman Rights Project, a nonprofit civil rights firm, has so far failed to convince a Hawaiʻi court that elephants Mari and Vaigai are eligible for state-ordered release. The group’s 2023 petition was dismissed by the Circuit Court in 2024, a decision the Intermediate Court of Appeals affirmed earlier this year.
The group has tried to get elephants and chimpanzees freed in other states, including California, Colorado, Michigan and New York, but courts there too have ruled against it.
If the project’s attorneys are successful, it could challenge the legal framework that allows humans to keep animals in captivity. This idea is being litigated at a time when Mayor Rick Blangiardi wants the Honolulu Zoo to become even more of a draw with the addition of giant pandas.
Asian Elephant Vaigai checks out Honolulu Zoo visitors in August in Honolulu. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
Justices expressed concern that a ruling in the elephant’s favor could lead to attempts to free other animals. They also questioned the city’s claim that only human beings are eligible for release from confinement.
“There’s a lot of animals that have autonomy,” Justice Sabrina McKenna said as she questioned where to draw the line.
Chief Justice Vlad Devens presided over the hearing, which took place in the auditorium at Punahou’s Dillingham Hall Monday morning. Media, members of the public, city officials including council members Esther Kiaʻāina and Tyler Dos Santos-Tam, and roughly 450 students from Punahou and beyond squeezed in to watch. 
They witnessed a debate that careened from deeply serious philosophical discussions of freedom, to questions about the rights of household pets and a comparison to a character in the 1960s Flintstones cartoons who was an alien.
Are Elephants ‘Persons?’
The question at Monday’s hearing was not whether Mari and Vaigai can go free tomorrow. The Nonhuman Rights Project is seeking a habeas corpus proceeding, which would determine whether the elephants have claim to individual liberty. If the court agrees, there would still need to be a separate hearing where each side could bring in expert witnesses to argue their case.
Davis’s organization argues that Mari and Vaigai – female Asian elephants who have been kept at the zoo since 1982 and 1992, respectively – are intelligent beings forced to live under oppressive conditions far smaller and more isolated than their natural habitats. In the wild, elephants roam far and live in complex social groups. Not so in Honolulu.
The Honolulu Zoo is far smaller than an elephant’s typical range out in the wild. (April Estrellon/Civil Beat/2026)
The zoo enclosure’s ground has little cushioning for the elephants’ joints, the petition says, and it lacks adequate shade or water features deep enough to bathe.
“They can’t be elephants,” Davis told Civil Beat before the hearing. “You aren’t seeing elephants at the Honolulu Zoo. You’re seeing artifacts.”
Zoo Director John Berry, meanwhile, described their lives differently in a recent Civil Beat Community Voice opinion piece. Berry said the elephants are active and happy, and that they have deep relationships not only with each other but with their human keepers.
A legal method does exist for freeing those kept in captivity, but it only applies to “persons,” as written in Hawaiʻi state law, and a fundamental disagreement at the core of the case centers on whether Mari and Vaigai count as “persons.” 
“You aren’t seeing elephants at the Honolulu Zoo. You’re seeing artifacts.”Nonhuman Rights Project attorney Jake Davis
The legal procedure habeas corpus, meaning “produce the body,” dates back to the Magna Carta when it was used to prevent the King of England from secretly disappearing people into dungeons. As a concept, it is over 800 years old. It is known as the Great Writ, and it has been used to protect formerly enslaved people as well as children in custody cases. Nowadays, it is a common tool in immigration detention cases. 
Davis told the justices he’s not alleging that Mari and Vaigai’s captivity at the Honolulu Zoo violates any specific statute written by Hawaiʻi lawmakers. Instead, he argued their confinement violates the common law – a concept that develops continuously via court decisions – and that the court should consider the elephants as “persons” eligible for habeas corpus. 
Honolulu Zoo Director John Berry, third from the right, listens as Hawaiʻi Supreme Court hears oral arguments in Nonhuman Rights Project vs. City and County of Honolulu. Other officials in the audience included council members Esther Kiaʻāina and Tyler Dos Santos-Tam. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
Although the common law interpretation of habeas corpus has not yet been successfully used to free elephants from a zoo anywhere in the U.S., Davis said that shouldn’t prevent justices from ruling differently in this case. 
“The common law evolves,” Davis said during the hearing. “It is responsive to the times. It changes as society changes.”
Underlying the case was a broader question: Would a ruling in the group’s favor challenge humanity’s entire relationship with animals kept in captivity? Justices expressed concern that it might even extend to pets.
“The argument is it does create a slippery slope,” Justice Sabrina McKenna said. “So the courts could be inundated with these requests. If we were to recognize this, we would have to set some reasonable parameters. So would you limit it to mammals? Would you exclude domesticated mammals?”
Davis sidestepped the question. He said he doesn’t know the science of all non-human intelligence, but that in this specific case, elephants’ self-awareness, empathy and long-term memory – their “autonomy” – should make them eligible for release from confinement. 
The city argued against this autonomy-based claim.
“Autonomy is not the standard for entitlement to habeas relief,” Deputy Corporation Counsel Patricia Sendao said. 
Habeas corpus is only available for human beings, she said. Even past cases that dealt with formerly enslaved people or women and children – demographics the country has not always treated as full legal “persons” – gained their freedom simply because they were human beings, she said, not because of a ruling in some evidentiary hearing.
But McKenna and Justice Todd Eddins challenged the view that animals automatically should be treated differently than human beings. 
City and County of Honolulu Deputy Corporation Counsel Patricia Sendao delivers oral arguments as Nonhuman Rights Project attorney Jake Davis takes notes in the background. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
On the continent, McKenna said, denying animals their freedom comes from a different point of view — one that harkens to biblical times — compared to what is enshrined in the Hawaiʻi’ State Constitution, which has local Indigenous roots.
“It’s really based on Western cosmology, and the concept that animals are beasts under Genesis that are to be dominated and exist for human beings who are much more superior,” McKenna said of the mainland cases that have ruled against the release of captive animals. “Hawaiian culture is that living things are our relatives. We are not dominating beasts – these are our relatives that we must respect. So should that be considered?”
“Hawaiian culture is that living things are our relatives. We are not dominating beasts – these are our relatives that we must respect.”Supreme Court Justice Sabrina McKenna
Other courts have expressed “great reverence,” for animals, Sendao replied, but that doesn’t mean it’s appropriate to shift their legal status to “persons.”
Similarly, Eddins referenced a Flintstones character called the Great Gazoo, “a last-dash effort to increase their ratings” in the form of an intelligent alien who came to earth. If humans were to detain the Great Gazoo, Eddins said, “would that alien ever be able to get out of confinement? Just because we have restricted it to persons, and that’s not a human being?”
Sendao said she thinks interplanetary relations would not hinge on an individual writ of habeas corpus. 
‘A Sweeping Pronouncement’
Given the potentially huge implications, Sendao said, courts should avoid making a decision that could upend the current system of animal captivity.
“This is such a sweeping pronouncement of how we are going to fundamentally alter our relationship to animals that it should be made through the legislative branch,” Sendao said. 
In an amicus briefing siding with the city, the Hawaiʻi Veterinary Medical Association makes a similar point. While animals are unquestionably more beloved than other forms of property, the group says, that doesn’t mean they are legally persons. They argued that animal welfare can be best facilitated by humans owning and caring for them — and presumably paying their veterinary bills.
“In Hawai’i and all other states, the legal system governing animals has always been based on ownership, which is not demeaning to animals,” the veterinarians say in their briefing.
A Myron B. Thompson Academy student takes notes during the hearing. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
But Mari and Vaigai’s attorney argues that habeas corpus by nature is decided on a narrow case-by-case basis, and that the court’s decision would not cause broader legal havoc.
“This case does not concern a sweeping pronouncement of animal personhood,” Davis said to the court. “It doesn’t concern wholesale recognition of animal personhood. It concerns the recognition of two innocent beings’ right to liberty.”
Justice Lisa Ginoza asked whether Nonhuman Rights Project has considered advocating for the elephants’ release through other channels such as the City Council or mayor. Davis responded that his group is focusing on the judiciary because that’s where decision-making power related to habeas corpus resides.
Ginoza said that’s all well and good, but deciding in favor of Mari and Vaigai could expand the courts’ power by reinterpreting the word “persons.”
“Courts are often very careful whether and when to exercise that authority,” she said.  
McKenna, for her part, noted the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark Citizens United case expands the definition of persons to encompass corporations. Davis made that point as well to show that the word’s definition can be flexible. 
He referenced the hundreds of students sitting in the audience behind him, saying, “What would we be telling these impressionable minds about our moral life to deny two innocent beings an evidentiary hearing they are entitled simply because they have the wrong biology?”
