title: Uthmeier subpoenas Democratic Socialists regarding alleged foreign contributions
description: A week after the first Democratic Socialist of America (DSA)-backed candidate won a seat in the Florida Legislature, Attorney General James Uthmeier is subpoenaing the organization, alleging possible violation of state laws against solicitation of funds from Cuba and China. “We are examining whether DSA accepted contributions or support from foreign sources [...]
text:
Florida Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier in Lakeland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)A week after the first Democratic Socialist of America (DSA)-backed candidate won a seat in the Florida Legislature, Attorney General James Uthmeier is subpoenaing the organization, alleging possible violation of state laws against solicitation of funds from Cuba and China.
“We are examining whether DSA accepted contributions or support from foreign sources of concern, including the regimes in Cuba and China,” Uthmeier said in a short video posted on his social media channels. “And whether its fundraising from Florida donors has been fully transparent and lawful.”
A delegation of DSA members — including members from Florida — joined a coalition of activist groups such as Code Pink and Progressive International on the “Nuestra America” convoy to Cuba in March. They reportedly brought medical and school supplies and solar panels and met with Cuban government officials.
The Florida Legislature has passed laws in recent years targeting foreign influence. That includes legislation passed in 2025 (SB 700) prohibiting nonprofits from accepting donations from entities or individuals associated with “foreign countries of concern” — which include China, Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Iran, Syria, and the Venezuelan government of Nicholas Maduro (removed by U.S. armed forces in January and awaiting trial on allegations of conspiring with drug cartels).
The DSA movement has burgeoned in the past couple of years, ignited by Zohran Mamdani’s election as New York mayor in the fall of 2025. Last week, six DSA candidates won election to Congress and, in Florida, Democrat Ashley Herrmann, backed by the DSA, ousted Republican incumbent Danny Alvarez in state House District 69 in Hillsborough County.
Uthmeier was on the ballot for the first time as a political candidate last week. He narrowly defeated Democrat José Javier Rodríguez  in the race for attorney general by less than 2 percentage points.
A spokesperson for the national DSA told the Phoenix that they “are aware of the situation and have no comment at this time.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Likely Speaker-elect Reives signals bipartisan approach as Democrats flip NC House
description: Republicans have controlled both legislative chambers since 2011, often with a veto-proof supermajority.
text:
North Carolina House Democratic Leader Robert Reives speaks to reporters on Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)With Democrats winning a near-supermajority in the North Carolina House, likely House Speaker-elect Rep. Robert Reives said Tuesday he’s open to bipartisan efforts to lower costs across the state.
“Compromise is not capitulation. Compromise is the job,” Reives, a Democrat from Chatham County, told reporters during a press conference Tuesday. 
Democrats flipped control of the North Carolina House during last week’s elections, gaining a majority for the first time in 15 years. They’ll hold a 71-48 advantage with one independent in the 2027 term. In the state Senate, in unofficial results, it appears Republicans will hold onto a narrow 26-24 majority, with one race possibly subject to a recount.
Reives said the House Democratic Caucus will meet early next week for an organizational meeting as lawmakers return to Raleigh for a lame duck session. Members will announce key legislative leadership roles after that. However, Reives announced last week he has secured majority support in his caucus for the speakership. 
Republicans have controlled both legislative chambers in North Carolina since 2011, often with a veto-proof supermajority. That’s allowed the party to sideline Democratic governors. Lawmakers passed measures to redraw congressional and legislative districts, limit reproductive freedom, boost private schools, and expand firearm access.
NC Senate Democratic leader sees a path to bipartisanship next year

When lawmakers return next week, Republicans will still hold veto-proof or near-veto-proof majorities in both chambers. Their terms don’t end until Dec. 31.
During past lame duck sessions, Republicans have stripped power from incoming Democratic elected officials and cut their agency staffing, as well as making changes to election law and proposing constitutional amendments, all along strict party lines. In 2024, lawmakers passed a 131-page bill branded as Hurricane Helene relief, but it also made drastic changes to state government. 
Reives is hoping this year will be different. 
“This is the first opportunity to show what kind of atmosphere we’re going to have next year,” Reives said. “If we come in here with the lame duck sessions that we’ve had every cycle since I’ve been here, then that will be a signal to the caucus that there is no interest in working with us and there’s no interest in any bipartisanism or camaraderie.”
Reives applauded his GOP counterpart, Speaker Destin Hall, for bipartisanship during the 2025-2026 legislative biennium. Republicans elected Hall, a representative from Caldwell County, to the position two years ago. Hall succeeded recently ousted Republican Congressman Tim Moore, who was state House Speaker for ten years.
“Speaker Hall did an amazing job of working with us, and we passed the budget,” Reives said. “First time that we passed a bipartisan budget in this building since Republicans took over, so I know the House Republicans are ready to get to work.”
Looking ahead to next year, Reives said he wants to tackle affordability issues when it comes to housing, groceries, energy and healthcare. 
“We’re going to work as hard as we can to make life more affordable,” he said. 
More than 3 million North Carolina voters are registered as unaffiliated with a party. An independent candidate, April Montgomery, won election to serve Lee and Moore counties in the House. She’s the first unaffiliated legislator elected in North Carolina since 2010.
Reives said Montgomery ran a great campaign.
“I want her in a position that she can operate in the way that is most comfortable and aligns with her philosophies,” he said. “I want her to know that she has got 70 people who are cheering for wherever she goes. If she decides she wants to caucus with Republicans, caucus with Democrats, if she wants to caucus with nobody, I want her to be supported because she’s been elected by our people.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Commentary: Dwindling margins: Can Tennessee Democrats build on an encouraging election?
description: The blue paint that Jackson Pollacked the canvas of American politics last week didn’t miss Tennessee, but there’s a case to be made that it landed with more of a sprinkle than a splash.  Gazing longingly at the midterm miracles that stunningly remade the political landscapes of Texas, Kansas, Iowa, South Carolina, and perhaps Mississippi, […]
text:
Also-rans who almost won: In Tennessee's 6th Congressional District, Democrat Mike Cooley, left, raised $117,000 but almost beat state Rep. Johnny Garrett, who raised more than $3 million. Marquita Bradshaw, right, came within 12 percentage points of beating incumbent U.S. Sen. Bill Hagerty, to whom she lost by 27 percentage points in 2020. (Photos by John Partipilo of Mike Cooley and Karen Pulfer Focht of Marquita Bradshaw/Tennessee Lookout)The blue paint that Jackson Pollacked the canvas of American politics last week didn’t miss Tennessee, but there’s a case to be made that it landed with more of a sprinkle than a splash. 
Gazing longingly at the midterm miracles that stunningly remade the political landscapes of Texas, Kansas, Iowa, South Carolina, and perhaps Mississippi, Volunteer State Democrats are left to ponder: is Tennessee on the same path, or is it just too stubbornly red to join the fun? 
If you glance at a national map showing Republican-to-Democrat voting shifts by county comparing 2026 to 2024, it sure looks like Tennessee with its dense cluster of blue arrows was right there in the middle of the wave last week. But the actual results for Dems here were more about dwindling margins than electoral wins. 
There were, of course, some blue successes. At the legislative level a surprising six state House seats flipped red to blue . In the race for governor Democrats won a half dozen counties they lost in 2022, including Hamilton, Knox, Montgomery and Rutherford. And the capper no one saw coming was Victoria Broderick’s astonishing win over 8-term GOP U.S.  Rep. Scott DesJarlais in the 4th Congressional District. 
The collapse of GOP voters for Blackburn in TN. Two years later, and 1M fewer votes.

But the math on the ground remains grim. With those legislative flips the Republican edge in the state House drops from 75% to 69%, and the state Senate didn’t change.  And Broderick’s signature win notwithstanding, the split in Tennessee’s nine-member congressional delegation remains the same it was before last Tuesday.
Republicans survived a close call at the top of the ticket. Gov. Bill Lee won his first term in 2018 by 21 points and his second term in 2022 by 32 points. Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn’s feeble 2.5% win last week over the energetic but underfunded Democrat Jerri Green speaks not just to Blackburn’s singular unpopularity even in her own party but also tells us this was a winnable contest for Dems given more resources and a better campaign. In other words, a missed opportunity. 
Congressional races beyond just the astounding 4th District outcome also showcased blue incursions into the minds and hearts of Tennessee voters. Amply funded Democrats Chaz Molder in the 5th District, Darden Copeland in the 7th District) and Rep. Justin J. Pearson in the (9th District all ran aggressive races, losing only by low single digits — much closer than Republicans thought possible when they drew the lines to make them safe red seats. 
A fascinating thing in the U.S. House races was that these well-financed, well-staffed Democrats fared no better than a couple of barely funded candidates who ran minimalist campaigns. The $90K that Broderick raised is peanuts for a congressional race, and she had only about $40K to work with in the general election, yet she won. 
Less noticed but just as stupefying is the 6th District, where unknown Democrat Mike Croley lost this supposedly safe GOP seat to Republican Rep. Johnny Garrett by just three points. Garrett spent over half a million dollars on the general election (after blowing through more than two million to win his primary), while Croley came out of his primary with less than $5,000 in his campaign account and rustled up only about $70K to spend on the general election. I’m a voter in the 6th and never once heard a peep from Croley’s campaign. 
What should we make of the fact that unknown Democrats with little money drawing zero outside attention running muted campaigns in districts nobody regarded as remotely competitive did just as well or better than the higher-profile Democratic contenders who enjoyed money, attention, and optimistic vibes?
Victoria Broderick claims victory over U.S. Rep. Scott DesJarlais in 4th Congressional District

The simple explanation is that big political waves powered by broad dissatisfaction with the party in power will naturally pull some small fish from the other party into the incoming tide. Last week saw a number of so-called accidental wins in several states that likely surprised the victors themselves as much as anyone else. It’s also the case that unsung, underfunded Democrats like Broderick and Croley were largely ignored by GOP campaigns. With no flurry of media defining the turf, voters would see them merely as the “D” option on a ballot, free of the woke-radical-lefty-commie-socialist labels that Republicans in competitive races spent every last dime this cycle slapping on their opponents. 
The wave dynamic also explains how the Democrat running for U.S. Senate, Marquita Bradshaw, managed to come within 12 points of the GOP incumbent Sen. Bill Hagerty, despite the fact that she raised virtually no money, ran virtually no campaign, and lost to Hagerty by 27 points when he first won the seat in 2020.
For years the working assumption has been that Democrats are structurally uncompetitive in much of the South, including Tennessee. Last Tuesday makes it clear that the footprint of Republican dominance has lost a few shoe sizes. So can Tennessee Democrats turn this new jolt of optimism into something more than just a mostly close-but-no-cigar outlier election that entices but doesn’t fulfill? Is there a path to membership in the newly growing club of Southern and Midwestern red states moving past the tyranny of one-party control?
One thing that would help Tennessee look like other red states turning purple is loosening the stranglehold Republicans have had on voters in growing suburban counties. Last week’s election teased us big time here. Two years ago in her U.S. Senate reelection,Blackburn waxed state Rep. Gloria Johnson by 20 points in each of the key high-growth suburban and exurban counties of Rutherford and Montgomery. In last Tuesday’s contest for governor Blackburn lost to Green in Rutherford by almost 9,000 votes and in Montgomery by over 3,500 votes. Even Bradshaw  won the U.S. Senate race in both counties. 
Going forward, turning this into something lasting for Democrats means throwing significant money and serious talent at every crucial race and doing so early. One of Blackburn’s first acts as governor in January will be to appoint someone to fill her Senate seat until it’s on the ballot in 2028. A serious Democrat who has the chops and wants that seat should be in the fray raising money and running hard by Valentine’s Day. Others who want to give congressional seats a go should also get started without delay, publicly and aggressively watchdogging these House Republicans from the minute they take the oath at the start of the new Congress in January.
Perhaps 2028 will be another big blue election year, but even if it is it probably won’t have coattails like this one. Tsunamis just don’t happen that often. To build on 2026 Tennessee Democrats need to find candidates, write checks, and open the throttle, but quick.

Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, Colorado's Democratic attorney general, spoke to reporters at a press conference on Nov. 4, 2026. name: WyoFile
title: Barlow announces first leadership picks as Wyoming’s incoming governor
description:
Eric Barlow, so far, has selected Erin Taylor as chief of staff, Walter Eggers as nominee for attorney general and Eydie Trautwein as chief operating officer.
The post Barlow announces first leadership picks as Wyoming’s incoming governor appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming Gov.-elect Eric Barlow announced the first members of his incoming administration Tuesday, tapping three leaders with experience in public policy, law and state government. 
The Republican selected Erin Taylor as chief of staff, Walter Eggers as nominee for attorney general and Eydie Trautwein as chief operating officer, according to a press release. 

Wyoming Gov.-elect Eric Barlow has selected Erin Taylor as chief of staff of his incoming administration. (Courtesy Office of Gov.-elect Eric Barlow) 

“Wyoming deserves a government that listens, spends responsibly and delivers dependable service,” Barlow said in the release. “Erin, Walter and Eydie understand our state and bring the experience and judgment needed to help lead this work. I will count on them to build strong relationships, address problems directly and keep our administration focused on serving the people of Wyoming.”
While Taylor and Trautwein’s positions are ultimately decided by the governor, Eggers is a nominee and will be subject to Wyoming Senate confirmation. 
As chief of staff, Taylor will lead the governor’s office with more than 25 years of public policy experience at the federal, state and local levels, and will help coordinate the administration’s priorities with legislators, state agencies and communities. 
In 2014, Taylor founded a consulting firm after serving eight years as executive director of the Wyoming Taxpayers Association. She also led U.S. Sen. Mike Enzi’s 2014 campaign and previously directed the Wyoming Association of Community College Trustees. Taylor holds two degrees from the University of Wyoming. 

Wyoming Gov.-elect Eric Barlow has selected Walter Eggers as nominee for attorney general. Eggers will be subject to the Wyoming Senate’s confirmation. (Courtesy Office of Gov.-elect Eric Barlow) 

Eggers began his legal career in Cheyenne after graduating from the UW College of Law in 1997, working as both a prosecutor and defense attorney. In 2000, he joined powerhouse Mountain West law firm Holland and Hart where he served as partner for about 16 years and led the firm’s Cheyenne office. 
He later led the firm’s Energy, Environment and Natural Resources Practice Group, which included overseeing more than 100 lawyers and legal professionals. Eggers’ practice has focused on administrative law, state and local taxation, litigation and appeals. 

Wyoming Gov.-elect Eric Barlow has selected Eydie Trautwein as chief operating officer of his incoming administration. (Courtesy Office of Gov.-elect Eric Barlow) 

At UW, Eggers has taught professional responsibility, evidence, and oil and gas law. He’s also worked to expand access to civil legal assistance with the Wyoming Access to Justice Commission and Equal Justice Wyoming. 
Trautwein, also a graduate of UW’s College of Law, will bring her experience in state administration, legal services and coordination across government to the position of chief operating officer. Her responsibilities will include overseeing the governor’s office operations and supporting implementation of the administration’s priorities. 
She previously served as Wyoming’s deputy state auditor, where her work included coordinating a major upgrade of the state’s financial, human resources and payroll systems. 
Trautwein also served as director of legal resources and judicial education for the Wyoming Supreme Court. 
Barlow, a veterinarian and longtime state lawmaker, is set to be inaugurated on Jan. 4.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Commentary: Possibly coming to a classroom near you: ‘Teacher, what does “adultery” mean?’
description: Imagine this coming to a South Carolina classroom near you. It could happen if the General Assembly follows Texas and Louisiana with a law requiring public school classrooms to display the Ten Commandments: (Scene: A lively second-grade classroom. Students settle into their desks. A hand is raised.) Student: Teacher, what is “adultery”? Teacher: What?! Where[...]
text:
The U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in February 2026 that a Louisiana law requiring displays of the Ten Commandments in classrooms can be enforced. The ruling removed an injunction that had blocked enforcement in a handful of parishes where plaintiff parents had challenged the law. (Photo by Michael Smith/Getty Images)Imagine this coming to a South Carolina classroom near you. It could happen if the General Assembly follows Texas and Louisiana with a law requiring public school classrooms to display the Ten Commandments:
(Scene: A lively second-grade classroom. Students settle into their desks. A hand is raised.)
Student: Teacher, what is “adultery”?
Teacher: What?! Where did you see a word like that?
5th Circuit upholds Louisiana law requiring Ten Commandments displays in classrooms

Student: It’s on the wall.
Teacher: Someone wrote that on the bathroom wall?
Student: No, it’s in the classroom. (Points to the Ten Commandments recently placed on the classroom wall.)
Teacher: Oh, you’re talking about the Ten Commandments. The Legislature required every classroom to post them on the wall.
Student: Why?
Teacher: Well, the Legislature says they’re important.
Second Student: Is the Legislature a church?
Teacher: No. It’s not a church.
First Student: OK, but I still don’t know what “adultery” means.
Teacher: I think the Legislature wanted you to read the commandments but not ask questions about them.
Third Student: But why can’t we ask questions? Didn’t you say we can’t learn if we don’t ask questions?
Teacher: Well, yes, but some of these commandments are not what we call “age appropriate.”
Third Student: But why would they put them on the wall then?
Teacher: (Sighs) I don’t know. No one asked me. State lawmakers don’t talk to teachers.
First Student: So, what is adultery?
Teacher: Heavens. That’s when a married person cheats on their husband or wife.
Fourth Student: Is that what they call “sex”?
Teacher: You know, you really need to ask your parents. It’s time for math.
Fifth Student: What’s a graven image? It says you can’t make a graven image.
Teacher: That’s an idol.
Sixth Student: Like “American Idol”? We can’t watch “American Idol”? My parents like “American Idol.”
Teacher: No, “American Idol” is an OK kind of idol. I mean, it’s different…
Seventh Student: Is an idol like a statue?
Teacher: Yes, sometimes.
Seventh Student: We have statues at school.
Teacher: Yes.
Seventh Student: Are those idols?
Teacher: No.
Seventh Student: How do you know?
Teacher: Let’s talk about fractions.
Eighth Student: What does “covet” mean? And what’s a “manservant”? Is that like a slave?
Teacher: Oh, my. Well, sometimes it was, but…
Ninth Student: What about “Thou shalt not kill”? My dad says we’re fighting a war. Are soldiers allowed to kill people?
Teacher: Is that the lunch bell? I feel like I heard the lunch bell.
Ninth Student: Are soldiers allowed to kill people?
Teacher: That’s … a very complicated question.
Ninth Student: But it’s right there on the wall.
Teacher: Yes, but…
Ninth Student: So, is the wall wrong?
Teacher: No, I mean, yes, I mean. … It should say “murder,” not “kill.”
Ninth Student: Who decided it should say, “kill,” not “murder”?
Teacher: That’s a very good question.
Principal Smith (Energetically pops his head into the classroom). Hello! How’s everything going today?
Teacher: Oh, Principal Smith, I have a question about the Ten Commandments.
Principal Smith: Oh, what’s your question?
Teacher: What am I supposed to tell the children when they ask what they mean?
Principal Smith: We’re waiting for guidance from the district.
Teacher: What does the district say?
Principal Smith: We’re waiting for guidance from the state.
Teacher: What does the state say?
Principal Smith: The Legislature says the commandments speak for themselves.
Teacher: Not to 7-year-olds.
Tenth Student: Teacher, who is the Lord?
Principal Smith: Laterz! (Principal Smith disappears.)
Teacher: The Lord?
Tenth Student: It says, “I am the Lord thy God.”
Teacher: That’s referring to God.
Tenth Student: Which god? My family is Hindu.
SC House approves bill requiring classrooms to post Ten Commandments

Teacher: Well … The Ten Commandments are part of Jewish and Christian religions.
Tenth Student: But we’re not all Jewish or Christian.
Teacher: No, we’re not.
Tenth Student: But they’re on our wall.
Teacher: Yes.
Tenth Student: So, are they everyone’s rules — no matter what my parents believe?
Teacher: OK, everybody, recess! (Students run out.)
Teacher: I have a question, too. (Looks at the Ten Commandments.) Am I a teacher? Or a preacher?
Editor’s note: The House passed legislation 84-31 in February that would require an 11-by-13-inch poster or framed copy in every classroom, alongside a “context statement.” The Senate never took up that bill, which officially died when the regular legislative session ended in May. Supporters could reintroduce the proposal for the session that starts in January.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico could soon require co-pays for high-earning families using universal childcare program
description: High-earning New Mexico families could soon pay monthly fees to keep their kids in the state’s first-in-the-nation universal childcare program. A state Early Childhood Education and Care Department spokesperson said co-pays would only apply to 10% of participating families.
text:
The New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department will hold a public hearing on Dec. 3, 2026, regarding a proposal to require co-pays for high-earning families who participate in the state’s universal childcare program. Above, Olga Grays reads to children in her class at Mrs. Olga's Daycare in Las Cruces in September of 2026. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)High-earning New Mexico families could soon pay monthly fees to keep their kids in the state’s first-in-the-nation universal childcare program.
The New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department will hold a hybrid public hearing from 9 to 11 a.m. on Dec. 3 in Santa Fe and online, regarding a proposal to require co-pays for high-earning families. The department is also accepting public feedback on the proposal by email.
The law establishing New Mexico’s universal childcare program specified that co-pays would take effect only in times of economic downturn, and that they would apply to families who make at least six times the federal poverty level — $163,920 for a family of three and $198,000 for a family of four.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Under the current proposal, those families could see monthly co-pays of $15 to $99 for one child, depending on their income level, and $22.50 to $148.50 for two or more children.
In a statement provided to Source NM, ECECD spokesperson Julia Sclafani said national inflation levels are responsible for the proposed co-pays, which would affect about 10% of families who participate in universal childcare.
“Under the Child Care Assistance Program Act, copay for families at the highest income levels take effect when certain national economic conditions are met. Those conditions have nothing to do with the health of the Early Childhood Trust Fund or the state budget,” she said.
During this year’s legislative session, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham criticized proposals to require co-pays — including one from the state House of Representatives that would have set a lower income threshold for the payments — as being, by definition, not universal. Sclafani said Lujan Grisham still opposes the co-pays.
“If anything, inflation makes it harder for households to take on additional bills,” she said. “ECECD is doing everything within its authority to limit the impact on them. Universal childcare is working, it is sustainable, and this administration will keep fighting to protect it.”
The rulemaking hearing is scheduled just weeks before Democratic Gov.-elect Deb Haaland is set to take office. On the campaign trail, she frequently cited her experience as a single working mother when expressing her support for the program.
When asked at a news conference last week whether she would support co-pays, she told reporters that she hoped to spare families from the payments “to the extent that we can.”
“It’s an economic driver for our state,” she said. “To the extent that we can keep anyone from having to make co-pays for early childhood education, I think we want to see if we can do that. This benefits our children.”

title: Whitmer asks Trump administration to end food tariffs, reimburse Michiganders for increased costs
description: Gov. Gretchen Whitmer is using her final months in office to attack food tariffs imposed by the administration of President Donald Trump. On Tuesday, Whitmer called for the U.S. Department of Treasury to end its tariffs imposed on food products, while also requesting that the federal government reimburse Michigan residents for the increased costs they’ve […]
text:
U.S. Customs station at the Blue Water Bridge in Port Huron, Michigan. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Gov. Gretchen Whitmer is using her final months in office to attack food tariffs imposed by the administration of President Donald Trump.
On Tuesday, Whitmer called for the U.S. Department of Treasury to end its tariffs imposed on food products, while also requesting that the federal government reimburse Michigan residents for the increased costs they’ve incurred from the tariff regime.
Whitmer, in a letter to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, noted that Trump’s federal tariff policies have had a disproportionate effect on Michigan families. She also pointed out that, according to the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, Michigan households have faced an average tariff burden of $6,485 per household since January 2025. Whitmer’s office said that burden was the highest in the country. Meanwhile, food prices have continued to rise, Whitmer wrote, and grocery prices have increased by 2.4% in 2025.
“Right now, Michigan families are paying the highest tariff burden in the nation because of DC Republicans’ agenda, and those costs are showing up every time they check out at the grocery store,” Whitmer wrote. “In Michigan, we’ve worked hard to put money back in people’s pockets, but we need a federal trade policy that works with our allies, brings supply chains home, and makes life more affordable. Families deserve relief from rising prices on the essentials they depend on every day.” 
Whitmer signs executive order to examine impact of Trump tariffs on Michigan’s economy

The letter also emphasized how the tariff regime has heavily damaged the U.S. relationship with Canada.
“Specifically, exports to Canada fell 12.3% last year, signaling severe strain with our strongest trading partner — these tariffs and sudden policy reversals have weakened Michigan’s competitiveness and disrupted long‑standing trade relationships,” Whitmer wrote. “Federal leaders can step up and make real change. I ask that you end the new food tariffs this administration has levied in 2025 and 2026, and reimburse Michiganders for the increased cost of food.” 
A request for comment was sent by Michigan Advance to the U.S. Treasury Department. This story will be updated when a response is received.

The money will target “diabetes and chronic-disease care, expand access to technology-enabled healthcare, improve care coordination, and build the rural healthcare workforce,” according to a news release. 
The Marshall Research Corporation, a nonprofit that finds grants for Marshall University, will receive $11.4 million for three separate programs for remote patient monitoring on patients with diabetes and hypertension, implement lifestyle and nutrition programs for managing diabetes and training for emergency medical care in rural areas. 
Another $1.5 million will go to Cabell-Huntington Hospital for helping rural patients with follow-ups and connecting with specialists. 
The West Virginia Primary Care Association will receive nearly $2.8 million to expand diabetes management at community health centers. 
Rural Outreach and Access to Medicine West Virginia, an organization that does diabetes and other medical monitoring in central West Virginia, will receive $1.2 million. The money will be used to recruit nurses and serve patients with high-risk for neuropathy or diabetes.

title: Winter is coming. Can Democrats succeed in chilling soaring energy prices?
description: WASHINGTON — Democrats during the midterm election campaign promised bold steps to make life more affordable if voters elected them to control Congress next year. They won, in a historic blue wave that’s already given them comfortable majorities in both the House and Senate. But Democrats likely will find that bringing down gasoline and other energy prices a[...]
text:
WASHINGTON — Democrats during the midterm election campaign promised bold steps to make life more affordable if voters elected them to control Congress next year. They won, in a historic blue wave that’s already given them comfortable majorities in both the House and Senate. But Democrats likely will find that bringing down gasoline and other energy prices as winter arrives will take more than an act or two of Congress. And it’s largely a process out of their control.“You can’t legislate your way out of high gasoline prices,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, which tracks prices.Since the United States attacked Iran on Feb. 28, fuel prices have soared. A gallon of regular gasoline averaged $3.98 Tuesday, AAA reported. While that’s down from recent weeks, it’s still well above the $3.07 of a year ago. Diesel prices Tuesday averaged $6.16 a gallon, ballooning from $3.73 a year ago.Home heating oil averaged a staggering $6.14 a gallon last week, up from $3.62 a year ago, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Electricity costs were up 3.8% and natural gas was up 4.4% over the 12 months ending in September, said the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics.Republicans will control Congress during the rest of this year’s session, and Democrats will be in charge beginning in January. Regardless of who has the majority, the government’s ability to bring consumer energy prices down over the short term is limited.Some Democrats are already blunt about what they can do about prices.“I’m not telling people I’m going to be able to lower X by X number of cents, but I’m telling them they’re going to have somebody who’s going to fight like hell for them,” Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, who’s in line to chair the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee next year, told reporters at the Capitol Monday. There are quick fixes. They can involve suspending fuel taxes, drawing from petroleum reserves and easing restrictions on certain products. Most of those strategies have been tried this year, and have had minimal if any impact.Lowering fuel taxes“The most obvious quick fix would be to eliminate the federal gas tax,” said Jeff Lenard, a vice president of the National Association of Convenience Stores, a trade group.He saw little else Congress could do quickly but added “if the federal tax is eliminated, that would create a budget hole elsewhere for the federal government,” and ending the gas tax would address only about 5% of the current cost of fuel.

 






Gas and diesel prices in Forest Glen, Maryland, on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom)

Proposals to suspend the 18.4-cents-a-gallon federal gasoline tax and the 24.4-cents-a-gallon tax on diesel fuel have been a popular, easily understandable way of trying to get prices down quickly.Members of Congress from both parties have been trying this year to push the legislation. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., wants a 90-day suspension. Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., wants an 18-month tax holiday and a phase-in of the full tax when that period ends. Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., has called for suspending the tax when the national average price of gasoline tops $4 a gallon.But, said the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service last month, suspension of the federal tax “may not reduce consumer prices at all. Gasoline suppliers, distributors, refiners, and blenders could choose to reduce prices by more or less than 18.4 cents per gallon or, in theory, not reduce prices at all.” While no legislation to curb federal taxes has been approved, fuel tax holidays have been tried in different states. Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, North Carolina, Ohio, and Utah are suspending gas taxes or delaying increases this year.Washington’s Tax Foundation found California’s taxes and fees are the nation’s highest at 73.6 cents a gallon, followed by Illinois at 70.4 cents. The lowest taxes and fees are in Alaska at 9 cents a gallon.The emergency supply One big strategy for keeping price and supply stable was supposed to be the nation’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve.Created in 1975 after the price and supply shocks of the previous two years, the oil filled underground salt caverns along the Gulf Coast in Texas and Louisiana.Fifteen years ago, the reserve had about 726 million barrels. At the end of October, the supply was down to 282 million barrels, its lowest level in 44 years. President Donald Trump authorized the release of millions of barrels of oil during the Iran war, and President Joe Biden ordered major drawdowns to counter supply disruptions after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.This year, the supply from the U.S. and other nations, as well as lower consumer demand because of higher prices, helped ease the economic pain, said an analysis from Washington’s Bipartisan Policy Center.But, it added, “The events of the last few months have also demonstrated the limitations of the SPR. The reserve’s lower stock levels in the run-up to the Iran conflict limited the volumes available for release.”What can the government do?Trump last month eased restrictions on dyed diesel, often called red diesel, widely used in agriculture, and made a deal to bring more diesel from Russia into world markets.None of these strategies, though, is likely to make a lot of difference to consumers. “You can pull small levers, but the president has pulled most of those levers,” said De Haan.The most powerful players in regulating electricity rates and home heating oil are largely state and local agencies. But, said Charles Hua, founder and executive director of PowerLines, a nonpartisan consumer education organization, “federal policymakers including Congress and the president can still have an impact over utility bills.”He cited the ability to pass “policies that can modernize grid planning and utility business models, using their platform to elevate these issues, and engaging with state and regional actors on grid decisions that can impact utility bills.” The Iran warTrump could take what’s arguably the fastest way to provide relief to consumers from the high oil prices this winter by reaching an agreement to end the war with Iran. Prior to the war, roughly 20% of the world’s oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway between Oman and Iran. The strait has been closed, or the site of attacks, since the war began.Here’s where the new Democratic-run Congress could have influence: It can pressure the administration to end the war. Serious talks are underway among Democratic leaders as to whether, or when, to cut off or at least severely limit  war funding, perhaps during the lame-duck session now underway.“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’ intransigence, of course not,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York told a forum at the progressive Center for American Progress last week.“And let’s not forget one of our most powerful tools: Democrats have power on spending bills that require our votes, and we should use it. No more funding for a forever war with Iran,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, told the 2026 Popular Mandate conference on Tuesday, a gathering of progressives. Even an end to the war is no guarantee of sharply lower prices. Oil is a globally traded commodity, its supply and price affected by all sorts of developments.In 2022, prices spiked to levels similar to and even higher than the current costs after the Russian invasion of Ukraine disrupted world markets that were concerned about losing Russian oil.That war continues, meaning tensions in the Middle East are likely to go on, raising questions about the security of Saudi Arabia’s oil fields.De Haan, like most analysts, is wary of any fast solution. Oil prices are affected by too many different developments.“There’s a lot of different things going on at the same time,” he said. “There is no magic wand.”

title: Pa. State Police report near-total compliance on skill games removal
description: More than 12,000 businesses and social clubs have removed skill games in the three weeks since Pennsylvania State Police started enforcing a court order that found the slot machine-like terminals fell under state gambling laws.  PSP reported that just 68 places held onto the devices after Oct. 14 out of the 12,202 establishments they visited. […]
text:
Karma, an LGBTQ+ bar near the Capitol in Harrisburg, calls for saving skill games on Nov. 2, 2026. Pennsylvania State Police report that most businesses removed that gaming terminals voluntarily. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)More than 12,000 businesses and social clubs have removed skill games in the three weeks since Pennsylvania State Police started enforcing a court order that found the slot machine-like terminals fell under state gambling laws. 
PSP reported that just 68 places held onto the devices after Oct. 14 out of the 12,202 establishments they visited. The agency said it had seized 14 machines and $1,913, but investigations are ongoing. 
The Attorney General’s Office previously estimated there were as many as 70,000 skill games machines around the state, many providing a vital stream of income to gas stations, grocery stores and laundromats. 
The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled in June that skill games must be regulated like other gaming, meaning the terminals could only be placed in businesses that are licensed by the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board.
 
The Pennsylvania State Police urge the public to report such devices by emailing tips@pa.gov or calling 1-888-292-1919.


Justices paused their ruling for 140 days, giving lawmakers time to craft legislation legalizing the machines, but no consensus was reached.
PSP emphasized that, contrary to “claims from manufacturers and operators,” machines that don’t accept money or operate like a “sweepstakes” still fall under the order and can be confiscated.
“No manufacturer or operator sought PSP’s input on the legality of these devices before placing them inside Pennsylvania businesses. Distributors of these devices and establishments hosting them could face criminal charges for unlawful gambling and other related offenses if they continue operating these machines,” the agency said.
Devices that accept “any form of compensation from a player to engage in slot-style games” that comes with a potential payout “is a slot machine and/or gambling device,” the statement continued. 
The agency directs businesses with these machines to discuss “immediate” removal with distributors and vendors, noting that criminal charges can be levied against the latter parties as well.

title: Senate Republicans select Johnson as nominee for speakership
description: Tennessee’s Senate Republican Caucus narrowly nominated its leader as speaker for the next session of the General Assembly in an election that saw the group allow one member to vote by proxy. The 27-member caucus chose Majority Leader Jack Johnson of Franklin to be its nominee for speaker, picking him over Sen. Paul Bailey of […]
text:
The Tennessee Senate Republican Caucus on Tuesday nominated Sen. Jack Johnson as its candidate for Senate Speaker. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s Senate Republican Caucus narrowly nominated its leader as speaker for the next session of the General Assembly in an election that saw the group allow one member to vote by proxy.
The 27-member caucus chose Majority Leader Jack Johnson of Franklin to be its nominee for speaker, picking him over Sen. Paul Bailey of Sparta. The caucus refused to divulge the vote count, a day after announcing it unanimously voted to let outgoing Sen. Brent Taylor cast a vote by proxy through an attorney.
Johnson, long a member of Senate leadership, is tied closely to Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn, also of Franklin, while Bailey is considered a candidate of rural and rank-and-file Senate members.
The nomination essentially makes Johnson the Senate speaker because Republicans hold a 27-6 supermajority in the Senate. A final vote of the full chamber will be held when the legislature convenes in January.
Johnson has led the legislature in a conservative direction, sponsoring legislation banning gender affirming care for minors in Tennessee, a law the U.S. Supreme Court upheld in a 2025 decision.
Johnson promised to improve communication, collaboration and cooperation within the Senate as he made his case for the post.
“When you succeed, the people you represent succeed,” Johnson told Senate colleagues.
Bailey harkened back to former Senate Speaker John Wilder, a West Tennessee Democrat who often said, “The Senate will be the Senate.”
In making his pitch for votes, Bailey said he would move the Senate back toward the “basics of governing,” making government smaller and focusing on conservative spending.
The caucus also allowed Sen. Kerry Roberts to vote absentee. The Senate clerk’s office conducted the ballot count.
By acclamation, the caucus selected Sen. Dawn White of Murfreesboro as majority leader.

description: Former Republican state lawmaker Elliott Pritt formally pleaded guilty Tuesday to a federal charge related to a sexual relationship with an underage student.
text:
The Robert C. Byrd United States Courthouse in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Lexi Browning/ West Virginia Watch)Former Republican state lawmaker Elliott Pritt formally pleaded guilty Tuesday to a federal charge related to a sexual relationship with an underage student. 
Del. Elliott Pritt, R-Fayette, was arrested July 22, 2026, and faces one count of enticement of a minor. (Photo courtesy of Carter County Detention Center)
As part of a plea agreement, Pritt admitted to one count of attempted production of child pornography. Attorneys representing the federal government agreed to dismiss two other charges: enticement of a minor to engage in sexual activity and attempt to persuade a minor not to tell law enforcement information related to a federal crime. 
Pritt resigned from the House of Delegates, where he represented Fayette County, when he was arrested on federal charges in July. He was a public school teacher at the time. 
Pritt told U.S. District Court Judge Irene C. Berger that he exchanged nude photos with the student, who was aged 14 to 15 at the time, on the social media platform Snapchat.
“We asked one another what we wanted to see, and that’s how it happened,” Pritt told the judge. He said the photos were exchanged more than 10 times. 
As part of the plea agreement, Pritt will surrender his cellphone along with a laptop computer, the judge said. 
According to the stipulation of facts in the case, Pritt told the student of his undying love for her in a typewritten letter. 
According to the plea agreement, attorneys will recommend Pritt serve a sentence of 15 to 30 years in prison. He’d be required to register as a sex offender, pay possible fines and restitution, and have supervisory release for five years to life.
Pritt appeared at the hearing Tuesday in an orange prison jumpsuit and shackles. He was escorted into Berger’s fifth floor courtroom by U.S. Marshals. 
Sentencing in Pritt’s case is set for 10 a.m. March 4 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia in Charleston.

title: New Mexico State University faculty union files ‘bad faith’ negotiations complaint
description: Members of New Mexico State University’s faculty union served a prohibited practice complaint against university administration Monday alleging the university has acted in “bad faith” in its negotiations. About 40 NMSU faculty members rallied outside Hadley Hall, the university administration building, to protest the delay in the union’s first contract negot[...]
text:
New Mexico State University English Professor Michelle Granger speaks to a gathering of university faculty on Nov. 9, 2026, during a union protest over contract negotiations. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)Members of New Mexico State University’s faculty union served a prohibited practice complaint against university administration Monday alleging the university has acted in “bad faith” in its negotiations.
About 40 NMSU faculty members rallied outside Hadley Hall, the university administration building, to protest the delay in the union’s first contract negotiations, which started in January of last year. Faculty organizers pointed to what they described as a “pattern of bad faith” negotiations regarding compensation, benefits, workload and parental leave.
NMSU’s Graduate Workers United filed a separate complaint against the university last week alleging the administration failed to notify members before they stopped deducting union dues from their checks.
“This seems like an attempt to weaken our union and our collective power,” Michelle Granger, NMSU NEA bargaining spokesperson and English Department professor, said to the crowd. “After 662 days, we ask that management come back to the table with the level of respect and accountability that we, the backbone of NMSU, deserve.”
The union’s complaint highlights more than 20 instances in which NMSU administration allegedly violated bargaining rules, including not responding to financial information requests; submitting fewer contract proposals than the faculty union; and removing proposals for family leave. The complaint also alleges the university general counsel stated, “Do you think that status quo is the lowest we can go?” in a bargaining meeting in September. 
The complaint, filed with the Public Employee Labor Relations Board, requests that the board find that the university engaged in prohibited practices and order administration not to interfere with timely negotiations.
“Faculty deserve a fair and timely process that respects our rights to bargain,” Granger said. “Faculty should not have to wait years for the protections and respect that we deserve.”
NMSU spokesperson Amanda Wyatt told Source NM in an emailed statement that university administration is aware of the union complaint and “remains committed to fulfilling its obligations under the Public Employee Bargaining Act and engaging in good-faith collective bargaining. We will not comment further on the specific allegations while the matter is pending.”
Jamie Bronstein, chief spokesperson for NMSU NEA and professor in the history department, told Source NM that despite the university seemingly maintaining the “status quo,” the union is willing to meet them at the table. 
“I don’t really understand it because New Mexico is a state that respects organized labor,” Bronstein said. “The teachers unions are very strong and everybody understands how beneficial unions can be, and so NMSU foot-dragging doesn’t make sense to me in the context of the wider state that we live in.”

Individuals representing the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot committee, Clean[...]
text:
Michiganders for Money Out of Politics submitted its signatures in Lansing to make the November 2026 ballot. May 27, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Three groups that supported and organized the “Michiganders for Money Out of Politics” ballot measure that passed on Nov. 3, as well as a recently elected state representative, have filed a motion to intervene in two First Amendment lawsuits filed against the measure.
Individuals representing the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot committee, Clean Water Action and Voters Not Politicians, as well as state Rep.-elect Joanna Whaley, argued in their brief that the current defendants — Attorney General Dana Nessel, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and, in the suit from the utilities, Director of Elections Jonathan Brater — “represent the public at large” and as such, have different considerations in defending the lawsuit.
“These include Defendants’ obligations to take account of enforcement priorities and resource limits and their interest in preserving enforcement discretion,” the brief argues. “These interests may lead Defendants to concede the invalidity of certain applications of Proposal 2 or agree to narrowing constructions to it, or even to enter into a settlement of the case. Proposed Intervenors, by contrast, have a direct stake in every provision of Proposal 2.”
Because of this, the groups argue that they should be included as defendants in the lawsuit in order to defend the interests of those who drafted and advocated for the proposal. All three organizations were involved in the creation of the ballot measure and collection of signatures on its petition, and each advocated for its passage. For Whaley, the motion states that during her 2026 campaign, she “faced advertisements, supported by outside spending, that did not use the ‘magic words’ of ‘vote for’ or ‘vote against’ and thus would not trigger disclosures under the law prior to Proposal 2 but that would trigger disclosures under Proposal 2. She intends to run for re-election and expects to confront similar outside spending in her reelection campaign.”
In support of their motion, the groups also argue that in the past, courts “have repeatedly granted permissive intervention to the sponsors of ballot initiatives in cases challenging the adoption or implementation of those initiatives.”
Both lawsuits — one brought by the right-leaning policy think tank Mackinac Center and the other brought by utility companies — were filed in the days after the election. The proposal to ban campaign spending from regulated electric and gas utilities and from major government contractors passed with over 80% support. 
In a press release from the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics campaign, longtime federal litigator Samuel Bagenstos says that the group is “fully confident in the legality of Proposal 2 and look forward to seeing this out in court.”
Bagenstos, who is representing the proposed intervenor-defendants along with Stephanie Command and Tracey Wigglesworth of The Political Law Group, added, “The language of Proposal 2 was carefully crafted with constitutionality in mind, and we are well prepared for this expected legal challenge. We intend to vigorously defend the will of Michiganders who overwhelmingly approved this measure just one week ago.”

text:
Chef Joseph Sakers of Delaware Tech will demonstrate how healthier food choices can help prevent chronic disease during a Nov. 16 event focused on nutrition, wellness, and practical cooking skills.
DOVER, Del. — Can the food on your dinner plate help you live a longer, healthier life?
The Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition hopes to help answer that question during its free Yes2Health Fall Retreat on Monday, Nov. 16, at Delaware Technical Community College in Dover.
The two-hour event, scheduled from 5 to 7 p.m., will feature Chef Joseph Sakers, chair of the Culinary Arts Department at Delaware Tech’s Terry Campus, demonstrating recipes built around the increasingly popular concept of “food as medicine.”
Participants will watch cooking demonstrations, sample healthier dishes and learn how everyday food choices can contribute to better health. The first 25 people to register will also receive a bag of fresh produce courtesy of the coalition.
What does ‘food as medicine’ mean?
The idea behind food as medicine is straightforward: What people eat can play a significant role in preventing illness, managing chronic conditions and improving overall health.
Rather than focusing exclusively on medications and medical treatments after a disease develops, the approach recognizes that good nutrition can be an important part of maintaining health.
The American Heart Association defines food as medicine more specifically as providing healthy foods through the health care system to help prevent, manage or treat diet-related chronic diseases. Such programs can include prescriptions for fresh produce, medically tailored groceries and meals designed for people with particular health conditions.
The concept has gained attention as medical professionals examine how nutrition can help address diabetes, heart disease, obesity and other chronic illnesses.
In June 2025, the American Heart Association released a review of 14 randomized clinical trials examining food-as-medicine programs. Researchers found improvements in participants’ diet quality and access to nutritious food, although evidence of long-term improvements in clinical outcomes remained inconsistent.
The findings suggest that nutrition-focused programs have potential, but researchers say more extensive studies are needed to determine their effectiveness in reducing disease and health care costs.
The connection to breast cancer prevention
For the Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition, the relationship between nutrition and disease prevention is particularly important.
According to the American Cancer Society, approximately one in five cancer cases is linked to a combination of excess body weight, physical inactivity, unhealthy diets and alcohol consumption.
The society recommends eating a variety of vegetables, fruits, whole grains and other nutrient-rich foods while limiting processed meats, sugary beverages and highly processed foods.
These recommendations are intended to reduce cancer risk and support overall health. No particular food or diet can guarantee that a person will avoid cancer, and healthy eating is not a substitute for recommended cancer screenings or medical treatment.
The coalition’s Yes2Health program puts these principles into practice by helping Delaware residents make healthier choices through nutrition education, physical activity and community support.
The program includes free 10-week health education sessions, walking activities and interactive cooking classes that teach participants how to prepare nutritious meals.
The coalition also offers online cooking programs and a cookbook club, creating opportunities for people to develop healthier habits without requiring expensive equipment or specialized culinary training.
Making healthy eating practical and enjoyable
Sakers will bring a professional chef’s perspective to the retreat, focusing on making nutritious food flavorful, approachable and enjoyable.
A graduate of Johnson & Wales University, where he earned a bachelor’s degree in 1997, Sakers serves as department chair and a culinary arts instructor at Delaware Tech.
His teaching emphasizes nutrition, wellness and practical cooking techniques alongside the professional skills students need for careers in the hospitality industry.
According to the event announcement, Sakers believes culinary professionals can help people make better food choices without sacrificing the enjoyment of eating.
His demonstration will give participants an opportunity to see those principles applied in the kitchen, with samples available during the event.
Small changes can make a difference
One of the challenges surrounding healthy eating is translating nutritional advice into meals that people can realistically prepare and afford.
Fresh produce, whole grains and healthier protein sources can be part of a nutritious diet, but cost, convenience, access to grocery stores and cooking knowledge can all influence what families put on their tables.
Food-as-medicine initiatives increasingly seek to address some of those barriers by connecting nutritional education with greater access to healthy foods.
For individuals, the changes do not necessarily require a complete overhaul of their diet. Choosing water instead of sugary drinks, adding vegetables to familiar meals, preparing more food at home or replacing some refined grains with whole grains can be useful starting points.
The American Cancer Society emphasizes that an overall pattern of healthy eating, maintained over time, matters more than any single ingredient or so-called superfood.
The Yes2Health Fall Retreat is designed to make that message tangible by showing participants how healthy ingredients can become appealing meals.
Through the event, the Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition hopes to encourage residents to view nutrition not simply as a matter of weight management but as an important part of lifelong health and disease prevention.
To Go: Yes2Health Fall Retreat

What: Free cooking demonstration and health education event hosted by the Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition.
When: Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, 5-7 p.m.
Where: Delaware Technical Community College, Terry Campus, Technology Drive, Room 723, Dover.
Featured presenter: Chef Joseph Sakers, culinary arts department chair at Delaware Tech.
Cost: Free.
What to expect: Cooking demonstrations, healthy food samples and a fresh produce bag for the first 25 registrants.
Registration: Seating is limited. Advance registration is encouraged at Yes2Health Fall Retreat registration.
More information: Visit Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition’s Yes2Health program or call 1-888-672-9647.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi’s newest barrier to voting is Experian data, brother of slain civil rights activist writes
description: Alcorn State University students Carson Posey, left,  and LaNise Chilton in white T-shirts work with the Andrew Goodman Foundation Vote Everywhere program to register students to vote in October 2026 at Alcorn State in Lorman, Mississippi.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.  

My brother Andrew was 20 years old when the Ku Klux Klan murdered him in Mississippi on June 21, 1964, along with James Chaney and Michael Schwerner. They were there to work alongside Black Mississippians registering to vote.
Sixty-two years later, students at Jackson State, Alcorn State, Tougaloo College and the University of Mississippi, campuses where the Andrew Goodman Foundation’s Vote Everywhere program is active, are likely among the thousands of Mississippi voters whose affidavit ballots remain unresolved. 
An affidavit ballot is what Mississippi calls a provisional ballot or ballots that for various reasons must undergo additional scrutiny. Some may have used an affidavit ballot because they did not have a photo identification on them. Others because a poll worker could not find their name on the rolls. Estimates of what is still unresolved statewide run from 12,000 to 18,000 ballots, in a U.S. Senate race that has not been called.

Before the election, Mississippi marked 230,107 registered voters inactive. Secretary of State Michael Watson’s office flagged them by using address data from Experian, the credit bureau, under a $50,000 contract last year to clean the rolls statewide. Mississippi Today has reported that the data is unverified and wrongly inactivated legitimate voters.
This is problematic for a college student. Dorms often lack an individual mailing address the voting system recognizes. A verification letter sent to a residence hall may have nowhere to land. The student never sees it, never responds and gets flagged. The Mississippi Free Press reported this problem a week before the election, and Election Day is when it came due.
No law was passed to do this. No legislator voted for it. A for-profit vendor’s address file decided which young voters would spend Election Day exercising their right to vote and which would spend it arguing with a poll worker. That is the newest barrier, and it sits on top of the old ones.
Mississippi is one of only three states with no in-person early voting. It is one of 13 states requiring an excuse to vote by mail. It has no online voter registration. Polls are open from 7 in the morning until 7 at night on a Tuesday, which is a workday. A Jim Crow era provision still imposes a lifetime voting ban for certain felony convictions, affecting nearly 70,000 Mississippi residents. When researchers rank the states on ballot access, Mississippi finishes last or next to last.
The remedy itself is problematic. Students who voted by affidavit because they had no photo ID have until close of business on Tuesday to appear in person at their county circuit clerk’s office with acceptable identification. Not online. Not by mail. In person, during business hours, in a short time frame.
For a student at Alcorn State in Lorman, it means getting to Port Gibson, 11 miles away, with no public transportation. A 19-year-old without a car has no way to make her or his  own vote count.
Here is what Mississippi students did anyway. Turnout rose about 35 percent over the last midterm in 2022, from roughly 710,000 votes to more than 950,000. Thirty Mississippi students trained as poll monitors with the Andrew Goodman Foundation, ACLU of Mississippi and Mississippi Votes, from Jackson State, Alcorn State and Tougaloo. Eleven of them drove up from Alcorn State for the training.
 Through our partnership with the ACLU, students worked 44 precincts, serving as nonpartisan poll observers in Florida, Georgia and Mississippi, and in Arkansas supporting ballot curing and watching the count.
That is the hard work the Andrew Goodman Foundation exists to do. We support nonpartisan student organizers with a modest stipend, and the campuses they organize are their own. They are not volunteers brought in from out of state. Some of them are the 19-year-olds waiting to find out whether their own ballots will count.
Andrew did not go to Mississippi because it was easy. He went as a student himself because it was the right thing to do even though it was hard work. People there had been asking for help from allies for a long time. What has changed in 62 years is not the difficulty. It is that the students doing the asking now live there.
So this is not a request for sympathy for Mississippi students. They do not need it. It is a request for three specific things.
Cease using unverified commercial credit data to decide who stays on the voter rolls. If a state buys a database and acts on it, the burden of proving an address wrong belongs to the state, not to a college sophomore.
Treat a dormitory as a residence. A student who lives in one has an address for every purpose except, apparently, this one.
And give Mississippians what voters in most other states already have: early voting, and the ability to register online.
Sixty-two years is a long time to still be arguing about whether young people in Mississippi have equal access to the ballot box. Those students have already made their case. They registered their classmates, they trained as poll monitors, they showed up on a Tuesday between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Many of them and other Mississippians are now waiting to learn whether the ballots they cast will be counted at all.

David Goodman is the brother of Andrew Goodman and a board member of the Andrew Goodman Foundation, a nonpartisan organization that trains and supports student voting advocates in 25 states and the District of Columbia.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: President Trump nominates former Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer as US ambassador to UAE
description: Former Republican Gov. Jeff Colyer is President Donald Trump's choice to serve as U.S. ambassador to United Arab Emirates.
text:
Former Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer, while a candidate for governor, appears on the Kansas Reflector podcast on Feb. 17, 2026, in Topeka. President Donald Trump nominated Colyer to be ambassador to United Arab Emirates. (Photo by Anna Kaminski)TOPEKA — President Donald Trump nominated former Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer to serve as U.S. ambassador to the United Arab Emirates.
Colyer, 66, campaigned for governor this year but chose not to file as a candidate in June. His departure from the campaign created an easier path for Trump-endorsed Senate President Ty Masterson to win the Republican Party’s nomination in August. Before the primary election, Colyer also endorsed Masterson’s candidacy for governor.
“My service will continue,” Colyer said at that time, “but I shall not be a candidate for governor in 2026.”
The White House announced the nomination of Colyer on Monday. The president didn’t issue a statement regarding Colyer’s selection. The nomination requires consent of the U.S. Senate. The UAE post is currently vacant.
Republicans currently hold a majority in the U.S. Senate, but Democrats in the November election won a majority that will be installed Jan. 3.
U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kansas, expressed support for Colyer’s nomination to serve as a diplomat in the Middle East.
“He has a proven record of public service, principled leadership and steadfast commitment to improving the lives of Kansans and the American people,” Moran said. “I am confident he will represent our country well on the world stage.”
Colyer, who served two years each in the Kansas House and Kansas Senate, gained greater prominence in Kansas politics when selected to be the lieutenant governor running mate of Republican Sam Brownback in 2010.
The duo was elected and Colyer was the state’s lieutenant governor until January 2018, when Brownback resigned to become Trump’s U.S. ambassador for international religious freedom.
Despite having represented Kansas for 14 years in the U.S. Senate, Brownback’s confirmation was hindered by the challenge of lining up votes to confirm his appointment as an ambassador. The Senate voted 49-49 on his nomination, and Vice President Mike Pence cast a tiebreaking vote.
Colyer was sworn into office as governor but narrowly lost the August 2018 GOP gubernatorial primary to Kris Kobach. Kobach lost the general election to Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, who is nearing completion of her second term in office.
Colyer abandoned plans to run for governor in 2022 after he was diagnosed in 2021 with prostate cancer.
Colyer’s professional career has been as a surgeon in Johnson County, and he has been a medical volunteer in conflict zones with the International Medical Corps.
He was in Ukraine for one month in 2024 and assisted local doctors for six weeks in Iraq during 2003. He also was posted to Rwanda, Afghanistan, Libya, Sierra Leone, Sudan, Cameroon and more than a dozen other locations.

text:
Sen. Chris Garten poses a question to the Secretary of State's Office during a budget committee on June 18, 2025. (Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana Senate has a whole new leadership look, including 14 new committee chairs.
Senate President Pro Tem-elect Chris Garten announced the changes Tuesday following last week’s election. He removed three existing committee chairs who supported the previous leader and also filled vacant posts due to retirements and losses.
“Hoosiers expect us to address the challenges impacting their everyday lives, from affordability and public safety to education, healthcare and economic opportunity,” he said in a news release. “Our committee chairs will play a critical role in advancing thoughtful, responsible policies that move Indiana forward. I expect them to challenge conventional thinking, encourage meaningful debate and approach their responsibilities with a sense of urgency.”
One of the biggest changes is Sen. Scott Baldwin to lead Tax and Fiscal Policy, a powerful committee overseeing tax-related legislation previously run by Travis Holdman, who was defeated in the May Republican primary.
Garten also split the Education and Career Development Committee into two — K-12 Education and Higher Education, to be run by Sen. Jeff Raatz and Sen. Greg Goode, respectively.
Goode, who fended off a Trump-endorsed challenger in the primary, also will lead the Ethics Committee.
Committee chairmen in the Senate receive additional pay to lead committees, between $1,000 and $5,500 depending on the workload of a panel. Other leadership roles also receive additional pay that varies.
The three chairs who were removed were Sen. Sue Glick of Natural Resources; Sen. Ed Charbonneau of Health and Provider Services and Sen. Jean Leising of Agriculture.

description: Local media reports say the FBI is raiding former London Mayor Randall Weddle’s house in Laurel County.  WKYT reported that the FBI was active in an area near an address where Weddle lives off of Highway 552.  In recent years, Weddle has made headlines around the state for his fiery public clashes with the London […]
text:
London Mayor Randall Weddle exits the courtroom at the Laurel County Judicial Center in London on April 15, 2026. Weddle was there to be arraigned on four felony counts of campaign finance violations. He entered pleas of not guilty. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Morgan Hornsby)Local media reports say the FBI is raiding former London Mayor Randall Weddle’s house in Laurel County. 
WKYT reported that the FBI was active in an area near an address where Weddle lives off of Highway 552. 
In recent years, Weddle has made headlines around the state for his fiery public clashes with the London City Council. He was impeached in 2025 after the council approved charges against him that included signing a $5 million mortgage without council approval. After challenging that in court, Weddle resigned from office after an appeals court upheld the council’s impeachment of him. 
Earlier this year, a Laurel County grand jury indicted Weddle on four felony counts, alleging he made $93,000 in excessive contributions to the 2023 campaign of Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear and the Kentucky Democratic Party. Weddle’s massive bundles of donations were first highlighted by the Kentucky Lantern in 2023. Weddle pleaded not guilty to the charges in April. 
Before resigning over the summer, Weddle was attempting to seek another term as mayor, but a Laurel County judge ruled Weddle was an ineligible candidate in London’s primary election because he did not reside within city limits. Weddle was the top vote-getter in the May primary election with 11 votes over second place winner, Matt Orr.

title: RI ethics rule limits Roger Williams, Fatima hospitals CEO’s interactions with state officials
description: Former Rhode Island Health and Human Services Secretary Richard Charest should avoid talking business with his former colleagues, as well as other state officials, for the first year in his new, private-sector gig, according to a recommendation unanimously adopted by the Rhode Island Ethics Commission Tuesday. The seven-page opinion answers the question pose[...]
text:
Former Rhode Island Executive Office of Health and Human Services Secretary Richard Charest, center, testifies before the House Committee on Finance regarding the sale of Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital on Tuesday, Feb. 2, 2026. Charest is now CEO for the hospitals. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Former Rhode Island Health and Human Services Secretary Richard Charest should avoid talking business with his former colleagues, as well as other state officials, for the first year in his new, private-sector gig, according to a recommendation unanimously adopted by the Rhode Island Ethics Commission Tuesday.
The seven-page opinion answers the question posed by Charest, who sought advice on the ethical implications of his career change. Charest began work on Nov. 1 as head of CharterCare Health of Rhode Island, the local subsidiary that owns Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital.
Before that, he spent nearly five years working for the state under Gov. Dan McKee, and for the last three years, led the massive state health and human services umbrella agency. 
RI Health and Human Services head to replace Roger Williams, Fatima hospitals CEO

News of Charest’s transition from government to industry raised immediate questions, including from Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha, about the revolving door clause of state ethics law. The clause limits state officials and administrators from representing themselves before state agencies where they worked for one year after leaving the public sector position.
In his Oct. 19 letter to Jason Gramitt, executive director for the ethics panel, Charest acknowledged the “limitations” that his government work might pose on his new job with CharterCARE. His contract with the hospital owners states that he would not interact with any state agencies until he received the Ethics Commission’s advice, he wrote in the letter.
The advice, presented Tuesday by Teodora Papa, a staff attorney for the commission, follows similar opinions for other former state officials who have transitioned to private-sector roles. Charest should not represent himself or his new employer before any division of the health and human services agency, the governor’s office, or the Department of Administration, for one year. 
That includes formal meetings and legislative activity, as well as informal interactions like phone calls and social gatherings.
“It is the content of the discussion, rather than the venue,” Papa said, adding that personal discussions with his former colleagues are not prohibited, only those that apply to business and industry.
Charest is also barred under state ethics law from using any confidential information gained from his government work to benefit his new employer.
Charest, who attended the meeting with his attorneys, did not speak except to confirm he understood the recommendation.
His attorneys, Marc DeSisto and Sarah Boucher of Providence-based DeSisto Law, did not immediately respond to requests for comment following the decision Tuesday. 
Charest’s appointment to CharterCARE, replacing retiring CEO Jeffrey Liebman, comes at a critical juncture for the newly formed healthcare operator. Since buying Roger Williams and Fatima hospitals from their bankrupt former owner in March, the local entity has struggled to revive the safety-net hospitals after years of financial and operational mismanagement. Contract disputes quickly soured the 1,200 union workers on their new leaders.
Neronha, whose office remains heavily involved in the transition, rejected an initial strategic plan, warning of imminent cash flow problems. After meeting with CharterCARE executives in late October, Neronha gave the hospital operator until Dec. 11 to submit a new plan that includes updated financial projections and input from Charest, according to a Nov. 2 letter from Neronha shared with Rhode Island Current.
Otis Brown, a spokesperson for CharterCARE, did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday.
Ethics Commission members Frank Cenerini and Emma Peterson were absent from the meeting.

title: Mya Adams is soaring toward a career in aviation
description:
